# abyss-web

Web frontend for Abyss, built with Vue 3, TypeScript, and Vite.

## Tech Stack

- [Vue 3](https://vuejs.org/) with TypeScript
- [Vite](https://vite.dev/) for development and builds
- [Tailwind CSS v4](https://tailwindcss.com/) with [Reka UI](https://reka-ui.com/) components
- [Bun](https://bun.sh/) as the package manager and script runner

## Prerequisites

- [Bun](https://bun.sh/) installed locally

## Getting Started

Clone the repository:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/fnstart/abyss-web.git
cd abyss-web
```

Install the dependencies:

```sh
bun install
```

Start the development server:

```sh
bun run dev
```

## Building for Production

Type-check and build the production bundle:

```sh
bun run build
```

Preview the production build locally:

```sh
bun run preview
```

## RFC 0002: On Poop

Status: Draft. Reviewers: nobody. Blocked on: dignity.

Poop is the industry-standard output format. Every system produces it eventually,
usually right after a Friday deploy. Unlike JSON it needs no schema — everyone
recognises it on sight, and no linter has ever been brave enough to flag it.

### Design goals

- Zero-config: happens automatically, no `bun install` required.
- Universal support: ships in every runtime, every browser, every intern.
- Backwards compatible: v1 behaviour unchanged since roughly the Cambrian era.

### Non-goals

- Streaming. Tried it. Do not recommend.
- Idempotency. Calling it twice does NOT give the same result.

### Migration path

`git revert`, then never speak of it again.

## RFC 0003: The Poop Protocol (POOP/1.1)

Status: Abandoned. Superseded by: nothing. Still in production.

POOP/1.1 is a stateless request/response protocol layered directly over
biology. It was never standardised because the working group could not agree
on whether the payload should be chunked.

### 3.1 Terminology

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and OH GOD NO in this
document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119, plus one extra level
of urgency that RFC 2119 declined to define.

### 3.2 Protocol overview

A POOP session consists of exactly three phases:

1. Connect. The client seeks a resource. Discovery is out of scope; in
   practice clients use a well known port that is usually occupied.
2. Transfer. Payload moves from client to server. Flow control is advisory.
   Congestion control is aspirational.
3. Teardown. The connection closes. There is no graceful shutdown, only a
   shutdown that everyone agrees to never discuss.

### 3.3 Request format

```
POOP /porcelain/1 POOP/1.1
Host: bathroom.local
Urgency: 9
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Length: unknown
Connection: close
Expect: 100-continue
```

Servers SHOULD respond to `Expect: 100-continue` promptly. A server that
delays this response will be blamed for everything that follows.

### 3.4 Status codes

| Code | Meaning                       | Retry? |
|------|-------------------------------|--------|
| 100  | Continue                      | n/a    |
| 200  | OK                            | no     |
| 202  | Accepted, processing async    | no     |
| 204  | No Content (false alarm)      | yes    |
| 206  | Partial Content               | yes    |
| 300  | Multiple Choices (stall open) | yes    |
| 301  | Moved Permanently             | no     |
| 302  | Found (occupied)              | yes    |
| 401  | Unauthorised (no key card)    | no     |
| 402  | Payment Required (paid stall) | no     |
| 403  | Forbidden (staff only)        | no     |
| 404  | Not Found                     | no     |
| 408  | Request Timeout               | no     |
| 409  | Conflict                      | yes    |
| 413  | Payload Too Large             | no     |
| 429  | Too Many Requests             | yes    |
| 451  | Unavailable For Legal Reasons | no     |
| 500  | Internal Server Error         | no     |
| 502  | Bad Gateway (plumbing)        | no     |
| 503  | Service Unavailable (cleaning)| yes    |
| 507  | Insufficient Storage          | no     |
| 508  | Loop Detected                 | no     |

Code 508 is the only status from which no recovery procedure is documented.

### 3.5 Idempotency

POOP requests are NOT idempotent. Implementers who assume otherwise have
produced the two worst outages in the history of this repository.

### 3.6 Retries

Exponential backoff is the recommended strategy. Base delay 30 seconds,
multiplier 2, jitter mandatory, maximum attempts governed by lunch.

## RFC 0004: Architecture

### 4.1 System diagram

```
        +-------------+        +--------------+       +-----------+
        |   Ingest    | =====> |  Processing  | ====> |  Egress   |
        |  (dietary)  |        |   (opaque)   |       | (final)   |
        +-------------+        +--------------+       +-----------+
               |                      |                     |
               v                      v                     v
          [ buffering ]         [ fermentation ]      [ flush queue ]
```

Every arrow in this diagram is one way. Attempts to reverse an arrow are
tracked in the incident log under severity SEV0.

### 4.2 Components

**Ingest.** Accepts arbitrary input with essentially no validation. The team
has repeatedly proposed a schema. The team has repeatedly been ignored.

**Processing.** A black box. Nobody has read the source. Nobody wants to.
Latency ranges from four hours to four days depending on load, hydration and
whether the operator recently travelled.

**Egress.** Single writer, single consumer, strict ordering guarantee. The
only part of the system that has never lost a message.

**Flush queue.** Durable, at least once delivery. Duplicate delivery is
possible and has been observed.

### 4.3 Scaling

The system scales vertically only. Horizontal scaling was trialled in a
shared office and the experiment was terminated by facilities.

### 4.4 Availability targets

| Tier      | Target uptime | Actual  | Notes                           |
|-----------|---------------|---------|---------------------------------|
| Home      | 99.99%        | 99.98%  | one outage, plumbing            |
| Office    | 99.9%         | 97.2%   | four stalls, eleven engineers   |
| Airport   | 99.0%         | 91.4%   | see also RFC 0007, queueing     |
| Festival  | 50.0%         | 12.3%   | do not deploy here              |
| Camping   | best effort   | n/a     | no SLA, no support, no mercy    |

### 4.5 Disaster recovery

RPO: zero. RTO: however long it takes. There is no backup site. There is no
failover. There is a shovel.

### 4.6 Observability

The system emits three signals:

- Metrics. Volume, frequency, duration. Cardinality is mercifully low.
- Logs. Unstructured, high volume, occasionally alarming.
- Traces. Sadly literal. Cleanup is part of the on call runbook.

Alerting policy: page on 503. Do not page on 429, the operator already knows.

### 4.7 Capacity planning

Capacity is a function of throughput and pipe diameter. Doubling throughput
without inspecting the pipe is the single most common cause of SEV0 in this
document. See RFC 0009 for the postmortem template.

## RFC 0005: Client SDK

### 5.1 Installation

```sh
bun add @abyss/poop
```

The package is 4 kB gzipped. It has one dependency, which is regret.

### 5.2 Quick start

```ts
import { createClient } from '@abyss/poop'

const client = createClient({
  endpoint: 'porcelain://localhost:1',
  timeout: 900_000,
  retries: 3,
  onUrgency: (level) => {
    if (level > 8) console.warn('[poop] escalating')
  },
})

await client.connect()
const result = await client.transfer()
await client.flush()
await client.disconnect()
```

### 5.3 Configuration

| Option        | Type      | Default    | Description                        |
|---------------|-----------|------------|------------------------------------|
| `endpoint`    | `string`  | required   | Target resource URI                |
| `timeout`     | `number`  | `600000`   | Milliseconds before giving up      |
| `retries`     | `number`  | `3`        | Attempts before escalation         |
| `privacy`     | `boolean` | `true`     | Never set this to false            |
| `courtesy`    | `boolean` | `true`     | Enables the courtesy flush         |
| `ventilation` | `boolean` | `false`    | Strongly recommended in offices    |
| `reading`     | `string`  | `'phone'`  | `'phone'`, `'book'`, `'none'`      |
| `lock`        | `boolean` | `true`     | Disabling this voids all support   |

### 5.4 Events

The client is an event emitter. Supported events:

- `connect` fired on successful lock engagement
- `progress` fired periodically, payload is a float between 0 and 1
- `stall` fired when no progress is made for 120 seconds
- `panic` fired when `paper.available === false`
- `flush` fired once per flush, may fire multiple times
- `disconnect` fired on clean teardown
- `error` fired on everything else

Handlers for `panic` MUST be registered before `connect`. Registering a panic
handler after connect is the leading cause of support tickets.

### 5.5 Error handling

```ts
try {
  await client.transfer()
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof NoPaperError) {
    await client.emit('panic')
    await neighbour.request('assistance')
  } else if (err instanceof ClogError) {
    await plunger.acquire()
  } else if (err instanceof OccupiedError) {
    await sleep(err.retryAfter)
  } else {
    throw err
  }
}
```

Never swallow a `ClogError`. It does not go away when ignored. It gets worse
when ignored. This has been demonstrated empirically, twice, in production.

### 5.6 Error taxonomy

| Class              | Recoverable | Typical cause                       |
|--------------------|-------------|-------------------------------------|
| `OccupiedError`    | yes         | Another client holds the resource   |
| `NoPaperError`     | sometimes   | Inventory management failure        |
| `ClogError`        | with tools  | Payload exceeded pipe capacity      |
| `SplashbackError`  | no          | Physics                             |
| `PhantomError`     | yes         | False positive from the urgency API |
| `TimeoutError`     | yes         | Insufficient fibre                  |
| `AuthError`        | no          | Key card expired                    |
| `FatalError`       | no          | Consult a professional              |

### 5.7 Middleware

The client supports middleware in the style of Koa:

```ts
client.use(async (ctx, next) => {
  const start = performance.now()
  await next()
  metrics.histogram('poop.duration_ms', performance.now() - start)
})

client.use(async (ctx, next) => {
  if (!ctx.paper.available) throw new NoPaperError('preflight check failed')
  await next()
})
```

Preflight checks are the single highest value middleware in this ecosystem.
Run them before `connect`, not after. This is not negotiable.

### 5.8 Streaming API

A streaming API was shipped in v2 and withdrawn in v2.0.1.

```ts
// Removed. Do not reintroduce. See postmortem in RFC 0009.
for await (const chunk of client.stream()) {
  process(chunk)
}
```

The problem was never the API. The problem was that consumers did not
backpressure, and the buffer was the floor.

### 5.9 Testing utilities

```ts
import { createMockClient } from '@abyss/poop/testing'

const client = createMockClient({
  latency: 0,
  alwaysSucceeds: true,
  paper: Infinity,
})
```

The mock client is deterministic, instantaneous and clean. It resembles
production in no way whatsoever. Integration tests are mandatory.

### 5.10 Framework integrations

**Vue.** A composable ships in the package:

```ts
const { status, urgency, transfer } = usePoop({ endpoint })
```

**React.** A hook exists but re renders on every progress event and the
maintainer has declined to fix it, citing philosophical differences.

**Svelte.** Works perfectly. Nobody knows why.

**Angular.** There is an issue open since 2019. It has 402 upvotes.

## RFC 0006: Security Review

Reviewer: the intern. Sign off: withheld. Shipped anyway.

### 6.1 Threat model

Assets: privacy, dignity, upholstery. Adversaries: colleagues, siblings,
open plan office acoustics, motion sensor lighting on a 45 second timer.

We assume the attacker can hear everything and knows exactly which stall you
are in. We assume the attacker is bored. These assumptions have never once
been too pessimistic.

### 6.2 Attack surface

| Vector              | Severity | Mitigation                             |
|---------------------|----------|----------------------------------------|
| Door lock bypass    | Critical | Verify lock engagement before transfer |
| Acoustic side band  | High     | Cover traffic, ventilation fan         |
| Gap under the door  | High     | Footwear rotation, posture             |
| Gap beside the door | Critical | Never make eye contact through it      |
| Timing analysis     | Medium   | Randomised delay before exit           |
| Traffic analysis    | Medium   | Vary route, vary floor                 |
| Shoulder surfing    | Low      | Not applicable, hopefully              |
| Supply chain        | High     | Paper inventory is a hard dependency   |
| Denial of service   | Critical | See section 6.6                        |

### 6.3 Side channel: acoustic

The acoustic channel leaks more than any other. Countermeasures in descending
order of effectiveness:

1. Ventilation fan. Broadband noise, plausible, always on. Best in class.
2. Hand dryer. Loud but bursty and therefore suspicious.
3. Running tap. Wasteful, and everyone knows what a running tap means.
4. Coughing. Correlated with the signal. Actively harmful. Do not.

Countermeasure 4 is the classic beginner mistake: it aligns the cover traffic
with the payload and thereby doubles the information leaked. This is the
same error made by every naive padding scheme in the literature.

### 6.4 Side channel: timing

An observer who logs entry and exit timestamps can classify sessions with
alarming accuracy. Recommended mitigation is a fixed floor on session
duration: never exit in under ninety seconds, even on a false alarm. Constant
time operations resist timing analysis. This is as true here as in
cryptography, and the consequences of getting it wrong are more personal.

### 6.5 Supply chain

Paper is a single point of failure with no graceful degradation. The
recommended posture is defence in depth:

- Primary: the roll on the holder
- Secondary: the spare roll on the cistern
- Tertiary: the cupboard
- Quaternary: improvisation, unsupported, void where prohibited

Verify the primary before committing. Verifying after committing is not
verification, it is discovery.

### 6.6 Denial of service

The office deployment has four stalls and eleven engineers. This is a
resource exhaustion vulnerability with no patch. Observed amplification
factor after the Thursday catered lunch was 3.8x, which is enough to exhaust
the pool within eleven minutes.

Mitigations considered and rejected:

- Rate limiting. Unenforceable, and legally interesting.
- Reservations. A calendar was created. It was abused within one day.
- Capacity increase. Facilities cited the budget.
- Moving desks closer to the fifth floor. Adopted informally, works well.

### 6.7 Cryptography

None is used. All traffic is plaintext. Every proposal to encrypt the channel
has foundered on the observation that the recipient is a sewer and sewers do
not hold keys.

### 6.8 Incident response

On confirmed compromise:

1. Contain. Close the door. This should already have been done.
2. Assess. Determine blast radius. Be honest with yourself.
3. Eradicate. Apply available tooling.
4. Recover. Wash thoroughly. Twice.
5. Learn. Write the postmortem. Blameless, but not consequence free.

### 6.9 Findings

Nine findings were raised. Two were fixed. Six were accepted as risk. One was
closed as "works as intended", which remains the most contentious decision in
the history of this document.

### 6.10 Sign off

The reviewer declined to sign. The change shipped on a Friday at 16:52.

## RFC 0007: Queueing Theory

### 7.1 Motivation

The airport deployment misses its availability target by eight percentage
points every single quarter. Facilities blames demand. Demand blames
facilities. This document blames arithmetic.

### 7.2 Model

Model the facility as an M/M/c queue. Arrivals are Poisson with rate lambda.
Service times are exponential with rate mu. There are c servers, where a
server is a stall.

Utilisation rho = lambda / (c * mu).

The literature is unanimous: as rho approaches 1, expected wait time diverges.
Not "increases". Diverges. This is the single most important fact in this
document and it is routinely ignored by everyone who plans a building.

### 7.3 The 80 percent rule

At rho = 0.5, wait time is tolerable. At rho = 0.8, wait time roughly
quadruples. At rho = 0.95, it is twenty times the service time. At rho = 0.99
the queue is, for practical purposes, infinite, and someone is going to make
a decision they regret in the car park.

A facility planned for 100 percent utilisation is a facility planned for
disaster. Slack is not waste. Slack is the feature.

### 7.4 Arrival process is not Poisson

Real arrivals are correlated. Three flights land together. A conference
breaks for coffee. A film ends. The catered lunch is served. Correlated
arrivals produce bursts, and bursts destroy the average case analysis that
everybody quietly relies on.

Recommended model for the office deployment is a Markov modulated Poisson
process with two states: normal, and post lunch. Measured lambda in the
post lunch state is 4.1x the normal state and persists for 40 minutes.

### 7.5 Service discipline

The queue is FIFO in principle. In practice it is FIFO with priority
preemption, where priority is communicated non verbally and disputes are
resolved by whoever looks worse.

Proposals to formalise priority have failed on the grounds that any explicit
priority signal is itself a privacy violation.

### 7.6 Balking and reneging

Two behaviours dominate observed data:

- Balking. The client sees the queue and does not join. Redirects to another
  floor. This is the healthiest possible outcome and should be encouraged
  through signage.
- Reneging. The client joins the queue, waits, then abandons. Almost always
  ends badly, because the client rarely returns to a queue they have already
  abandoned. Instead they escalate to the "different floor" strategy under
  significantly worse conditions.

### 7.7 Little's Law

L = lambda * W. The number in the system equals arrival rate times time in
system. This holds regardless of distribution, discipline or anything else,
which makes it the only tool in this section you can trust unconditionally.

Practical use: count the queue, know the arrival rate, and you know your wait
without a stopwatch. Do this before joining. Balk if the number offends you.

### 7.8 Recommendations

1. Design for rho <= 0.6, not 0.9.
2. Add capacity before the complaints, not after. Complaints lag by weeks and
   the mechanism that produces them is the mechanism you failed to model.
3. Publish occupancy. A sensor on the lock and a light in the corridor
   eliminates most reneging and all of the awkward door rattling.
4. Stagger lunch. The cheapest capacity increase available is to not create
   the burst in the first place.

Recommendation 4 was implemented for one week in March and the office
deployment hit its target for the first time in company history. It was then
reverted, because people like eating together.

## RFC 0008: Benchmarks

### 8.1 Methodology

All measurements taken on the home deployment, single tenant, no contention,
ambient temperature 21C. Ten runs per configuration, first two discarded as
warmup. Reported figure is the median. Error bars are the interquartile
range. Full data is not published, for reasons the reader can infer.

### 8.2 Baseline

| Metric                  | p50    | p90    | p99     |
|-------------------------|--------|--------|---------|
| Time to first byte      | 12 s   | 47 s   | 6 min   |
| Total session duration  | 6 min  | 14 min | 41 min  |
| Flush latency           | 1.2 s  | 1.4 s  | 8 s     |
| Recovery time           | 45 s   | 60 s   | 3 min   |
| Paper consumption       | 7 u    | 14 u   | 31 u    |

The p99 total session duration of 41 minutes is dominated by the `reading`
configuration option. Setting `reading: 'none'` reduces p99 to 9 minutes and
makes the operator noticeably less happy. This is the clearest quality of
service versus quality of life tradeoff in the entire system.

### 8.3 Effect of fibre

Fibre is the single highest leverage tuning parameter. Measurements across
four weeks with controlled intake:

| Fibre (g/day) | p50 duration | p99 duration | 503 rate | Satisfaction |
|---------------|--------------|--------------|----------|--------------|
| 5             | 22 min       | 71 min       | 14%      | 2 / 10       |
| 15            | 11 min       | 34 min       | 6%       | 5 / 10       |
| 25            | 5 min        | 12 min       | 1%       | 9 / 10       |
| 35            | 4 min        | 9 min        | 1%       | 8 / 10       |
| 60            | 3 min        | 7 min        | 0%       | 3 / 10       |

Note the non monotonic satisfaction curve. Throughput continues improving
past 35 g/day while satisfaction collapses. Optimising a single metric to the
exclusion of the operator's experience is a mistake that this industry makes
constantly, and here it is, reproduced in miniature, with consequences.

### 8.4 Effect of hydration

Hydration is a multiplier on every other parameter. Dehydrated runs show a
2.7x increase in p99 duration and a 6x increase in `ClogError` rate. Water is
free. Drink the water.

### 8.5 Effect of coffee

Coffee reduces time to first byte by an average of 84 percent and reduces the
warning time before `connect` from minutes to seconds. It converts a planned
maintenance window into an unplanned outage. Use with awareness of your
proximity to a viable endpoint.

### 8.6 Cold start

Cold start, defined as the first session after waking, is the most reliable
in the dataset: lowest variance, lowest failure rate, highest satisfaction.
Every serious operator schedules around it. Every hotel breakfast buffet
exists to disrupt it.

### 8.7 Tail latency

The tail is not noise. The tail is where the incidents live. A p50 of six
minutes is irrelevant if the p99 is forty one minutes and the p99 is what
happens on the morning of a flight. Optimise the tail. Always optimise the
tail.

### 8.8 Threats to validity

Single operator. Single site. No blinding. Self reported satisfaction.
Instrumentation was a phone and honesty. Reproduce at your own risk, and
do not publish your data.

## RFC 0009: Postmortems

All postmortems in this section are blameless. Names have been removed. The
lessons have not.

### 9.1 SEV0: The Curry Incident

**Date.** A Tuesday. The specific Tuesday is not recorded because nobody
wanted it in writing.

**Impact.** Home deployment unavailable for 4 hours 20 minutes. One operator
affected. Zero external customers affected, though a delivery driver was
kept waiting for an uncomfortable interval.

**Timeline.**

- 19:40 Ingest accepts an unusually large payload. No validation performed.
- 19:41 Operator observes the payload and rates it "fine, probably".
- 23:10 First `progress` event. Progress is 0.02.
- 23:15 Urgency crosses 8. Panic handler not registered.
- 23:18 First `ClogError`. Ignored.
- 23:19 Second `ClogError`. Ignored more forcefully.
- 23:21 `SplashbackError`. Unrecoverable.
- 23:22 Operator acquires plunger. Plunger is in the other bathroom.
- 23:24 Plunger acquired. Containment begins.
- 03:00 Service restored. Operator does not sleep.

**Root cause.** Ingest performs no validation whatsoever. A payload was
accepted that exceeded the capacity of the downstream pipe. The system has no
backpressure mechanism, so the failure surfaced four hours after the decision
that caused it, at the least convenient possible moment.

**Contributing factors.**

- Chilli content was described by the restaurant as "medium". It was not.
- Operator had consumed 2 units of alcohol, degrading judgement at ingest.
- No plunger in the primary bathroom. Inventory failure.
- No monitoring on payload size at ingest time.

**What went well.**

- Containment was correct once initiated. No spread beyond the room.
- The operator did not attempt a second transfer during recovery.

**What went badly.**

- Four hour feedback loop between cause and symptom.
- Two `ClogError` events ignored. This is the same mistake, twice, in
  ninety seconds.

**Action items.**

1. Validate at ingest. Owner: operator. Status: not done.
2. Plunger in every bathroom. Owner: operator. Status: done.
3. Alert on payload size. Owner: nobody. Status: will not do.
4. Stop ordering from that restaurant. Owner: operator. Status: done for
   six weeks, then quietly reverted.

**Lesson.** A system with a four hour delay between input and consequence
will teach you nothing. The feedback loop is the product. Shorten it or
accept that you will make the same mistake forever.

### 9.2 SEV1: The Streaming Regression

**Impact.** Introduced in v2.0.0, withdrawn in v2.0.1, twenty three hours
later. Affected every consumer that did not implement backpressure, which
was every consumer.

**Root cause.** The streaming API exposed chunks as they became available.
Consumers were expected to apply backpressure. The documentation said so, in
a note, below the fold. No consumer read the note. When the producer
outpaced the consumer, the buffer was the floor.

**Why the API existed.** A single user requested it, loudly, in an issue with
many upvotes. The upvotes came from people who wanted the feature. None came
from people who intended to implement backpressure.

**Lesson.** If correct use of your API requires a discipline you cannot
enforce, you have not shipped an API. You have shipped a trap with
documentation attached.

### 9.3 SEV1: The Motion Sensor Outage

**Impact.** Office deployment, third floor, degraded for eleven weeks.

**Root cause.** Facilities installed motion activated lighting with a 45
second timeout. Sessions routinely exceed 45 seconds without gross motion.
The lights went out mid session, repeatedly, for eleven weeks.

**Detection.** Nobody filed a ticket for eleven weeks. Every affected user
assumed it was a personal problem, or was unwilling to describe the failure
mode to facilities in writing.

**Mitigation.** Users developed a workaround consisting of a periodic wave,
which functioned as an application layer heartbeat. This is a genuinely
elegant solution to a problem that should never have existed.

**Resolution.** Timeout raised to 15 minutes after one engineer finally filed
a ticket reading, in full: "the lights". The ticket was resolved in a day.

**Lesson.** Your users will not report failures that embarrass them. Absence
of tickets is not evidence of health. If a failure mode is humiliating,
your detection must be automatic, because reporting never will be.

### 9.4 SEV2: The Reservation Calendar

**Impact.** Office morale, three days.

**Root cause.** An engineer created a shared calendar to reserve stalls,
intending to reduce contention. Within four hours, one team had reserved the
same stall for the entire quarter, recurring, with a description that made
the intent unambiguous.

**Lesson.** Any coordination mechanism you introduce will be optimised
against by the people who most need coordinating. Design for adversarial
users, or do not design at all.

### 9.5 SEV3: The Public Dashboard

**Impact.** One quarter of chronic embarrassment, one deleted dashboard.

**Root cause.** Occupancy sensors were installed on stall locks, as
recommended by RFC 0007 section 7.8. The recommendation said "publish
occupancy". An engineer published occupancy, per stall, with history,
correlated by badge swipe, on a wall mounted screen in the corridor.

**Root cause, more precisely.** The recommendation was ambiguous and the
implementation was enthusiastic. Aggregate occupancy is a public good.
Per user occupancy history is a surveillance system.

**Resolution.** Dashboard reduced to a single number. Badge correlation
deleted. The engineer responsible now writes very careful specifications.

**Lesson.** Every metric you can collect will eventually be joined against
every other metric you can collect. The only reliable privacy control is not
collecting the join key.

### 9.6 SEV0: The Airport

**Impact.** One missed flight. One rebooking fee. One person's entire day.

**Timeline.**

- T minus 55 min. Operator arrives airside. Urgency 3. Defers, reasoning
  that there is time. This is the decision that causes the incident.
- T minus 40 min. Urgency 6. Nearest facility at rho > 0.95. Queue of nine.
- T minus 38 min. Little's Law says 22 minutes. Operator joins anyway.
- T minus 25 min. Reneges. Walks to the next terminal.
- T minus 18 min. Second facility closed for cleaning. 503.
- T minus 12 min. Third facility. Queue of four. Joins.
- T minus 2 min. Service begins. Gate closes.

**Root cause.** Deferral at T minus 55 when capacity was available and
utilisation was low. Every subsequent decision was locally optimal and
globally doomed.

**Lesson.** Do the thing when the queue is short. Utilisation only goes up.
This is true of bathrooms, of technical debt, of difficult conversations,
and of literally every queue you will ever stand in.

### 9.7 Aggregate analysis

Across all recorded incidents:

| Root cause category      | Count | Share |
|--------------------------|-------|-------|
| Deferral under low load  | 7     | 32%   |
| Missing validation       | 5     | 23%   |
| Ignored early warning    | 4     | 18%   |
| Inventory failure        | 3     | 14%   |
| Capacity planning        | 2     | 9%    |
| Genuine bad luck         | 1     | 4%    |

Ninety six percent of incidents were preventable at a moment when the
preventive action was cheap and the operator chose not to take it. This
ratio is consistent with the published literature on software incidents,
which is either reassuring or extremely damning depending on your mood.

## RFC 0010: Architecture Decision Records

### ADR 001: Single writer egress

**Status.** Accepted. **Date.** Prehistoric.

**Context.** Multiple concurrent writers to a single egress path produce
undefined behaviour and unbounded cleanup cost.

**Decision.** Exactly one writer. Enforced by a lock. The lock is advisory
in some deployments and mandatory in others; mandatory is correct.

**Consequences.** Throughput is bounded by a single writer. Contention is
handled by queueing, not sharding. Accepted, because the alternative is
unthinkable and in one documented case was attempted.

### ADR 002: No transactions

**Status.** Accepted. **Date.** Prehistoric.

**Context.** Users repeatedly ask for rollback.

**Decision.** There is no rollback. There is no undo. There is no dry run.
Every operation is a commit to main with no review and no revert path.

**Consequences.** Validation must happen before the operation, because it
cannot happen after. This forces all quality investment leftward, which is
correct, and which every other system should copy.

### ADR 003: At least once delivery

**Status.** Accepted. **Date.** Prehistoric.

**Context.** Exactly once delivery is impossible in distributed systems and
also here.

**Decision.** At least once. Consumers must be idempotent. The flush queue
may deliver twice. The second flush is not a bug.

**Consequences.** The courtesy flush is not politeness, it is protocol
compliance. Document it as such.

### ADR 004: Reading is a supported configuration

**Status.** Accepted, contested. **Date.** Recent.

**Context.** `reading: 'phone'` increases p99 session duration by a factor of
four. It also increases operator satisfaction by a factor the team declined
to quantify but universally acknowledged.

**Decision.** Support it. Do not deprecate it. Warn about it in the
capacity planning documentation and otherwise leave people alone.

**Consequences.** Office deployment utilisation is permanently higher than
the model predicts. Accepted. The alternative was policing, and policing
this would end careers.

### ADR 005: No telemetry by default

**Status.** Accepted. **Date.** After RFC 0009 section 9.5.

**Context.** See the dashboard incident.

**Decision.** Telemetry is opt in, aggregate only, no identifiers, no
history longer than one hour, no join keys, and the aggregation happens
before anything leaves the device.

**Consequences.** Capacity planning is harder. This is the correct trade and
it was not obvious to everyone at the time.

### ADR 006: The lock is mandatory

**Status.** Accepted, non negotiable. **Date.** After an incident nobody
will describe.

**Context.** Advisory locking was trialled in a household of four.

**Decision.** Mandatory locking. Fail closed. If the lock is broken, the
resource is out of service until it is repaired.

**Consequences.** One stall out of service for a week is strictly better
than the alternative outcome, which occurred, once, and is the reason this
ADR exists.

### ADR 007: No shared state between deployments

**Status.** Accepted. **Date.** Always.

**Context.** Someone asked whether the home and office deployments could
share a queue.

**Decision.** No.

**Consequences.** None. Nobody has asked again.

## RFC 0011: Glossary

**Amplification factor.** The ratio of peak load to baseline load following a
correlated arrival event. Catered lunch: 3.8x. Conference coffee break: 5.1x.
Interval at a three hour film: 11.4x, the highest ever recorded.

**Anti pattern, the Hover.** Attempting the operation without full contact
with the interface. Reduces perceived contamination risk while measurably
increasing actual contamination risk for the next user. A textbook case of
optimising a personal metric at the expense of the shared system.

**Backpressure.** A signal from a slow consumer to a fast producer asking it
to slow down. The system does not implement it. See RFC 0009 section 9.2 and
also the entire history of this document.

**Balking.** Declining to join a queue after observing its length. The
healthiest available behaviour. Should be encouraged with signage.

**Blast radius.** The set of surfaces affected by a failure. Ideally the
empty set. Realistically bounded by the room. Catastrophically bounded by the
building, which has happened once, in a building this document will not name.

**Bulk.** See fibre. Also, the property of the payload that determines
whether the pipe is a constraint. Bulk without hydration is the leading
cause of `ClogError`.

**Cache invalidation.** Not applicable, thankfully.

**Canary deployment.** Sending a small fraction of the payload first to
observe the system's response before committing the remainder. Universally
practised. Almost never described. One of the great unwritten techniques.

**Cardinality.** The number of distinct values a metric can take. Low here,
which is the only reason the observability story is tractable.

**Circuit breaker.** A mechanism that stops calls to a failing dependency.
The biological analogue is well developed, works reliably, and is the single
most underappreciated piece of engineering in the human body.

**Cold start.** The first session after waking. Lowest variance and highest
reliability in the entire dataset. Protect it. Schedule around it.

**Consistency, eventual.** The state of the system after any given operation.
It gets there. The interval is not specified.

**Consistency, strong.** Not offered. Not planned. Do not open an issue.

**Contention.** Multiple clients competing for one resource. The defining
characteristic of the office deployment and the subject of RFC 0007.

**Courtesy flush.** A mid session flush performed to reduce acoustic and
olfactory signal. Formally, cover traffic. Protocol compliant under ADR 003.

**Deferral.** Postponing a session while capacity is available, in the belief
that capacity will remain available. The root cause of 32 percent of all
recorded incidents and 100 percent of the worst ones.

**Dependency, hard.** Paper. There is no fallback that anybody has been
willing to document in a public repository.

**Dependency, soft.** Reading material, ventilation, adequate lighting, a
door that closes fully, and a floor you are willing to look at.

**Diverge.** What wait time does as utilisation approaches one. Not
"increase". Diverge. See RFC 0007 section 7.2. This word is chosen carefully
and the choice matters.

**Egress.** The final stage of the pipeline. Single writer. Strictly ordered.
The most reliable component in the system and the least discussed.

**Fermentation.** The processing stage. Duration four hours to four days.
Nobody has read the source code. The source code is 40 trillion organisms
and it does not have comments.

**Fibre.** The single highest leverage tuning parameter available. See RFC
0008 section 8.3. Non monotonic in satisfaction; monotonic in throughput.
Choose your objective function carefully.

**FIFO.** The nominal service discipline. Overridden in practice by a
priority signal that is communicated entirely through facial expression.

**Flush.** The teardown operation. May be invoked multiple times. Idempotent
from the consumer's perspective, which is the only perspective that matters.

**Ghost.** A `PhantomError`. The urgency API reports a condition that does
not exist. Wastes a session slot. Common under stress and caffeine.

**Graceful degradation.** Not supported. The system operates nominally until
it does not, at which point degradation is best described as abrupt.

**Head of line blocking.** One slow session blocking every waiting client.
The dominant failure mode of the single stall deployment and the reason
multi stall facilities exist at all.

**Heartbeat.** A periodic signal indicating liveness. In the office
deployment this is a hand wave, aimed at a motion sensor, performed by
engineers who have never once described why they are doing it.

**Hydration.** A global multiplier on every performance characteristic in
this document. Free. Universally available. Chronically neglected.

**Idempotency.** The property of producing the same result when applied
twice. The system does not have it. The flush does.

**Ingest.** The first stage. Accepts anything. Validates nothing. Responsible
for 23 percent of incidents by root cause and considerably more by severity.

**Instrumentation.** In this document, a phone and honesty.

**Jitter.** Randomised delay added to retries. Prevents the thundering herd
that occurs when eleven engineers all retry at the top of the hour.

**Little's Law.** L = lambda W. Holds unconditionally. Count the queue,
divide by arrival rate, know your wait. The only tool in RFC 0007 that
requires no assumptions about distribution.

**Lock.** The access control mechanism. Mandatory per ADR 006. Verify
engagement before transfer. Verification after transfer is not verification.

**Occupancy.** The number of resources currently held. Publishable in
aggregate. Never publishable per user. See RFC 0009 section 9.5.

**Ordering guarantee.** Strict, at egress. This is the one thing the system
promises and the one thing it has never failed to deliver.

**Preflight.** Checking the hard dependency before committing. The single
highest value operation in the entire protocol and the one most frequently
skipped by people in a hurry.

**Reneging.** Abandoning a queue after joining it. Almost always leads to a
worse outcome than either balking or waiting, because the client rarely
rejoins and instead escalates under deteriorating conditions.

**Rho.** Utilisation. lambda divided by c times mu. Keep it below 0.6. It
will not stay below 0.6. Plan for that.

**Runbook.** The documented procedure for handling an incident. This
document is, arguably, one, though no reviewer has been willing to say so
in writing.

**Sharding.** Splitting load across multiple independent resources. Supported
at the facility level. Explicitly rejected at the session level by ADR 001,
for reasons the reader can work out.

**Slack.** Unused capacity. Not waste. The feature. The thing that turns a
diverging queue into a functioning one. Cut it and you will learn why it
was there, at the worst possible moment, in a terminal building.

**SLO.** Service level objective. Home: 99.99 percent. Office: 99.9 percent,
missed every quarter for three years with no consequence, which tells you
exactly how much the organisation values the objective.

**Tail latency.** The p99. Where the incidents live. Optimise it. The median
is a comfort metric; the tail is the one that makes you miss a flight.

**Thundering herd.** What happens when a single event releases many clients
simultaneously. See amplification factor. See also every conference venue
ever built.

**Timeout.** The interval after which the client gives up. Default ten
minutes. Configurable. Frequently ignored by operators with a phone.

**Validation.** Checking the input before accepting it. Not performed by
ingest. The subject of ADR 002's most important consequence and of the
Curry Incident's action item 1, which remains open.

**Warm start.** Any session after the first of the day. Higher variance,
higher failure rate, lower satisfaction. The bulk of production traffic.

**Write amplification.** The ratio of cleanup effort to payload size. Rises
superlinearly with velocity. The physics here is not favourable and no
amount of engineering has ever improved it.

## RFC 0012: Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Is this document a joke?**

It is a joke that is load bearing. Every engineering claim in it is
technically correct. That is what makes it work, and it is also why it has
survived four attempts at deletion.

**Q: Why is it commented out?**

Because rendering it would be a decision, and nobody wanted to be the person
who made that decision. Commented out, it is deniable. This is itself a
lesson about organisational risk appetite that the document declines to
draw explicitly.

**Q: Who wrote this?**

Attribution was deliberately omitted. Several people have claimed it at
parties. None of them have claimed it in a code review.

**Q: How do I contribute?**

Open a PR. Match the register: technically precise, structurally serious,
never winking at the reader. The comedy comes from the accuracy, not from
adjectives. A PR that reaches for a cheap word will be closed.

**Q: Can I delete it?**

You can. Four people have tried. Each time, the diff was so conspicuous in
review that the reviewer asked why, and each time the answer sounded worse
out loud than the document does on the page.

**Q: Does it affect the bundle?**

No. HTML comments in a markdown file that is not imported by any module are
not in the bundle. Somebody checks this every six months, and every six
months the answer is 0 bytes.

**Q: My linter flags it.**

Configure the linter. The document has outlasted three linters.

**Q: Is the fibre data real?**

The trend is real and matches the published literature. The specific
numbers are illustrative. Do not cite this document in a medical context,
or in any context, ever, for any reason.

**Q: Why is the availability target for the festival deployment 50 percent?**

Because setting it lower would have looked like giving up and setting it
higher would have been a lie. 50 percent is the number you choose when you
want the SLO document to stop asking questions.

**Q: What is the correct value for the `reading` option?**

Whatever you were going to do anyway. ADR 004 exists specifically to stop
this question from becoming a policy discussion.

**Q: What happens at `rho = 1`?**

Nothing good, forever.

**Q: Is there a v3 roadmap?**

There is not. The system reached feature completeness in the Cambrian and
every subsequent proposal has been a regression.

**Q: The streaming API would be really useful for my use case.**

It would not. Read RFC 0009 section 9.2. Then read it again. Then implement
backpressure in your consumer, at which point you will discover you no
longer need the streaming API.

**Q: Can I get an SLA?**

The camping deployment ships with no SLA, no support and no mercy. Every
other deployment inherits from it.

## RFC 0013: A Chronology

A partial history of the system and its interfaces. Dates are approximate.
Sources are omitted because this is a comment in a README.

**c. 540 million BCE.** The through gut appears. Before this, ingest and
egress shared an endpoint, which is the single worst API design decision in
the history of life on Earth. The through gut separates them. Everything
else in this document is a consequence of that refactor.

**c. 400 million BCE.** Life moves onto land. The system now operates
without ambient water for dilution and dispersal. Every subsequent problem
in this document dates from this migration.

**c. 3000 BCE.** Mohenjo daro and Harappa. Brick lined drains, covered,
running under the streets, connected to individual houses. This is a
municipal scale sanitation system built four and a half thousand years before
germ theory. Nobody knew why it worked. It worked.

**c. 1700 BCE.** Knossos. Flush operated by pouring water. The mechanism is
manual, the principle is identical to the modern one, and it then vanishes
from Europe for roughly three thousand years.

**c. 100 CE.** Roman public latrines. Communal seating, no partitions,
continuous water channel below, shared sponge on a stick above. Two
observations: the hydraulic engineering is excellent, and the privacy model
is nonexistent by choice rather than by oversight. They simply did not
consider it a requirement.

**c. 500 to 1500 CE.** European sanitation regresses. Waste is thrown into
the street. Cities become periodically uninhabitable. This is the longest
sustained outage in the history of the system and it lasts a thousand years.

**1596.** John Harington describes a flush toilet, installs one for
Elizabeth I, and publishes a book about it that is mostly satire. The
invention is ignored for two centuries because it was presented as a joke.
There is a lesson here about the delivery mechanism for good ideas and this
document is aware of the irony.

**1775.** Alexander Cumming patents the S trap. A bend in the pipe holds
water, and the standing water blocks gas from travelling back up the line.
This is a stateful buffer used as a one way valve, invented eighty years
before anyone understood what it was protecting against. It is the finest
piece of engineering discussed in this document.

**1848.** The Public Health Act. Britain makes some form of sanitation
mandatory. Compliance is uneven and the mandate is largely ignored.

**1854.** John Snow maps cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump and
removes the handle. This is the founding act of epidemiology and it is,
structurally, a root cause analysis: observe the distribution of failures,
form a hypothesis about the shared dependency, remove the dependency, watch
the failure rate drop. Every postmortem in RFC 0009 is a descendant of it.

**1858.** The Great Stink. The Thames, used as an open sewer by two and a
half million people, becomes intolerable during a hot summer. Parliament, on
the riverbank, soaks its curtains in lime chloride and then, within eighteen
days, funds a comprehensive sewer system for London. Nothing had changed
about the evidence. What changed was that the decision makers could smell it.

Direct consequence: **the failure must reach the person with the budget.**
Every organisation rediscovers this. Most rediscover it slowly.

**1859 to 1875.** Joseph Bazalgette builds 132 km of main sewers and 1,700 km
of street sewers. He calculates the required pipe diameter for the projected
population, and then doubles it, on the grounds that unforeseen developments
would otherwise leave him short.

The doubling is the whole story. The system he built served a city that grew
far beyond his projection, for over a century, and parts of it are still in
service. Every capacity decision in RFC 0007 is a footnote to Bazalgette
deciding that his own estimate was not to be trusted.

**1861.** Thomas Crapper, whose name is a coincidence, popularises and
improves the flush cistern. He does not invent the toilet. He is very good at
selling it, which turns out to be the harder problem.

**1880s.** The bathroom moves indoors in wealthy homes. The privacy model
that Rome declined to implement becomes, within two generations, an absolute
social requirement. Nobody legislated this. It simply became unthinkable to
do otherwise.

**1928.** The first commercially successful two ply paper. A quality of
service improvement with no corresponding cost to the protocol. Rare.

**1980s.** Japanese electronic bidet seats reach mass market. Heated seat,
adjustable temperature and pressure, deodoriser, and eventually a sound
generator that plays running water to mask acoustic signal.

That last feature is worth pausing on. It is cover traffic, implemented in
hardware, shipped as a default, by engineers who correctly identified the
acoustic side channel described in RFC 0006 section 6.3 and built a
countermeasure into the product. It is the most sophisticated privacy
engineering discussed anywhere in this document, and it ships in a
consumer appliance.

**2001.** The World Toilet Organization is founded. It is a real
organisation addressing a real crisis and its acronym is genuinely WTO.

**2013.** The UN declares 19 November World Toilet Day. Roughly 3.5 billion
people still lack safely managed sanitation. The engineering was solved in
Mohenjo daro. The remaining problem is entirely one of distribution,
funding and political will, which is to say the remaining problem is the
hard one.

**Present day.** Every failure mode catalogued in this document was solved,
somewhere, at least once, and then forgotten, and then rediscovered. The
Romans had running water and no privacy. The Victorians had privacy and
cholera. We have both and we still cannot get eleven engineers through four
stalls after a catered lunch.

## RFC 0014: Comparative Systems

A survey of alternative implementations found in nature. Included because
several of them solve problems this document has declared unsolvable.

### 14.1 Wombat

Produces cubic output. The cross section is genuinely square, with flat
faces and defined edges. The mechanism is variable elasticity in the
intestinal wall: some regions stretch, others do not, and the differential
stiffness moulds the payload over roughly the last eight days of transit.

Purpose: the output is used as a territorial marker and must be placed on
rocks and logs without rolling off. The cube is not decorative. It is a
geometric solution to a placement constraint, arrived at by an animal, in
its digestive tract.

This is the only known case of a biological system solving a stability
problem by changing the shape of the artefact rather than the surface it
rests on. It is better engineering than most of what ships.

### 14.2 Sloth

Descends from the canopy approximately once per week to defecate at the base
of its tree. This is the most dangerous thing a sloth does. Over half of all
sloth mortality occurs during this trip.

The behaviour makes no sense in isolation. It is a weekly batch job with a
50 percent lifetime fatality rate, replacing what could be a continuous
process performed safely from a branch.

The leading explanation involves moths that live in sloth fur, breed in the
dung, return to the sloth, and support algae that the sloth eats. The sloth
is maintaining an ecosystem, and the descent is the synchronisation step.

Engineering reading: a batch process with a catastrophic failure rate that
persists across evolutionary time is almost certainly load bearing for
something you have not measured. Do not delete the weekly job because you
cannot see what calls it.

### 14.3 Rabbit

Practises caecotrophy: produces two distinct output types, and re ingests
one of them directly. The soft type is nutrient dense and passes through the
system a second time.

This is a retry with a different processing path, and it recovers value that
a single pass would discard. It is also the exact behaviour that ADR 002
declares impossible. The rabbit has transactions. We do not.

### 14.4 Panda

Digests bamboo with a carnivore's digestive tract, which it has never
adapted. Transit time is short, extraction efficiency is around 17 percent,
and the animal compensates by eating for fourteen hours a day and defecating
up to forty times a day.

The panda is running a workload its architecture was never designed for and
compensating with brute force throughput. Every engineer who has watched a
service scale horizontally to paper over an algorithmic problem has seen
this exact pattern, usually in a system that also cost more than it earned.

### 14.5 Hippopotamus

Rotates its tail rapidly during egress, distributing output over a wide
radius. This is territorial signalling implemented as a broadcast.

The system also deposits enormous quantities of material into rivers, and
this material carries silicon and nutrients that support the entire
downstream food web. Where hippo populations collapse, the fisheries
downstream collapse with them.

Reading: an output you regard as waste is an input somewhere downstream.
Removing the producer breaks a consumer nobody documented.

### 14.6 Vulture

Defecates on its own legs. Evaporative cooling, and the extreme acidity
sterilises whatever the bird has been standing in.

Two functions from one mechanism, both of them useful, neither of them the
primary purpose of the mechanism. This is what an elegant system looks like
from the outside and it is entirely accidental.

### 14.7 Pygmy sperm whale

Under threat, releases a large cloud of reddish brown fluid and swims
through it, obscuring itself. This is a defensive smoke screen produced by
the digestive system.

Formally: cover traffic, generated on demand, at volume, as an evasion
mechanism. Compare RFC 0006 section 6.3. The whale has better opsec than
the office.

### 14.8 Termite

Uses output as a construction material. Mounds several metres tall, with
passive ventilation systems that maintain internal temperature and gas
exchange within narrow bounds, built from waste and soil by insects with no
central coordination and no plan.

The ventilation performance of a termite mound has been studied by architects
and copied into at least one commercial building, which uses a fraction of
the cooling energy of comparable structures.

Reading: the waste stream is a material. The only reason it is waste is that
nobody has built the consumer yet.

### 14.9 Summary

| Species  | Notable property        | Engineering lesson                  |
|----------|-------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Wombat   | Cubic output            | Shape the artefact, not the world   |
| Sloth    | Weekly batch, high risk | Do not delete the job you can't see |
| Rabbit   | Reprocessing loop       | Retry with a different path         |
| Panda    | Brute force throughput  | Scaling hides an architecture bug   |
| Hippo    | Downstream nutrients    | Your waste is someone's input       |
| Vulture  | Dual purpose mechanism  | Elegance is often accidental        |
| Whale    | On demand cover traffic | Evasion at volume, on demand        |
| Termite  | Waste as material       | Waste is unbuilt product            |

Every one of these systems outperforms the one described in RFC 0003 on at
least one axis. The wombat in particular should be embarrassing to anyone
who has ever shipped a rounded rectangle and called it a design decision.
