## RFC 0015: Onboarding

For new team members. Read before your first week. Do not print this.

### 15.1 Your first day

The office deployment is on floors 2, 3 and 5. Floor 2 is closest to the
kitchen and therefore has the worst contention profile in the building.
Floor 5 has three stalls and is used almost exclusively by finance, who
keep predictable hours. Learn the timetable. It will serve you for years.

Floor 3 is the default and the trap. It is nearest to engineering, which
means every engineer treats it as the only option and rho sits above 0.9
from 09:30 to 11:00. There is a lift. Use it.

### 15.2 The unwritten rules

1. Never take the stall adjacent to an occupied one if a non adjacent stall
   is free. This is the buffer allocation problem and the optimal strategy is
   to maximise distance. Everyone knows this. Nobody says it.
2. If all stalls are occupied, do not wait inside the room. Wait outside.
   Waiting inside converts a queue into an audience.
3. Do not rattle a locked door. The lock is the answer. A rattle is a demand
   for a second answer and it will be remembered.
4. Do not greet colleagues by name. Recognition is a violation. The correct
   protocol is mutual, sincere, permanent non recognition.
5. Conversation is not held. Not at the sink, not at the urinal, not through
   a partition, and above all not by someone who has recognised your shoes.
6. Phone calls are never taken. The other party can hear the room. They will
   know. They will tell people.
7. The last person to use the last of the paper replaces it. Failure to do
   so is the single most antisocial act available in this building.

### 15.3 Escalation paths

- Out of paper, stall level: use another stall.
- Out of paper, room level: use another floor. Then file a ticket.
- Out of paper, building level: this has happened once and the postmortem
  is sealed.
- Clog: do not attempt heroics. Facilities has tooling and no emotional
  investment. Their number is on the wall.
- Lock broken: report it immediately. Per ADR 006 the stall must be taken
  out of service, and someone has to be the one who says so.
- Anything else: floor 5, and tell nobody.

### 15.4 The lunch problem

Catered lunch is served Thursdays at 12:30. Peak load lands between 13:10
and 13:50. Measured amplification is 3.8x with a queue depth of nine at
peak. Little's Law puts the wait at 22 minutes.

Every new hire discovers this in their second week, and every new hire
believes they have discovered it first. You have not. It is in RFC 0007.
The mitigation is to go at 12:25, before the food arrives, which feels
absurd and works perfectly.

### 15.5 What to do in your first month

Find your floor. Learn your window. Establish your default. Do not
experiment during a deadline.

Read RFC 0009. Every incident in it was preventable at a moment when
prevention was free, and you will be offered that moment roughly twice a
week for the rest of your career.

### 15.6 Buddy system

Your onboarding buddy will not discuss any of this with you. That is why
this document exists. It is the only written onboarding material in the
company that covers the thing every employee does every day, and it is
commented out in a README, which tells you something about the company.

## RFC 0016: Style Guide

Rules for contributing to this document.

### 16.1 Register

Write as though the subject were a distributed system and you were unaware
of the second reading. The comedy is produced entirely by the collision
between a serious frame and an unserious subject. Any sentence that winks at
the reader destroys the effect for the whole section.

Never write "if you know what I mean". Never write "so to speak". Never
follow a joke with an explanation of the joke. The reader arrived here
voluntarily, in a comment block, in a README. They are ahead of you.

### 16.2 Precision

Every technical claim must be true. Little's Law is stated correctly.
Queueing behaviour near rho = 1 is stated correctly. The S trap does what
this document says it does. Bazalgette did double the pipe diameter. The
wombat cube mechanism is as described.

The accuracy is not decoration. It is the entire load bearing structure. A
false claim in a document like this reads as laziness and it cheapens every
true claim around it.

### 16.3 Vocabulary

Prefer the clinical term to the crude one, always, without exception. The
document is funnier in a register it never breaks. There is exactly one
crude word permitted in this file and it appears only in the title of RFC
0002, where it functions as the premise rather than as a joke.

### 16.4 Structure

Numbered sections. Tables where data exists. Timelines for incidents.
Status fields on decisions. Follow the shape of the genuine artefact you
are parodying, precisely, including the parts that are boring. The boring
parts are where the effect comes from.

### 16.5 Length

Long. The joke is not the content of any single section. The joke is that
somebody maintained this at length, with discipline, over time, in a file
nobody reads, and never once broke character.

### 16.6 What is out of bounds

- Anything about a specific colleague.
- Anything that would be unkind read aloud.
- Anything medical presented as advice.
- Any claim that is false.
- Any sentence that explains the joke.

### 16.7 Review

Two approvals. One for technical accuracy, one for tone. In practice the
tone reviewer is stricter, because a factual error can be corrected and a
broken register requires rewriting the section.

## RFC 0017: Interview Questions

Proposed for the systems design loop. Never approved. Occasionally used.

### 17.1 Design a bathroom for a 200 person office

Assess whether the candidate asks about arrival distribution before
proposing a number of stalls. Most candidates propose a number immediately.
The number is always wrong because the question is underspecified and the
correct first move is to say so.

Strong signal: candidate asks whether arrivals are correlated. Immediately
recognises the catered lunch problem without being told. Proposes measuring
before building.

Strong signal: candidate targets utilisation well below 100 percent and can
explain why the wait time curve makes 90 percent unacceptable.

Weak signal: candidate divides 200 by some number and moves on.

Disqualifying: candidate proposes a booking system. See RFC 0009 section 9.4
for what happens next.

### 17.2 Your service has a p50 of 6 minutes and a p99 of 41 minutes. Where do you look?

Correct answer identifies that the p99 is a different population, not a
slower version of the same one. Something categorically different is
happening in the tail. In this system it is the `reading` configuration.

Candidates who propose optimising the median have failed the question and,
in a small way, the profession.

### 17.3 A failure mode embarrasses your users. How do you find out about it?

Tests whether the candidate understands that reporting rates are not failure
rates. The eleven week motion sensor outage is the reference case.

Strong answer: instrument it, because they will never tell you. Provide an
anonymous channel. Assume that the absence of complaints about an
embarrassing failure means the failure is total, not absent.

### 17.4 Design an API that cannot be misused

Reference implementation: there isn't one, and the streaming regression is
why. If correct use requires a discipline you cannot enforce in the type
system or the runtime, you have shipped a trap.

Look for candidates who make the wrong thing impossible rather than
documented. Documentation is not a control. Nobody reads the note below
the fold.

### 17.5 You have a four hour delay between a decision and its consequence. How do you improve quality?

The Curry Incident question. The correct answer is that you cannot improve
quality through experience when the feedback loop exceeds the memory of the
decision. You must move the check to the moment of the decision, or accept
the failure rate forever.

Candidates who propose "be more careful" have described the state of the
world, not an intervention.

## RFC 0018: Economics

### 18.1 Unit economics

The cost per session, fully loaded, at the office deployment:

| Component            | Cost per session | Notes                          |
|----------------------|------------------|--------------------------------|
| Water                | 0.004            | 6 litre cistern, metered rate  |
| Paper                | 0.021            | 7 units at bulk purchase price |
| Cleaning, amortised  | 0.180            | Contract divided by volume     |
| Floor space          | 0.410            | Rent per square metre, per use |
| Facilities overhead  | 0.090            | Maintenance, consumables       |
| Engineer time        | 4.900            | 6 minutes at loaded rate       |
| **Total**            | **5.605**        |                                |

Engineer time is 87 percent of the cost and it is the only line item nobody
tries to reduce. Every cost saving initiative in the history of this
building has targeted paper, which is 0.4 percent of the total.

### 18.2 The queueing cost

Time spent in queue is pure loss. At the office deployment, with a mean
queue of 4 minutes across 2.1 sessions per person per day, across 200
people, at the loaded rate, the annual cost of insufficient capacity is
approximately 340,000 currency units.

The cost of building four additional stalls was quoted at 60,000, one time.

The proposal was rejected on the grounds that it was not in the budget. The
340,000 is also not in the budget, but it is distributed across two hundred
timesheets where nobody has to sign for it. This is the most honest thing
this document has to say about how organisations actually work.

### 18.3 The paper procurement incident

Facilities switched to a supplier whose product was 22 percent cheaper per
unit. Consumption rose 41 percent, because the product required more units
per session to reach the same outcome.

Net effect: costs rose 10 percent, satisfaction fell measurably, and one
person kept a personal supply in their desk for the remainder of the
contract.

Lesson: per unit cost is not cost. If your unit is not the thing the user
actually needs, your cost per unit is a fiction and your savings are a
transfer to your users' patience.

### 18.4 Build versus buy

The bidet seat question comes up every eighteen months.

Capital cost per unit is high. Consumable cost falls by roughly 70 percent.
Payback period at office volume is 2.4 years. Nobody has ever been willing
to present this analysis in a meeting where it would be minuted.

Status: perpetually deferred. Not on cost grounds. On grounds of who would
have to say the words out loud, in front of finance, with their name on
the slide.

### 18.5 The externality

The system's outputs enter a municipal treatment network whose costs are
socialised and whose capacity was, in this city, sized by a Victorian
engineer who deliberately doubled his own estimate.

Every organisation in the city benefits from that decision and none of them
pay for it. This is what good infrastructure looks like from the inside: it
is invisible, it is free at the point of use, and nobody thanks the person
who oversized the pipe.

## RFC 0019: Philosophy

### 19.1 On the universal and the unmentionable

There are two facts about this subject that are both true and difficult to
hold at once. The first is that it is entirely universal: every person
reading this does it, has always done it, and will continue to do it. The
second is that it is essentially unmentionable: not one of them will discuss
it, not with colleagues, not with friends, and in many cases not with a
doctor when they should.

The gap between those two facts is where every failure in this document
lives. The motion sensor outage lasted eleven weeks because reporting it
required saying the thing out loud. The bidet analysis is deferred forever
because presenting it requires a slide. The paper supplier stayed under
contract because complaining required specificity.

An organisation's capacity to fix a problem is bounded by its willingness to
name it. This is not a fact about bathrooms.

### 19.2 On the seriousness of unserious subjects

The engineering discussed in this document is real engineering. The S trap
is a genuinely elegant solution to a hard problem. Bazalgette's decision to
double his own estimate is one of the great acts of engineering humility.
The Japanese sound generator is competent privacy engineering shipped as a
consumer default.

None of it is taken seriously, because of what it is attached to. Sanitation
is the single largest contributor to human life expectancy in the modern
era, larger than antibiotics, larger than surgery, and it is the subject
nobody wants on their slide.

The field with the highest ratio of impact to prestige is the field where
the most valuable unclaimed work is sitting.

### 19.3 On feedback loops

The Curry Incident is not really about curry. It is about a four hour delay
between a decision and its consequence, and what that delay does to
learning.

A system with a fast feedback loop teaches you whether you meant to be
taught or not. A system with a slow one lets you make the same mistake for
a decade with complete confidence. Most of the important decisions in a
career have feedback loops measured in years, which is why experience is
worth so much less than people assume and why writing things down is worth
so much more.

That is what a postmortem is for. It is an artificial feedback loop,
bolted onto a system that does not have one.

### 19.4 On deferral

Thirty two percent of recorded incidents share a root cause: the operator
had capacity available, judged the urgency insufficient, and deferred.

Every single one of those deferrals was locally rational. Capacity was
available. Urgency was low. There was time. The mistake is not in any
individual decision. The mistake is in modelling capacity as a constant
when it is a queue, and in modelling urgency as a level when it is a
derivative.

Do it while the queue is short. This is the whole of RFC 0007, the whole
of the airport incident, and, if the reader will forgive one moment of
overreach in a document that has otherwise stayed in character, most of
what anyone needs to know about technical debt.

### 19.5 On privacy as a default

Rome built superb hydraulics and no partitions. They did not overlook
privacy; they did not consider it a requirement. Within two generations of
the bathroom moving indoors, privacy became so absolute a requirement that
its absence is now unthinkable.

No committee decided this. No standard was published. The requirement was
constructed socially, completely, and in living memory.

Reading: the things you believe are inherent properties of your problem
domain include at least one requirement that was invented recently by
people who could have chosen otherwise, and at least one absence that will
be unthinkable to your successors.

### 19.6 On the document itself

This document has survived four deletion attempts, three linters, two
migrations and one acquisition. It has never rendered. Nobody is assigned
to it. It has no owner, no tests, no CI job, and no reason to exist.

It is also the only written onboarding material in this company that covers
something every employee does every single day, and the only place where
the queueing analysis that would save 340,000 a year is written down.

Both of those sentences are true. Neither is a joke. That is why it is
still here.

## RFC 0020: Internationalisation

### 20.1 Scope

The protocol is universal. The interface is not. This section catalogues
regional variation for engineers who travel, which is to say for engineers
who will otherwise learn this material the hard way.

### 20.2 Interface variants

| Variant          | Posture   | Water   | Paper    | Notes                  |
|------------------|-----------|---------|----------|------------------------|
| Western seated   | Seated    | Cistern | Primary  | Global default         |
| Squat            | Squatting | Cistern | Optional | Biomechanically better |
| Bidet, separate  | Seated    | Fixture | Drying   | Two step workflow      |
| Bidet, integrated| Seated    | Nozzle  | Drying   | Best in class          |
| Bucket and jug   | Squatting | Manual  | None     | No dependency on paper |
| Composting       | Seated    | None    | Primary  | Batch, not streaming   |
| Aircraft vacuum  | Seated    | Vacuum  | Primary  | 2 bar pressure delta   |
| Long drop        | Squatting | None    | Varies   | No recovery path       |

### 20.3 The squat variant

Anorectal angle is more favourable when squatting. Transit is faster and
the required intra abdominal pressure is lower. This is measurable and
uncontroversial.

The Western seated variant is worse on the metric that matters and won on
distribution, comfort and manufacturing. This is the most complete example
in the document of a dominant design that is technically inferior to its
alternative, and it is why the footstool exists as an aftermarket patch.

### 20.4 The paper versus water divide

Roughly two thirds of the world's population uses water as the primary
mechanism and paper, if at all, as a drying step. Roughly one third uses
paper alone.

Neither population finds the other's approach reasonable, and each is
confident that the other has not thought about it. Every engineer who has
argued about tabs and spaces has participated in a smaller version of this
disagreement.

The water primary approach uses less consumable, produces less waste,
performs better on the outcome metric, and is unavailable in most Western
buildings because the plumbing was never run. Path dependence, again.

### 20.5 Aircraft

The vacuum variant operates on a pressure differential rather than gravity
and water. It uses roughly 0.2 litres per flush against 6 litres for a
domestic cistern, because water is mass and mass is fuel.

It is also extremely loud, which produces a well documented behavioural
adaptation in which passengers close the lid before actuating, and a less
well documented one in which nobody actuates until they are standing.

### 20.6 Localisation failures

- Paper dispensers that require two hands in facilities with no shelf.
- Sensor flush systems calibrated for a posture the local population does
  not use, producing spurious mid session flushes.
- Hand dryers loud enough to defeat the acoustic countermeasure in section
  6.3, installed in rooms with no ventilation fan.
- Doors with a gap at eye level. There is one country responsible for the
  overwhelming majority of these and this document declines to name it.
- Signage that assumes literacy in one language, in an airport.

### 20.7 Recommendation

Support both primary variants where plumbing permits. Where it does not,
document what you have, clearly, at the entrance, so that a traveller can
form a correct model before committing. The worst experience is not an
unfamiliar interface. It is an unfamiliar interface discovered late.

## RFC 0021: Accessibility

### 21.1 Position

An inaccessible facility is not a degraded facility. It is an absent one.
There is no partial credit here and no graceful degradation. Either a
person can use the room or they cannot, and if they cannot, they leave the
building, and shortly afterwards they leave the job.

### 21.2 Requirements

- Door clear width sufficient for a wheelchair, measured, not estimated.
- Turning circle inside the room with the door closed.
- Grab rails on both sides, fixed to structure, not to plasterboard.
- Transfer space beside the fixture, kept clear, permanently.
- Emergency cord reaching the floor, and staff trained on what it means.
- Fixtures at reachable height including the lock, the paper and the flush.
- Lighting that does not depend on gross motion. See RFC 0009 section 9.3.
- Signage legible to someone who cannot read the language.

### 21.3 Common failures

**The storeroom failure.** The accessible stall is the largest, so it
accumulates cleaning equipment, spare stock and a broken chair. The room
still technically exists. It is no longer usable. This is the most common
failure in the entire category and it is committed by people who would
never remove a grab rail.

**The cord failure.** The emergency cord is tied up out of the way because
it dangles. It is tied up by cleaning staff who were never told what it is
for. This has killed people.

**The lighting failure.** Motion sensors calibrated for a standing person
walking across the room do not detect a seated person. The eleven week
outage on floor 3 was an inconvenience for most users. For at least one it
was a categorical failure that nobody heard about, because the reporting
problem in section 9.3 applies with more force to the people who most need
the report to be acted on.

**The locked door failure.** The accessible facility is locked and the key
is at reception. The person must identify themselves and request access,
every single time, in public. The facility exists. The dignity does not.

### 21.4 Testing

Test with the users. Not with a checklist, not with a tape measure, and
not with an able bodied engineer sitting in a borrowed wheelchair for an
afternoon, which produces confident conclusions and misses everything that
matters.

The checklist is a floor, not a specification. Every item in section 21.3
passes a standard compliance audit.

### 21.5 On this section

This is the only section of this document written without a joke in it.
The subject does not need one and the register would not survive it.

## RFC 0022: Test Plan

### 22.1 Unit tests

Unit tests cover the components in isolation with all dependencies mocked.
Coverage is 94 percent. The uncovered 6 percent is where every production
incident has occurred, which is the normal relationship between coverage
and reality.

```ts
describe('preflight', () => {
  it('throws when paper is unavailable', async () => {
    const client = createMockClient({ paper: 0 })
    await expect(client.preflight()).rejects.toThrow(NoPaperError)
  })

  it('passes when paper is available', async () => {
    const client = createMockClient({ paper: 1 })
    await expect(client.preflight()).resolves.toBeUndefined()
  })

  it('throws when the lock is not engaged', async () => {
    const client = createMockClient({ locked: false })
    await expect(client.preflight()).rejects.toThrow(LockError)
  })
})
```

The third test was added after the incident described in ADR 006 and is the
only test in the suite with a comment explaining why it exists. The comment
reads, in full: "ask nobody".

### 22.2 Integration tests

Integration tests run against a real facility with a real payload. They are
slow, non deterministic, impossible to parallelise, and cannot be run in CI.

They are also the only tests that have ever caught a real defect.

### 22.3 Load tests

Load testing is performed once per quarter by catering.

The test is uncontrolled, unannounced, unrepeatable and produces no
artefacts other than complaints. It is nonetheless the most informative
signal the organisation receives about its own capacity, and it is the only
reason anyone knows what the amplification factor is.

### 22.4 Chaos engineering

Chaos experiments run continuously in production without anybody's consent:

- Paper is removed at random intervals by an unknown process.
- One stall is taken out of service for cleaning at peak load.
- The lighting fails on a 45 second timer.
- The lock on stall 2 has been degraded for eight months.
- Hot water availability is stochastic and correlated with nothing.

The system's resilience to these experiments is not measured, because
measuring it would require asking people about them.

### 22.5 Regression suite

One test per incident in RFC 0009. The suite is the incident history made
executable, which is the only defensible reason to write a regression test
at all.

| Test                          | Incident | Status  |
|-------------------------------|----------|---------|
| `rejectsOversizedPayload`     | 9.1      | SKIPPED |
| `requiresBackpressure`        | 9.2      | PASS    |
| `lightingIndependentOfMotion` | 9.3      | PASS    |
| `reservationsAreImpossible`   | 9.4      | PASS    |
| `noPerUserOccupancy`          | 9.5      | PASS    |
| `doesNotDeferUnderLowLoad`    | 9.6      | FLAKY   |

`rejectsOversizedPayload` has been skipped since the day it was written,
because it fails, because the fix was never made, because action item 1 of
the Curry Incident postmortem is still open. The skip has a link to the
postmortem. Nobody has followed the link in three years.

`doesNotDeferUnderLowLoad` is flaky because the system under test is a
person.

### 22.6 Manual QA

There is one manual QA procedure and it is performed by every user, several
times a day, without training, documentation or a reporting channel. It has
caught every defect in the system's history and reported approximately four
percent of them.

### 22.7 Acceptance criteria

A release is acceptable when it does not embarrass anyone. This criterion
is subjective, unfalsifiable, and has correctly gated every release.

## RFC 0023: Monitoring and Alerting

### 23.1 Signals

Three signals, in descending order of usefulness:

**Olfactory.** Highest information density, lowest latency, no
instrumentation required, universally available and universally ignored in
formal monitoring design because nobody will write it in a document. It is
in this one.

**Acoustic.** Medium latency, high false positive rate, extremely high
social cost on a true positive. Cannot be sampled without the sampling
being detected, which makes it the only signal in this document that
observes its observer.

**Visual.** Lowest latency of all, but only available at a range where the
information is no longer actionable and the observer wishes very much that
it were not available.

### 23.2 SLIs

| Indicator                | Definition                          | Target  |
|--------------------------|-------------------------------------|---------|
| Availability             | Fraction of attempts finding a stall| > 99%   |
| Queue depth              | Clients waiting at arrival          | < 2     |
| Time to service          | Arrival to lock engagement          | < 90 s  |
| Paper availability       | Stalls with non zero paper          | 100%    |
| Successful completion    | Sessions ending in 200              | > 98%   |
| Cleanliness              | Subjective, 1 to 10, sampled daily  | > 7     |

Cleanliness is the only subjective indicator and the only one anybody
checks. This is not a coincidence. The measurable indicators are measured
by nobody and the unmeasurable one is measured by everybody, continuously,
without being asked.

### 23.3 Alerting policy

Page on:

- Zero available stalls for more than 10 minutes.
- Paper availability below 100 percent.
- Any `ClogError` reported by a user.
- Lock failure on any stall, immediately, per ADR 006.

Do not page on:

- Queue depth. The affected users are already aware.
- Cleanliness below target. Ticket it. Paging helps nobody at 03:00.
- A single 503. Cleaning is scheduled and expected.

### 23.4 Alert fatigue

The facilities ticket queue contains 340 open tickets. Median age is 8
months. Nobody reads it. Every user knows nobody reads it. Ticket creation
rate has fallen 70 percent over two years while the underlying defect rate
has risen.

This is the failure mode of every monitoring system that outlives the
attention paid to it: the signal does not stop, the listener does, and the
absence of alerts is then read as health by people who have stopped
counting how many alerts they ignored.

### 23.5 Dashboards

One dashboard exists. It shows a single integer: the number of available
stalls, aggregated across all floors, with no history and no identifiers.

It is the second version. The first version is described in RFC 0009
section 9.5 and is the reason this one has exactly one number on it.

It has reduced reneging by an estimated 60 percent and it cost 90 currency
units in parts. It is, by return on investment, the most successful project
in the building's history.

### 23.6 On measuring what matters

The organisation measures paper cost to four decimal places and does not
measure queue time at all. Paper is 0.4 percent of unit cost. Queue time is
approximately 340,000 a year.

What gets measured is not what matters. What gets measured is what is easy
to measure and safe to discuss.

## RFC 0024: Performance Tuning

### 24.1 Before you tune

Measure. Almost every intervention attempted in this domain is applied
without measurement, to a system whose baseline the operator has never
established, targeting a symptom whose cause is elsewhere.

Establish a baseline over two weeks. Change one variable. Wait two weeks.
This is slower than everybody wants and it is the only method that produces
knowledge rather than folklore.

### 24.2 Tuning parameters, ranked by leverage

**1. Hydration.** Free. Immediate. Affects every other parameter
multiplicatively. Chronically under applied. If you change one thing,
change this.

**2. Fibre.** The highest leverage dietary parameter. See RFC 0008 section
8.3 for the dose response curve, including the non monotonic satisfaction
relationship that makes 25 g/day the recommended target rather than the
maximum tolerated dose.

**3. Timing consistency.** The system entrains to a schedule. A consistent
daily window reduces variance more than any dietary change. Cold start is
the highest quality window available and it is free.

**4. Posture.** A footstool raising the knees above the hips approximates
the squat variant's anorectal angle. Cheap, effective, and universally
mocked until tried.

**5. Not deferring.** Ignoring the signal degrades the signal. Repeated
deferral raises the threshold at which the signal is generated at all,
which is a documented feedback loop with unpleasant long run behaviour.

**6. Movement.** Walking increases motility. Sedentary work degrades it.
The office deployment's poor performance relative to the home deployment
is partly contention and partly the fact that its users have not stood up
since 09:30.

### 24.3 Anti tuning

Interventions that are widely applied and either useless or harmful:

- Straining. Increases pressure, increases risk, does not increase
  throughput. The single most counterproductive technique in common use.
- Extending session duration in the absence of progress. After ten minutes
  with no progress the correct action is to terminate the session and
  retry later. This is documented nowhere and known by nobody.
- Stimulants applied as a routine rather than as a rescue. Tolerance
  develops. Baseline degrades. The intervention becomes the dependency.
- Optimising throughput without regard to comfort, per the 60 g/day row in
  the benchmark table, which is the best throughput and the worst life.

### 24.4 When to escalate

Persistent deviation from your own baseline for more than two weeks, blood,
pain, or an abrupt change with no dietary explanation, are all reasons to
consult a professional rather than a README.

This document is a joke. That sentence is not.

## RFC 0026: Migration Guide

### 26.1 Migrating from v1 to v2

Do not. v2 is v1 with a streaming API that was removed in a patch release
twenty three hours later. There is nothing in v2 for you.

### 26.2 Migrating from the outdoor deployment

The outdoor deployment has no cistern, no trap, no lighting and no lock.
Migration is a full rewrite and the only shared component is the operator.

Checklist:

1. Verify plumbing exists before decommissioning the old deployment. This
   ordering has been got wrong, in this country, within living memory.
2. Verify the trap. A drain without a trap is worse than no drain, because
   it connects your building to the sewer's gas volume directly.
3. Verify ventilation before you verify anything else you consider more
   important, because you will not be able to.
4. Keep the old deployment available during cutover. The rollback path is
   the whole reason it is still standing.

### 26.3 Migrating between regional variants

Travellers migrating from paper primary to water primary deployments
should expect a two week adaptation period and should not form an opinion
before it has elapsed. Every recorded opinion formed in the first 48 hours
has been reversed.

Travellers migrating in the other direction have no adaptation period and
form their opinion immediately. It does not improve.

### 26.4 Migrating to an integrated bidet

Payback period at office volume is 2.4 years. Payback period at household
volume is 4.1 years. Neither number is why anybody has ever installed one,
and neither number is why anybody has ever refused.

Prerequisites: a power outlet within reach of the fixture, which most
bathrooms outside East Asia do not have, for reasons of electrical code
that were written before anybody imagined the requirement.

That missing outlet is why this variant has not spread. Not cost, not
preference, not culture. A socket location decided by a committee in the
1960s.

### 26.5 Rollback

There is no rollback for any migration in this section. Per ADR 002, there
is no rollback for anything. Verify before you commit.

## RFC 0027: Environments

### 27.1 Environment matrix

| Environment | Tenancy      | SLA        | Rollback | Observability |
|-------------|--------------|------------|----------|---------------|
| Home        | Single       | 99.99%     | None     | Total         |
| Office      | Multi        | 99.9%      | None     | Aggregate     |
| Airport     | Multi, hostile| 99.0%     | None     | None          |
| Train       | Multi, moving| 90.0%      | None     | None          |
| Festival    | Multi, feral | 50.0%      | None     | None          |
| Camping     | Single, none | Best effort| None     | None          |
| Aircraft    | Multi, sealed| 99.5%      | None     | None          |

### 27.2 Home

The reference environment. Single tenant, no contention, full control over
every configuration parameter, complete observability, and the only
environment in which the operator can influence the supply chain.

All benchmarks in RFC 0008 were taken here, which is the principal threat
to their validity: this environment resembles production the way a mock
client resembles a facility at an airport.

### 27.3 Office

Multi tenant with soft isolation. The isolation is social rather than
technical: nothing prevents a co tenant from observing your session except
a convention that everybody upholds and nobody has written down.

This document has now written it down, in section 15.2, which is either
useful onboarding or a violation of the convention it documents.

### 27.4 Airport

Hostile multi tenancy. High arrival correlation, high urgency distribution,
users under time pressure with no fallback and no local knowledge.

Utilisation runs above 0.95 for most of the operating day, which per RFC
0007 means wait times are not merely long but unbounded in the practical
sense: the queue does not clear, it is drained continuously by departures
and refilled continuously by arrivals, and the depth is set by whatever
equilibrium the building's geometry happens to produce.

Every airport built in the last thirty years has been sized by someone who
had access to this arithmetic.

### 27.5 Train

Moving multi tenant environment with a hard capacity limit, no resupply for
the duration, no cleaning during service and a floor that is never level.

The vacuum variant is standard. The failure mode is total: when the tank
fills, the environment is out of service for the remainder of the journey,
with no recovery path and no alternative within reach, at speed, for hours.

This is the only environment in the matrix where a single component failure
takes out every tenant simultaneously with no possibility of failover, and
it is the only one where the users are physically unable to leave.

### 27.6 Festival

Feral multi tenancy. Capacity is provisioned for a fraction of demand.
Resupply is scheduled and inadequate. Lighting is absent after dark. The
supply chain fails on the first evening and is not restored.

The 50 percent availability target is not a target. It is a description,
written afterwards, by somebody who had been there.

Recommended posture: bring your own supply chain, arrive early in the
lifecycle, and treat every facility you pass as an opportunity rather than
a resource that will be there later. This is the deferral lesson from
section 19.4 applied under adversarial conditions, and the people who
learn it here learn it permanently.

### 27.7 Camping

Single tenant, zero infrastructure, full operator responsibility for the
complete lifecycle including disposal.

Best practice is well established and widely ignored: 200 m from water, 60
m from camp and trail, a hole of adequate depth, everything non organic
carried out. The operator is simultaneously the ingest layer, the egress
layer, the treatment plant and the regulator.

It is the only environment in the matrix where the externality described in
RFC 0018 section 18.5 is fully internalised, and consequently the only one
where people think carefully about it.

### 27.8 Aircraft

Sealed multi tenant environment at 0.75 bar with a 2 bar differential
across the flush valve, a total water budget measured in litres, and a
queue that forms in an aisle where standing is periodically prohibited.

Notable property: the seatbelt sign is an externally imposed, non
negotiable freeze on the entire queue, applied without warning, for an
unknown duration. No other environment in the matrix has a mechanism that
can halt service for every tenant simultaneously at the discretion of a
third party who cannot see the queue.

### 27.9 Promotion between environments

There is none. Every environment is production. Every session is a deploy
to production on a Friday afternoon with no review, no staging and no
revert. This is stated in ADR 002 and it is worth restating, because the
entire discipline of this document follows from it: when you cannot roll
back, verification moves to the front, and the front is where all the
value is anyway.

## RFC 0028: Contributing

### 28.1 Before opening a PR

Read RFC 0016. The register is the product. A technically correct addition
in the wrong register is worse than no addition, because it teaches the
next contributor that the register is negotiable.

### 28.2 Scope

In scope: new RFCs, new incidents, benchmark data, historical material,
comparative systems, glossary entries.

Out of scope: anything naming a colleague, anything unkind, anything false,
anything medical stated as advice, and any sentence that explains a joke.

### 28.3 Review

Two approvals: one technical, one tonal. The tonal reviewer is stricter and
this is correct. A wrong number can be fixed in a line. A broken register
requires rewriting the section and usually the two around it.

### 28.4 Commit messages

Conventional commits. `docs(readme):` scope. The scope is accurate: this
is documentation, it is in the readme, and it has never rendered.

Real examples from the history:

```
docs(readme): add RFC 0007 queueing analysis
docs(readme): correct Little's Law statement (was inverted)
docs(readme): remove joke that explained itself
docs(readme): add accessibility section, no jokes, deliberate
docs(readme): revert bidet cost analysis (finance saw the diff)
```

The fifth is the only revert in the history of this file and it was not
reverted for accuracy.

### 28.5 On the four deletion attempts

Each of the four attempts to delete this document was made in good faith by
somebody with a reasonable case. Each stalled at review, when the reviewer
asked why, and the answer had to be typed into a public comment box on a
pull request, under a real name, in a company chat that is archived.

Nobody has yet been willing to write "I want to remove the only document
that explains the queueing problem, because it is about defecation" in a
place where it would be retained.

This is not a defence of the document. It is an observation about the
mechanism that has kept it alive, and it is the same mechanism, exactly,
that kept the motion sensor outage unreported for eleven weeks.

## RFC 0029: Compliance

### 29.1 Regulatory landscape

Workplace sanitation is mandated by statute in every jurisdiction this
company operates in. The mandates specify minimum fixture counts as a
function of headcount, and every one of them specifies a floor that is
substantially below the point at which utilisation becomes tolerable.

The regulation is a compliance threshold, not a capacity target. A building
that meets the mandate exactly will operate at rho above 0.9 and will be
fully compliant while being, in the sense that matters, broken.

This is the general case of every compliance regime ever written. The
standard describes the point below which you are negligent. It says nothing
whatsoever about the point above which you are good.

### 29.2 Fixture ratios

| Headcount | Statutory minimum | rho at minimum | Recommended |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|-------------|
| 25        | 2                 | 0.71           | 3           |
| 50        | 3                 | 0.79           | 5           |
| 100       | 5                 | 0.85           | 9           |
| 200       | 8                 | 0.91           | 16          |
| 500       | 15                | 0.94           | 38          |

The recommended column is derived from targeting rho below 0.6 with the
measured post lunch amplification factor applied. It is roughly double the
statutory figure at every scale, which is Bazalgette's rule arrived at
independently by arithmetic ninety years later.

The building we occupy was provisioned at the statutory minimum.

### 29.3 Data protection

Occupancy data is personal data the moment it can be joined to a person.
A sensor on a lock is not personal data. A sensor on a lock plus a badge
reader on the door is a record of which employee was in which stall at
which time, retained indefinitely, on a screen in a corridor.

The distinction is not the sensor. The distinction is the join. See RFC
0009 section 9.5 for the case where this was learned expensively.

Current posture, per ADR 005: aggregate before it leaves the device, no
identifiers, no retention beyond one hour, no join key collected at all.
The last clause is the only one that is actually a control. The others are
promises about behaviour and promises are not controls.

### 29.4 Records retention

This document is retained because it is in git and git retains everything.
Four attempted deletions are in the history. The diffs are readable. The
review comments are readable.

Nothing has ever been removed from this repository. Contributors should
write accordingly, in this file and in every other.

### 29.5 Audit findings

The last facilities audit raised three findings:

1. Accessible facility on floor 3 used for storage. **Repeat finding, third
   consecutive audit.** Closed after the audit. Reopened within a month,
   every time.
2. Emergency cord secured out of reach. **Critical.** Closed same day. Root
   cause is that cleaning staff were never told what the cord is for, and
   the corrective action was a sign, and signs do not survive staff
   turnover, and staff turnover is quarterly.
3. Paper stock below reorder threshold on two floors. Closed.

Finding 1 has been raised and closed three times without ever being fixed,
which is the definition of a control that does not work. Finding 2 has a
corrective action with a half life shorter than the audit cycle.

Both findings will appear in the next audit. This is knowable now, is
written down now, and will surprise everybody involved.

## RFC 0031: Materials

### 31.1 The consumable

The hard dependency identified in RFC 0006 section 6.5 is a low grade
tissue optimised on three axes that trade against each other: absorbency,
tensile strength when wet, and dispersibility in the sewer.

The third axis is the one nobody thinks about and the one that determines
whether the municipality has to send a crew.

### 31.2 Ply

| Ply | Absorbency | Wet strength | Units per session | Blockage risk |
|-----|------------|--------------|-------------------|---------------|
| 1   | Low        | Very low     | 14                | Low           |
| 2   | Good       | Moderate     | 7                 | Low           |
| 3   | High       | High         | 5                 | Moderate      |
| 4   | Very high  | Very high    | 4                 | High          |

Two ply is the optimum and has been since 1928. Everything above it trades
a marginal comfort gain for a disproportionate rise in blockage risk, and
the blockage risk is borne by the building rather than by the person who
chose the product.

The paper supplier incident in RFC 0018 section 18.3 was a move down this
table dressed as a cost saving. Consumption rose almost exactly in the
ratio the table predicts.

### 31.3 The wet wipe problem

Wet wipes are marketed as flushable. They are not flushable in any sense
that matters. They do not disperse. They accumulate at every restriction
in the network, bind with fat, and form masses that require excavation.

London removed one weighing 130 tonnes. It was 250 m long. It had a name.

The regulatory position is that "flushable" is unregulated as a term. The
engineering position is that anything which retains tensile strength when
wet is, by definition, not dispersible, and the wet strength is the entire
product feature.

This is a case where the consumer's local optimum and the network's global
optimum are in direct opposition, the consumer has no visibility of the
cost, and the label actively misleads. Every externality problem has this
shape.

### 31.4 Fixture materials

Vitreous china. Fired at 1200 C, glazed, non porous, chemically inert,
mechanically brittle, and essentially unchanged as a material choice since
the 1880s.

It is one of very few components in daily use whose design converged over a
century ago and has resisted every attempt at improvement since. The
material is correct, the shape is correct, and the failure mode, sudden
brittle fracture under point load, is rare enough that nobody has been able
to justify replacing it.

Compare: everything else in the building has been replaced three times.

### 31.5 The trap

Water sits in a bend and blocks gas. The mechanism is that simple.

Failure modes:

- **Evaporation.** An unused fixture loses its seal in roughly three weeks.
  This is why a house that has been empty smells the way it does, and why
  the fix is to pour a jug of water down every drain.
- **Siphonage.** A fixture on the same stack, discharging at volume, can
  pull the seal out of a neighbouring trap. Prevented by venting, which is
  the pipe on the roof that everybody sees and nobody has ever wondered
  about.
- **Back pressure.** The opposite case. Same fix.
- **Capillary action.** A thread or hair over the weir wicks the seal away
  slowly. Rare, maddening, and invisible on inspection.

Every one of these is a state loss in a stateful component whose state is
invisible and whose failure is silent until the consequence arrives through
the air.

### 31.6 On the vent stack

The vent stack is a pipe that does nothing, costs money, occupies space,
penetrates the roof, and must be maintained. It carries no water. Its only
function is to hold pressure constant so that a different component can
keep its state.

It is the first thing a value engineer proposes to remove, and removing it
breaks a system two rooms away in a manner that nobody will connect back to
the decision.

Every codebase has one. Learn to recognise it before you delete it.

## RFC 0032: Field Notes

Traveller observations. Unverified. Contributed over several years.

### 32.1 Japan

The best in the world and not close. Public facilities are clean, free,
numerous, and equipped to a standard that Western private homes do not
reach. Integrated bidet, heated seat, sound generator, and in some
installations an occupancy display at the entrance to the room so that
nobody enters a full facility.

That last feature is the dashboard from RFC 0023 section 23.5, shipped as
standard infrastructure, decades ago, by people who did not need an
incident to work out that it was a good idea.

### 32.2 Germany

Historically the shelf variant, which places the payload on a dry ledge
for inspection before flushing. Now largely replaced.

Every explanation offered for the shelf involves either parasite
inspection or coal gas, and neither survives scrutiny. The honest position
is that it was a local optimum in a design space with weak selection
pressure, and it persisted for a century.

The relevant engineering property is that it converts the acoustic profile
substantially and increases the requirement for the countermeasure in
section 6.3 by a wide margin.

### 32.3 France

Historically the squat variant in public facilities, now mostly replaced.
The self cleaning street unit is the notable contribution: a fully
automated cycle between users, unattended, in public, at scale, which is a
genuinely hard robotics and hygiene problem solved competently in the
1980s.

The failure mode is that the cycle takes 90 seconds and the queue does not
understand why the door will not open, which is a user interface problem
attached to a solved mechanical one, which is where most problems live.

### 32.4 United States

The gap. Every partition has a gap at the door, at eye level, of a width
that is not an accident and is not required by any code.

Explanations offered locally include cost, ventilation, maintenance access
and safety monitoring. None of them survives comparison with any other
country that has solved all four constraints with a door that closes.

It is a norm that persists because it is invisible to the people who
specify buildings and unmentionable by the people who use them. See
section 19.1.

### 32.5 India and much of South Asia

Water primary, bucket and jug or spray. Better outcome, lower consumable
cost, no dependency on the supply chain that fails in RFC 0006 section 6.5.

The technique has a two week learning curve for a paper primary traveller
and is preferred by essentially everybody who completes it.

### 32.6 Nordic countries

Public facilities are clean, well maintained and charge a fee. The fee is
resented by every visitor and is the reason the facilities are clean and
well maintained.

There is a whole essay in the relationship between those two sentences and
it is the same essay as the one about the 340,000 in section 18.2.

### 32.7 Airports, ranked

Singapore Changi rates each facility with a touchscreen at the exit, feeds
it to a cleaning dispatch system, and responds within minutes. It is
closed loop monitoring with an actual actuator on the end of it, which is
more than can be said for the ticket queue in section 23.4.

Most others provision to the statutory minimum, at rho above 0.95, and
absorb the resulting queue as a cost paid entirely by passengers in a
currency the operator does not measure.

### 32.8 Motorway services, United Kingdom

Consistently better than expected. High throughput, aggressive cleaning
schedules, and a business model that depends on people stopping, which
aligns the operator's incentive with the user's experience.

Alignment of incentives produces better outcomes than regulation, exhortation
or good intentions. It is the only mechanism in this entire document that
has ever reliably worked.

## RFC 0033: Failure Atlas

A catalogue of failure modes, their signatures, and their handling. Ordered
by frequency rather than severity.

### 33.1 Resource contention

**Signature.** All stalls occupied. Queue forming. Arrival rate exceeds
service rate.

**Frequency.** Daily at the office deployment, 13:10 to 13:50.

**Handling.** Balk. Use another floor. Do not renege after joining; the
data in RFC 0009 is unambiguous that reneging produces the worst outcomes.

**Prevention.** Shift your window fifteen minutes earlier. Contention is
almost entirely produced by synchronisation, and desynchronising costs you
nothing.

### 33.2 Supply exhaustion

**Signature.** Preflight fails. Discovered at preflight if you are
disciplined, and considerably later if you are not.

**Frequency.** Weekly across the building.

**Handling.** Abort before committing. There is no recovery path after
commitment that does not involve another person, and involving another
person is a permanent change to that relationship.

**Prevention.** Preflight. Every time. It costs two seconds and it is the
highest expected value action available anywhere in this document.

### 33.3 Capacity exceeded downstream

**Signature.** `ClogError`. Water level rising rather than falling.

**Frequency.** Rare at the home deployment, more common at the office,
where the pipe runs are longer and the payload distribution has a fatter
tail because the population is larger.

**Handling.** Stop. Do not flush again. A second flush on a blocked line
adds six litres to a volume that is already exceeding its container, and
converts a contained failure into an uncontained one. This is the single
most common escalation error and it is always committed in panic.

Wait. The level falls on its own in most cases within two minutes. If it
does not, tooling is required.

**Prevention.** Validate at ingest, which nobody does, or split the payload
across sessions, which everybody discovers independently and nobody
discusses.

### 33.4 Uncontained failure

**Signature.** Material outside the intended vessel.

**Frequency.** Rare, catastrophic, memorable.

**Handling.** Contain first: close the door, which should already be
closed. Assess honestly. Clean thoroughly. Report if it affects a shared
facility, because the alternative is that somebody else finds it, and
being found is worse in every dimension than reporting.

**Prevention.** Velocity control. Write amplification rises superlinearly
with velocity, per the glossary entry, and the physics has never once been
negotiable.

### 33.5 False positive

**Signature.** `PhantomError`. Urgency signal present, no payload
available.

**Frequency.** Common under stress, caffeine and anxiety.

**Handling.** Terminate the session after five minutes. Do not persist.
Persistence under a false positive produces strain, and strain is the most
counterproductive technique in RFC 0024 section 24.3.

**Prevention.** Not really available. The signal is noisy by design and
the cost of a false negative is so much higher than a false positive that
the biological threshold is set exactly where you would set it.

### 33.6 Timeout

**Signature.** Session exceeds ten minutes with no progress.

**Frequency.** Correlated with `reading: 'phone'`, and this correlation is
not causal in the direction most people assume: the phone does not cause
the timeout, it makes the timeout comfortable, and comfort removes the
pressure that would otherwise terminate the session.

**Handling.** Terminate. Retry later. The queue outside is real.

### 33.7 Lock failure

**Signature.** Lock does not engage, or engages and cannot be released.

**Frequency.** Once per stall per two years.

**Handling.** The first case: do not use the stall. Per ADR 006 it is out
of service. The second case: this is the only failure in the atlas where
shouting is the correct response, and the social cost of shouting is why
people wait an average of eleven minutes before doing it.

**Prevention.** Maintenance. Locks are mechanical, wear is predictable,
and replacement is cheap relative to the incident.

### 33.8 Environmental failure

**Signature.** Lighting fails mid session. Ventilation stops. Hot water
absent. Door does not latch.

**Frequency.** Continuous, at low severity, everywhere.

**Handling.** Adapt. Report if shared. The reporting rate for this class is
approximately four percent and everybody involved knows it.

### 33.9 Cascading failure

**Signature.** Two or more of the above, simultaneously, compounding.

**Reference case.** The airport incident: contention, then a 503, then
contention again, under a hard external deadline, with the operator's
decision quality degrading at each step as urgency rose.

**Handling.** Recognise that your decision quality is degrading and reduce
your ambition accordingly. The operator at T minus 25 made a decision that
was reasonable at T minus 55 and catastrophic at T minus 25, because they
were still using the model they had formed when they were calm.

**Prevention.** Do not enter the cascade. Every cascade in this document
has a first step that was cheap to avoid and was avoided by nobody.

## RFC 0034: Capacity Planning, Worked

### 34.1 Inputs

Take the actual building.

- Headcount: 200.
- Sessions per person per day: 2.1.
- Mean service time: 6.0 minutes.
- Operating window: 09:00 to 18:00, 9 hours.
- Stalls: 8 (statutory minimum for this headcount).

### 34.2 Naive calculation

Total demand: 200 x 2.1 x 6.0 = 2,520 stall minutes per day.

Available: 8 x 9 x 60 = 4,320 stall minutes per day.

Utilisation: 2,520 / 4,320 = 0.58.

At rho = 0.58 the queueing model predicts a mean wait of well under a
minute. On this arithmetic the building is comfortably provisioned and no
further action is required.

This is the calculation that was performed. It is wrong.

### 34.3 Why it is wrong

Demand is not uniform across the window. It is concentrated.

Measured arrivals by hour, as a fraction of daily total:

| Hour  | Share | Effective rho |
|-------|-------|---------------|
| 09:00 | 14%   | 1.13          |
| 10:00 | 11%   | 0.89          |
| 11:00 | 8%    | 0.65          |
| 12:00 | 6%    | 0.49          |
| 13:00 | 19%   | 1.54          |
| 14:00 | 12%   | 0.97          |
| 15:00 | 9%    | 0.73          |
| 16:00 | 8%    | 0.65          |
| 17:00 | 7%    | 0.57          |

Two hours of the day exceed rho = 1.0. During those hours the queue does
not reach equilibrium; it grows for the duration of the peak and drains
afterwards. The daily average of 0.58 is a true number that describes
nothing anyone experiences.

### 34.4 The correct target

Size for the peak, not the mean. Target rho <= 0.6 at the 13:00 hour.

Required stalls at 13:00: demand in that hour is 0.19 x 2,520 = 479 stall
minutes, against 60 minutes of wall clock, giving 8.0 stalls at rho = 1.0
and therefore 13.3 stalls at rho = 0.6.

Round up: 14 stalls. The building has 8.

### 34.5 The cheaper answer

Alternatively: flatten the peak.

If the 13:00 share falls from 19 percent to 12 percent by staggering lunch
across two sittings, required stalls at rho = 0.6 drop from 13.3 to 8.4.
The building's existing 8 stalls are then within rounding of adequate.

Cost of building 6 stalls: approximately 90,000 currency units, one time,
plus the floor space forever.

Cost of two lunch sittings: zero.

### 34.6 What happened

Neither was done. The staggered lunch was trialled for one week, worked
exactly as the arithmetic predicted, and was abandoned because people like
eating together, which is a completely legitimate reason and which nobody
has ever written down as the actual decision.

The decision on record is "no budget", which refers to the option that was
not chosen for a different reason entirely.

### 34.7 Lesson

The mean hides the peak. The peak is the whole problem. And when the
cheapest fix is behavioural rather than capital, the reason it does not
happen will not be the reason in the minutes.

## RFC 0035: On Call Runbook

For the facilities rotation. Print and laminate. Do not print this document.

### 35.1 Severity definitions

**SEV0.** Building level. No usable facility on any floor. Page
immediately, any hour.

**SEV1.** Floor level. No usable facility on one floor, or an accessible
facility out of service anywhere. Page during working hours.

**SEV2.** Stall level. One stall out of service. Ticket, same day.

**SEV3.** Degraded. Lighting, ventilation, hot water, supply low. Ticket,
next business day.

Note that an accessible facility out of service is SEV1 regardless of how
many other stalls are available, because for its users it is a total
outage. This was previously SEV3 and the change came out of the audit
described in RFC 0029 section 29.5.

### 35.2 First response

1. Confirm the report. Roughly a third are stale, because the reporter
   waited two days to work out how to phrase the ticket.
2. Establish scope. One stall, one room, one floor, or the building.
3. Take out of service if unsafe. Signage on the door, not on the stall,
   because signage on a stall inside a room means somebody has to walk in
   and read it.
4. Communicate. One line, to the floor, with the expected restoration
   time. Nobody needs detail. Everybody needs the estimate.

### 35.3 Blockage

Escalation order:

1. Wait two minutes. Most clear without intervention.
2. Plunger. Seal the outlet, sharp strokes, maintain the seal.
3. Auger, if available and if you have used one before.
4. Contractor.

Do not add water. Do not flush to test. A flush on a blocked line adds six
litres to a container that is already at capacity and is how a SEV2 becomes
a SEV1 with a cleaning contract attached.

Do not use chemical drain cleaner on a fixture blockage. It will not reach
the obstruction, it will sit in the trap, and the next person to work on
the line will put their hands in it.

### 35.4 Supply

Reorder threshold is 20 percent of stock. Lead time is 5 days. Consumption
is 41 percent higher on the current supplier than the previous one and the
threshold was never recalculated after the switch, which is why two floors
appear in every audit.

Recalculate the threshold when the product changes. This is written here
because it is not written anywhere else.

### 35.5 Lock failure

Immediate SEV2. Take out of service. Replace, do not repair. A lock that
has failed once has worn, and a lock that is repaired will fail again in a
manner that ADR 006 exists to prevent.

If somebody is inside and cannot release: this is the one case where
protocol is suspended entirely. Speak through the door, keep speaking,
and get the tool. Do not go and find a colleague to discuss it with first.

### 35.6 Emergency cord activation

Respond immediately, in person, and speak through the door before opening
anything. Announce yourself. Ask before entering.

Verify weekly that the cord reaches the floor and that it is not tied,
looped or tucked behind a rail. It will be, again, within a month of every
correction, because the corrective action is a sign and the population it
addresses turns over quarterly.

The durable fix is a cord with a weighted end that cannot be tucked, which
costs eleven currency units and has been on the maintenance backlog for two
years behind items with clearer owners.

### 35.7 Post incident

Every SEV0 and SEV1 gets a written postmortem within five days. Blameless.
Published to the facilities channel.

Every postmortem gets one action item, not six. Six action items is a way
of not choosing, and a list of six will produce zero completions, which is
demonstrably what happened to the Curry Incident's list of four.

### 35.8 Handover

At rotation end, hand over: open incidents, stock levels by floor, any
stall out of service and why, and anything that has failed twice in the
same month. The last category is the only one that predicts the next
incident and it is the one that never gets written down.

## RFC 0036: Vendor Evaluation

### 36.1 Scope

Evaluation of managed facility services, conducted over one quarter, at
the request of a director who had read a slide.

### 36.2 Criteria and weights

| Criterion             | Weight | Rationale                           |
|-----------------------|--------|-------------------------------------|
| Response time         | 25%    | Drives SEV1 duration                |
| Consumable quality    | 20%    | See RFC 0018 section 18.3           |
| Cleaning frequency    | 20%    | Only SLI anybody actually checks    |
| Cost                  | 15%    | Deliberately not the top weight     |
| Reporting             | 10%    | Aggregate only, per ADR 005         |
| Accessibility audit   | 10%    | Repeat finding, needs an owner      |

Cost was deliberately weighted below quality after the paper incident. The
director asked twice why cost was not the top weight and accepted the
answer on the second occasion.

### 36.3 Findings

**Vendor A.** Cheapest by 18 percent. Response time SLA of 4 hours,
measured from ticket acknowledgement rather than ticket creation, with
acknowledgement unbounded. This is a 4 hour SLA on a clock the vendor
starts.

**Vendor B.** Mid price. Response measured from creation. Provides per
stall usage reporting as a headline feature, which is precisely the data
ADR 005 exists to prevent us from collecting, and which they could not
disable without a custom contract.

**Vendor C.** Most expensive by 9 percent. Response from creation, 2
hours. Aggregate reporting only. Would not commit to an accessibility
audit without a scope document, which is the only honest answer anybody
gave to that question.

### 36.4 Recommendation

Vendor C. Selected on response time and on the fact that they were the
only vendor whose reporting did not require us to build a privacy control
around their product.

### 36.5 Outcome

Vendor A was selected. Cost.

Six months later, mean SEV1 duration had risen from 3.1 hours to 9.4
hours, entirely explained by the acknowledgement clock. The contract has
eighteen months to run.

### 36.6 Lesson

Read the clock definition. Every SLA in this industry is a promise about
an interval, and the party writing the promise chooses when the interval
starts. If you do not control the start, you do not have an SLA, you have
a number.

## RFC 0037: Organisational Design

### 37.1 Conway's Law

An organisation designs systems that mirror its own communication
structure. This building is a proof of the theorem.

Facilities owns the fixtures. IT owns the sensors. HR owns the policy.
Finance owns the budget. Nobody owns the outcome.

The result is a system in which the sensor exists, the data is collected,
the policy prohibits its use, the budget for the fix sits with a fifth
party, and the queue continues.

### 37.2 Ownership

Every recurring failure in this document maps to an ownership gap rather
than a technical one:

| Failure                      | Technically hard? | Owned? |
|------------------------------|-------------------|--------|
| Accessible facility storage  | No                | No     |
| Emergency cord tucked away   | No                | No     |
| Reorder threshold stale      | No                | No     |
| Lighting timeout             | No                | No     |
| Peak capacity                | No                | No     |
| Vendor clock definition      | No                | No     |

Not one of these required an engineer. Every one of them required a person
whose job it was to care, and in each case that person did not exist.

The technical work in this building was finished in 1880.

### 37.3 The specification gap

RFC 0007 section 7.8 recommended "publish occupancy". An engineer
published occupancy per stall with badge correlation on a corridor screen.

The engineer did exactly what the specification said. The specification was
written by somebody who assumed a shared understanding that did not exist,
and the gap between what was written and what was meant was filled with
enthusiasm.

Every specification you write will be read by somebody with more energy
than context. Write for that person.

### 37.4 The reporting gap

Four percent of environmental failures are reported. This is not a
motivation problem and it will not be fixed by a poster.

The reporting rate for a failure is a function of how embarrassing the
report is, and no amount of encouragement changes the embarrassment. The
only interventions that work are removing the person from the loop
entirely, through instrumentation, or removing the identification, through
anonymity.

The dashboard in RFC 0023 section 23.5 works because it needs no reporter.

### 37.5 The budget gap

The queue costs 340,000 a year. The fix costs 60,000 once. The fix has not
been funded for three years.

This is not irrationality. It is an accounting artefact: the 340,000 is
distributed across two hundred timesheets and appears in no line item,
while the 60,000 appears in one line item with one signature required.

Distributed costs do not compete with concentrated costs, regardless of
magnitude. Every organisation works this way. Knowing it does not fix it,
but it tells you which number to put on the slide: not the 340,000, which
is abstract, but the 22 minutes, which everybody in the room has stood in.

### 37.6 The RACI

Somebody once produced a RACI matrix for this domain. It was four pages.
It listed nine parties. Under "Accountable" for the outcome "facilities are
available and adequate", the cell was blank.

It went through review with the blank cell. Six people approved it.

### 37.7 Recommendation

One owner. One number. Publish it monthly.

The number should be the peak hour queue depth, because it is the thing
users experience, it cannot be gamed without actually fixing the problem,
and it is not embarrassing to say out loud in a meeting, which is the
binding constraint on every intervention in this document.

## RFC 0038: An Interview with the Maintainer

Conducted anonymously. Lightly edited. The maintainer requested that no
identifying details be retained and this request has been honoured, which
is itself consistent with everything else in this file.

**Q: Why did you start it?**

I wrote the first section during a deploy freeze. The build was broken,
nobody could merge anything, and I had a queueing textbook open for an
unrelated reason. Then the catering arrived and the floor emptied, and I
realised I was looking at a worked example.

**Q: Did you expect it to survive?**

No. I expected it to be deleted in the first review. The reviewer approved
it with the comment "lol" and that was the entire gate. Nobody has applied
a stricter one since, which tells you exactly how much attention a README
diff receives.

**Q: When did it stop being a joke?**

The queueing section. I did the arithmetic properly because doing it badly
would have been worse than not doing it, and when I finished I had the
number for what the peak costs us. Nobody in the building had that number.
The only place it existed was inside a joke about defecation.

I raised it in a planning meeting once, without the surrounding document.
It went nowhere. It goes nowhere every time. The number is not the problem.

**Q: The accessibility section has no jokes.**

It cannot have any. I tried, early on, and the draft was unpublishable.
The subject does not tolerate the register, and a document that breaks
character once has no character.

Also, the storeroom failure is real and it is in this building right now.
I have reported it four times. It is in three consecutive audits. Writing
it here is not activism, it is just the only place I can write it where it
stays written.

**Q: Four people have tried to delete it.**

Five. One withdrew before the review, which is why it is not in the
history, and that one was me. I opened the PR, looked at the diff, and
could not construct a sentence in the description field that I was willing
to have archived.

That is the mechanism. It is not that people love the document. It is that
removing it requires saying why, in writing, under your name, and the
sentence sounds worse than the file does.

**Q: Is that a good reason for something to survive?**

No. It is exactly the mechanism that kept the lights broken on floor 3 for
eleven weeks. The same social force that protects this file suppresses the
tickets. I am not comfortable with it and I have not resolved it.

**Q: What would you change?**

I would delete the anthology. The verse is weak and it was where the
project started performing rather than documenting.

**Q: What are you proudest of?**

The line about slack not being waste. It is four words long, it is true of
every system I have ever worked on, and I have watched two people quote it
in design reviews without knowing where it came from.

**Q: Will you keep maintaining it?**

Until the queue is fixed or I leave. Whichever is first. It will be the
second one.

### A.7 Satisfaction survey

Anonymous, n = 143, single question, five point scale: "The facilities in
this building meet my needs."

| Response          | Count | Share |
|-------------------|-------|-------|
| Strongly agree    | 6     | 4.2%  |

Net: 50.4 percent negative against 21.0 percent positive.

The free text field received 89 responses. The word "queue" appears 51
