This is the evidence behind RFC 0035 section 35.7. A postmortem with six
action items is a postmortem with no action items and a longer document.

### C.1 Incidents not indexed

Three incidents are referenced elsewhere in this document and do not appear
in the index.

One is sealed. One involves a named individual and is therefore out of
scope per RFC 0028 section 28.2. One was never written up, because writing
it up would have required the person who caused it to describe it, and that
person was the only witness.

The third case is the interesting one. It is not in the index, it is not in
the ticket queue, and the only evidence it happened is a maintenance
invoice with a line item nobody has ever queried.

Your incident history is the subset of your incidents that somebody was
willing to write down. Every organisation's postmortem archive has this
shape and every organisation treats it as complete.

## RFC 0039: Roadmap

### 39.1 Status

There is no roadmap.

### 39.2 Why there is no roadmap

The system reached feature completeness in the Cambrian, per the changelog
entry for v0.1.0. Every subsequent release in the changelog is either an
interface improvement, an infrastructure improvement, or a regression that
was reverted within a day.

The protocol has not changed and will not change. The proposals that
arrive are, without exception, proposals to change the interface, and the
interface converged in the 1880s and has resisted improvement since.

### 39.3 Proposals received and rejected

**Gamification.** A leaderboard. Rejected on privacy grounds, on dignity
grounds, and on the grounds that the proposer had not read RFC 0009
section 9.5, which is the same proposal with worse framing and a real
incident attached.

**A mobile app.** For what.

**Machine learning.** A model predicting peak occupancy from historical
data. Rejected because peak occupancy is at 13:30, this is known, it is
written in Appendix A, and no model is required to read a table. The
proposal was for a two quarter project.

**Blockchain.** Received twice, in different years, from different people,
both sincere. No.

**A Slack integration.** A bot posting current availability to a channel.
This is the dashboard from RFC 0023 section 23.5 with a worse interface, a
retention problem, and a permanent searchable log of who asked when.

**Dynamic pricing.** Received once. The proposer was serious. The
discussion that followed is the only time this document's maintainer has
used the word "no" as a complete review.

### 39.4 The one accepted proposal

The aggregate occupancy display. One integer, no history, no identifiers,
90 currency units in parts, an estimated 60 percent reduction in reneging,
and the highest return on investment of any project in the building.

It was proposed by somebody who had read the incident that produced ADR
005 and designed within the constraint rather than around it, which is why
it shipped and why the five proposals above did not.

### 39.5 What is actually needed

Six more stalls. It is in RFC 0034. It has been in RFC 0034 for three
years. It is not a roadmap item because it is not a technology problem and
this document has no budget authority, which is the summary of RFC 0037
and, on a bad day, the summary of this entire file.

## RFC 0040: Retrospective

Conducted at the four year mark. Attendance: three people, voluntarily, at
lunch, off site, which is where every honest retrospective in the history
of this company has been held.

### 40.1 What went well

**The arithmetic held.** Every quantitative claim made in year one has
survived four years of measurement. The queueing analysis predicted the
peak, the amplification factor, the effect of staggered lunch, and the
outcome of the paper supplier change, in advance, correctly.

**The register held.** Four years, forty odd sections, multiple
contributors, and the document has never once broken character or
explained a joke. Two PRs were rejected on tonal grounds and both authors
resubmitted better versions.

**The dashboard shipped.** One concrete improvement to the physical world
came out of this document, and it works, and it cost ninety units.

**Nobody was hurt.** No section names a colleague. No section is unkind.
The accessibility section has no jokes in it and never did.

### 40.2 What went badly

**Nothing structural changed.** Six stalls are still not built. The peak
is still at 13:30. The queue is still nine deep on a bad Thursday. Four
years of correct analysis produced one integer on a wall.

**The action items.** Forty eight percent completion. The single most
important one, validation at ingest, has been open since the first
incident and will be open when this document is deleted.

**The audience.** The document is read by people who already agree with
it. The people who could fund six stalls have never seen it and could not
be shown it, because the delivery mechanism is a joke in a comment block
and the joke is the reason it exists and also the reason it cannot travel.

That is the central failure and it was designed in from the first section.

### 40.3 What we would do differently

Extract the queueing analysis into a document with no jokes in it and put
that in front of finance. This was proposed in year two. It was not done,
because the version with no jokes in it is four pages of arithmetic about
bathrooms and nobody would attach their name to it.

The joke is what makes it writable and what makes it unpresentable. There
is no version of this document that is both.

### 40.4 Actions

One action item, per section 35.7:

Extract section 34 into a standalone memo, unsigned, and leave it in the
facilities channel.

Owner: unassigned. Status: open.

## RFC 0041: The Zero Gravity Deployment

### 41.1 Why this section exists

Every assumption in this document rests on gravity. Ingest is gravity fed.
Egress is gravity fed. The trap in RFC 0031 section 31.5 is a column of
water held in place by gravity. The entire architecture is a gravity
dependent design that has never once declared the dependency.

Remove gravity and every component fails simultaneously.

### 41.2 The problem statement

In free fall there is no separation between phases. Nothing falls away from
anything. Liquid adheres to surfaces in whatever shape surface tension
dictates. Solids remain where they are produced, in contact with the
producer, indefinitely.

There is no drain because there is no down. There is no flush because water
does not go anywhere. There is no trap because a trap is a shape that holds
water against gravity and gravity is the thing that is missing.

This is a total architectural rewrite, forced by the removal of a single
environmental assumption that nobody documented because nobody imagined it
could be absent.

### 41.3 The solution

Airflow replaces gravity. A fan draws air through the seat and into the
system, and the air carries the payload where gravity would have.

This is the entire design. Everything else is packaging.

Consequences:

- The seal between operator and interface becomes load bearing. On Earth a
  poor seal is a comfort issue. Here it is a containment failure, and
  containment failure in a sealed volume with recirculated air is the
  worst failure mode in this document by a wide margin.
- The fan must run continuously during the session. Fan failure mid
  session is an emergency and there is a checklist for it.
- Airflow must be filtered before return, because the air goes back into
  the cabin, because there is nowhere else for it to go.

### 41.4 Separation

Liquid and solid are separated at source rather than downstream, because
downstream does not exist. Liquid is collected by a funnel with individual
attachments per crew member, processed, and recovered as drinking water at
a recovery rate above 90 percent.

Solid is collected in a bag, compacted, and stored. On the ISS it is
loaded into a departing cargo vehicle which burns up on reentry.

The station therefore drinks its own recovered urine and incinerates the
remainder in the upper atmosphere, which are the two most extreme answers
to the questions "where does it go" and "what is it worth" that anyone has
ever implemented.

### 41.5 The training rig

Crew train on a positioning trainer: the same interface, with a camera
inside, and a screen showing the operator their own alignment.

The opening is approximately 10 cm across. Alignment tolerance is a few
centimetres and a miss is a containment failure in a shared sealed volume
with people in it who cannot leave.

So the training is instrumented, with visual feedback, on a rig, with a
camera, and every astronaut does it, and it is the least discussed item in
the entire training programme.

Engineering reading: when the failure cost is high enough, the
embarrassment stops being a reason not to instrument. Section 19.1 says
that an organisation's capacity to fix a problem is bounded by its
willingness to name it. NASA's willingness is bounded by a sealed volume,
and so they named it, built a rig, and pointed a camera at it.

The office cannot get the lights fixed for eleven weeks.

### 41.6 Failure history

The ISS toilet has failed. Repairs have been performed in orbit, by crew,
on a system carrying the load of the entire station, with the alternative
being a contingency arrangement nobody wants to use.

The 2008 failure on the Russian segment ran for weeks on a workaround
while a replacement part was launched. The part was flown on a Shuttle
mission. There is a cargo manifest, in the public record, listing a
toilet pump as flight critical.

Every engineer who has ever been paged for a system nobody respects should
read that manifest.

### 41.7 Apollo

Before the airflow design there was a bag with an adhesive flange, applied
manually, used in a shared cabin with no privacy of any kind and no
separation between the crew.

The transcripts are public. There is a passage in the Apollo 10 air to
ground loop concerning an object observed floating in the cabin, and the
subsequent discussion between three astronauts and mission control
regarding its provenance, and it is a matter of permanent public record in
the archive of the most technically accomplished programme in human
history.

The lesson is not that it is funny, although it is. The lesson is that a
requirement dismissed as beneath consideration will surface at the worst
possible moment in the most consequential system you have, and it will be
recorded, and it will be read for as long as the archive exists.

### 41.8 Lunar and Martian deployments

Long duration surface missions cannot store and cannot incinerate. The
material must be processed locally, and local processing means either
biological treatment, which needs a functioning ecosystem, or chemical
treatment, which needs power.

There is an active research programme on using the material as radiation
shielding, as feedstock for construction, and as substrate for growing
food, all of which are the termite mound from RFC 0014 section 14.8
rediscovered by people with a much larger budget and the same conclusion.

Waste is unbuilt product. The termites knew. The mound is still standing.

### 41.9 Summary

| Constraint          | Earth        | Orbit                 |
|---------------------|--------------|-----------------------|
| Transport mechanism | Gravity      | Airflow               |
| Separation          | Downstream   | At source             |
| Water use           | 6 L          | 0 L                   |
| Liquid recovery     | Municipal    | 90%+ on board         |
| Solid disposal      | Sewer        | Stored, then burned   |
| Seal requirement    | Comfort      | Life safety           |
| Training            | None         | Instrumented, camera  |
| Failure severity    | SEV2         | Station critical      |
| Privacy             | Absolute     | A curtain             |

Every row in the right hand column is the result of removing one
undocumented environmental assumption from the left hand column.

Audit your assumptions. The one that will destroy you is the one so
obvious that it never made it into the document.

## RFC 0042: Physics

### 42.1 Scope

The mechanical behaviour of the system. Included because several failure
modes catalogued in RFC 0033 are consequences of physics that the operator
can influence and generally does not.

### 42.2 Impact dynamics

A falling body entering a liquid surface displaces liquid. The displaced
liquid forms a crown, the crown collapses, and the collapse produces a jet
which produces droplets.

Droplet velocity scales with impact velocity, and impact velocity scales
with the square root of drop height. Halving the effective drop height
reduces impact velocity by 29 percent and droplet energy by half.

This is the entire physics of the failure mode everybody has experienced
and nobody discusses. It is governed by one variable and the variable is
under the operator's control.

### 42.3 Mitigations, ranked

**1. Reduce drop height.** The dominant term. Nothing else in this section
comes close.

**2. Break the surface.** A layer of paper on the surface before the
session absorbs impact energy and suppresses crown formation almost
entirely. It is the single most effective known mitigation, it costs three
units, and it is passed between people as folklore rather than appearing
in any documentation anywhere. It is in this one now.

**3. Angle of entry.** Oblique entry produces a directional splash rather
than a radial crown. This trades a symmetric low energy failure for an
asymmetric higher energy one and is not recommended.

**4. Surface tension modification.** Detergent reduces surface tension and
suppresses jet formation. Effective, and impractical as a routine.

### 42.4 The plume

Flushing aerosolises a fraction of the contents. The plume rises, disperses
through the room, and settles on every horizontal surface within roughly
two metres.

Measured particle counts remain elevated for over a minute after actuation.
Particles are detectable at 1.5 m above the fixture.

The mitigation is a closed lid, which reduces the plume by roughly 80
percent and takes half a second.

The lid is present on essentially every domestic fixture and absent on
essentially every commercial one, because commercial procurement optimises
for cleaning cost and a lid is a surface to clean. The commercial decision
is defensible on its own terms and is made by somebody who has never seen
the particle count data, which nobody has ever put in front of them, and
which is the same structural failure as every other failure in this
document.

### 42.5 Fluid dynamics of the flush

A gravity flush works by siphon. Water enters the bowl fast enough to fill
the trap completely, which starts a siphon, and the siphon empties the
bowl to below the trap weir, at which point air breaks the siphon with the
sound everybody recognises as the end of the cycle.

Two failure modes follow directly:

- **Insufficient rate.** Water enters too slowly, the trap never fills
  completely, no siphon starts, and the bowl drains slowly without
  clearing. This is the symptom of a partially blocked inlet and it is
  routinely misdiagnosed as a blocked outlet, which is the opposite end of
  the system.
- **Insufficient volume.** The siphon starts and breaks early. Partial
  clearance. This is what a low volume retrofit on a fixture designed for
  higher volume produces, and it is why some water saving conversions
  require two flushes and save nothing.

The 6 litre standard is not arbitrary. It is the volume at which a
correctly designed bowl reliably establishes and sustains a siphon. Below
it requires a redesigned bowl, not a smaller cistern, and the market has
spent thirty years learning this the expensive way.

### 42.6 Write amplification

Cleanup effort scales superlinearly with velocity, per the glossary. The
mechanism is section 42.2: droplet count rises with impact energy, droplet
dispersal radius rises with droplet velocity, and cleanup area scales with
the square of the radius.

Doubling velocity therefore roughly quadruples the affected area. The
physics has never been negotiable and no engineering intervention has ever
improved it.

Control the velocity. It is the only variable you have.

### 42.7 Thermal

Ceramic has high thermal mass and conducts well enough to feel cold. A
seat at 18 C removes heat quickly and the operator's session is measurably
shorter as a result.

The heated seat is therefore not a luxury feature. It is a deliberate
extension of session duration, and it is why the environments that have it
report higher satisfaction and worse throughput. It is the `reading`
option implemented in hardware, and the same tradeoff applies.

### 42.8 Acoustics

The room is small, hard surfaced and reverberant. Reverberation time is
typically 0.8 to 1.4 seconds, which is concert hall territory in a space of
four square metres, and it is why the acoustic side channel in RFC 0006 is
as strong as it is.

Soft furnishing would fix it and is prohibited on hygiene grounds. A
ventilation fan raises the noise floor and is the accepted mitigation. The
Japanese sound generator raises it selectively and is better.

Nobody has ever specified reverberation time in a bathroom tender.

## RFC 0043: The Processing Layer

### 43.1 Scope

What happens between ingest and egress. Included for completeness and
because the component is routinely described as a black box in this
document when in fact it is the most studied part of the system.

### 43.2 Composition

Roughly 100 trillion microorganisms, several thousand species, with a
composition that is individual, stable over years, and different from every
other person's.

By mass the output is approximately 75 percent water. Of the dry remainder,
roughly a third is bacterial biomass, a third is undigested fibre, and a
third is everything else including shed intestinal cells, fats and
inorganic material.

A meaningful fraction of the output is therefore the processing layer
itself, continuously shed and continuously replaced. The system's exhaust
includes its own workers.

### 43.3 Transit

Total transit time is typically 24 to 72 hours. The colon is not a pipe. It
is a fermentation vessel with active mixing, selective absorption and
retrograde motion, and material moves backwards as often as forwards until
it does not.

This is why the four hour delay in the Curry Incident is a floor rather
than a typical figure, and why dietary interventions take two weeks to
evaluate rather than two days. The feedback loop is genuinely that long.

### 43.4 The fermentation product

Gut bacteria ferment fibre and produce short chain fatty acids, chiefly
butyrate, which is the primary energy source for the cells lining the
colon.

The colon does not primarily feed itself from the bloodstream. It feeds on
the output of the bacteria it hosts, which feed on the material the host
cannot digest.

The host eats what it can. The bacteria eat what the host cannot. The
colon eats what the bacteria produce. This is a three tier system in which
each tier's waste is the next tier's input, running continuously, in
everyone reading this, and it is the clearest example available anywhere of
the principle stated in RFC 0014 section 14.5.

This is also why fibre is the highest leverage parameter in RFC 0024. It
is not bulk. It is feedstock.

### 43.5 Gas

Approximately 0.5 to 1.5 litres per day, produced by fermentation, mostly
nitrogen, hydrogen, carbon dioxide and methane, none of which have an
odour.

The odour is produced by sulphur compounds present at concentrations
measured in parts per million. The detection threshold for hydrogen
sulphide is around 0.5 parts per billion, which is roughly a thousand times
more sensitive than the concentration present.

The signal to noise ratio on the olfactory channel is therefore
extraordinary, which is exactly what RFC 0023 section 23.1 claimed and
declined to substantiate. It is substantiated here.

### 43.6 Colour and what it indicates

Bile is green when secreted and browns as it is processed in transit.
Colour is therefore a transit time indicator.

- Brown: nominal.
- Green: fast transit, bile not fully processed, or dietary.
- Pale or clay: bile not reaching the system. Escalate.
- Black: upper system bleeding, or iron supplementation, or bismuth.
  Escalate unless you know which.
- Red: lower system bleeding, or beetroot. Escalate unless you are certain.

Two of those five require a professional and three of them have benign
explanations that people reach for first. RFC 0024 section 24.4 applies.

### 43.7 Individuality

Microbiome composition is individual enough to function as an identifier.
Studies have re identified individuals from their microbiome across
intervals of months.

This is a biometric that every person continuously sheds, in volume, into
a shared municipal system, with no consent framework, no retention policy
and no deletion mechanism.

Nobody is currently collecting it at scale. The relevant sentence in RFC
0029 section 29.3 was about badge readers. It applies here with
considerably more force, and this document notes the fact and declines to
elaborate on it.

## RFC 0044: Distributed Systems

### 44.1 The building as a distributed system

Three floors, eleven stalls, two hundred clients, no coordinator, no
consensus protocol and no shared clock.

Every property that makes distributed systems hard is present. Every
solution the literature offers is unavailable, because the nodes are people
and people will not run your protocol.

### 44.2 CAP

Consistency, availability, partition tolerance. Choose two.

The building chooses availability and partition tolerance. Each floor
operates independently. A client on floor 3 has no consistent view of
floor 5's state, acts on stale information, and frequently walks two
flights to discover a condition that changed while they were on the stairs.

The occupancy display is a consistency improvement bought at the cost of
building a coordinator, and it is deliberately weakly consistent: a single
integer, updated on a delay, with no per node detail, because a strongly
consistent view would require exactly the per stall data that ADR 005
prohibits.

The privacy constraint forced a weaker consistency model and the weaker
model turned out to be sufficient. This happens more often than anybody
admits.

### 44.3 Consensus

There is no consensus protocol. There is a convention, described in RFC
0015 section 15.2, maintained entirely by social pressure, unwritten until
this document wrote it down, and honoured by essentially everybody.

It is a Byzantine fault tolerant protocol with no messages, no rounds and
no leader, and it works because defection is punished by a mechanism
stronger than any technical control available: the defector has to keep
working with everyone else.

Reputation solves coordination problems that consensus algorithms cannot.
This is true in buildings and it is true in open source, and it is why the
maintainer of a package with no tests is more reliable than a contract
with penalties.

### 44.4 Leader election

None. Any client may act at any time. The system has no leader and needs
none, because the resource enforces mutual exclusion locally through the
lock in ADR 006.

This is the correct design. A leader would be a queue manager, a queue
manager would need to observe the queue, and observing the queue is the
surveillance problem from RFC 0009 section 9.5.

Distributed mutual exclusion via local locks, with no coordinator, is
strictly better here than any centralised alternative, and the reason is
privacy rather than performance.

### 44.5 The thundering herd

Two hundred clients released simultaneously by an external event with no
jitter. See amplification factor. See RFC 0034.

Every mitigation the literature offers applies directly: add jitter,
stagger the release, increase capacity, or shed load. The building has
implemented none of them, trialled one, and reverted it because people
like eating together.

The load shedding option, in this domain, means telling people they may not
go. It has never been proposed. It is the only option that would work
without spending money and it is unspeakable, which is a complete
description of the constraint space this document operates in.

### 44.6 Backpressure

The system has none, at any layer. Ingest accepts what it is given.
Processing accepts what ingest produces. Egress accepts what processing
delivers.

The only backpressure signal in the entire architecture is urgency, and it
is a signal from the middle of the pipeline to a component that has
already finished its work and cannot act on it.

Backpressure that arrives after the decision is not backpressure. It is
notification. Every queue you have ever built with an unbounded input has
this shape.

### 44.7 Idempotency and retries

Sessions are not idempotent, per RFC 0003 section 3.5. Retries are
therefore not safe in the general case and the client library's retry logic
applies only to connection establishment, never to transfer.

Retrying a connection is safe. Retrying a transfer is a category error that
the type system prevents and that users request support for approximately
twice a year.

### 44.8 The circuit breaker

The biological circuit breaker is the best implemented component in the
system: it opens under load, it holds, it degrades gracefully as pressure
rises, and it fails closed rather than open.

Half open state exists and is well calibrated. The system permits a small
trial release to assess conditions before committing, which is the canary
deployment from the glossary, and it is implemented in hardware, and it
works, and nobody has ever written it down before.

### 44.9 Split brain

Two clients, two floors, one believing floor 3 has capacity and one
believing floor 5 does, both acting on stale reads, arriving simultaneously
at the same stall from opposite stairwells.

Resolution is by a social protocol with no formal specification and a wide
variance in outcome quality. There is no tiebreaker rule. There is only
politeness, and politeness is not a consistency model.

### 44.10 Summary

| Distributed systems problem | Solution here          | Works? |
|-----------------------------|------------------------|--------|
| Mutual exclusion            | Local lock             | Yes    |
| Consensus                   | Social convention      | Yes    |
| Leader election             | None needed            | Yes    |
| Consistency                 | Weak, one integer      | Mostly |
| Thundering herd             | None implemented       | No     |
| Backpressure                | None exists            | No     |
| Split brain                 | Politeness             | Sometimes |
| Circuit breaking            | Biological, excellent  | Yes    |

The problems solved well are the ones solved locally, without a
coordinator, by a mechanism the participants understand. The problems
solved badly are the ones requiring somebody to act on behalf of the whole
system, and there is nobody, per RFC 0037.

## RFC 0045: Game Theory

### 45.1 The paper replacement game

The last person to use the last of the paper faces a choice: replace it, at
a personal cost of thirty seconds, or leave, at a personal cost of zero and
a cost to the next user that is substantial.

The dominant strategy is to leave. The socially optimal strategy is to
replace. This is a straightforward defection game and the building plays it
several times a day.

Observed defection rate is roughly 40 percent, which is far below what the
payoff matrix predicts and is explained entirely by the fact that the game
is iterated and the players share a lift.

### 45.2 The last unit problem

A subtler version. The stock is not zero but is low. Replacing it now is
easy. Leaving it is defensible, because there is still some.

Nobody replaces at 20 percent. Everybody agrees somebody should. The
threshold at which action becomes obligatory is undefined, and an
undefined threshold is where every diffusion of responsibility problem
lives.

The fix is to define the threshold. Facilities defines it for stock rooms
and nobody has ever defined it for a stall, which is why the failure
recurs weekly in a building with an eight week supply on site.

### 45.3 The adjacency game

Given a choice of stalls, the optimal individual strategy is to maximise
distance from occupied stalls. Given that everybody plays this strategy,
the equilibrium is an alternating pattern that wastes 50 percent of
capacity at moderate load.

At high load the equilibrium breaks and everybody accepts adjacency,
abruptly, at a threshold nobody has ever articulated but everybody
recognises.

This is a phase transition in a social protocol and it is the most elegant
thing in this document that nobody designed.

### 45.4 The queue position game

A client arriving at a full facility may wait inside the room or outside.
Waiting inside gives a positional advantage: they will hear the lock first.

Waiting inside also converts the queue into an audience, which imposes a
cost on the person currently in service.

The convention prohibits waiting inside. It is unenforceable, it is
honoured by most people, and it is honoured most reliably by people who
have been on the other side of it.

Experience of the externality produces compliance where rules do not. This
is the entire theory of change behind every incident review this document
has ever recommended.

### 45.5 The disclosure game

An operator who has caused a condition requiring attention may report it,
at a cost of embarrassment, or leave, at a cost of zero and a cost to the
next user.

The reporting rate is approximately four percent, per RFC 0037 section
37.4.

This is the same game as section 45.1 with the embarrassment term added,
and the difference between a 40 percent defection rate and a 96 percent
defection rate is the entire quantitative measure of what embarrassment
costs a system.

Ninety six versus forty. That is the number. Every organisation that
wonders why its incident reports are thin should write it on a wall.

## RFC 0046: The Actual Problem

### 46.1 Scale

Roughly 3.5 billion people lack safely managed sanitation. Roughly 400
million practise open defecation.

Diarrhoeal disease, overwhelmingly a sanitation and water problem, kills
several hundred thousand children under five every year. Every one of those
deaths is preventable with technology that was working in Mohenjo daro four
and a half thousand years ago.

### 46.2 Why it is not solved

Not technology. The engineering was finished before germ theory. A pit, a
slab, a vent pipe and a lid is a functioning solution costing tens of
currency units and it works.

The constraints are:

**Capital and operating cost at municipal scale.** A sewer network is one
of the most expensive pieces of infrastructure a city can build, it must be
built before the demand it serves is visible, and it produces no revenue.
Bazalgette's network required a legislature that could smell the river.

**Land tenure.** People without secure tenure do not build permanent
sanitation, because they may not be there. This is a legal problem wearing
an infrastructure costume.

**Water.** Flush based systems consume water at a rate unavailable in many
of the places that need sanitation most. The Western default is the wrong
architecture for a water scarce deployment and exporting it is a category
error that has been made repeatedly and expensively.

**Maintenance.** Pit latrines fill. A facility with no emptying service is
a facility with a lifespan. Enormous numbers of installations built by
well meaning programmes were built with no operating model and are now
full, abandoned, and counted in nobody's statistics.

**Dignity and use.** A facility that is unsafe to reach at night, or that
lacks privacy, or that is shared in a way a woman will not use during
menstruation, is a facility with a much lower effective availability than
the count of installations suggests. Installations are counted. Use is not.

### 46.3 The counting problem

Programmes report facilities built. Facilities built is the easiest metric
to collect and the least correlated with outcome.

The metric that matters is safe use, sustained, over years, which requires
survey work, longitudinal data and honest reporting of failures, all of
which are expensive and none of which produce a good slide.

RFC 0023 section 23.6 said what gets measured is what is easy to measure
and safe to discuss. Here that observation has a body count.

### 46.4 What works

Community led approaches that generate demand before supply outperform
installation programmes consistently. A facility somebody wanted is
maintained. A facility somebody was given is not.

Sanitation marketing, local supply chains for parts, and emptying services
run as businesses outperform donated infrastructure, because they have an
operating model and donated infrastructure has an opening ceremony.

Container based sanitation, where a sealed container is collected on a
schedule and treated centrally, works in dense informal settlements where
neither a pit nor a sewer is possible, and it is unglamorous, and it is one
of the more promising things in the field.

### 46.5 The pit emptying problem

Somebody has to empty the pits. In much of the world this is done manually,
by hand, by people in the lowest social position available, without
protective equipment, at direct risk to their lives.

Mechanised emptying exists, costs money, and requires access roads that
informal settlements do not have. Small vehicle solutions designed for
narrow lanes exist and are underfunded.

This is the part of the sector that receives the least attention and
carries the most human cost. It is invisible for exactly the reasons this
whole document has been describing: it is unmentionable, it is done by
people with no power, and nobody wants it on a slide.

### 46.6 Why this section is in a joke document

Because the joke is the delivery mechanism, and this is the payload.

Every reader who reached section 46 arrived through forty five sections
about queueing theory and wombats. Nobody arrives at a document titled
"Global Sanitation Access" voluntarily. The engagement numbers on that
document are zero and the engagement numbers on this one are, apparently,
whatever brought you here.

RFC 0040 section 40.3 identified the central failure of this document: the
joke makes it writable and unpresentable, and there is no version that is
both. That is true of the queueing memo and finance.

It is not true here. Here, the joke is the only reason the section gets
read at all, and the section is the only part of this entire file that is
about something that kills people.

Sanitation is the single largest contributor to human life expectancy in
the modern era. It is not on anybody's slide. This is the one place the
maintainer of this file has been able to write that sentence and have it
land in front of an engineer.

## RFC 0047: Bibliography

An informal reading list. Nothing here is cited in the text because the
text is a comment in a README, but everything in the text came from
somewhere.

### 47.1 On queueing

The standard treatment of M/M/c and the behaviour of wait time as
utilisation approaches unity appears in any operations research text.
Little's Law is a page. The 80 percent rule, the divergence, and the
correct response to correlated arrivals are the three ideas worth taking
and they fit on a card.

Recommended: any introductory operations research textbook, read only as
far as the chapter on queues, which is chapter three in most of them and
is the only chapter most engineers need.

### 47.2 On sanitation history

The Broad Street pump, the Great Stink, and Bazalgette's network are
covered in the standard popular histories of Victorian London, and the
primary sources are accessible. The parliamentary record around the 1858
funding decision is public and reads exactly as this document describes it.

The Indus Valley drainage is archaeological and the interpretations vary,
but the brick lined covered drains are physically present and datable.

### 47.3 On the microbiome

Fast moving field with a large gap between what is established and what is
claimed. Established: composition is individual and stable, short chain
fatty acids feed the colonic epithelium, fibre is the substrate. Claimed,
frequently, on thin evidence: nearly everything else.

Treat any claim connecting gut bacteria to mood, personality or disease
causation as provisional regardless of how confidently it is stated.

### 47.4 On global sanitation

The WHO and UNICEF joint monitoring programme publishes the figures used
in RFC 0046. The service ladder framework, distinguishing open
defecation, unimproved, limited, basic and safely managed, is worth
understanding because it is the reason headline numbers differ so widely
between sources.

The manual pit emptying literature is thin and mostly grey. That is itself
a finding.

### 47.5 On spaceflight sanitation

Primary sources are excellent. NASA publishes design documents, the
training materials are described in crew memoirs, and the Apollo
transcripts are public and searchable.

The waste collection system sections of the Apollo mission reports are
written in the most rigorously neutral technical prose ever produced by
human beings and are, for that exact reason, extremely funny.

### 47.6 On the register

Nothing. There is no literature on how to write this. RFC 0016 was derived
empirically, over four years, mostly from rejected pull requests.

## RFC 0048: Naming

### 48.1 The naming problem

There is no neutral word. Every term available is either clinical, crude,
childish or evasive, and choosing between them is a register decision that
the speaker cannot avoid making and cannot make correctly.

This is the only subject in ordinary life with no unmarked vocabulary. You
cannot say the thing plainly. There is no plain.

### 48.2 The register ladder

| Register   | Example        | Usable with            |
|------------|----------------|------------------------|
| Clinical   | defecation     | Doctors, this document |
| Formal     | bowel movement | Doctors, reluctantly   |
| Neutral    | (none exists)  | n/a                    |
| Euphemism  | going          | Everyone, vaguely      |
| Childish   | various        | Children               |
| Crude      | various        | Friends, sometimes     |
| Metaphor   | various        | Nobody, ever           |

The gap at the neutral row is the entire problem. Every conversation about
this subject must be conducted in a register that signals something about
the speaker, because there is no register that signals nothing.

### 48.3 The room

The room itself has more names than any other room in a building, and they
are all evasions:

Bathroom, in a room with no bath. Restroom, where nobody rests. Washroom,
which is closer. Lavatory, from the Latin for washing, same evasion.
Toilet, from the French for a small cloth, originally the process of
dressing, drifted to the furniture and then to the room. Loo, contested
etymology, possibly from *gardyloo*, the warning shouted before emptying a
chamber pot from an Edinburgh window. Water closet, the only honest term
in the list, now archaic everywhere except plumbing schedules and the
letters WC.

Every one of these is a word for something else, borrowed to avoid the
word for the thing. The pattern is called a euphemism treadmill: each term
becomes tainted by what it refers to, and a new evasion is recruited, and
the cycle has run for centuries and is still running.

### 48.4 The treadmill

Toilet was itself the polite word. It replaced privy, which replaced
jakes, which replaced words this document will not list. Toilet has now
become slightly impolite in American English, replaced by bathroom, which
will in time become impolite, and be replaced.

You cannot fix this with vocabulary. The taint attaches to the referent,
not the word, and travels to whatever word you appoint next. Renaming a
thing does not change how people feel about the thing. Every rebranding
exercise in the history of commerce is this, and most of them fail for this
reason.

### 48.5 In code

Identifier naming in the client SDK was a genuine problem. The options
were clinical, which is unreadable, or euphemistic, which is imprecise, or
crude, which is unmergeable.

The resolution was to name every identifier after its systems function
rather than its referent: `transfer`, `flush`, `preflight`, `urgency`,
`ClogError`. Nothing in the public API names the subject at all.

The result reads as a perfectly ordinary networking library, which is the
joke, and which is also genuinely better naming than the alternatives,
because the identifiers describe what the code does rather than what it is
about. That is the correct principle in every codebase and it was arrived
at here for entirely the wrong reasons.

### 48.6 The one crude word

Appears once, in the title of RFC 0002, where it functions as the premise
rather than as a joke, per RFC 0016 section 16.3.

Two contributors have attempted to add a second instance. Both PRs were
rejected. The second author argued, correctly, that the rule is arbitrary.
The rule is arbitrary. It is also the reason the document has a register
at all, and an arbitrary rule consistently applied is worth more than a
principled rule applied by judgement.

## RFC 0049: Onboarding a New Node

### 49.1 Scope

Provisioning a human. Eighteen months to four years, highly variable, no
rollback, and the most consequential deployment most people will ever
perform.

### 49.2 Readiness signals

Deployment cannot be scheduled by the operator. The node signals readiness
and the signals are:

- Sustained dry intervals, indicating buffer capacity has developed.
- Awareness of the internal state before the event rather than after.
- Physical capability: walking, sitting, managing clothing.
- Interest in the interface.
- Capacity to follow a two step instruction.

Attempting deployment before these signals appear produces a longer
process, not a shorter one. Every published dataset agrees and every
generation of parents attempts it early anyway, because the peer group is
a stronger signal than the evidence.

### 49.3 The regression

Regression is normal, expected, and universal. A node that has been stable
for months will regress on a new sibling, a house move, an illness, or
starting school.

Regression is not a failure of the deployment. It is the node shedding a
recently acquired capability under load, which is exactly what every
system does, and the correct response is to reduce load rather than to
increase pressure on the capability.

This is written in every parenting book and is understood by essentially
nobody in the moment, including the maintainer of this document.

### 49.4 Failure modes

**Escalation.** The operator applies pressure. The node associates the
process with conflict. The process becomes a negotiation the node can win,
because the node holds the only lever that matters and will discover this
within days.

Never make it a contest. You will lose, and losing costs months.

**Premature declaration.** Success declared, equipment removed, regression
follows, and the reversal is more damaging than the delay would have been.

**Environmental mismatch.** The node is provisioned for one environment and
fails in another: nursery, grandparents, public facilities. Deployment is
per environment and each environment needs its own commissioning.

**The public facility problem.** Loud, unfamiliar, automatic flush systems
that actuate unpredictably while the node is in place. A single such event
can set the process back weeks and no adult present has ever anticipated
it.

Sensor flush systems are calibrated for adults. Nobody tested them with
small children and the failure mode is a child who will not use a public
facility for a month.

### 49.5 Timeline

| Age        | Typical state                                    |
|------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| 18 months  | Signals appearing in some nodes                  |
| 2 years    | Deployment commonly attempted                    |
| 2.5 years  | Daytime stability in many nodes                  |
| 3 years    | Daytime stability in most nodes                  |
| 4 years    | Night time stability in most nodes               |
| 5 years    | Night time stability considered typical          |
| 7 years    | Night time variance still within normal range    |

The variance is enormous and almost entirely uncorrelated with anything the
operator did. The spread between an early node and a late node is years,
both are normal, and the discourse around it causes more harm than the
variance does.

### 49.6 The comparison problem

Operators compare nodes. The comparison is meaningless, the variance is
constitutional, and the confidence with which advice is delivered by
operators of early nodes is inversely proportional to its value.

An operator whose node completed at two years believes they have a method.
They have a node. This is survivorship bias operating in a domain where
the sample size per operator is one or two, and it is the single most
reliable source of bad advice in the entire subject.

## RFC 0050: Non Human Clients

### 50.1 Scope

Clients sharing the deployment who did not agree to any of this and cannot
read the documentation.

### 50.2 Cat

Self provisioning. Given a substrate, a cat will locate it, use it, and
bury the result without instruction. The behaviour is instinctive and the
success rate on first exposure is close to total.

This is the only client in the entire document that onboards itself. RFC
0049 describes eighteen months of effort to achieve what a cat does in one
afternoon with no supervision.

Failure modes are almost always environmental rather than behavioural: the
substrate is wrong, the location is exposed, the tray is dirty, or another
cat controls the approach. A cat that stops using the tray is reporting a
fault in the facility, not misbehaving, and the fault is usually one of
those four.

Substrate preference is strong and specific. Changing brands is a
migration, requires a transition period, and produces exactly the same
user revolt as changing a paper supplier.

The covered tray is a design that optimises for the operator's experience
at the expense of the user's: it contains odour for the human and
concentrates it for the cat, and it removes the sightlines that a prey
animal requires while occupied. Cats reject them at measurable rates and
the industry sells them anyway, because the purchaser is not the user.

Every enterprise software procurement decision has this exact shape.

### 50.3 Dog

Requires full onboarding, comparable in effort to RFC 0049 and considerably
faster. Four to six months typical.

The mechanism is scheduling rather than instruction: frequent opportunity,
consistent location, immediate reward on success, no punishment on failure.
Punishment after the event teaches concealment rather than compliance,
because the animal cannot connect the punishment to a decision made
minutes earlier.

This is the four hour feedback loop problem from RFC 0009 section 9.1 with
a shorter constant and identical consequences. A delayed signal does not
teach the thing you think it teaches. It teaches something, and what it
teaches is worse.

Collection and disposal by the operator is a legal requirement in most
jurisdictions and a social one everywhere. The compliance rate is a
function of observation, which is the disclosure game from RFC 0045
section 45.5 with the anonymity term inverted.

### 50.4 The urban dog problem

A city with a high dog population and no collection compliance has a
sanitation problem of genuine scale. Enforcement is difficult because the
event is brief, unobserved and untraceable.

One municipality trialled DNA registration of licensed animals and
matching against uncollected samples. It worked, it was extremely
unpopular, and it is the single most invasive control described anywhere
in this document, including RFC 0009 section 9.5.

It also has an interesting property: the control identifies the animal,
which identifies the household, which is a join key on a biological
sample collected without consent from a party who cannot give it. RFC
0043 section 43.7 declined to elaborate on the human version. This is the
version that has actually been deployed.

### 50.5 Livestock

Volume changes the problem category entirely. A dairy herd produces
material at a rate that makes it an industrial waste stream with
regulatory oversight, storage requirements and runoff controls.

Improperly managed, it reaches watercourses, and nutrient loading produces
algal blooms, oxygen depletion and fish kills. This is the hippo mechanism
from RFC 0014 section 14.5 operating at the wrong concentration: the same
material that supports a river system in one dose destroys it in another.

Properly managed, it is fertiliser and feedstock for anaerobic digestion,
which produces methane, which produces electricity. Several farms run
entirely on it.

Waste is unbuilt product, again, for the third time in this document, and
the difference between a pollutant and a fuel is a capital investment and
somebody willing to make it.

### 50.6 The shared household deployment

A household with animals runs a multi tenant deployment with clients who
have different interfaces, different substrates, different schedules and no
shared protocol.

Contention is real: the dog requires the operator to be present and
available at intervals that do not align with the operator's schedule, and
the failure mode is borne entirely by the floor.

Nobody has ever modelled this and this document is not going to be the
first, because the maintainer has a dog and knows exactly how the analysis
would end.

## RFC 0051: Diagnostics

### 51.1 The signal

The output is the most information rich diagnostic signal the body
produces without instrumentation, it is available daily, it is free, and it
is looked at by approximately nobody.

This is a monitoring system with perfect coverage, zero cost, daily
granularity, and a four percent read rate. It is section 23.4 again: the
signal does not stop, the listener does.

### 51.2 The classification scale

There is a standard seven point scale, developed at a British university,
used clinically worldwide, describing form from separate hard lumps
through to entirely liquid.

Types 3 and 4 are the target. Types 1 and 2 indicate slow transit. Types 6
and 7 indicate fast transit. Type 5 is borderline.

The scale exists because clinicians needed patients to describe something
patients would not describe, and the solution was a diagram with numbers,
so that the patient could say a number.

That is a superb piece of interface design. It removes the vocabulary
problem from RFC 0048 entirely by replacing language with an index, and it
raised diagnostic quality across an entire field by giving people a way to
report something they were unwilling to say.

If your users will not report a thing, do not ask them to describe it.
Give them a number to point at.

### 51.3 What to watch

- **Sustained change in your own baseline** over more than two weeks.
  Baseline is individual. The comparison that matters is against yourself,
  not against a scale.
- **Blood.** Any. Escalate.
- **Black, tarry output** not explained by iron or bismuth. Escalate.
- **Pale or clay coloured output.** Escalate.
- **Pain.** Escalate.
- **Unexplained weight loss** alongside any change. Escalate.
- **New and persistent urgency or frequency.** Escalate.

### 51.4 Screening

Population screening programmes exist in most developed countries, are
typically offered from age 50 or 45, use a sample collected at home, and
are among the most cost effective interventions in medicine.

Uptake is well below target everywhere. The barrier is not access, cost or
awareness. The barrier is that the test requires the participant to
collect a sample and post it, and the embarrassment of that act outweighs,
for a large fraction of the eligible population, a materially reduced
chance of dying of a preventable cancer.

That sentence is the entire thesis of this document, stated in its most
serious form, with the highest possible stakes.

Section 19.1: an organisation's capacity to fix a problem is bounded by its
willingness to name it. So is a person's. The people who die of this are
not killed by the disease's aggressiveness. They are killed by a two week
delay that turned into a two year delay because the first conversation was
uncomfortable.

### 51.5 The recommendation

Do the screening test when it arrives. Look at the thing before you flush.
If something has changed and stayed changed for two weeks, say so out loud
to a professional, using the number from the scale if the words are hard.

This document is a joke. RFC 0024 section 24.4 already said that sentence
is not. This section says it again, in more detail, because it is the only
part of this file that has ever been worth writing.

## RFC 0052: Marine Deployments

### 52.1 Constraints

A vessel is a sealed environment with finite storage, no municipal
connection, a legal prohibition on discharge within defined distances of
shore, and a client population that cannot leave.

It is the aircraft environment from RFC 0027 section 27.8 with a longer
duration and worse motion.

### 52.2 The holding tank

Storage is finite and the fill rate is a function of crew and duration.
When the tank is full the system is out of service for every client
simultaneously, with no failover, for the remainder of the voyage or until
a pump out facility is reached.

This is the train failure mode with a longer interval to recovery, and it
is the reason experienced crews monitor the tank level as a primary
operational metric rather than as a maintenance detail.

Tank level is one of very few metrics in this document that is measured,
watched, acted on, and universally respected. The reason is that the
consequence of ignoring it is shared, immediate and inescapable.

Metrics get respected when the consequence cannot be externalised. In the
office building the consequence is externalised onto whoever is next, which
is why nothing is watched.

### 52.3 Discharge regulation

International and national regulation prohibits discharge of untreated
material within defined distances of shore, with treated discharge
permitted further out and in some areas prohibited entirely.

Enforcement is by inspection of equipment and by dye testing. Compliance in
practice varies with the probability of inspection, which is the disclosure
game again with a fine attached instead of embarrassment.

Adding a financial penalty to a defection game raises compliance. It does
not raise it as much as making the consequence visible to the defector's
peers, which is the finding from RFC 0045 section 45.4 and is consistently
underused by regulators.

### 52.4 The marine head

Manual pump, seawater intake, macerator, discharge to tank. Every
component is a failure point and the failure modes are all unpleasant.

The universal rule, printed on placards on essentially every vessel afloat,
is that nothing enters the system that has not been consumed first. The
macerator is small, the pipework is narrow, and anything with wet tensile
strength blocks it.

This is the wet wipe problem from RFC 0031 section 31.3 at a scale where
the consequence is immediate, local, and repaired by the person who caused
it. Compliance on vessels is dramatically higher than compliance ashore
for exactly that reason.

Internalise the externality and behaviour changes without any enforcement
at all. It is the only reliable mechanism in this document, stated for the
third time, in a different domain, with the same conclusion.

### 52.5 Motion

The vessel moves in six degrees of freedom. The interface does not. The
operator must maintain position, alignment and balance simultaneously in a
compartment approximately one metre square with hard surfaces on every
side.

Handholds are mandatory in any serious installation and are absent in most
recreational ones, where the compartment was designed at a boat show by
somebody optimising for the impression it makes at a dock.

Designing for the showroom rather than the sea is a failure that recurs in
every product category and it is more obvious here than most, because the
consequence of a poor design at anchor is nothing and the consequence
underway is an injury.

### 52.6 The bucket

Every experienced sailor's contingency plan. Simple, reliable, no moving
parts, no blockage mode, no regulatory ambiguity when used correctly, and
universally derided until the day the macerator fails four hundred miles
from anywhere.

The simplest possible implementation, kept available, in case the
sophisticated one fails, is a pattern with a name in software and no name
at sea, where it is simply what everybody does.

## RFC 0053: Institutional Deployments

### 53.1 Hospital

Highest stakes deployment in this document. Clients are unwell, frequently
immobile, sometimes unable to communicate, and the material is a
transmission vector in a population with compromised immunity.

Requirements that do not appear in any other environment:

- Assisted use as a designed workflow rather than an exception.
- Measurement and recording of output as clinical data.
- Isolation protocols where the material is infectious.
- Disposal systems handling material that cannot enter the normal stream.
- Dignity preservation for clients who have lost the capacity to manage
  the process themselves.

The last requirement is the one that determines whether a hospital is a
good hospital, it is invisible in every quality metric published, and the
staff who do it well are the least paid people in the building.

### 53.2 The clinical record

In a hospital, output is recorded, charted, and reviewed. Frequency, form,
volume and appearance are clinical observations with defined vocabulary
and a standard scale, per RFC 0051 section 51.2.

The same information that is unmentionable everywhere else is, inside a
ward, ordinary data written on a chart by a professional and discussed at
a handover without embarrassment.

The taboo is contextual, not inherent. A profession that needs the
information has simply decided not to have the taboo, and the decision was
sufficient. That is worth knowing: the constraint that governs this entire
document is a norm, and norms can be locally suspended by a group that
decides they are inconvenient.

### 53.3 Prison

Multi tenant, involuntary, no exit, and in shared cells no privacy of any
kind, permanently, for years.

The absence of privacy is not incidental to the punishment. Whether it
should be part of the punishment is a policy question this document is not
equipped for, but the engineering observation is available: a facility
design that removes privacy removes it for the cellmate as well, who is
subject to it as an externality of somebody else's sentence.

Every jurisdiction that has invested in single occupancy with a partition
has reported reductions in violence. The finding is consistent enough to
be worth stating plainly.

### 53.4 School

The deployment with the worst outcomes relative to its cost, anywhere.

Facilities are commonly locked between periods, monitored, unsupervised
when open, inadequately stocked, and unpleasant. Children respond by not
drinking water, not using the facilities all day, and holding.

The physiological consequences of sustained holding in childhood are real
and documented. The behavioural consequence is a population learning, at
the age at which such things are learned permanently, that this need is
shameful and must be suppressed.

Every adult described in this document who would not file a ticket about
the lights on floor 3 learned that in a school toilet.

Fixing school facilities is cheap, has a documented health return, and
would over one generation alter the reporting behaviour that RFC 0037
section 37.4 identifies as the binding constraint on every other problem
in this file.

Nobody will fund it. It has no constituency, the beneficiaries cannot
vote, and the metric would take twenty years to move.

### 53.5 Care homes

Everything in section 53.1 applies with less funding, less staff, less
oversight, and clients who have less capacity to report and less prospect
of leaving.

The quality of a care home is more accurately predicted by its bathrooms
than by anything in its brochure, and every family that has chosen one
knows this, and no inspection regime measures it directly.

## RFC 0054: Disaster Response

### 54.1 The order of operations

In a disaster, the sequence is water, then shelter, then sanitation, then
food, and the third item is the one that is consistently deprioritised and
consistently produces the deaths.

An earthquake or flood destroys the network. The population concentrates.
Water sources become contaminated by material that has nowhere to go.
Cholera and dysentery follow within days, in a population already injured,
displaced and immunocompromised.

The disease does not come from the disaster. It comes from the sanitation
failure that follows the disaster, and it arrives on a predictable schedule
that responders have known for a century.

### 54.2 Provisioning

Emergency standards specify a ratio of facilities to population, a maximum
distance from shelter, separation by gender, lighting, and lockable doors.

The last three exist because a facility that is unsafe to reach at night is
a facility that is not used at night, and a population that will not use a
facility at night will use the ground behind the shelter, and the outbreak
follows.

The specification is not about counting. It is about whether the thing is
usable by the person who needs it at the moment they need it, which is the
distinction that RFC 0046 section 46.3 identified as the difference between
what is counted and what matters.

### 54.3 The first 72 hours

Before any structure can be built, the immediate requirement is
containment: define locations, mark them, keep them away from water, and
prevent the ad hoc distribution that otherwise establishes itself within
hours and is very hard to reverse once habitual.

The intervention that works in the first day is a shovel, some tape, and
somebody with authority pointing at a spot. It costs nothing and it is
routinely omitted because it is nobody's job.

Section 37.2 again. The recurring failure is never technical.

### 54.4 Household preparedness

For a household facing a multi day utility interruption:

- Water off means the fixture still functions if you pour water into the
  bowl. A bucket of any non potable water flushes it. This is the single
  most useful fact in this section and most people do not know it.
- Sewer backup or main break means the fixture must not be used at all,
  and using it produces a contained failure inside your own home.
- The contingency is a lined container, sealed, with an absorbent
  material, stored until collection resumes. Unglamorous, effective, and
  the thing every preparedness list mentions last if at all.
- Hand hygiene without running water requires stored water or alcohol gel.
  This is the control that actually prevents transmission and it is the
  one that runs out first.

### 54.5 The psychological dimension

Populations under stress will not report sanitation problems, will not
discuss them with responders, and will conceal illness because illness
implies a cause and the cause is unmentionable.

Responders are trained to ask directly, in specific terms, because the
information will not be volunteered. The training exists because the
alternative was learned the hard way, repeatedly, in field conditions.

RFC 0037 section 37.4 said the reporting rate is a function of
embarrassment and only instrumentation or anonymity changes it. Disaster
response adds a third mechanism: a professional who asks the question
plainly, first, so that the client does not have to raise it.

That mechanism is available in ordinary life too and essentially nobody
uses it.

## RFC 0055: Field Deployments

### 55.1 Military doctrine

Field sanitation is a command responsibility in every serious army, taught
formally, inspected, and enforced, because the historical record is
unambiguous: disease has killed more soldiers than combat in most conflicts
before the twentieth century, and sanitation failure is the mechanism.

The doctrine is old, well tested, and consists almost entirely of things
that are obvious in retrospect: site downhill and downwind of water and
camp, dig to depth, cover after use, mark the location, close and mark when
full, never site near the kitchen.

It is enforced because armies learned that units do not do it voluntarily,
that the failure is invisible for a week, and that by the time it is
visible a third of the unit is unfit.

### 55.2 The delay again

One week between the sanitation failure and the disease it produces. Long
enough that no individual connects their own decision to the outcome, short
enough that the outcome is catastrophic.

Every failure mode in this document with a delayed consequence produces the
same result: individuals defect rationally, the system degrades invisibly,
and the correction arrives after the cost.

The military solution is not education. It is inspection: a person whose
job is to look, on a schedule, with authority. This works, it is expensive,
and it is precisely the ownership that RFC 0037 section 37.2 found missing
in every civilian failure catalogued here.

### 55.3 Expedition practice

Small teams in remote environments follow essentially the same rules with
a stronger constraint: in fragile environments, everything is carried out.

On high mountains and in polar regions, waste does not decompose. It
accumulates in place, indefinitely, and the accumulation on the popular
routes of major peaks is now a documented environmental problem, with
material deposited over decades emerging as glaciers retreat.

Some permits now require a sealed container and its return, weighed, as a
condition. Compliance is high, because it is checked, and because the
alternative is losing the permit.

Enforcement plus a consequence the individual bears. It works. It always
works. The problem is never finding a mechanism that works, it is finding
one that somebody is willing to operate.

### 55.4 The leave no trace hierarchy

For general wilderness use, in order of preference:

1. Carry out. Always correct, always available, always the best option.
2. Cathole: 15 to 20 cm deep, 60 m from water, trail and camp, covered and
   disguised.
3. Nothing else is acceptable and the alternatives people improvise are
   worse than they imagine.

Paper is carried out. Paper does not decompose at altitude, in arid
conditions, or under snow, and it is the single most visible evidence of
poor practice on any popular route.

### 55.5 Why the rules are specific

Sixty metres from water is not arbitrary. It is derived from measured
transport of contamination through soil under typical conditions, with
margin.

Fifteen to twenty centimetres is the depth of the biologically active soil
layer, where decomposition actually happens. Deeper is worse: below that
layer the material is preserved rather than processed.

Every number in the guidance has a mechanism behind it. The guidance is
distributed as a list of numbers with no mechanisms, which is why people
treat them as arbitrary and round them down.

Publish the reason with the rule. A rule with a visible mechanism is
followed. A rule without one is negotiated.

## RFC 0056: Event Operations

### 56.1 The problem shape

A temporary population, concentrated, with synchronised demand driven by
an external schedule that the operator controls and does not use.

A stadium empties at the interval. A festival stage finishes. A cinema
screening ends. In each case, thousands of people are released
simultaneously into a facility count fixed months earlier by somebody
applying a ratio.

Amplification factor at a three hour film interval was measured at 11.4x,
the highest figure recorded anywhere in this document.

### 56.2 Provisioning

Event guidance specifies units per thousand attendees, adjusted for
duration, alcohol availability and whether food is served. The numbers are
well established, published, and routinely undercut by organisers because
units cost money and the queue costs the organiser nothing.

The externality is borne entirely by attendees, in a currency the organiser
does not measure, at an event the attendee has already paid for and cannot
leave.

Every incentive points the wrong way. This is the only environment in the
document where the operator profits from under provisioning, and it is,
predictably, the worst provisioned environment in the document.

### 56.3 The servicing schedule

Units fill. A unit at capacity is out of service and, worse, degrades the
adjacent units by displacing their demand.

Servicing requires vehicle access, which requires routes kept clear, which
conflicts with crowd flow, which is why servicing is scheduled overnight
and why the second day of a festival is materially worse than the first.

The failure is not capacity. It is that capacity was sized for a peak and
the servicing interval was sized for a mean.

### 56.4 The interval problem

An organiser who staggers the release flattens the peak entirely. Two
screens finishing fifteen minutes apart halves the amplification factor at
zero cost.

Cinemas with multiple screens schedule start times to optimise projection
staffing and concession queues. The same scheduling lever, applied to the
other constraint, is free and unused.

RFC 0034 section 34.5 found the same thing in an office: the cheapest fix
is behavioural, it works, and it is not done, and the reason it is not done
never appears in the minutes.

### 56.5 What good looks like

Large events that get this right share three properties: they provision
above guidance rather than to it, they service continuously rather than
overnight, and they publish queue information so attendees can balk toward
under used blocks.

All three are the same three recommendations as RFC 0007 section 7.8, and
they were arrived at independently by event operations people who have
never heard of Little's Law and did not need to, because they could see
the queue.

Seeing the queue is worth more than modelling it. The model exists for the
people who cannot see it, which is always the people holding the budget.

## RFC 0057: Provisioning Ratios and Who Waits

### 57.1 The observation

In venues with equal floor area allocated to men's and women's facilities,
the women's queue is longer, consistently, in essentially every venue, at
essentially every event, everywhere.

This is not a perception. It is measured, it is large, and it has a
mechanism.

### 57.2 The mechanism

Three factors compound:

**Effective capacity per unit area.** Urinals occupy less area per fixture
than stalls. Equal floor area therefore yields substantially more fixtures
on one side than the other. Equal area is not equal capacity and building
codes wrote equal area for most of a century.

**Service time.** Mean service time is longer, for reasons including
clothing, the higher probability of accompanying a child, and menstrual
management. Estimates commonly put the ratio near 1.5 to 2.

**Arrival rate.** Higher, on average, driven by physiology, pregnancy and a
higher incidence of relevant conditions.

Take capacity ratio, multiply by service time ratio, multiply by arrival
rate ratio, and the compounded disparity in utilisation is large enough to
push one side of the wall to rho above 1.0 while the other sits at 0.5.

One side queues. The other does not. Both sides conclude that this is
simply how it is.

### 57.3 The arithmetic

Model both sides as separate M/M/c queues, which is what they are, since
there is no sharing across the wall.

Take a venue with equal area, yielding 12 fixtures on one side and 6 on the
other. Take arrival rates in a 1.15 ratio and service times in a 1.6 ratio.

Utilisation on the 12 fixture side at a given event: 0.52. Utilisation on
the 6 fixture side: 1.19.

One side is comfortably provisioned. The other is above 1.0, which per RFC
0007 means the queue does not reach equilibrium at all; it grows for the
entire duration of the peak.

That is the whole explanation. It is one line of arithmetic and it has been
available since queueing theory was formalised in 1909.

### 57.4 Why it persisted

Codes specified equal area or equal fixture counts, both of which are
inputs rather than outcomes. Nobody specified equal wait time, which is the
outcome anybody actually cares about.

Specifying an input and hoping for an outcome is the same error as
provisioning to the statutory minimum in RFC 0029 section 29.1, and the
same error as counting facilities built in RFC 0046 section 46.3.

It is the most repeated mistake in this entire document: measure the thing
you can count, ship it, and never check whether the thing you wanted
happened.

### 57.5 The fix

Many jurisdictions now mandate ratios of 2:1 or higher in new construction
for exactly this reason, and the legislation is generally known by a name
this document will not use because the name is a joke and this section is
not.

Where the ratios have been applied, the disparity closes. The arithmetic
was right. It was right for a hundred years before anybody applied it.

### 57.6 Universal and single occupancy designs

A row of individual lockable rooms, each with a fixture and a basin,
serving everybody, solves several problems at once: it removes the fixed
allocation entirely so capacity flows to demand, it accommodates carers and
parents with children of any age, it accommodates people whose use of a
gendered facility is contested or unsafe, and it improves privacy for
everyone.

It costs more per fixture in floor area and less in duplicated
infrastructure. Venues that have built it report shorter queues on
aggregate, because a fixed partition between two pools of demand is a
capacity model that cannot adapt, and removing it is strictly better on
every queueing metric that exists.

Partitioned capacity is worse than pooled capacity. This is a load
balancing result that has been known since the earliest work on the
subject, it holds for servers, for tills at a supermarket, and for
bathrooms, and it is the single most transferable finding in this file.

The supermarket worked it out. One queue, many tills. Everybody accepted it
within a decade and nobody now remembers arguing about it.

## RFC 0058: Downstream

### 58.1 Where it goes

The question nobody asks. The answer is a sequence of unit operations, most
of them mechanical, running continuously, in a facility nobody visits, paid
for by everybody, thought about by no one.

### 58.2 The stages

**Screening.** Bar screens remove anything that should never have entered
the system. The removed material is skipped, landfilled, and consists
overwhelmingly of wet wipes, sanitary products and cotton buds, in that
order, at a volume measured in tonnes per day for a medium city.

Every item in that skip was flushed by somebody who believed it was fine.

**Grit removal.** Sand, grit and road detritus settle out. This exists
because the network carries surface water in many cities, which is a
design decision from the nineteenth century that has consequences at every
subsequent stage.

**Primary settlement.** Solids settle by gravity over hours. Roughly half
the suspended solids and a third of the biological oxygen demand is removed
here, by doing nothing, slowly, in a large tank. It is the cheapest stage
and the most effective per unit cost.

**Secondary, biological.** Aerated tanks where bacteria consume the
dissolved organic load. This is the processing layer from RFC 0043
reproduced industrially: the same organisms, the same reactions, at scale,
in concrete, with blowers supplying the oxygen.

A treatment works is a cultivated microbiome. The operators are keeping
bacteria alive and healthy, and the failure mode of the plant is that the
culture dies, which takes weeks to recover.

**Settlement, again.** The biomass settles out. Some is returned to keep
the culture going. The rest is surplus and becomes sludge.

**Tertiary, where required.** Filtration, nutrient removal, disinfection.
Required where the receiving water is sensitive, expensive, and the first
thing to be skipped when a plant is over capacity in a storm.

### 58.3 The sludge

The surplus biomass is the actual product. It is digested anaerobically,
which produces methane, which is burned to generate electricity, which in
well run plants covers a large share of the plant's own consumption and in
some cases exports.

The digested residue is dewatered and, subject to regulation, applied to
agricultural land as fertiliser.

So: material enters as waste, is processed by cultivated bacteria, produces
fuel that powers its own processing, and leaves as fertiliser that grows
food. The loop closes.

This is the termite mound and the hippo river and the rabbit's second pass,
built in concrete, at municipal scale, and it works, and almost nobody
knows it is there.

### 58.4 Combined sewer overflow

Where the network carries both foul and surface water, heavy rain exceeds
capacity, and the overflow discharges untreated to the river by design,
because the alternative is that it discharges into houses.

The overflow is a designed relief valve on a system whose capacity was
fixed by pipe diameters laid down over a century ago, in cities that have
since paved every surface that used to absorb rainfall.

The volume of discharge is now measured and published in some
jurisdictions. Publishing it produced immediate political consequences that
a century of unpublished discharge did not.

Measurement changes nothing. Publication changes everything. This is the
Great Stink mechanism again: the evidence existed, the smell did not reach
the people with the budget, and then it did.

### 58.5 The people

A treatment works runs continuously, is staffed at night, and requires
people to enter confined spaces containing gases that kill.

Deaths in this sector happen, are investigated, and produce guidance that
is followed unevenly. The workers who maintain the network below the
street do the most dangerous and least regarded work in municipal
engineering.

The single most useful thing anybody reading this can do about that is
already stated: do not flush anything that has wet tensile strength.
Nearly every blockage that requires a person to go down there is one of
those.

### 58.6 The cost

A household's wastewater charge covers collection, treatment, sludge
processing, and the capital cost of a network built by somebody who died a
century ago.

It is one of the lowest cost, highest return services any household
purchases, it is invisible, and it is the only line on a utility bill that
anybody has ever tried to have removed on the grounds that they were not
sure what it was for.
