## RFC 0059: The Public Facility

### 59.1 The disappearance

Public facilities in most Western cities have declined sharply over three
decades. Councils closed them because they cost money, generate no
revenue, attract maintenance costs and antisocial behaviour, and have no
constituency that will vote on them.

Each individual closure decision was defensible on its own budget line.
The aggregate outcome is a city that people with certain medical
conditions, older people, parents with young children, taxi drivers,
delivery workers and anybody without the money to buy a coffee cannot
navigate.

### 59.2 The externality, reversed

RFC 0018 section 18.5 described infrastructure whose cost is socialised and
whose benefit is invisible. This is the same asset being decommissioned.

When the facility closes, the demand does not. It relocates: to cafés,
where it becomes a cost borne by businesses who now police access with
door codes; to shop doorways, where it becomes a cleaning cost borne by
the council on a different line; and to people simply not going out, which
is a cost borne entirely by them and recorded nowhere.

The saving is real, appears in one budget, and is smaller than the sum of
the costs it creates in three other budgets and one population that does
not have a budget.

Every closure of a shared resource works this way. The saving is
concentrated and visible, the costs are distributed and invisible, and the
decision is therefore always to close.

### 59.3 The access economy

Door codes on café facilities, printed on receipts, are now standard in
several cities.

This converts a public good into a purchase requirement. It is a rational
response by each business to a cost that the council stopped bearing, and
in aggregate it means that the right to relieve yourself in a city centre
now costs the price of a coffee, and is unavailable to anybody who cannot
pay it or is not welcome in the room.

Nobody designed this. It is an emergent property of a thousand individually
sensible decisions and it is worse than any of the alternatives anybody
would have chosen deliberately.

### 59.4 The community scheme

Some councils pay businesses a small annual sum to open their facilities
to the public without purchase, with a sticker in the window.

Cost per facility is a fraction of operating a standalone unit. Coverage
is better. Maintenance is handled by an existing operator with an existing
cleaning routine.

The schemes work, they are cheap, and their adoption is limited by the fact
that nobody's job title contains the words that would make them the person
who champions it.

Section 37.2, for the last time: the recurring failure is never technical.

### 59.5 The Changi counterexample

RFC 0032 section 32.7 described the airport with a rating screen at every
exit feeding a dispatch system with a response time in minutes.

That is not a technology difference. The technology is a touchscreen and a
work order queue, both of which every airport already has.

It is an ownership difference. Somebody's performance is measured on that
number. That is the entire mechanism, it is the mechanism recommended in
RFC 0037 section 37.7, and it is the only intervention in this document
that has ever been observed to work at scale.

One owner. One number. Published.

## RFC 0060: On Documentation

### 60.1 Why this section exists

Four years in, the document has become an argument about documentation
itself, and it may as well say so.

### 60.2 What this document got right

**It was written down.** Everything in it was known by somebody before it
was written. The queueing peak was known. The floor 5 timing was known. The
lights being broken was known by everybody on the floor for eleven weeks.

None of it existed as an artefact anybody could hand to a new hire. Now
some of it does.

**It was specific.** Numbers, times, floors, tables. A document that says
"the facilities get busy at lunch" is worth nothing. A document that says
the peak is 13:30, the queue is 6.7 deep on average, and floor 5 is empty
because finance keeps different hours, changes behaviour on first reading.

**It survived.** Because it was entertaining enough to be read and
awkward enough to delete. Both properties were accidents and both were
load bearing.

### 60.3 What it got wrong

**The audience.** Written for engineers, by an engineer, in a repository
engineers read. The people who could act on it never saw it. Four years of
correct analysis, one integer on a wall.

**The format.** A comment block in a README is not a document. It is not
searchable by anybody who does not know it exists, it has no title anybody
would search for, and it is invisible to every tool the organisation uses
to find anything.

**The escalation path.** There is none. The document describes problems,
assigns them to nobody, and has no mechanism for anything in it to become
work. RFC 0040 identified this at year four and the action item is still
open, unassigned, which is a fitting final entry in a document whose most
repeated finding is that nothing without an owner gets done.

### 60.4 The general lesson

Documentation fails in three ways and only one of them is about writing.

It fails because it is not written. It fails because it is written and
cannot be found. And it fails because it is written, found, read, agreed
with, and connected to nothing that can act.

Most organisations only address the first. This document addressed the
first, failed the second by design, and failed the third completely.

### 60.5 On writing things nobody asked for

Nobody asked for this. It has no ticket, no owner, no budget and no
mandate. It was written during a deploy freeze by somebody with a
queueing textbook open for an unrelated reason.

It is also, by a wide margin, the most read document this team has
produced, and the only one that has ever caused a physical change to the
building.

That is not an argument that unmandated work is better than mandated work.
It is an observation that the ratio of value to authorisation is not one,
and that a person who notices something and writes it down carefully, with
correct numbers, in a register people will actually read, occasionally
produces more than a quarter of planned work.

Occasionally. The base rate on unmandated documents is dreadful and most
of them deserve their obscurity.

### 60.6 To the next maintainer

The numbers are in Appendix A. Recollect them if they are older than two
years; the building changes.

The register is in RFC 0016 and it is the whole product. Guard it. A
document that breaks character once has no character.

The accessibility section has no jokes and never will.

The queueing memo in RFC 0040 section 40.4 is still unwritten. It is four
pages and it would save 340,000 a year and it needs somebody willing to
attach their name to four pages of arithmetic about bathrooms.

It will not be you either. That is fine. Add a section instead.

## RFC 0061: Alternative Architectures

### 61.1 Why alternatives exist

The flush architecture takes a small quantity of material and mixes it
into a large quantity of clean drinking water, then spends significant
energy separating them again at a facility downstream.

Stated that way it is obviously absurd, and it is the dominant global
design because it solves the local problem completely: the material leaves
immediately, the operator never handles it, and the cost is borne
elsewhere.

Every alternative asks the operator to accept some part of the cost back.
That is why the alternatives lose.

### 61.2 Composting

Solids collected in a chamber with a carbon source, aerated, allowed to
decompose over months. Liquid separated at source, because the mixture is
what produces the odour and the mixture is what fails.

Output after full processing is a soil amendment. Water consumption is
zero. Energy consumption is a small fan.

The design works, it is well understood, and it fails in practice for one
reason: it is a batch process with a maintenance requirement, and the
maintenance is performed by the operator, who is the same person who
chose the system for environmental reasons and who has now discovered what
the third month involves.

Systems maintained by enthusiasts work. Systems maintained by whoever
happens to live there do not. This is the single most reliable predictor of
success for any alternative in this section.

### 61.3 Incinerating

Electric or gas, burns the material to sterile ash, no water, no plumbing,
minimal maintenance.

Consumes significant energy per cycle, requires a flue, and cannot be used
during the cycle, which imposes a service interval on a resource that
already has contention.

Used in remote installations where the alternative is a pit and the ground
is frozen. Correct in its niche and absurd anywhere with a sewer.

### 61.4 Vacuum sewerage

Small diameter pipes under vacuum rather than large pipes under gravity.
No gradient required, so it works in flat terrain, high water tables and
retrofits where excavating for gravity runs is impossible.

Used at scale in some Northern European towns and in essentially every
aircraft, train and ship. Requires a vacuum station, which requires power,
which means a network failure is total rather than local.

Trades a passive system that fails locally for an active system that fails
globally. That trade is correct where gravity is unavailable and incorrect
everywhere else, and it is exactly the trade you make when you replace a
static file with a service.

### 61.5 Container based

Sealed container, collected on a schedule, treated centrally. No plumbing,
no water, no excavation.

Works in dense informal settlements where neither a pit nor a sewer is
possible. Requires a functioning collection service, which requires an
operating model, which is precisely what donated infrastructure programmes
do not build, per RFC 0046 section 46.4.

It is the most promising thing in the sector and it is unglamorous, because
its innovation is logistics rather than hardware, and logistics does not
photograph well for a funding round.

### 61.6 Urine diversion

Separate the liquid at source. The liquid is nearly sterile, contains most
of the nitrogen and phosphorus, and is a viable fertiliser after simple
treatment. The solid fraction, undiluted, is far smaller and easier to
process.

The engineering is sound, the agronomy is proven, and adoption is limited
by an interface change: the fixture has two openings and requires the
operator to align correctly, every time.

An architecture that requires precise user cooperation on every single
operation will fail at the rate that people fail, which is not zero, and
the failure contaminates the stream the whole design exists to keep clean.

Do not build a system whose correctness depends on every user doing a
fiddly thing correctly every time. This is RFC 0017 section 17.4 in
porcelain.

### 61.7 Why nothing displaces the flush

The flush architecture has one property no alternative matches: it
requires nothing of the operator beyond a lever, it never requires the
operator to see the material again, and its costs are fully externalised
to a municipal system funded by everyone.

Any alternative that asks the operator to handle, store, maintain or think
about the material is competing against a system that asks for none of
those things.

This is why the technically superior option loses. The technically
superior option is superior on axes the user does not pay for, and it is
inferior on the one axis the user experiences, which is effort.

Every product decision you will ever make has this shape.

## RFC 0062: Historical Interfaces

### 62.1 The garderobe

A stone chute in a castle wall, discharging outside the curtain wall or
into the moat. Cold, exposed, and entirely effective.

The name is the origin of the modern word wardrobe: clothing was stored in
the same shaft, because the ammonia atmosphere deterred moths.

A latrine used as a pest control system for textiles, deliberately, as a
design feature. Dual use, entirely intentional, and better documented than
most of the vulture material in RFC 0014 section 14.6.

### 62.2 The chute as an attack surface

At least one castle is recorded as having fallen to attackers who climbed
the garderobe shaft.

This is a documented physical intrusion through an unmonitored egress
path in an otherwise well defended perimeter, and it is the single best
security parable available anywhere in engineering.

Your outbound path is an inbound path. Somebody will climb it. Nobody is
watching it, because nobody wants to be assigned to watch it.

### 62.3 The gong farmer

The trade of emptying cesspits in medieval and early modern cities. Worked
at night, paid comparatively well, socially excluded, and subject to
recorded fatalities from asphyxiation and drowning.

The same work, the same conditions and the same social position as the
manual pit emptying described in RFC 0046 section 46.5, separated by five
hundred years and no meaningful change in how the people doing it are
regarded.

### 62.4 The chamber pot and the street

Household waste emptied from windows into the street, with a shouted
warning in some cities and no warning in most.

The consequence was that streets were open sewers, that the raised
pavement and the practice of walking on the inside were both practical
responses to it, and that European cities were, for centuries,
substantially less sanitary than cities that had solved this thousands of
years earlier.

Progress is not monotonic. A working solution can be lost for a millennium
and rebuilt from scratch by people who do not know it existed.

### 62.5 Versailles

A palace of extraordinary expense with almost no sanitary provision, a
court of thousands, and a documented odour that visitors recorded.

The building was optimised entirely for display. The functional
requirements that everybody present had, several times daily, were not
considered part of the design brief, because they were not the part
anybody would be shown.

Every system built to impress a stakeholder rather than serve a user is
Versailles, and the smell is the integration test.

## RFC 0063: Water

### 63.1 The budget

A 6 litre flush, at roughly five sessions per person per day counting all
uses, is around 30 litres per person per day. In a typical developed
country household that is between a quarter and a third of total domestic
water consumption.

A third of the treated drinking water delivered to a house, at the cost of
abstraction, treatment, pumping and distribution, is used to move material
a distance of approximately two metres.

### 63.2 The reduction path

**13 litres to 6 litres.** Achieved through bowl redesign, not cistern
reduction, per RFC 0042 section 42.5. This is the single largest domestic
water saving of the last fifty years and it was achieved by changing the
shape of a ceramic object.

**6 litres to 4.5 litres dual flush.** Real savings where the mechanism is
understood by users, which it frequently is not, because the two buttons
are unlabelled on most units and a large fraction of people press both.

An interface with two options, no labels, and no feedback on which one was
used, deployed to the entire population, with the saving contingent on the
user choosing correctly. It saves less than the specification claims and
the gap is entirely interface design.

**Dual flush leakage.** Dual flush valves leak at a much higher rate than
the flap valves they replaced. Estimates in several countries put the
leakage from faulty dual flush units at a volume comparable to the savings
the technology produced.

A water saving technology whose failure mode wastes more water than it
saves, deployed at national scale, discovered years later, because nobody
measured the installed base and everybody measured the specification.

### 63.3 Greywater

Shower, basin and laundry water, reused for flushing. Halves the treated
water requirement in principle.

Requires separate plumbing, storage, filtration and a mains top up for
when the greywater runs out. Cost effective in new construction at scale,
uneconomic as a retrofit, and installed in almost nothing because the
decision is made by a developer who does not pay the water bill.

The person who chooses the system and the person who pays for its
operation are different people. There is a name for this in economics and
it explains approximately half of everything in the built environment.

### 63.4 Waterless variants

The urinal without water works, saves substantial volume, and requires a
sealing cartridge changed on a schedule.

Where the schedule is followed, it is excellent. Where it is not, the
result is worse than the fixture it replaced, and the schedule is followed
by a contractor whose contract was awarded on price.

Every water saving technology in this section has the same shape: it works
if maintained, it is deployed to environments that will not maintain it,
and the specification is written as though maintenance is free.

### 63.5 Scarcity

In water scarce regions the flush architecture is not merely wasteful, it
is unavailable. There is no volume of treated water to spend on transport.

Exporting the Western default to those regions is the category error noted
in RFC 0046 section 46.2, and it has been made repeatedly, at cost, by
programmes that measured facilities built.

The correct architectures there are dry: pit with a vent and a lid,
composting, container based collection. They are technically adequate,
culturally contested, and consistently under funded relative to hardware
that photographs like development.

### 63.6 The future

The likely path is not a new architecture. It is the existing architecture
with the water source changed: local greywater reuse, recycled municipal
supply, and eventually a residential loop resembling the one the ISS
operates, per RFC 0041 section 41.4.

The ISS drinks its recovered urine at above 90 percent recovery. The
technology exists, works, has operated continuously for years, and the only
barrier to its terrestrial adoption is that people know what it is.

Somebody will eventually deploy it under a name that does not say so, and
it will be adopted, and this document will consider that outcome both
dishonest and correct.

## RFC 0064: Folklore

### 64.1 Superstition

Practices that are widespread, sincerely held, and mostly wrong.

**The lid.** Closing the lid before flushing is often framed as luck,
tidiness or a household rule. It is actually the plume mitigation in RFC
0042 section 42.4 and it reduces aerosol dispersal by roughly 80 percent.

Here a piece of folklore is correct, is universally transmitted as
superstition, and would be more widely followed if anyone had ever
explained the mechanism. Publish the reason with the rule.

**The running tap.** Believed to mask sound. It does, poorly, and it
signals intent precisely. Ranked third of four in RFC 0006 section 6.3 and
adopted by more people than any option above it.

**The paper layer.** Believed to be about hygiene, in which capacity it
does very little, since the barrier is porous and the contact is brief.
Its actual function is the splash suppression in RFC 0042 section 42.3,
where it is genuinely the most effective mitigation available.

Right practice, wrong reason, transmitted as folklore, and effective
regardless. Most of what works in most fields has this history.

**The phone.** Believed by the operator to be a private act. It is a
device that has been in a bathroom, and the surface contamination
literature on personal devices is unambiguous and unpleasant.

Nobody cleans the phone. Everybody washes their hands. The hands then touch
the phone.

### 64.2 The reading habit

Documented across cultures and centuries, from newspapers to phones, and
consistently the single largest driver of session duration.

The explanation usually offered is boredom. The better explanation is that
it is, for a large fraction of adults, the only reliably uninterrupted
solitary time in the day.

That is not a joke about the modern condition. It is the actual finding
behind ADR 004, it is why the option was never deprecated, and it is why
the office deployment's utilisation will never match the model.

### 64.3 Regional taboos

Which hand is used, whether the feet may face a particular direction,
whether the door may face a particular way, whether discussion is
permissible at all and with whom.

The constant across every culture surveyed is that there is a taboo. The
content varies completely. The existence does not.

RFC 0048 concluded that there is no neutral vocabulary in English. The
comparative picture is stronger: there is no culture with a neutral
practice. Every human society has built a set of rules around this and no
two sets agree.

Whatever is unmentionable in your organisation is unmentionable by
convention, not by nature, and somewhere there is a group that mentions it
freely and finds your reticence strange.

### 64.4 The graffiti

The only genuinely anonymous written medium most people ever encounter,
and the content is consistently: territorial marking, sexual boasting,
political slogans, and, in a persistent minority, extremely sincere advice
to strangers.

The last category is the interesting one. People write earnest,
unprompted, unrewarded encouragement to an unknown reader, in a locked
room, anonymously.

Remove the possibility of attribution and a measurable fraction of people
become kinder rather than worse. Every model of online anonymity assumes
the opposite and the bathroom door is the counterexample nobody cites.

## RFC 0065: Adjacent Shared Resources

### 65.1 The kitchen

The other contended shared resource on every floor, governed by the same
dynamics and studied by nobody.

One microwave, eleven engineers, a lunch peak at 12:30, and a service time
distribution with a fat tail because somebody is always reheating
something for four minutes that should have been split into two portions.

Utilisation at peak exceeds 1.0. The queue forms in a corridor. Nobody has
ever modelled it and the model is identical to RFC 0007 with different
nouns.

### 65.2 The fridge

A shared resource with unbounded input, no eviction policy, and no owner.

Items enter. Nothing leaves except by consumption or by an annual purge
announced with three days notice and executed with a bin bag.

This is a cache with no TTL, no LRU, and a manual flush performed by
whichever person's tolerance breaks first. The person who performs the
purge is resented. The people who filled it are not identified, because
identifying them would require the same disclosure mechanism that fails
everywhere else in this document.

Set a TTL. Label everything with a date. Automate the eviction. This is
the entire solution, it costs a marker pen, and no office has ever
implemented it.

### 65.3 The last cup

Whoever takes the last cup of coffee makes the next pot. The compliance
rate is roughly comparable to the paper replacement game in RFC 0045
section 45.1, which is to say around 60 percent, and for the same reason:
iterated game, shared lift.

The interesting difference is that coffee compliance is higher than paper
compliance despite the cost being higher, because coffee defection is
observable and attributable, and paper defection happens behind a locked
door.

Observability drives compliance more than cost does. Every incentive design
in every organisation is built on the opposite assumption.

### 65.4 The meeting room

Booked, held, and abandoned. The room shows as occupied and is empty.

Ghost bookings are the reneging behaviour from RFC 0007 section 7.6 with
the resource still held, which is worse: the resource is neither used nor
released, and the queue behind it cannot see that it is free.

The fix is a sensor and an automatic release after ten minutes of
vacancy. It exists, it is sold, it works, and it is the same intervention
as the occupancy display in RFC 0023 section 23.5, applied to a resource
that people are willing to discuss in a meeting.

The meeting room got the sensor in year one. The bathroom took three
years and an incident.

### 65.5 The general form

Every shared resource in an office has the same four properties: demand is
correlated by an external schedule, capacity is fixed by a decision made
before anybody measured, contention is resolved by an unwritten social
protocol, and nobody owns the outcome.

The bathroom is the extreme case because the taboo prevents even the
unwritten protocol from being discussed, and this document is what
happened when one person wrote it down anyway.

## RFC 0066: The Remote Deployment

### 66.1 What changed

Widespread home working moved a large fraction of daily load from the
office deployment to the home deployment.

For the individual this was, on every metric in this document, an
unambiguous improvement: single tenancy, zero queueing, full configuration
control, complete supply chain control, no acoustic side channel, no
timing analysis, no colleague recognition problem.

The best environment in the matrix in RFC 0027 became the default
environment for the first time in the history of office work.

### 66.2 The measurable effect

Office building occupancy fell. Peak utilisation fell with it. The queue
that this document spent three years analysing simply stopped forming,
not because anything was fixed but because the load left.

The six stalls were never built. The problem went away. The analysis was
correct and irrelevant.

Every capacity problem has this possible ending and nobody plans for it.
The demand curve is not a law of nature; it is a consequence of
arrangements that can change faster than the building.

### 66.3 The return

Then attendance mandates arrived, load returned partially and, critically,
in a correlated way: three fixed days rather than five, with everybody on
the same three days.

Total weekly demand fell. Peak demand rose.

A building sized for its old mean now serves a higher peak with a lower
average, which is the worst possible combination for a fixed capacity
system, and is exactly the pattern RFC 0034 warned about when it said the
mean hides the peak.

The organisation reduced its headcount in the building and made the queue
worse. Both facts are true and only one of them is in a report.

### 66.4 The hybrid arithmetic

| Scenario          | Weekly demand | Peak day demand | Peak rho |
|-------------------|---------------|-----------------|----------|
| Full attendance   | 100%          | 20%             | 1.54     |
| Fully remote      | 12%           | 3%              | 0.19     |
| Hybrid, staggered | 60%           | 12%             | 0.92     |
| Hybrid, fixed days| 60%           | 20%             | 1.54     |

The last two rows have identical total demand and completely different
outcomes. The only difference is whether the mandated days are the same
days for everybody.

Staggering the days costs nothing, has no downside anybody has articulated,
and is not done, because the mandate is written by somebody optimising for
the appearance of a full office rather than for the function of one.

### 66.5 The lesson, again

Correlated arrivals are the whole problem. This document has now found the
same finding in an office, an airport, a cinema, a festival, an aircraft
and a hybrid working policy.

It is the single most transferable result in this file and it can be
stated in one line: the thing that breaks your system is not how much
demand there is, it is how much of it arrives at once.

## Appendix G: Metric Definitions

Precise definitions for every metric used in this document. Included
because the most common failure in metrics is not measurement error, it is
two people using the same word for different quantities.

**Arrival rate (lambda).** Clients per unit time attempting to acquire a
resource. Measured at the door, not at the fixture, because a client who
balks still arrived.

**Service rate (mu).** Completions per unit time per server, at
saturation. The reciprocal of mean service time. Measured only during
periods when a queue exists, because measuring it when the resource is
idle measures the client's leisure rather than the server's capacity.

**Servers (c).** Fixtures available for use. A fixture out of service is
not a server. A fixture in the accessible facility is not a general
purpose server and must not be counted as one, which is an error made in
every fixture count this building has ever published.

**Utilisation (rho).** lambda / (c mu). Dimensionless. Above 1.0 the queue
grows without bound for the duration of the condition.

**Queue depth (L_q).** Clients waiting, excluding those in service.
Counted, not modelled, wherever possible.

**Wait time (W_q).** Arrival to service start. The metric users
experience. The metric nobody publishes.

**Service time (W_s).** Lock engagement to lock release. Includes
everything the client does inside, which is why the `reading` option
appears in this metric and not in any other.

**Time in system (W).** W_q + W_s.

**Balk rate.** Fraction of arrivals that observe the queue and leave
without joining. High balk rates make availability metrics look excellent
while the service is unusable, which is the single most misleading
interaction in this appendix.

**Renege rate.** Fraction of joined clients who abandon before service.
Correlated with the worst outcomes in the incident record.

**Amplification factor.** Peak arrival rate divided by baseline arrival
rate, over the window in which the peak is sustained. Meaningless without
the window.

**Availability.** Fraction of arrival attempts that find at least one
usable fixture. Not the fraction of time fixtures are working, which is a
maintenance metric and is what facilities reports.

The gap between those two definitions is why facilities reports 99.4
percent and users report queueing daily. Both numbers are correct. They
measure different things and only one of them is about the user.

**Successful completion rate.** Sessions terminating in a 2xx status.
Self reported and therefore an upper bound.

**Paper availability.** Fraction of fixtures with non zero primary supply
at time of check. A binary per fixture, not a volume. A fixture with one
unit remaining passes this metric and fails the user, which is why
`reserve` in Appendix B section B.4 defaults to 1 and not 0.

**Cleanliness.** Subjective, 1 to 10, sampled daily by a single observer.
Unreliable, uncalibrated, uncomparable between observers, and the only
metric anybody in the building acts on.

## RFC 0067: Hand Hygiene

### 67.1 Why this section is here

It is the control. Everything else in this document is about moving
material somewhere. This is the part that stops the material reaching the
next person, and it is the highest impact intervention discussed anywhere
in this file.

### 67.2 The evidence

Handwashing with soap reduces respiratory infection and diarrhoeal disease
by margins that are large, replicated, and consistent across every
population studied.

At population scale it is among the most cost effective health
interventions that exists. It costs soap.

### 67.3 The mechanism

Soap is a surfactant. It does not kill most pathogens. It lifts them off
the skin, along with the oils they are bound to, and the water carries
them away.

The mechanical action is therefore the active component, not the soap
itself, and the duration of the mechanical action is what determines the
outcome. This is why every guideline specifies a time, and why the time
feels absurdly long to everybody performing it.

Twenty seconds. Measured. Almost nobody does twenty seconds.

### 67.4 Observed compliance

Studies using direct observation, rather than self report, consistently
find compliance far below what self report claims.

Self reported handwashing after using a facility: typically above 90
percent. Observed: substantially lower, with the gap widest for men and
widest in facilities where nobody else is present.

The observation studies are conducted by a person standing in the room
with a clipboard, which is the single most awkward research role in public
health, and the presence of the observer raises compliance, which means
the true unobserved rate is lower than the observed rate that is already
much lower than the reported rate.

Two nested layers of measurement bias, both in the same direction. Assume
the real number is worse than anything published.

### 67.5 The interventions that work

**Sinks in the path.** A sink the user must pass is used more than a sink
they must turn toward. Layout beats signage by a wide margin.

**Visible soap.** Empty dispensers are the single largest cause of non
compliance and are reported at the four percent rate from RFC 0037.

**Water temperature.** Cold water discourages duration. Warm water does
not clean better, but it keeps people at the sink longer, which does.

**Mirrors.** A mirror at the sink raises compliance measurably. The
mechanism is self observation and it is one of the cheapest behavioural
interventions in the literature.

**Another person present.** The largest single effect of all. Compliance
rises sharply when somebody else is in the room.

That last finding is the disclosure game from RFC 0045 section 45.5,
inverted: observation drives compliance where rules do not, exactly as
section 65.3 found for coffee.

### 67.6 Drying

Drying matters. Wet hands transfer bacteria far more readily than dry
ones, so an incomplete dry undoes a substantial part of the wash.

The literature on paper versus air dryers is contested, is funded on both
sides by parties with a commercial interest, and should be read with that
in mind.

The findings that are reasonably robust: paper towels dry faster and more
completely in typical use, jet dryers disperse more material into the room
air, and warm air dryers are used for less than the time required to dry
properly because people give up.

The findings that are contested: essentially everything else, and the
contest is between two industries.

A literature where every study is funded by a manufacturer is not a
literature, it is a marketing budget with citations. This is worth
recognising, because it is the state of the evidence in several fields
that engineers routinely treat as settled.

### 67.7 The phone

Hands are washed. The phone is not. The phone was in the room. The clean
hands then pick up the phone.

The control is defeated at the last step by a device that nobody has ever
included in a hygiene guideline, and the reason it is not in the
guidelines is that the guidelines predate the device and nobody has
revised them.

Your control is only as good as the step after it. Check what happens
after the step you are proud of.

## RFC 0068: Signage

### 68.1 The genre

Bathroom signage is the most read and least considered writing in any
building. It is seen by everybody, several times a day, for years, and it
is typically produced by whoever had access to a label printer.

### 68.2 What signs are asked to do

Signs in this domain attempt four distinct jobs, and confusing them is the
source of every bad sign:

1. **Wayfinding.** Where is it. Must work at distance, at speed, in a
   second language, for someone in a hurry.
2. **Identification.** Which one is which. The pictogram problem.
3. **Instruction.** How does this fixture work. Required far more often
   than anybody admits, especially for sensor and dual flush systems.
4. **Exhortation.** Please do or do not do a thing. Almost never works.

### 68.3 Why exhortation fails

"Please leave this facility as you found it." "Employees must wash hands."
"Please do not flush sanitary products."

These target behaviour with information the reader already has. Nobody
flushes a wipe because they were unaware wipes should not be flushed. They
do it because the bin is across the room, or absent, or open, or full.

Signage substitutes for design. A sign asking people not to do a thing is
almost always evidence that the room makes the thing convenient and the
alternative inconvenient.

Move the bin. Remove the sign.

### 68.4 The pictogram problem

The standard figures are a poor system by any evaluation: they encode
clothing conventions from a particular time and place, they are ambiguous
at distance, and they fail entirely for anybody the binary does not fit.

Attempts to improve them have produced sets that are clearer, sets that
are more inclusive, and sets that are neither and were designed to be
noticed, which is the worst possible failure mode for wayfinding.

The unglamorous correct answer for a single occupancy room is a sign
describing the fixtures inside, because that is the information the person
actually needs and it is true regardless of who is reading it.

### 68.5 Instruction

The dual flush buttons in RFC 0063 section 63.2 are unlabelled on most
units, save water only when used correctly, and are used incorrectly by a
large fraction of users.

An unlabelled two state control with no feedback, deployed globally,
whose entire justification depends on correct use.

Two words on the buttons would recover a meaningful share of the promised
saving. Nobody has done it because the button is manufactured by one
company, specified by another, installed by a third, and the water bill is
paid by a fourth.

### 68.6 The out of service sign

The most important sign in the building and the worst executed.

It must be on the outside of the room when the whole room is affected,
because a sign inside means somebody has to walk in to learn they should
not have. It must say when service is expected. It must be removed
promptly when service resumes, and it never is, which trains everybody to
ignore it.

A sign that is wrong half the time is worse than no sign, because it
destroys the credibility of every other sign in the building. This is
alert fatigue from RFC 0023 section 23.4, printed on paper, taped to a
door.

### J.1 Analysis

Median age of open tickets: 8 months. Median age of resolved tickets: 3
days.

The distribution is strongly bimodal. Tickets that name a broken object
are fixed within days. Tickets that name a systemic condition are open for
years or closed with a comment.

The queue is not a backlog. It is two queues sharing a tool: a maintenance
queue that works well, and a everything else queue that is a filing cabinet
with a status field.

Nothing in the second queue has an owner. Every single one of them appears
in RFC 0037 section 37.2 as a row in the ownership table.

### J.2 The response comments

"Working as designed." "Not a facilities issue." "Stock levels within
policy." "No storage available."

Every one of these is factually correct and every one of them terminates a
conversation about an outcome by answering a question about a process.

This is the most common failure in support interaction anywhere: the
responder answers the question they can answer, correctly, and the user's
actual problem leaves the system permanently.

### J.3 Ticket #4003

"What is it an issue of."

No response. Three years.

That ticket is the entire document in five words, and the maintainer has
asked that it never be closed.

## RFC 0069: Instrumentation

### 69.1 What can be sensed

The technology available is unremarkable and cheap: a reed switch on a
lock, a passive infrared sensor in a room, a load cell under a dispenser,
a differential pressure sensor on a vent, a door counter.

None of it is new, none of it is expensive, and almost none of it is
installed anywhere.

### 69.2 What each sensor tells you

| Sensor            | Direct measurement    | Derived                  |
|-------------------|-----------------------|--------------------------|
| Lock switch       | Occupied / free       | Occupancy, service time  |
| Door counter      | Entries               | Arrival rate             |
| Dispenser weight  | Stock remaining       | Consumption, reorder     |
| Air quality       | Particulates, VOC     | Cleaning demand          |
| Flow meter        | Water per flush       | Leak detection           |
| Vent pressure     | Fan operating         | Ventilation availability |

Arrival rate plus service time gives utilisation, which gives predicted
wait, which is every number this document spent four years arguing about,
available continuously, from two sensors costing less than a keyboard.

### 69.3 What must not be sensed

Identity. In any form. Directly, or by join, or by inference from
timestamp correlation with any other system in the building.

ADR 005 and RFC 0009 section 9.5 cover this. The engineering restatement
is simple: aggregate at the sensor, transmit counts not events, retain
nothing at event granularity, and collect no field that could serve as a
join key.

If the data leaving the device cannot reconstruct an individual's
sequence, the system is safe regardless of who later gets access to it.
Every other control depends on somebody's continued good behaviour.

### 69.4 The leak

A flow meter on the supply detects a continuously running fixture, which
is the single largest source of water waste in most buildings and is
frequently undetected for months because a slow leak into a bowl is silent
and invisible.

Detection is trivial: nonzero flow during a period with zero door entries.
Two sensors, one comparison, and it catches something that costs real money
and that nobody currently looks for at all.

This is the most straightforwardly valuable idea in this entire document
and it took sixty nine sections to arrive at it, because it is unglamorous,
and unglamorous is where the value has been the whole time.

## RFC 0070: Depiction

### 70.1 The absence

Characters in film and television do not use bathrooms. Across the entire
history of the medium the function is essentially absent, except where it
is the point of the scene.

This is not squeamishness alone. It is that any depiction becomes a
statement, because there is no neutral register, per RFC 0048 section 48.2.
A scene cannot show it casually; showing it at all makes it significant.

The result is that the most universal human activity is invisible in the
medium that depicts human activity.

### 70.2 When it appears

Three uses account for nearly all of it:

**Vulnerability.** A character is interrupted, exposed, or trapped. The
setting is used because it is the one place a person has no defences,
which is exactly the property that makes the privacy requirement absolute
in RFC 0021 and section 19.5.

**Comedy.** The oldest available gag, deployed continuously since theatre
began, and deployed most often by writers with the least to say.

**Realism as signal.** A director includes it specifically to signal that
this work is unflinching. The inclusion is itself a statement about the
work rather than about the character, which proves the point in section
70.1: there is no casual depiction available.

### 70.3 The exception

Long form prose handles it better, because prose can be brief and
unemphatic in a way that a camera cannot. A sentence can pass over it. A
shot cannot.

Medium constrains subject. The things your medium cannot say casually
become the things your medium cannot say at all, and after a generation
the audience forgets they were ever sayable.

### 70.4 Architecture and the plan

Architectural drawings label the room, place the fixtures, and move on.
The room receives the least design attention per square metre of any space
in a building, and it is the space most users form their opinion of the
building from.

Ask anybody about a building they disliked. A large fraction of the
answers will be about the bathrooms, the queue for them, or the walk to
them.

The space nobody designs is the space everybody judges. This is true of
buildings, of software installers, of error messages and of the
onboarding flow.

## RFC 0071: Procurement

### 71.1 The split incentive

The developer specifies. The landlord installs. The tenant occupies. The
employee uses. The facilities budget maintains. The water bill is paid by
whoever the lease says.

Six parties, five of whom make decisions, one of whom experiences the
outcome, and no path connecting the last to any of the others.

Section 63.3 named this and it is worth stating as the general rule: the
person choosing a system and the person living with it are different
people, and every property that only the second person notices will be
optimised away by the first.

### 71.2 What gets optimised

**Capital cost.** Visible to the specifier. Optimised hard.

**Installation time.** Visible to the builder. Optimised hard.

**Cleaning cost.** Visible to facilities. Optimised, which is why
commercial fixtures have no lids, per RFC 0042 section 42.4.

**Water consumption.** Visible to whoever pays, who is frequently not the
specifier. Optimised only where regulation forces it.

**Queue time.** Visible to nobody with a budget. Never optimised.

**Acoustic privacy.** Visible to nobody with a budget. Never specified.
Reverberation time in a bathroom has never appeared in a tender document,
per RFC 0042 section 42.8.

**Dignity.** Not a line item anywhere.

### 71.3 The bottom two rows

The two properties users care about most are the two that appear in no
specification, because there is no party in the chain whose budget they
affect.

This is not a moral failure by any participant. Every party is optimising
what they can see and are accountable for. The system produces a bad
outcome from six locally rational actors, which is the definition of a
coordination failure and the reason regulation exists at all.

### 71.4 The fix that would work

Specify outcomes rather than inputs. Not fixture counts, but a maximum
wait time at design occupancy. Not equal floor area, but equal wait time,
per RFC 0057 section 57.4.

Outcome specifications are harder to write, harder to verify, and would
change what gets built. Input specifications are easy, verifiable and
produce the building this document has spent seventy one sections
describing.

Every standards body in every field faces this choice and nearly all of
them choose the verifiable input, because a standard that cannot be
checked cannot be enforced, and so the industry optimises the checkable
thing and the outcome drifts away unmeasured.

## RFC 0072: Continence

### 72.1 Scope

The failure mode that this document has, until now, discussed only as a
system property. Here it is discussed as it actually occurs: in people, at
a prevalence far higher than anybody assumes, across every age group.

### 72.2 Prevalence

Urinary incontinence affects a large minority of women over fifty and a
substantial minority of men over seventy. Faecal incontinence is less
common, more distressing, and far more under reported.

Both are strongly associated with age, childbirth, surgery and several
common conditions. Both are treatable, frequently curable, and both are
presented to a clinician years after onset, on average, if at all.

### 72.3 The delay

The average interval between onset and seeking help is measured in years.
Not weeks. Years.

The reason is entirely the reason this document has given for everything
else: the report requires naming the thing, the naming is humiliating, and
the person waits until the condition makes the humiliation unavoidable.

Section 51.4 said the same thing about cancer screening. This is the same
mechanism applied to a condition that is not fatal but that removes
people's ability to leave their homes.

### 72.4 The consequence

The practical effect of untreated incontinence is that a person maps their
world by facility availability. Journeys are planned around it. Events are
declined. Travel stops. Social contact narrows.

RFC 0059 documented the closure of public facilities as a budget decision
with distributed costs. This is who bears them. Not inconvenience: a
progressive withdrawal from public life, imposed on the people least able
to advocate against it, by a series of individually defensible council
budget lines.

### 72.5 The engineering response

Nothing in this section is a software problem, and the document is not
going to pretend otherwise.

What is available: public facility provision, which is the intervention
that matters most and is being withdrawn; radar key schemes giving access
to locked accessible facilities without requesting a key at a desk, which
removes the public identification from the transaction; published facility
maps, which are cheap and useful; and workplaces that do not require an
explanation for frequency of use.

The last one costs nothing at all and is entirely within the gift of every
manager who will read this.

### 72.6 Why it is in this file

Because it is the point where every abstraction in this document resolves
into a person who did not go to a friend's wedding.

The queue analysis, the reporting rate, the closure economics, the taboo:
they all terminate here. Section 19.1 said an organisation's capacity to
fix a problem is bounded by its willingness to name it.

This is what is on the other side of not naming it.

## RFC 0073: Energy

### 73.1 The hidden load

The energy cost of the system is not the flush. It is everything around
it: heating the water for the basin, heating the room, running the
ventilation continuously, running hand dryers, and pumping and treating
the water at both ends of the network.

Wastewater treatment is among the largest single consumers of electricity
in many municipalities, frequently the largest line in a council's energy
budget, and it runs continuously.

### 73.2 Where the energy goes

| Component                  | Share of system energy |
|----------------------------|------------------------|
| Water heating (basin)      | 31%                    |
| Space heating              | 24%                    |
| Ventilation                | 18%                    |
| Treatment (municipal)      | 15%                    |
| Pumping (supply and waste) | 9%                     |
| Hand drying                | 3%                     |

The debate that consumes all the public attention is the last row.

The two largest rows are addressed by insulating the pipe run and by not
overheating a room that is occupied intermittently, both of which are
unglamorous, cheap, effective, and discussed by nobody.

Optimising the visible three percent while ignoring the invisible
fifty five is the most common pattern in energy discourse and it recurs
everywhere.

### 73.3 Heat recovery

Wastewater leaves a building warm. A drain heat exchanger recovers a
significant fraction of that heat to preheat incoming cold water.

The technology is a coil around a pipe. It has no moving parts, requires
no maintenance, and pays back within years in any building with
substantial hot water use.

It is installed in very little, because it is invisible, it appears on the
capital line, and the saving appears on somebody else's operating line.
Section 71.1, again, for the last time.

### 73.4 Embodied carbon

A ceramic fixture is fired at 1200 C and shipped heavy. The embodied
carbon is significant and is entirely front loaded.

The fixture then lasts, in practice, for decades, and is frequently
replaced during refurbishment while fully functional, for aesthetic
reasons, and disposed of as rubble because vitreous china is not
practically recyclable.

The most environmentally significant decision available with a bathroom
fixture is to keep the one that already exists. This is true of nearly
everything and it is never the decision that gets made, because
refurbishment is a project and maintenance is a cost.

### 73.5 The ventilation trade

Continuous ventilation is required for the odour control that everything
in RFC 0006 depends on, and it exhausts heated air.

Heat recovery ventilation solves this, is standard in new construction in
some countries, and is absent in most retrofits, where the choice is
between a heated room that smells and a cold room that does not.

Most buildings choose neither deliberately. They run an extract fan on a
timer sized by nobody and accept both problems partially.

## RFC 0074: The Night Shift

### 74.1 The 24 hour deployment

Hospitals, data centres, factories, warehouses, transport hubs and
newsrooms operate continuously. Their facilities do not.

Cleaning is scheduled overnight because daytime cleaning disrupts
occupancy, which means the night shift consistently occupies a facility at
the moment it is least serviced and most likely to be out of service.

The night population is smaller, has less voice in the organisation, and
reports less. Their experience of the building is materially worse and
appears in no survey, because the surveys are sent during the day.

### 74.2 The measurement gap

Every metric in Appendix A was collected between 08:00 and 18:00.

This document has spent seventy four sections arguing that measurement
determines what gets fixed, and its own dataset excludes a third of the
day and the people who work it.

The maintainer noticed this in year three and has not corrected it,
because correcting it would require standing in a corridor at 03:00 with a
notebook and nobody volunteered.

A limitation acknowledged and not fixed is still a limitation. It is
recorded here so that the next maintainer does not mistake this document
for complete.

### 74.3 Lone working

A person alone in a building at night who becomes unwell in a locked room
has no colleague to notice.

This is the emergency cord scenario from RFC 0035 section 35.6 with nobody
to respond, and it is the strongest argument in this document for
occupancy sensing, which is also the technology that RFC 0009 section 9.5
demonstrated can be abused.

The resolution is the same as everywhere else: sense the state, not the
person. A stall occupied continuously for ninety minutes is an alert. Who
is in it is not required to generate that alert, is not required to
respond to it, and must not be collected.

Safety and surveillance are separable. They are conflated by every vendor
in the market because the surveillance product is easier to sell.

**Year 1, Q3.** RFC 0007, the queueing analysis. The document stops being
purely a joke at this point and nobody notices for another year.

**Year 2.** The benchmarker contributes Appendix A. The counter stands in a
corridor for ten days. RFC 0009 begins accumulating real incidents. The

**Year 2, Q4.** Second deletion attempt. Stalls at review. RFC 0016 is
written in response, to make the register explicit so that the next
contributor does not have to guess.

**Year 3.** The occupancy dashboard ships. One integer, ninety units. The
only physical change the document has caused.

**Year 3, Q2.** The accessibility section is written after an audit
finding. Three drafts with jokes are discarded. Third deletion attempt,
stalls at review.

**Year 3, Q4.** RFC 0046 written. The document acquires a payload it did
not start with, and the maintainer begins describing the joke as a

**Year 4.** Fourth deletion attempt, stalls at review. RFC 0040
retrospective conducted at lunch, off site, by three people. Action item
recorded: extract the queueing memo. Owner: unassigned. Status: open.

**Year 4, Q3.** Hybrid working policy introduced with fixed days. Peak rho
returns to pre pandemic levels at 60 percent of the demand. The document
predicted this in a table and nobody read the table.

**Now.** Seventy four RFCs, eleven appendices, one dashboard, one memo
unwritten, and a ticket numbered 4003 that has never been closed.

## RFC 0075: Retail

### 75.1 The customer facility

A shop, café or restaurant provides facilities as a cost of doing
business, not as a product. The provision is therefore minimal, the
maintenance is a low priority for staff with other duties, and access is
frequently conditioned on purchase.

Retailers who have measured it consistently find that facility provision
increases dwell time, dwell time increases spend, and the effect is larger
than the cost of provision by a wide margin.

The measurement exists. It is not acted on, because the cost sits in one
budget and the revenue in another, which is section 71.1 for the sixth
time in this document and the reason it keeps recurring is that it is the
single most common structural failure in commercial buildings.

### 75.2 The department store counterexample

Large department stores historically provided generous facilities,
deliberately, as part of a strategy of keeping customers in the building
for a whole day.

They understood that a customer who has to leave to find a bathroom does
not come back, and that facilities were therefore a retention mechanism
rather than a cost.

That understanding was lost along with the format. The stores that
replaced them provide the minimum, have shorter dwell times, and attribute
the difference to consumer behaviour.

### 75.3 The staff facility

Frequently worse than the customer facility, in the same building, for the
people who spend forty hours a week there rather than forty minutes.

Where break duration is short and the facility is distant, the effective
provision is lower than the count suggests, which is the availability
definition problem from Appendix G.

Warehouse operations have been the subject of specific reporting on this
point, and the reporting is consistent enough across employers and
countries to indicate a structural rather than an isolated failure.

Where a system measures productivity continuously and provides facilities
at a fixed distance, the worker is placed in a direct trade between a
measured metric and a physiological need. The system does not have to
prohibit anything. The metric does the prohibiting.

Any metric that a person can improve by neglecting themselves will be
improved that way by somebody, and the fact that nobody instructed them is
not a defence.

## RFC 0076: On Measurement

### 76.1 The recurring theme

Seventy five sections have converged on the same finding from every
direction: what gets measured gets managed, what is easy to measure gets
measured, and the gap between those two facts is where every failure in
this document lives.

Recorded instances:

- Fixture counts measured, wait time not. RFC 0029.
- Facilities built measured, safe use not. RFC 0046.
- Paper cost measured, consumption not. RFC 0018.
- Maintenance uptime measured, availability at arrival not. Appendix G.
- Specification compliance measured, installed base leakage not. RFC 0063.
- Tickets filed measured, failures occurring not. RFC 0037.
- Daytime experience measured, night shift not. RFC 0074.
- Productivity measured, the trade it forces not. RFC 0075.

Eight instances, eight domains, one mechanism.

### 76.2 Why the easy metric wins

It is not laziness. The easy metric wins because it is verifiable,
auditable, comparable between sites, and defensible in a meeting.

A fixture count can be checked by walking around with a clipboard. A wait
time distribution requires instrumentation, a definition, a sampling
strategy and somebody to argue with about the definition.

Organisations select for metrics that survive scrutiny, not metrics that
describe reality. A number that can be challenged is a number that creates
work for the person who published it, and so the numbers that get
published are the ones nobody can argue with, which are precisely the ones
that describe nothing anybody experiences.

### 76.3 What to do about it

Publish the bad metric anyway, alongside the good one. Label its
weaknesses. A wait time estimate with an error bar is worth more than a
fixture count with a decimal place, and the error bar is what makes it
publishable without being indefensible.

Measure the outcome even if you can only measure it badly. Badly measuring
the right thing beats precisely measuring the wrong thing, and every
serious field learns this eventually and every new field learns it late.

### 76.4 The ethical limit

Some things must not be measured even though measuring them would help.

Per stall occupancy by individual would improve capacity planning
substantially. It is prohibited, correctly, permanently, and the loss in
analytic power is the price of a control that does not depend on anybody's
future good behaviour.

The full statement of the principle: the fact that data would be useful is
not an argument that it should be collected. That sentence is the only
thing in this document the maintainer has ever quoted in a design review
outside this file, and it worked, and nobody asked where it came from.

## RFC 0077: The Simulation

### 77.1 Why simulate

The analytic queueing results in RFC 0007 assume Poisson arrivals and
exponential service times. Real arrivals are correlated and real service
times are bimodal, per Appendix A section A.4.

When the assumptions fail, simulate. The code below is the model that
produced the tables in RFC 0034 and RFC 0066.

### 77.2 The model

```ts
type Arrival = { t: number; serviceTime: number }

interface Config {
  stalls: number
  windowMinutes: number
  arrivalsPerHour: (hour: number) => number
  serviceTime: () => number
  balkThreshold: number
  renegeAfter: number
}

function simulate(cfg: Config, seed: number) {
  const rng = mulberry32(seed)
  const arrivals: Arrival[] = []

  for (let h = 0; h < cfg.windowMinutes / 60; h++) {
    const lambda = cfg.arrivalsPerHour(h)
    let t = h * 60
    while (t < (h + 1) * 60) {
      t += -Math.log(1 - rng()) / (lambda / 60)
      if (t < (h + 1) * 60) {
        arrivals.push({ t, serviceTime: cfg.serviceTime() })
      }
    }
  }

  const free: number[] = new Array(cfg.stalls).fill(0)
  const queue: Arrival[] = []
  const waits: number[] = []
  let balked = 0
  let reneged = 0

  for (const a of arrivals) {
    const available = free.filter((f) => f <= a.t).length
    if (available === 0 && queue.length >= cfg.balkThreshold) {
      balked++
      continue
    }

    const idx = free.indexOf(Math.min(...free))
    const start = Math.max(a.t, free[idx])
    const wait = start - a.t

    if (wait > cfg.renegeAfter) {
      reneged++
      continue
    }

    free[idx] = start + a.serviceTime
    waits.push(wait)
  }

  return {
    n: arrivals.length,
    served: waits.length,
    balked,
    reneged,
    meanWait: mean(waits),
    p50: quantile(waits, 0.5),
    p90: quantile(waits, 0.9),
    p99: quantile(waits, 0.99),
  }
}
```

### 77.3 The service time distribution

Bimodal, per Appendix A section A.4. Modelling it as a single exponential
understates the tail by a factor of roughly three and is the reason the
naive calculation in RFC 0034 section 34.2 was wrong twice over.

```ts
function serviceTime(): number {
  // 60% short sessions, 40% with `reading: 'phone'`
  return Math.random() < 0.6
    ? exponential(4.0)   // mean 4 minutes
    : exponential(11.0)  // mean 11 minutes
}
```

### 77.4 Correlated arrivals

The whole point. A Poisson process with the correct daily mean produces
almost no queue. The same daily volume delivered in a burst produces the
observed one.

```ts
function arrivalsPerHour(hour: number): number {
  const shares = [0.14, 0.11, 0.08, 0.06, 0.19, 0.12, 0.09, 0.08, 0.07]
  return DAILY_ARRIVALS * shares[hour]
}
```

Nine numbers. Everything in this document that matters follows from those
nine numbers not being equal to each other.

### 77.5 Results

Ten thousand runs, current building, current policy.

| Config                   | p50 wait | p90 wait | p99 wait | Balk % |
|--------------------------|----------|----------|----------|--------|
| 8 stalls, fixed lunch    | 2.1 min  | 11.4 min | 24.8 min | 18.2%  |
| 8 stalls, staggered      | 0.3 min  | 2.2 min  | 6.1 min  | 2.4%   |
| 14 stalls, fixed lunch   | 0.2 min  | 1.4 min  | 4.2 min  | 1.1%   |
| 14 stalls, staggered     | 0.0 min  | 0.4 min  | 1.6 min  | 0.2%   |
| 8 stalls, hybrid fixed   | 2.4 min  | 12.1 min | 26.0 min | 19.8%  |
| 8 stalls, hybrid stagger | 0.4 min  | 2.6 min  | 7.0 min  | 3.1%   |

Row 2 and row 3 are close. Row 2 costs nothing. Row 3 costs ninety
thousand.

Row 6 is the current state under the hybrid policy if the mandated days
were staggered. It is better than the pre pandemic baseline, at zero cost,
by changing which three days appear in a calendar invitation.

### 77.6 Why the simulation exists

Because a table of numbers from a model can be put in front of somebody
who will not read a queueing textbook, and because the maintainer, having
concluded in RFC 0040 that the memo would never be written, wrote the
model instead and left it here.

It is forty lines of TypeScript. It has been run by three people. Two of
them were the same person twice.

## Appendix N: Errata

Corrections to earlier versions of this document, retained because a
document that quietly fixes its errors teaches nobody anything.

**E1.** RFC 0007 originally stated Little's Law as W = L / lambda in one
place and L = lambda W in another, which are the same equation, but the
first was written with the wrong variable defined. Corrected in year one
by the reviewer, who noted: "it is the one thing in here that holds
unconditionally, so it had better be right."

**E2.** RFC 0013 originally attributed the flush toilet to Crapper.
Corrected. Harington described one in 1596, Cumming patented the S trap in
1775, and Crapper popularised and improved the cistern in the 1860s. The
error survived four months and was corrected by the historian, twice,
because the maintainer reintroduced it once by editing an old paragraph.

**E3.** RFC 0008 originally reported the fibre satisfaction relationship
as monotonic. It is not. The 60 g/day row was collected later and reversed
the conclusion. The original text was left in place with a strikethrough
for one release and then removed, and the maintainer has since decided the
strikethrough was the better choice and should have stayed.

**E4.** RFC 0014 originally claimed the wombat cube forms in the final
metre of the intestine. The mechanism operates over a considerably longer
section and a longer time. Corrected by a reader who works in veterinary
science and who found this document by searching for the mechanism, which
remains the strangest arrival path in the analytics.

**E5.** RFC 0029 originally cited a fixture ratio table from a code that
had been superseded. Corrected. The direction of the finding, that
statutory minima correspond to utilisation above 0.85, held under the new
table as well, which is the only reason the section survived the
correction.

**E6.** Appendix A section A.5 originally reported the festival
availability as beating its SLO. It does not; it fails more often than
promised. The sentence now says so and observes that nobody complained,
which was the actual point and was obscured by the error.

**E7.** RFC 0018 originally computed the annual queueing cost as 410,000.
Recomputed at 340,000 after the hybrid policy reduced attendance. The
older figure appeared in a slide that circulated internally and the
maintainer has been unable to recall it.

A number that escapes into a slide deck cannot be corrected. It is now
independent of you and it will outlive the document it came from. Check
twice before publishing a figure that is easy to quote.
