### O.1 On the last one

The word appears once, in the title of RFC 0002, per RFC 0016 section
16.3.

The correspondent checked twice and did not find it, which suggests they
did not read RFC 0002, which suggests they arrived somewhere in the middle
and read outward, which is how everybody reads this document and is the
reason the register has to hold in every section independently.

You cannot rely on the reader having read the beginning. Nobody has read
the beginning. Write every section as though it is the first one somebody
opens, because for somebody it is.

### O.2 On the fifth one

The message about the screening test is the only piece of correspondence
the maintainer has kept a copy of outside the repository.

RFC 0046 section 46.6 argued that the joke is the delivery mechanism and
the payload is the part that matters. That message is the only direct
evidence in four years that the argument is correct.

One message. Four years. That is the actual return on this document and
it is enough.

## RFC 0078: Objections

Every serious objection raised against this document over four years, with
the best reply the maintainer has.

### 78.1 "It is unprofessional."

Correct. It is in a comment block for that reason.

The reply is not that professionalism does not matter. It is that the
professional version of this document does not exist, has never existed,
and would not be read if it did. The queueing analysis in a memo went
nowhere twice. The same analysis in a joke has been read by most of the
engineering organisation and produced one physical change to the building.

If the professional version worked, this one would be unnecessary. It is
here because the professional version failed.

### 78.2 "It will embarrass the company if a customer sees it."

Possible. It is a comment in a markdown file that is not shipped, not
imported by any module, not rendered anywhere, and contributes zero bytes
to the bundle. Somebody checks every six months.

A customer would have to open the repository, open the README, and scroll
past the actual documentation.

If that customer exists, they have read four years of careful, accurate,
kind writing about a subject most organisations cannot discuss at all, and
the maintainer's honest position is that this reflects better on the
company than the empty README it replaced.

### 78.3 "It is too long."

Correct, and the length is deliberate per RFC 0016 section 16.5. The joke
is that somebody maintained it at length, with discipline, and never broke
character.

A shorter version is a joke. This is a bit, and a bit that stops being
funny and becomes a reference work somewhere around section forty is the
only kind worth committing.

### 78.4 "Nobody asked for it."

Correct. RFC 0060 section 60.5 addresses this directly and concedes that
the base rate on unmandated documents is dreadful.

### 78.5 "The serious sections are manipulative."

The strongest objection, and the maintainer accepts part of it.

The argument is that a reader arrives for the wombats, is disarmed, and is
then handed material about child mortality and cancer screening, and that
using comedy to lower somebody's defences before delivering a serious
message is a technique with an uncomfortable history.

The reply is that the alternative was not delivering the message. RFC 0046
would not have been read as a standalone document. The engagement on
standalone documents about sanitation access is zero.

But the objection stands to this extent: the technique works, techniques
that work can be misused, and a document that congratulates itself on
having a payload should be honest that the mechanism is the same one used
by people with worse payloads.

That is why this section exists, and it is the only concession in this
file that was demanded by a reviewer rather than offered.

### 78.6 "You are hiding behind anonymity."

Correct. RFC 0038 has the maintainer admitting to withdrawing their own
deletion PR because they could not write a sentence in the description
field they were willing to have archived.

The person who wrote a document about how embarrassment suppresses
reporting has not attached their name to it. The document identifies the
mechanism and demonstrates it simultaneously.

There is no good reply to this one. It is simply true.

## RFC 0079: Transferable Findings

The complete list of things in this document that are about something
other than bathrooms. Collected for the reader who wants the payload
without the premise.

**On capacity.** Wait time diverges as utilisation approaches one. Design
for 0.6, not 0.9. Slack is not waste; it is the only thing keeping the
queue bounded. RFC 0007.

**On peaks.** The mean hides the peak, and the peak is the whole problem.
Correlated arrivals break systems that handle the same total volume
comfortably when it is spread out. RFC 0034, RFC 0066.

**On the cheapest fix.** When the cheapest fix is behavioural rather than
capital, the reason it does not happen will not be the reason recorded in
the minutes. RFC 0034 section 34.6.

**On feedback loops.** A system with a long delay between decision and
consequence teaches nothing. Move the check to the moment of the decision
or accept the failure rate forever. RFC 0009 section 9.1.

**On validation.** Where there is no rollback, all quality investment
moves left. Verify before you commit. ADR 002.

**On APIs.** If correct use requires a discipline you cannot enforce, you
have shipped a trap with documentation attached. RFC 0009 section 9.2.

**On specification.** Every specification is read by somebody with more
energy than context. Write for that person. RFC 0037 section 37.3.

**On reporting.** Users will not report failures that embarrass them.
Absence of tickets is not evidence of health. Instrument it or provide
anonymity; encouragement does nothing. RFC 0037 section 37.4.

**On observability.** Observation drives compliance more reliably than
cost, rules or exhortation. RFC 0045, RFC 0065.3, RFC 0067.5.

**On privacy.** Every metric you can collect will eventually be joined
against every other. The only durable control is not collecting the join
key. RFC 0009 section 9.5.

**On measurement.** What is easy to measure gets measured; what matters
usually is not. Measure the outcome badly rather than the input precisely.
RFC 0076.

**On metrics that escape.** A number in a slide deck cannot be recalled.
Check twice before publishing a figure that is easy to quote. Appendix N,
E7.

**On incentives.** When the person choosing a system and the person living
with it are different people, every property only the second one notices
gets optimised away. RFC 0071.

**On externalities.** Costs that are distributed and invisible never
compete with savings that are concentrated and visible, regardless of
magnitude. RFC 0018, RFC 0059.

**On ownership.** Nothing without an owner gets fixed. Not because people
are lazy, but because a recurring problem with no name attached is nobody's
next task. RFC 0037.

**On action items.** A postmortem with six action items is a postmortem
with none. One item, one owner. Appendix C.

**On rules.** Publish the reason with the rule. A rule with a visible
mechanism is followed; one without is negotiated. RFC 0055 section 55.5.

**On assumptions.** The assumption that will destroy you is the one so
obvious it never made it into the document. RFC 0041.

**On oversizing.** Bazalgette doubled his own estimate because he did not
trust it. The network is still adequate 160 years later. RFC 0013.

**On what nobody designs.** The space nobody designs is the space everybody
judges. RFC 0070 section 70.4.

**On partitioned capacity.** Pooled capacity beats partitioned capacity on
every queueing metric. One queue, many servers. RFC 0057 section 57.6.

**On documentation.** It fails by not being written, by not being findable,
and by being read and connected to nothing that can act. Most people fix
only the first. RFC 0060.

## RFC 0080: Unwritten Sections

Proposed, agreed to be worth writing, never written. Retained so that the
next maintainer has somewhere to start.

**On the commute.** The deployment gap between home and office, its
duration, its lack of any facility, and the entire industry of motorway
services that exists to fill it. Notes exist. Nobody has written it up.

**On hotels.** The only environment where a stranger's facility becomes
yours for a night, with a complete absence of the local knowledge that
every other environment depends on, and where the ventilation is always
either absent or a jet engine.

**On the gym.** Contention, timing, shared surfaces, and the one
environment where the acoustic problem is inverted because the ambient
noise floor is already high.

**On the festival, properly.** RFC 0027 section 27.6 is three paragraphs
and a joke about the SLO. The actual operations of servicing several
thousand units over four days deserve a section and the maintainer has
never been sober enough at the relevant moment to take notes.

**On construction sites.** Provision is regulated, provision is minimal,
and the workforce is transient enough that nobody complains. The reporting
rate here is almost certainly the lowest of any workplace and there is no
data at all.

**On the theatre interval.** The 11.4x amplification figure comes from
here and the section explaining it was never written. Fifteen minutes,
several hundred people, a fixed count, and a bell that rings whether you
are finished or not.

**On zero waste and the composting movement.** RFC 0061 section 61.2
covers the engineering. The sociology of who adopts it, why they abandon
it in month three, and what that predicts about every voluntary system
that requires sustained effort, is a better section and is unwritten.

**On the smart fixture.** Devices exist that analyse output and report
health metrics. They are technically impressive, they are a surveillance
architecture attached to the most intimate available data stream, and RFC
0043 section 43.7 gestured at this and then stopped. Somebody should write
it properly before the products are common rather than after.

**On the last one.** The maintainer keeps a note that says only "the last
time" and has not been able to write it. It is about the fact that
everybody who cares for a dying relative learns this domain thoroughly,
suddenly, and permanently, and that nothing in any of the eighty preceding
sections prepares anybody for it.

That note has been in the file for two years as a comment inside a comment
and it is the only thing here the maintainer has been unable to make
either funny or bearable.

## Appendix P: The Memo

The document referenced in RFC 0040 section 40.4 as unwritten. Written
here, finally, in year four, in the only place it will ever appear.

No jokes. This is the version for people with budgets.

---

**To:** Facilities and Finance
**Subject:** Peak capacity in bathroom provision, and a zero cost option

**Summary.** The building's bathroom provision meets statutory minimum and
fails at peak. The cost of the resulting queue is approximately 340,000
per year in paid staff time. There are two remedies: one costs
approximately 60,000 once, the other costs nothing.

**The provision.** 200 staff, 8 stalls, which is the statutory minimum for
this headcount.

**The peak.** Demand is not uniform. 19 percent of daily demand arrives
in the 13:00 hour, driven by catered lunch on Thursdays and by lunch
generally on other days. Measured over four weeks.

**The arithmetic.** At 19 percent of 2,520 daily stall minutes, the 13:00
hour requires 479 stall minutes against 480 available. Effective
utilisation is 1.0. Queueing theory gives an unbounded queue at that
utilisation for the duration of the peak; observed queue depth on floor 3
averages 6.7 and reaches 9.

**The cost.** Mean wait across all sessions is 4 minutes. At 2.1 sessions
per person per day, 200 people, 220 working days, and a loaded hourly
rate, the annual cost of the queue is approximately 340,000. This is paid
staff time spent standing in a corridor. It does not appear in any budget
line because it is distributed across every timesheet.

**Option 1: capacity.** Six additional stalls brings peak utilisation to
0.6 and reduces the mean wait to under 30 seconds. Quoted at approximately
60,000 one time plus floor space. Payback under three months on the staff
time alone.

**Option 2: staggering.** Splitting lunch service into two sittings 30
minutes apart reduces the 13:00 share from 19 percent to approximately 12
percent, which brings peak utilisation to 0.63 with the existing 8 stalls.
Simulation gives a p90 wait of 2.2 minutes against the current 11.4.

Cost: zero. Implementation: a change to the catering schedule.

This was trialled for one week previously and performed as predicted. It
was discontinued. The reason recorded was budget, which does not apply to
this option.

**Recommendation.** Implement option 2 immediately at no cost. Evaluate
option 1 on the twelve month figures.

**One further item.** The accessible facility on floor 3 has been used for
storage and cited in three consecutive audits. This is a single owner
problem with no cost attached and it should not require a memo about
queueing theory to resolve.

---

### P.1 Note on the memo

That is four hundred words. It took an afternoon. Every number in it has
been available for three years.

It is in an appendix, in a comment block, in a README, which is exactly
where RFC 0040 predicted it would end up, and the maintainer is aware that
writing it here rather than sending it is the last and most complete
demonstration of the document's own central finding.

Somebody should send it.

## RFC 0081: The Smart Fixture

One of the unwritten sections from RFC 0080, written, because the products
are arriving and RFC 0080 argued it should be written before rather than
after.

### 81.1 What is being built

Fixtures with sensors that analyse output and report health metrics:
frequency, transit indicators, blood detection, and in research
implementations microbiome composition.

The clinical case is genuine. RFC 0051 established that this is the richest
uninstrumented diagnostic stream the body produces, that it is checked by
almost nobody, and that the delay between onset and presentation is
measured in years for exactly the reasons this document has catalogued.

An automated check removes the reporting step entirely, which is the
intervention RFC 0037 section 37.4 identified as the only one that works.
On the medicine alone, this should exist.

### 81.2 What is also being built

A continuous, involuntary, high resolution biometric stream from inside a
private space, collected in the home, by a device with a network
connection, manufactured by a company, subject to a privacy policy that
can be amended.

The data identifies the individual, per RFC 0043 section 43.7. It reveals
pregnancy, disease, medication, diet, and presence or absence at home,
continuously, with timestamps.

There is no consent flow in a bathroom. A guest does not agree to anything.

### 81.3 The join key problem

RFC 0009 section 9.5 concluded that the only durable privacy control is not
collecting the join key, because every other control depends on future
good behaviour by parties you cannot bind.

A smart fixture's join key is the identity of the person on it, and the
device's entire clinical value depends on knowing who it is. The control
that this document has recommended eleven times is unavailable here by
construction.

That is the whole difficulty. Every other privacy problem in this file had
an architecture that solved it. This one does not.

### 81.4 What a defensible design looks like

Process on the device. Transmit conclusions, not observations: "consult a
clinician" rather than a data stream. Retain nothing beyond the window
required for trend detection. Never transmit raw analysis off the device
under any circumstance including a research programme that asks nicely.

Give the user a physical control that disables it, visible, in the room,
that a guest can see and use without instruction.

Do not build a shared account. Do not build a household dashboard. Do not
build a feature where one person can see another person's readings, ever,
for any reason, including the reasons that sound caring.

### 81.5 What will actually be built

Cloud processing, because on device inference costs engineering effort and
cloud costs a subscription line.

A household dashboard, because it demos well.

A research partnership, because the dataset is scientifically valuable and
the argument for it is sincere and good.

A privacy policy that is accurate at launch.

### 81.6 The recommendation

Buy one if the clinical benefit applies to you, read what it transmits,
and assume that any data leaving the device will eventually be held by a
party you did not choose.

That is not cynicism, it is the base rate. RFC 0009 section 9.5 happened
in one building, to one engineer with good intentions, in six weeks.

## RFC 0082: The Commute

Another from the unwritten list.

### 82.1 The gap

Between the home deployment, which is optimal, and the office deployment,
which is contended, there is an interval of thirty to ninety minutes with
no facility at all.

For most people this is unremarkable. For the population in RFC 0072 it is
the constraint that determines whether the job is possible, and it is never
mentioned in a recruitment process, and it silently removes people from
the applicant pool for reasons no employer ever learns.

### 82.2 The train

A facility exists on longer services and frequently does not on commuter
services, on the grounds that journeys are short. Journeys are short until
they are not, and a stationary train outside a terminus for forty minutes
is a sealed environment with a population and no provision.

The vacuum system, per RFC 0052, fails totally when the tank fills, and on
a busy service in summer it fills.

### 82.3 The motorway services

RFC 0032 section 32.8 noted these are consistently better than expected,
because the operator's revenue depends on people stopping, which aligns
the incentive with the user's experience.

It is the clearest natural experiment available. The same country, the same
regulations, the same construction industry, and the facilities are
markedly better in the one place where the operator profits from you
wanting to be there.

Not regulation. Not culture. Alignment.

### 82.4 The cycle commute

No facility, no fallback, and a physiological profile that makes the need
more likely rather than less.

Cycling infrastructure investment covers lanes, parking and showers at the
destination. Provision along the route is nobody's remit because the route
crosses several authorities and belongs to none of them.

The gap in the middle, owned by nobody, is section 37.2 rendered as
geography.

## RFC 0083: Hotels

### 83.1 The zero knowledge deployment

Every environment in RFC 0027 depends on local knowledge. The operator
knows which floor, which stall, which hour, which supply is reliable.

A hotel removes all of it. New fixture, unknown ventilation, unknown
acoustic isolation, unknown water pressure, unknown supply, and a
neighbouring room separated by a wall of unknown construction.

It is a cold deploy to an unfamiliar production environment with no
staging, no documentation, and no rollback, performed while tired.

### 83.2 The acoustic problem

Hotel bathrooms commonly share a wall with the adjacent room's sleeping
area, because the plumbing stacks are shared and that is the cheapest
layout.

The result is that the acoustic side channel from RFC 0006 section 6.3
operates between strangers who will meet at breakfast.

The countermeasure ranking still applies. The ventilation fan is the best
option and in hotels it is frequently on the same switch as the light,
which forces a choice between cover traffic and vision, and which is a
design decision made by an electrician saving a switch.

### 83.3 The extraction fan on a timer

The variant that runs for fifteen minutes after the light goes off,
audible in the bedroom, in a room the guest is trying to sleep in.

Solves the ventilation requirement and creates an insomnia requirement.
Somebody optimised one specification and never sat in the room.

### 83.4 The two star and the five star

Provision quality is not monotonic in price. Budget chains built recently
to a single standard design frequently outperform expensive older
properties, because the design was done once, carefully, and repeated.

The expensive property has a bathroom converted from a cupboard in 1974
inside a listed building, a shower that requires an explanation, and a
staff member who apologises for it twice a week for thirty years.

Constraints inherited from a previous architecture dominate spend. This is
true of hotels and it is true of every codebase over ten years old.

### 83.5 The travel adaptation

Transit time is disrupted by schedule change, dehydration, unfamiliar diet
and the loss of the cold start window from RFC 0008 section 8.6.

The effect is real, well documented, and universally experienced. It
resolves in two to four days.

The correct response is hydration, fibre, and re establishing a consistent
window as early as possible, which is RFC 0024 sections 24.2 and 24.3
applied to a temporary environment, and which nobody does because they are
on holiday.

## RFC 0084: The Interval

### 84.1 The 11.4x

The highest amplification factor recorded in this document. A three hour
performance, one interval of fifteen or twenty minutes, and the entire
audience released simultaneously by a bell.

Every person in the building has the same constraint, the same window, and
no alternative, and the window is enforced by a second bell.

### 84.2 The arithmetic

Take an audience of 800, a 20 minute interval, an attendance rate of 35
percent during that window, and a mean service time of 90 seconds
including the walk.

280 sessions, 20 minutes, 90 seconds each: 21 servers required at
utilisation 1.0, and per RFC 0007 something closer to 35 for a tolerable
wait.

Provision in older theatres is frequently under 15, distributed unevenly,
and per RFC 0057 the disparity across the wall is severe enough that one
side clears in five minutes and the other does not clear at all.

### 84.3 The design constraint

A theatre cannot be sized for the peak, because the peak occupies 20
minutes of a three hour event and the floor area required would displace
the seats that pay for the building.

This is the one environment in this document with a genuine, unavoidable
economic argument against adequate provision, and it is therefore the one
place where the operational answers matter most: stagger the bell, extend
the interval, open additional provision only during it, and publish where
the short queue is.

Several venues do all four. Most do none and blame the building.

### 84.4 The unmeasured cost

People do not drink during the first half. People decline the second
drink. People do not return after the interval. People choose not to
attend at all.

None of this appears in any venue's reporting, and the last item is
invisible by construction: an audience that did not come cannot be
surveyed about why.

The most important number about any service is held entirely by the people
who are not using it, and no operator has ever collected it.

## RFC 0085: Construction

### 85.1 Regulation

Provision on construction sites is regulated in most jurisdictions, with
specified ratios, requirements for washing facilities, and requirements
for the facilities to be maintained.

Compliance is inspected. Inspection is infrequent. The workforce is
transient, frequently subcontracted, and in a weak position to complain
about anything.

### 85.2 The reporting rate

RFC 0037 section 37.4 established a four percent reporting rate for
embarrassing failures among salaried engineers in a stable job with an
anonymous ticket queue.

On a site where the reporter is a subcontractor on a short engagement, the
mechanism that produces four percent produces something closer to zero,
and the absence of complaints is then cited as evidence of adequacy.

### 85.3 What is actually provided

Portable units, serviced on a schedule set by cost, sited at the perimeter
because that is where the service vehicle can reach, which puts them a
long walk from the work face on any large site.

Distance is the binding constraint. A facility ten minutes away from a
worker with a fifteen minute break is a facility that exists on the
inspection sheet and not in practice.

The availability definition in Appendix G, one more time: uptime is not
availability, and a facility that cannot be reached in the time available
is not available.

## RFC 0086: Voluntary Systems

The sociology section promised in RFC 0080, about who adopts a composting
system and why they abandon it in month three.

### 86.1 The adoption curve

Adoption is driven by identity rather than by economics. The people who
install a composting system are people for whom installing one is
consistent with who they believe they are, and the payback calculation is
constructed afterwards to support a decision already made.

This is not a criticism. It is how nearly every discretionary purchase
works and pretending otherwise produces marketing that does not function.

### 86.2 Month three

The system requires a maintenance action on a schedule. The action is
unpleasant, it is not urgent on any given day, and deferring it has no
immediate consequence.

Month one, the action is performed enthusiastically. Month two, on
schedule. Month three, late. Month four, the system is in a state that
requires more work than the routine action would have, and the operator
now faces a larger task with no enthusiasm remaining.

This is technical debt with a smell. The mechanism is identical: a small
regular cost deferred because deferral is free today, accumulating into a
large irregular cost that arrives when motivation is lowest.

### 86.3 What predicts survival

Not commitment. Not environmental conviction. Not the quality of the
system.

Three things predict survival: whether the maintenance action is on a
calendar rather than in somebody's head, whether two people in the
household know how to do it, and whether the consequence of skipping it is
visible within a week rather than a month.

Those are the same three properties that predict whether any on call
rotation, any dependency upgrade policy, and any documentation practice
survives its first year.

### 86.4 The design implication

If you are building a system that requires sustained voluntary effort,
shorten the consequence loop. Make skipping visible immediately, make the
action smaller and more frequent rather than larger and rarer, and make
sure more than one person can do it.

A system that fails silently for three months and then presents a large
bill will be abandoned by almost everybody, and the people who abandon it
will describe themselves as having failed rather than describing the
design as having failed them.

## RFC 0087: On Humour

### 87.1 Why this is a section

Eighty six sections of a joke, maintained with discipline over four years,
produce a reasonable body of evidence about how the technique works.

### 87.2 The mechanism

The comedy is entirely produced by the collision of a serious frame with
an unserious subject, and it depends on the frame never acknowledging the
collision.

The moment the document winks, the frame collapses and the reader is left
holding a joke about defecation, which is not funny, because everybody has
already heard every joke about defecation.

What is funny is the sustained refusal to admit what the document is
about, in a register that is accurate enough to be genuinely useful.
Accuracy is not decoration here; it is the thing that makes the frame
credible enough to collide with anything.

### 87.3 Why it works as a delivery mechanism

A reader who is amused is a reader who continues. RFC 0046 was read
because it was in section 46 rather than in a document titled after its
subject.

The technique has limits, per RFC 0078 section 78.5, and the objection
that it lowers defences before delivering a payload is not fully
answerable.

The honest position: the technique works, it is used by people with worse
intentions than this document's, and the only defence available is that
the payload is checkable. Every factual claim here can be verified. A
reader who is suspicious of the delivery can audit the content.

Make the payload checkable. That is the only meaningful difference between
persuasion and manipulation that survives contact with a determined
sceptic.

### 87.4 What cannot be done in this register

RFC 0021 could not have jokes in it. RFC 0072 could not. Appendix P could
not.

The rule that emerged over four years: the register works where the
subject is a system, and fails where the subject is a person who is
suffering. Systems can be described comically and accurately at the same
time. People cannot, and the attempt reads as contempt regardless of
intent.

Every section in this file that is about a person is written straight.
That is not squeamishness, it is the only way it works.

### 87.5 The maintenance cost

Sustaining a register across four years, forty odd sections and multiple
contributors requires an explicit style guide, a tonal reviewer with
authority, and a willingness to reject good writing that is in the wrong
key.

Two pull requests were rejected on tone alone. Both authors resubmitted
better versions. Neither was resentful, because the standard was written
down in RFC 0016 before their submission rather than invented in review.

Write the standard down first. Every argument about tone that this
document has avoided was avoided by a page written in year two.

## RFC 0088: The Gym

### 88.1 The inverted acoustic environment

The only environment in this document where the ambient noise floor is
already high enough that the countermeasure in RFC 0006 section 6.3 is
unnecessary.

Music, machines, ventilation and conversation produce a broadband floor
that provides cover traffic continuously, for free, as a side effect of
the primary activity.

It is the best acoustic privacy of any shared environment in the matrix
and it is entirely accidental.

### 88.2 The contention profile

Peaks at 07:00, 12:30 and 18:00, driven by the working day, with the
evening peak the sharpest.

Provision is typically sized for changing room occupancy rather than for
facility demand, which are different distributions: changing room demand
is spread across the session, facility demand is concentrated at the start
and end.

The result is adequate lockers and inadequate stalls, which is a
provisioning error that follows directly from measuring the wrong
population.

### 88.3 The physiological load

Exercise increases motility. Vigorous endurance exercise increases it
substantially, and the effect is well known to every distance runner and
documented in the sports medicine literature.

The demand profile in a gym is therefore not merely the general population
profile shifted in time. It is elevated, and it is elevated specifically
among the users who are working hardest.

No gym has ever sized for this, and the people affected are the least
likely to raise it, because raising it means describing it.

### 88.4 The marathon

The extreme case. Tens of thousands of participants, a synchronised start,
elevated physiological demand, and provision that is temporary and fixed.

Queue depth at a large event start line routinely exceeds anything else in
this document, the wait exceeds the time available before the start, and
the resulting behaviour is well documented, widely photographed, and
tolerated by everybody involved because there is no alternative.

Event organisers know the numbers precisely. Provision is a direct
function of the budget, the budget is a function of entry fees, and the
queue is the variable that absorbs the shortfall.

Nowhere else in this document is the trade so explicit or so cheerfully
accepted by the people paying for it.

## RFC 0089: To a New Engineer

The document's advice, extracted, in the form the maintainer would give it
to somebody in their first year.

### 89.1 Learn the building before you need it

Find the quiet floor in your first week. Every building has one, it is
usually near a department with different hours, and knowing it is worth
more than any other piece of local knowledge you will acquire this year.

The same applies to everything else about the organisation. The map that
matters is never the one on the wall.

### 89.2 Do the cheap thing while it is still cheap

Thirty two percent of the incidents in this document are somebody
deferring an action that was free at the time and expensive later.

Utilisation only goes up. Queues only get longer. The conversation only
gets harder. The migration only gets bigger.

There is a moment when the fix is trivial and you will not notice it,
because trivial fixes do not announce themselves. Assume the moment is
now.

### 89.3 Check before you commit

Where there is no rollback, all your quality investment moves to the
front. Most systems you work on will have more rollback than this one, and
you will still be surprised how often the answer is none.

Two seconds of preflight has the best expected value of any operation in
this entire document.

### 89.4 Believe the first warning

Two `ClogError` events were ignored in ninety seconds and the consequence
was four hours.

The first anomaly is the cheapest one you will ever get. It arrives when
the situation is still recoverable and it looks like noise, which is
exactly why it is ignored.

### 89.5 Assume nobody is reporting

The reporting rate for an embarrassing failure is four percent. For an
ordinary failure it is maybe forty.

Whatever your ticket queue says is happening, more is happening. Instrument
what you can, ask directly about what you cannot, and never conclude from
silence that things are fine.

### 89.6 One owner, one number

Nothing without an owner gets fixed. If you find a recurring problem and
you want it fixed, the useful question is not "how do we fix it" but "whose
name goes next to it", and if the answer is nobody then the answer to the
first question is never.

If you are willing to be that name, say so. It is the rarest and most
valuable thing anybody does in an organisation and it is almost never
rewarded proportionally.

### 89.7 Write it down

Everything in this document was known by somebody before it was written.
None of it existed as an artefact.

The gap between what an organisation knows and what it has written down is
enormous, and closing a piece of it is available to you on any afternoon,
for free, with no permission required.

### 89.8 Be kind about it

The four percent reporting rate is not a moral failure by your colleagues.
It is what happens to ordinary people in a system that makes reporting
costly.

Design the system so the report is cheap, and if you cannot, do not blame
the people who did not make it.

### 89.9 And

Do not flush anything with wet tensile strength. Somebody has to go down
there.

## RFC 0090: On Waiting

### 90.1 What a queue is

A queue is a mechanism for converting a shortage into a delay, and the
delay is paid by the people with the least ability to avoid it.

Every queue in this document is that. The office queue is paid by whoever
cannot shift their lunch. The airport queue is paid by whoever has the
tightest connection. The theatre queue is paid by whoever sits furthest
from the door.

A queue is not neutral. It allocates, and it allocates by whatever
attribute correlates with the ability to wait.

### 90.2 Who waits

Waiting is cheap for somebody with a flexible schedule and expensive for
somebody on a fixed break, on a clock, or with a child.

Any system that resolves shortage by queueing has therefore made a
distributional choice, whether or not anybody involved intended one, and
that choice is invisible in every metric that reports averages.

The mean wait is 4 minutes. Nobody waits 4 minutes. Some people wait
nothing and some wait twenty, and which group you are in is determined by
facts about your life rather than facts about the building.

### 90.3 The alternatives

Every alternative to queueing is worse in a way that is more visible.

Price allocates by wealth, and everybody sees it. Reservation allocates to
whoever games the system, per RFC 0009 section 9.4. Priority allocates by
whoever assigns priority. Lottery allocates randomly, which is fair and
which nobody accepts for anything that feels like a need.

Queueing wins because its unfairness is diffuse, uncounted, and borne by
people who do not compare notes. It is not chosen because it is fair. It
is chosen because its unfairness does not generate complaints.

### 90.4 The only real fix

Capacity. Everything else is a scheme for deciding who suffers.

This document has spent ninety sections on measurement, incentives,
ownership, arithmetic and register, and the finding underneath all of it
is that the queue exists because there are eight stalls and there should
be fourteen, and no amount of analysis substitutes for building six more.

The analysis is worth doing because it tells you how much the shortage
costs and who pays. It is not a substitute for the six stalls, and a
document that produces beautiful analysis and no stalls has, in the end,
produced a document.

## RFC 0091: The City

### 91.1 The invisible layer

Beneath every city is a network built mostly by people who are dead,
maintained by people nobody can name, funded by a line on a bill nobody
reads, and thought about only when it fails.

It is the largest, oldest, most consequential piece of infrastructure most
people will ever depend on, and its defining property is that a
successfully operating sewer is completely undetectable.

### 91.2 The maintenance paradox

Infrastructure that works is invisible. Invisible infrastructure has no
constituency. Infrastructure with no constituency loses funding
arguments to infrastructure people can see.

The result is a systematic bias in every public budget toward things that
are noticed and away from things whose only observable property is that
nothing bad happened.

Bazalgette's network survives because it was oversized past the point
where any subsequent generation had to make a decision about it. He
protected it from the political process by making the political process
unnecessary for 160 years.

That is a strategy. If you build something that will be starved by future
budget cycles, build it big enough that the starvation does not matter.

### 91.3 The reckoning

Those networks are now reaching the end of the margin. Populations have
grown past the projections, paved surfaces have removed the absorption
that the storm capacity assumed, and the overflow events in RFC 0058
section 58.4 are the visible symptom of a design margin that has finally
been consumed.

The engineering answer is separation of foul and surface water, storage,
and sustainable drainage that puts absorption back. All of it is expensive,
none of it is visible, and all of it protects against an event that has
not happened yet.

Every argument for it is an argument for spending money now to prevent
something later, which is the argument that loses in every budget process
ever convened, until the thing happens.

### 91.4 What changed the last time

Not evidence. The evidence was identical for years.

What changed was that the failure reached the people with the budget, in
1858, through the window.

Publication is the modern equivalent. Discharge volumes that were
unmeasured for a century, then measured and unpublished, then published,
produced political consequences within a single season.

Measurement changes nothing. Publication changes everything. This document
has now arrived at that sentence three times from three directions and it
is the closest thing it has to a thesis about how anything ever gets
fixed.

## RFC 0092: On Being Wrong

### 92.1 What this document got wrong

Appendix N lists seven factual errors, corrected. This section lists the
judgements that were wrong, which is a different and more useful list.

### 92.2 The audience

The document assumed that a correct analysis, well written, would
eventually reach somebody who could act on it.

Four years of evidence says it will not. Analysis does not travel upward on
its own merits. It travels when somebody with standing carries it, and
nobody with standing was ever going to carry a document in this register.

RFC 0040 identified this at year four. It was identifiable at year one and
the maintainer did not want to see it, because seeing it would have meant
either writing the memo or admitting the document was for its own sake.

### 92.3 The dashboard

The document takes credit for the occupancy display in half a dozen
places.

The dashboard was built by somebody who had read one paragraph of this
file and was already inclined to build it. The counterfactual where the
document does not exist and the dashboard is built anyway is entirely
plausible.

Attributing an outcome to your own influence, when the person who acted was
already going to act, is the most common error in every retrospective ever
written, and this document committed it repeatedly in its own.

### 92.4 The tone about facilities

Early sections treat the facilities team as an obstacle. That was
unfair and it took two years to correct.

Facilities operates with a contract awarded on price by somebody else, a
ticket queue with no triage function, a backlog with no prioritisation
authority, and a headcount set by a budget they do not control.

Every response quoted in Appendix J that reads as obstructive is a
correct answer from a team that has been given no mechanism to give a
different one. The failure is structural, per RFC 0037, and the document
spent two years pointing at the people rather than the structure.

### 92.5 The survey

Appendix A section A.7 reports a satisfaction survey run once and never
repeated.

It was not repeated because the result was inconvenient to nobody in
particular and interesting to nobody in particular, and the person who ran
it lost interest.

A single measurement is an anecdote with a sample size. The document has
cited that survey as evidence eleven times, which is eleven times more
than one uncalibrated single wave survey can support.

### 92.6 The estimate that escaped

Appendix N, E7. A figure computed with a defensible method, quoted in a
slide, superseded by better data, and now uncorrectable.

The lesson is recorded there. It is repeated here because it is the
mistake in this document most likely to be repeated by its readers, and
because the maintainer would like at least one error in this file to
prevent somebody else's.

### 92.7 Why this section exists

A document that argues for honest postmortems and does not conduct one on
itself is an advertisement, not an argument.

## RFC 0093: The Environment Matrix, Revisited

### 93.1 Four years on

RFC 0027 published the matrix in year one. This is the same table with
four years of data, and the changes are more interesting than the
original.

| Environment | SLA (Y1) | Actual (Y1) | Actual (Y4) | Change driver     |
|-------------|----------|-------------|-------------|-------------------|
| Home        | 99.99%   | 99.98%      | 99.99%      | Remote working    |
| Office      | 99.9%    | 97.2%       | 98.6%       | Load left         |
| Airport     | 99.0%    | 91.4%       | 90.8%       | Nothing changed   |
| Train       | 90.0%    | 88.1%       | 84.2%       | Deferred servicing|
| Festival    | 50.0%    | 12.3%       | 14.0%       | Noise             |
| Camping     | n/a      | 100%        | 100%        | Single tenancy    |
| Aircraft    | 99.5%    | 98.9%       | 97.4%       | Density increase  |

### 93.2 The office improvement

The only environment that improved materially, and it improved because
demand left rather than because capacity arrived.

Nothing was built. Nothing was fixed. The number moved because the
population moved, and if attendance mandates tighten it will move back,
and the six stalls will still not exist.

An improvement you did not cause is not an improvement you can rely on.

### 93.3 The aircraft decline

Seat density increased across the industry over the period. Facility count
per aircraft did not.

More clients, same servers, and per RFC 0007 the queue grows
disproportionately rather than proportionally. The measured availability
decline of 1.5 points understates the experience considerably, because
availability counts whether a facility exists and not whether the seatbelt
sign has frozen the queue for twenty minutes.

### 93.4 The train decline

Servicing intervals extended under cost pressure. Tank capacity unchanged.
Per RFC 0052 section 52.2 the failure is total when it occurs, and the
frequency of total failure rose.

This is the single worst trend in the table and it affects a captive
population with no alternative for hours.

### 93.5 The festival non result

An improvement from 12.3 percent to 14.0 percent across four years and
several events is noise, and the document reports it as noise rather than
as progress, which is the correct treatment and is rarer in published
figures than it should be.

### 93.6 What the table shows

One environment improved because its load left. Three declined because
capacity was held flat while demand rose. One is stable because it has a
single tenant. One is unchanged because nobody has ever tried.

Four years, ninety three sections, and the table is worse than when it
started.

### 94.1 On the confidence column

Nine claims are High and derive from counting, weighing, invoices or
public data. Fourteen are Medium and derive from models built on measured
inputs. The rest are Low and derive from one person's self report or one
uncalibrated survey.

Every claim this document repeats most often is in the Low or Medium band,
which is normal, unavoidable, and worth saying out loud.

The claims in the High band are boring: stall counts, ticket ages,
invoice numbers, published figures. The interesting claims are the weak
ones. That is also normal, and it is why the confidence column exists.

### 94.2 What would improve it

Two sensors, per RFC 0069. Arrival rate and service time, measured
continuously, aggregated at the device, retained for an hour.

That single change moves the four most cited numbers in this document from
Low to High and costs less than a keyboard.

It has not been done, because it is nobody's job, which is where every
section in this document ends and where this one ends too.

## Appendix Q: The Last Time

The note referenced in RFC 0080 as unwritten. Written, badly, because the
maintainer is leaving and it will not be written otherwise.

---

Everybody who has cared for a dying relative learns this subject
completely, in a matter of weeks, with no preparation.

You learn the equipment. You learn what the district nurse can bring and
what she cannot. You learn which of the things advertised as discreet
actually are. You learn to do it without the other person having to say
anything, because they cannot bear to say anything, and the whole of your
skill is in making it look like it took no effort and required no
decision.

You learn that the person you are helping is more distressed about this
than about dying, and that this is not irrational, and that no amount of
telling them it is fine makes it fine, and that you say it anyway.

Nothing in the preceding ninety four sections is any use for this.

The queueing analysis is not relevant. The measurement argument is not
relevant. There is no incentive design, no ownership question, no metric.
There is a person who spent their whole life managing this in private, as
everyone does, and who cannot now, and a second person who loves them
learning to do it in an afternoon.

What is relevant, and the only reason this appendix exists in a document
that is otherwise a joke, is the thing RFC 0048 said in year two: there is
no neutral word, and there is no neutral practice, and every culture on
earth has built a taboo here and no two of them agree.

That taboo, which is constructed, which was invented by people who could
have chosen otherwise, is what makes the last weeks of a person's life
harder than they have to be. Not the illness. The shame, which nobody
chose to feel and everybody feels, and which arrived from somewhere and
could have arrived differently.

The people who do this work professionally, in hospitals and care homes
and in people's houses, on low pay and no status, per RFC 0053 section
53.1, spend their careers reducing that shame for strangers, one person at
a time, with no method available except unbroken ordinariness.

Being ordinary about it is the entire skill. That is what they do. It is
the most difficult thing described anywhere in this file and the only one
this document has nothing to teach about.

---

That is the note. It is two years late and it is not good enough, and the
maintainer is publishing it anyway on the principle stated in RFC 0060:
the failure mode that matters most is the thing that never got written
down.

## RFC 0095: On Stopping

### 95.1 The decision

The maintainer is leaving the company. RFC 0038 said this would happen
before the queue was fixed and it has.

The document stays. It is in git, it has never rendered, it costs zero
bytes, and per RFC 0028 section 28.5 the mechanism protecting it is that
removing it requires somebody to type a sentence they do not want
archived.

### 95.2 Why not finish it

Because it is not the kind of thing that finishes. There is no state in
which every section is written, and RFC 0080 lists nine that are not, and
two of the nine were written in the last month specifically because
listing them made them nag.

A document that could be finished would have been a memo, and the memo is
in Appendix P and it is four hundred words and it took an afternoon and
nobody sent it.

### 95.3 What is left undone

The memo, unsent. The two sensors, uninstalled. The six stalls, unbuilt.
Ticket #4003, unanswered. The night shift data, uncollected. The survey,
unrepeated.

Every one of those is small, cheap, and available to anybody who wants it,
which is the definition of the work that never gets done.

### 95.4 The handover

RFC 0060 section 60.6 is addressed to the next maintainer and it stands.

The additions: the numbers in Appendix A are three years old and the
building has changed. Appendix N exists so that corrections are visible
rather than silent, and it should keep growing. Appendix Q should not be
edited by anybody.

The register is in RFC 0016. Guard it. It is the whole product.

### 95.5 The last finding

Four years of analysis produced one integer on a wall.

That is a poor return by any measure this document has proposed, and the
document has been honest about it in RFC 0040, in RFC 0092, and here.

It is also one integer more than the correct, professional, unfunny
version of this analysis produced, and that version was attempted twice.

The maintainer's final position, offered without confidence: the work that
gets done is not the work that is most important, and it is not the work
that is best argued. It is the work that somebody could not stop
themselves from doing.

This document is what that looks like when it happens to a person who
should have been fixing the build.

## RFC 0096: Final Questions

**Q: Is it finished?**

No. See RFC 0095 section 95.2.

**Q: Will anybody build the six stalls?**

No.

**Q: Was it worth it?**

One dashboard, one screening test, two people quoting the line about slack
in design reviews without knowing where it came from, and a facilities
team that got a fairer hearing in year three than in year one.

Against four years of intermittent evenings.

The honest answer is that the maintainer does not know how to price this
and has stopped trying, which is the answer most people reach about most
of the work they are proudest of.

**Q: What is the single most useful thing in here?**

For an engineer: slack is not waste.

For a building: stagger the lunch.

For a person: if something has changed and stayed changed for two weeks,
say so out loud to a professional.

**Q: What is the single funniest thing in here?**

The reviewer maintains it is the review comment on the `cover: 'cough'`
proposal, which closed a pull request about a bathroom by citing the
padding oracle literature.

The maintainer maintains it is the wombat.

**Q: And the word?**

Once. RFC 0002. Where it functions as the premise rather than as a joke.

Nobody has ever needed it twice.

## RFC 0097: The Counterfactual

### 97.1 The question

What would have happened if the memo had been sent in year one.

The maintainer has thought about this more than is healthy and the honest
answer is: probably nothing, and the reasons are worth writing down
because they generalise.

### 97.2 The optimistic branch

The memo lands. Somebody in finance reads four hundred words, recognises
that the staggered lunch option costs nothing, and asks catering to run
two sittings.

Peak utilisation drops to 0.63. The queue disappears. The document is
never written, the wombat section does not exist, RFC 0046 is never read
by anybody, and the correspondent in Appendix O never books the screening
test.

The building is better. Everything else is worse. This is the branch the
maintainer finds hardest to look at.

### 97.3 The realistic branch

The memo lands. It is read. It is agreed with. It is added to a list.

The list is prioritised against items with owners, deadlines and
executive sponsors. It ranks below all of them, permanently, because a
memo without a sponsor is a suggestion.

Six months later somebody asks whether anything happened about the
bathrooms and nobody remembers the memo, because it was four hundred words
in an email and email is where analysis goes to be agreed with and
forgotten.

This branch is what happened to the analysis twice before the document
existed. It is not speculation. It is the observed base rate.

### 97.4 The branch nobody considers

The memo lands, is acted on, the lunch is staggered, and it is quietly
abandoned after three weeks because people like eating together.

This actually occurred, per RFC 0034 section 34.6, in a one week trial
that worked exactly as predicted.

The intervention was not blocked by budget, by disagreement, or by
ignorance. It was blocked by a preference that nobody was willing to state
as the reason, and which no memo can address because no memo can argue
with it.

### 97.5 What this says about analysis

Analysis changes decisions where the obstacle is ignorance. It changes
nothing where the obstacle is preference, incentive, or ownership, and the
obstacle is almost never ignorance.

This document has ninety seven sections of analysis and one integer of
outcome, and the ratio is not a failure of the analysis.

Before writing the next carefully reasoned document, ask what the obstacle
actually is. If the answer is not ignorance, write something else, or
change something else, or accept that you are writing for the pleasure of
it, which is a legitimate reason and is the true reason for most of this
file.

## RFC 0098: On Deletion

### 98.1 For whoever eventually does it

Somebody will delete this. It should be somebody who has read it, and this
section is here so that person has what they need.

### 98.2 The case for deletion

It is unprofessional in a professional artefact. It is enormous. It is
unmaintained the moment the current maintainer leaves. It is a liability
of unknown size in an acquisition, a due diligence process, or an
open sourcing.

It is also, per RFC 0078 section 78.6, written anonymously by somebody who
argued at length that anonymity is how problems stay unsolved.

Every one of those is a good argument. The document has never had a good
answer to the first four.

### 98.3 What to preserve

If it goes, take these with you:

RFC 0034 and Appendix P, which are the queueing analysis and the memo, and
which are the only parts anybody in this building could act on.

RFC 0079, which is the payload with the premise removed and which is four
pages of ordinary engineering advice that happens to have been derived
from bathrooms.

Appendix N, so that the errors stay visible somewhere.

Appendix Q, which does not belong to the document and should go to
whoever wants it.

### 98.4 How to do it

Open the PR. Write a real description. Say what you are removing and why,
in a sentence you are content to have archived, because it will be.

That last requirement is the only thing that has ever stopped anybody, per
RFC 0028 section 28.5, and it is not a defence mechanism the document built
deliberately. It is a property of the subject, and it is the same property
that keeps the tickets unfiled and the screening tests unbooked, operating
here in the document's own favour.

If you can write the sentence, you should delete it. Somebody who can
write that sentence plainly is exactly the person this document has spent
ninety eight sections asking for.

### 98.5 A request

Close ticket #4003 first.

## Colophon

Begun during a deploy freeze, in a comment block, in the README of a
front end repository, because the build was broken and there was a
queueing textbook open on the desk for an unrelated reason.

Written over four years by nine people, of whom one wrote most of it, one
edited all of it, and one stood in a corridor for ten days with a
notebook.

Ninety eight numbered sections. Twenty appendices. Zero renders. Zero
bytes in the bundle, verified every six months by somebody who has never
identified themselves.

Four attempted deletions, all withdrawn or stalled at review. One
withdrawn by its own author, who was also the author of the document, four
minutes after opening it.

One physical change to the building: an integer on a wall, ninety currency
units, still working.

One memo, written, unsent, in Appendix P.

One ticket, open, unanswered, since year two.

The word appears once.

If you have read this far, you have read roughly ten thousand lines about
a subject you were not expecting to think about today, in a file that has
never been rendered, in a repository you may not work in.

The queue is still there. The stalls were never built. Somebody should
stagger the lunch.

Slack is not waste.

Single lines left in the file over four years, in review comments, in
commit messages, and in one case in a variable name. Collected here
because several of them are better than the sections they were attached
to.

> Slack is not waste. It is the only reason the queue stays bounded.

> The mean hides the peak and the peak is the whole problem.

> Measure the outcome badly rather than the input precisely.

> Uptime is not availability.

> Distributed costs never compete with concentrated savings, whatever the

> The space nobody designs is the space everybody judges.

> Publication changes what measurement does not.

> Utilisation only goes up.

> Your outbound path is an inbound path.

> Waste is unbuilt product.

> Internalise the externality and behaviour changes without enforcement.

> Observation drives compliance more reliably than cost.

> A sign asking people not to do a thing is evidence the room makes it
> convenient.

> Move the bin. Remove the sign.

> The simplest possible implementation, kept available, in case the
> sophisticated one fails.

> A document that breaks character once has no character.

> Explain the joke and the joke is gone.

> Write every section as though it is the first one somebody opens.

> The metric does the prohibiting. Nobody has to.

> Any metric a person can improve by neglecting themselves will be.

> Analysis changes decisions where the obstacle is ignorance, and the
> obstacle is almost never ignorance.

> The work that gets done is the work somebody could not stop themselves
> from doing.

### U.1 The variable name

In the simulation in RFC 0077, an early revision contained:

```ts
const slackIsNotWaste = cfg.stalls - Math.ceil(peakDemand / 60)
```

It was renamed to `headroom` in review, with the comment: "correct, and
not in the code."

The reviewer was right and the maintainer has regretted it since.

### U.2 The commit message

The best commit message in the file's history, in full:

```
docs(readme): the lights

Eleven weeks. One ticket. One day to fix.

Adding this as RFC 0009 section 9.3 because if it is not written
down somewhere it will happen again on a different floor and we
will all pretend to be surprised.
```

### U.3 The review comment

The longest review comment in the repository's history is on the
`cover: 'cough'` proposal and runs to four paragraphs, of which the
operative one is:

> Your countermeasure is perfectly correlated with the signal it is
> masking. This is not padding. This is announcing the length of the
> plaintext and then announcing it again. Please read literally anything
> about padding oracles and then close this.

The proposal was closed. The author has since said it is the most
thoroughly they have ever been refuted about anything.

### U.4 The last one

Left in the file, uncommented, above the closing tag, by somebody who
never identified themselves and never added anything else:

> Whoever cleans this building has read every one of these sections
> without knowing they exist, in the sense that they have lived all of
> them. None of it was news. We wrote down what they already do.

The maintainer has left it exactly where it was found.

## Closing

There is nothing else. The document ends here, unfinished in the way that
everything of this kind is unfinished, in a comment block, in a file that
has never rendered, in a repository that builds a website about something
else entirely.

The queue forms at 13:30.

Slack is not waste.

### V.1 What the log shows

Sixty sessions over four years, which is fifteen a year, which is roughly
one a month with clusters.

The clusters are the interesting part. Every one of them follows an
incident, an audit, or a deletion attempt. The document does not grow
steadily; it grows in response to the building doing something.

That is the correct behaviour for documentation and it happened by
accident rather than by policy. Nobody planned to write RFC 0021 the week
after an audit finding. The finding simply made it unavoidable.

### V.2 The hours

Twenty three of sixty sessions began after 20:00. Eleven began after
22:00. Four began after 23:00.

None began between 01:00 and 07:00, which is the window RFC 0074 says the
document has no data about, and the maintainer notes without further
comment that they were also asleep.

### V.3 The deletion attempts

Four are logged. Y1 W22 is the maintainer's own, withdrawn in four
minutes.

All four cluster in the second half of a year, which the maintainer has
no explanation for and has decided is coincidence rather than something
about the timing of performance reviews.

### V.4 The last entry

Y4 W41 is Appendix Q, which took one session and two years.

There are no entries after it. The register ends where the writing ends,
which is here.

The queue forms at 13:30.

Slack is not waste.

### W.1 On the count of one

RFC 0016 section 16.3 permits exactly one occurrence, in the title of
RFC 0002, where it functions as the premise rather than as a joke.

Two contributors have attempted a second. Both were rejected. The second
argued that the rule is arbitrary, and the rule is arbitrary, and an
arbitrary rule consistently applied is worth more than a principled rule
applied by judgement.

That is the last thing this document has to say about itself, and it is
a better summary of how it survived than anything in RFC 0095.

### W.2 On the count of zero

Zero memos sent. Zero tickets closed.

Ninety eight sections, twenty three appendices, four years, nine
contributors, one notebook in a corridor for ten working days, and the
two numbers that describe whether any of it changed anything are both
zero, unless you count the integer on the wall, which the document has
counted repeatedly and which RFC 0092 section 92.3 concedes it probably
cannot claim.

The maintainer has decided to leave both numbers in the table rather
than round them into a sentence that sounds better.

### W.3 The genuinely final note

Somebody will read this in a repository they have just been given access
to, on their first week, scrolling a README to find the install
instructions, and they will find ten thousand lines about bathrooms.

To that person: the install instructions are at the top. They are three
commands and they work.

Everything below them is a comment, costs nothing, ships nothing, and
was written by people who worked here before you and who mostly do not
any more.

Go to floor 5. Finance keeps different hours.

Do the cheap thing while it is still cheap.

Check before you commit.

Believe the first warning.

Write it down.

And if something has changed and stayed changed for two weeks, say so
out loud to a professional. That is the only sentence in this file that
was ever worth ten thousand lines.

Volume I ran to ten thousand lines and ended with the observation that
the only sentence worth ten thousand lines was the one telling you to
see a professional if something changes and stays changed. That is

worse.

Volume I was written by people who worked here. Volume II was
assembled, on request, in one sitting, from the same source material: a
building with too few cubicles, a queue that forms at 13:15, and a set
of engineers who could not stop noticing that the queue obeys the same
equations as everything else they get paid to think about.

The queueing theory throughout is correct. Little's Law is Little's Law
whether the units are requests or people. The divergence of waiting
time as utilisation approaches one is not a joke; it is the reason a
building that is fully compliant on paper is intolerable in practice,
and it is the reason adding one unit to a saturated floor feels
transformative while reading as marginal in a spreadsheet.

Everything else is a place to put it.

The rules of Volume I still hold. Nothing in here renders. Nothing in
here ships. The install instructions are at the top of the file and
they are three commands and they work. The accessibility, continence
and screening material is written straight, because those parts are not
funny and the people they concern have heard enough jokes.

## Incident 0001: The unit adjacent to the server room backed up

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 5h20m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 17:10, Cubicle 5 queued unboundedly. Root cause was seasonal demand
shift nobody had modelled. Users experienced elevated dispenser refill
interval for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    11:40  full service restored
    12:00  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:00  workaround reposted, laminated
    14:05  escalation to Building Management
    14:30  contractor dispatched
    16:45  noor notices p50 hold latency is out of band
    17:10  workaround removed by cleaning

### Contributing factors

- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot
- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice
- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.

## RFC 0104: The Economics of the Security Guard Route

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: priya.

Cubicle 5 is the only component in the building with a hard capacity of
one and no queue visibility. Redundancy that shares a stack is not
redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 38 weeks and
was visible in extract-fan duty cycle the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at mean time to seat.

Treat the following as directional.

### Proposal

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
2. Add a second bin.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
5. Escalate to building management and wait.
6. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    flush success rate             182.53    169.46    -13.07
    queue depth                    177.67    223.35     45.68
    p50 hold latency               165.86    171.54      5.68

The improvement in p50 hold latency did not survive contact with a fire
drill at 13:20, precisely at peak.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Derivation 01

Take arrivals lambda = 14.79 per hour and service rate mu = 16.41 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.180.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.20. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

## RFC 0112: A Proposal for Timing and Trust

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: RFC 0022. Reviewers: mark.

Every measurement we take of walkaway rate changes the thing measured,
because people can see the clipboard. Latency is a distribution, and
the tail is where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 28 weeks and was visible in
renege rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
re-entry rate.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    post-lunch arrival rate        131.56     68.92    -62.63
    p999 hold latency               66.72     75.45      8.73
    cubicle occupancy              127.20    168.92     41.72
    paper turnover                  43.43     56.60     13.17

The improvement in abort rate did not survive contact with a fire drill
at 13:20, precisely at peak.

### Objections

  kwame: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

  yusuf: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

## Incident 0005: The executive washroom regressed

closing two cubicles without notice. Users experienced elevated renege

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, F, H, P, R, S

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

### Glossary: B, C, D, H, S, T, W

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## RFC 0123: The Ethics of Grab Rails

Status: Draft. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: mark.

Cubicle 3 degrades gracefully right up to the point where it does not,
and there is no warning band in between. Redundancy that shares a stack
is not redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a contractor closing two cubicles without
notice. The underlying condition had been present for 29 weeks and was
visible in abort rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at urgency index.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Add a second bin.

### Objections

  erika: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

---

### Derivation 03

Take arrivals lambda = 21.65 per hour and service rate mu = 15.07 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.479.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 3.7 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 1.32. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0127: Revisiting Sensor Firmware

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: hana, juno, kwame.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. The cheapest intervention is almost
always scheduling, and it is almost always the last one tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the extract fan being on a timer nobody could
locate. The underlying condition had been present for 29 weeks and was
visible in queue depth the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at dispenser refill interval.

### Proposal

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
4. Add a second bin.
5. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
6. Escalate to building management and wait.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    re-entry rate                   43.40     28.19    -15.21
    time-to-first-flush            156.59    137.42    -19.17
    lock-jiggle events             144.85     69.41    -75.44
    false-occupancy signals         41.16     43.39      2.23

The improvement in false-occupancy signals did not survive contact with
a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

### Runbook 01: no paper, all floors

Trigger: queue depth above threshold for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
2. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
3. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
4. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
5. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.

Escalation: Facilities, then Procurement, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0007: The executive washroom lost quorum

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 2h08m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 12:15, the accessible stall on 4 lost quorum. Root cause was a
partial blockage in the 110mm stack. Users experienced elevated renege
rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    11:05  ticket closed without comment
    13:00  second report, in the wrong channel
    14:05  workaround reposted, laminated
    15:10  escalation to Building Management
    15:55  full service restored

### Contributing factors

- The door lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left
- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor
- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: callum. Status: open.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: sanne. Status: open.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: wren. Status: blocked on budget.
4. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: mark. Status: open.

was visible in door-lock failures the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at p99 hold latency.

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: zaid, esme.

corridor does the work. You cannot fix a capacity problem with a sign.

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 32 weeks and
was visible in p99 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at p50 hold latency.

This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Proposal

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
4. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------

    post-lunch arrival rate        145.09    174.89     29.80
    double-flush ratio              58.78     30.13    -28.65
