    Bristol score                    5.60      6.60      1.00

The improvement in cubicle occupancy did not survive contact with the
vending machine restock arriving three days late.

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

### Derivation 04

Take arrivals lambda = 9.90 per hour and service rate mu = 6.34 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.781.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 33.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 5.57. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0138: Deprecating Sampling

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: ivo.

The building was designed for a headcount we exceeded in the second
year and never revisited. The cheapest intervention is almost always
scheduling, and it is almost always the last one tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled.
The underlying condition had been present for 34 weeks and was visible
in time-to-first-flush the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at re-entry rate.

Treat the following as directional.

### Proposal

1. Add a second bin.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team.

### Objections

  mira: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

  hendrik: we should measure for another quarter before touching
  anything

  vermingov: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

## RFC 0139: Failure Modes in Spare Parts

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

Every measurement we take of time-to-first-flush changes the thing
measured, because people can see the clipboard. Every shared resource
eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.
The underlying condition had been present for 30 weeks and was visible
in balking probability the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at seat-cold complaints.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Add a second bin.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Move the all-hands to 15:00.

### Objections

  zaid: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

  esme: this is a building problem being solved with a process document

  wren: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

## RFC 0140: In Defence of Escalation Paths

Status: Living. Supersedes: RFC 0089. Reviewers: callum, lotte, milo.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. Utilisation above 0.8 is not a
target. It is a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the second-floor block being locked for a
photoshoot. The underlying condition had been present for 28 weeks and
was visible in service time variance the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at hand-wash compliance.

This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Proposal

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    flush success rate              97.12    122.58     25.46
    Bristol score                   74.82     38.62    -36.21
    dispenser refill interval      230.47    317.51     87.05

The improvement in walkaway rate did not survive contact with the hot
tap being isolated during unrelated works.

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

## RFC 0141: Deprecating Emergency Cords

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: esme, ivo.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. You cannot fix a capacity problem with a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled.
The underlying condition had been present for 17 weeks and was visible
in abort rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at mean
time to seat.

This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Proposal

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
3. Add a second bin.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
5. Escalate to building management and wait.
6. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

## Incident 0009: Cubicle 2 wedged

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 1h58m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 13:30, the third-floor west block stalled. Root cause was the hot
tap being isolated during unrelated works. Users experienced elevated
Bristol score for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround reposted, laminated
    11:40  Building Management acknowledges
    12:35  ivo notices flush success rate is out of band
    13:15  second report, in the wrong channel
    14:05  partial service restored
    15:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    17:10  full service restored
    17:50  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate
- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently. Owner: ivo. Status: open.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: ivo. Status: closed, unclear why.

## Incident 0010: The gym changing room unit lost quorum

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 6h26m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 13:00, the sixth-floor facility queued unboundedly. Root cause was
an unannounced change to the building water pressure. Users experienced
elevated Bristol score for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround posted on the door
    10:20  partial service restored
    13:00  workaround reposted, laminated
    13:15  ticket closed without comment
    15:55  escalation to Building Management
    16:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    17:10  root cause identified, retroactively

### Contributing factors

- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate
- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window
- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: tomasz. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: sanne. Status: blocked on budget.

### Runbook 02: smell of unknown origin

Trigger: lock-jiggle events above 0.85 for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
2. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
3. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
4. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
6. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
7. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.

Escalation: Backend, then the plumbing subcontractor, then stop and wait.

**Decision.** We will stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

**Consequences.** We buy eighteen months. We do not use them.

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, H, L, R, S, T, W

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

## ADR 008: Preliminary Findings on the Silent Failure

Date: 4 May. Status: Obsolete.

**Context.** Every measurement we take of renege rate changes the thing measured, because people can see the clipboard.

**Decision.** We will buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

**Consequences.** Nothing measurable changes and morale improves anyway.

### Field note, day 8

A person waited, checked their phone, left, returned four minutes
later, waited again, and got in. Logged as one visit. Should be two.
Our instrumentation cannot tell the difference and this is probably the
largest error in the dataset.

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, H, P, R, S, T, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## RFC 0148: Notes on the Badge Reader

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: juno.

The immediate trigger was a contractor closing two cubicles without
notice. The underlying condition had been present for 21 weeks and was
visible in false-occupancy signals the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at lock-jiggle events.

### Runbook 03: accessible stall unavailable

Trigger: double-flush ratio above the March baseline for 30 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
2. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
3. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
4. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
5. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
6. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
7. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.

Escalation: Support, then Procurement, then stop and wait.

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: RFC 0050. Reviewers: lotte, priya.

and was visible in flush success rate the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at queue depth.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

## Incident 0012: The contractor portacabin regressed

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 1h44m. Detected by: nobody, in time.

### Summary

Root cause was a contractor closing two cubicles without notice. Users
experienced elevated mean time between visits for the duration. No data
was lost. Some dignity was.

- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.

### Action items

2. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: rune. Status: done.

## RFC 0166: Against Cistern Refill Time

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: bea.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. Every shared resource eventually
acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the coffee machine on 3 being repaired,
redirecting demand to 4. The underlying condition had been present for
30 weeks and was visible in cubicle occupancy the whole time, to anyone
who had thought to look at service time variance.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
4. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
5. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    renege rate                     51.98     69.23     17.26
    time-to-first-flush            225.22    259.34     34.12
    double-flush ratio             186.04    205.23     19.19

The improvement in paper turnover did not survive contact with the
coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4.

### Objections

  priya: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

  kwame: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Derivation 05

Take arrivals lambda = 8.18 per hour and service rate mu = 16.50 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.165.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.7 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.10. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen

## RFC 0175: Formalising Sensor Firmware

Status: Living. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: rune, dev.

We instrumented false-occupancy signals for six weeks and learned that
the interesting variance is entirely social. The cheapest intervention
is almost always scheduling, and it is almost always the last one
tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 8 weeks and was visible in
seat-cold complaints the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at mean time between visits.

The sample is small and self-selecting.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
4. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    paper turnover                  70.33     36.86    -33.47
    door-lock failures              90.91     69.70    -21.21
    utilisation rho                212.83    231.75     18.92
    cubicle occupancy               31.25     18.69    -12.56

The improvement in paper turnover did not survive contact with a fire
drill at 13:20, precisely at peak.

### Objections

  hendrik: we are solving for the average and the average is not the
  problem

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

## RFC 0176: Capacity Planning for the Return-to-Office Mandate

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: RFC 0163. Reviewers: nobody.

We instrumented mean time between visits for six weeks and learned that
the interesting variance is entirely social. Every shared resource
eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 23 weeks
and was visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at time-to-first-flush.

### Proposal

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
5. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
6. Move the all-hands to 15:00.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p50 hold latency               233.86    216.15    -17.71
    lock-jiggle events             230.39     84.84   -145.55
    paper turnover                 179.83    164.29    -15.54

The improvement in hand-wash compliance did not survive contact with an
off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware.

### Objections

  vermingov: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

### Derivation 08

Take arrivals lambda = 13.31 per hour and service rate mu = 7.02 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.379.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 5.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 1.16. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0015: The basement facility entered a hold-and-wait state

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 6h43m. Detected by: the queue.

### Summary

At 14:30, the executive washroom queued unboundedly. Root cause was the
hot tap being isolated during unrelated works. Users experienced
elevated p99 hold latency for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    11:40  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:35  workaround posted on the door
    13:15  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    13:30  escalation to Building Management
    15:55  second report, in the wrong channel
    16:20  ticket closed without comment
    17:10  contractor dispatched

### Contributing factors

- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: rune. Status: open.
2. Escalate to building management and wait. Owner: sanne. Status: blocked on budget.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: wren. Status: closed as wont-fix.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: erika. Status: closed, unclear why.

## Incident 0016: The loading-bay unit fell over

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 3h55m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 17:10, the sixth-floor facility fell over. Root cause was the
extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate. Users experienced
elevated p50 hold latency for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  full service restored
    13:15  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:30  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    14:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    15:55  first report, verbally, to the wrong team

### Contributing factors

- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper
- The wrong bin liners, which fit nothing
- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

## RFC 0186: Standardising Fair Queueing

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The sixth-floor facility is operationally invisible, and has been since
before anyone currently employed here arrived. You cannot fix a
capacity problem with a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the vending machine restock arriving three
days late. The underlying condition had been present for 21 weeks and
was visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at false-occupancy signals.

The sample is small and self-selecting.

### Proposal

1. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p50 hold latency               149.79    104.16    -45.62
    p99 hold latency               124.27    154.82     30.55
    floor-hop rate                 128.41    146.01     17.60

The improvement in p999 hold latency did not survive contact with a new
hire cohort of eleven starting on the same Monday.

### Objections

  hendrik: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Derivation 09

Take arrivals lambda = 6.59 per hour and service rate mu = 17.51 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.188.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.09. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 10

Take arrivals lambda = 13.39 per hour and service rate mu = 6.12 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 2.186.

rho exceeds one. The queue is unstable. No amount of politeness
recovers this; the only outcomes are balking, reneging, or somebody
taking the stairs to another floor, which is load shedding by another
name.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 30 weeks
and was visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at cubicle occupancy.

accordingly.

## RFC 0195: Measuring Tailgating

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. Every shared resource eventually
acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the vending machine restock arriving three
days late. The underlying condition had been present for 31 weeks and
was visible in mean time between visits the whole time, to anyone who
had thought to look at extract-fan duty cycle.

### Proposal

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
4. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    balking probability             74.47     92.26     17.79
    mean time to seat               91.69     55.30    -36.39
    p99 hold latency                 2.20      0.98     -1.22
    utilisation rho                 98.86     44.92    -53.94

The improvement in p999 hold latency did not survive contact with a
soap dispenser that dispensed only air.

### Objections

  priya: we are solving for the average and the average is not the
  problem

  roshan: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

  dev: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

---

### Field note, day 15

Queue formed at 13:11 and cleared at 13:38. Four walkaways, all toward
the stairs, none toward the lift. People will climb rather than wait in
view of the kitchen.

  The instrument drifted. We do not know by how much.

### Derivation 11

Take arrivals lambda = 7.19 per hour and service rate mu = 24.71 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.097.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.03. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.09. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0020: The lobby singles fell over

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 5h13m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 13:30, the gym changing room unit degraded. Root cause was a leak on
5 that was in fact condensation. Users experienced elevated lock-jiggle
events for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:00  Building Management acknowledges
    13:00  ticket closed without comment
    13:30  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:45  full service restored
    14:30  yusuf notices post-lunch arrival rate is out of band
    17:10  contractor dispatched

### Contributing factors

- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak
- The door lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: zaid. Status: open.
2. Escalate to building management and wait. Owner: noor. Status: open.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: erika. Status: open.
4. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: nils. Status: done.

---

### Runbook 04: lock reporting false occupancy

Trigger: cubicle occupancy above threshold for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
2. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
3. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
4. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
5. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
6. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
7. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
8. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: Legal, then Platform, then stop and wait.

### Field note, day 18

Arrived 08:50. Two units free on 3, four on 4. Nobody queueing. Wrote
nothing for ninety minutes.

  This survived review only because review was cancelled.

corridor does the work. The cheapest intervention is almost always
scheduling, and it is almost always the last one tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an unannounced change to the building water
pressure. The underlying condition had been present for 30 weeks and
was visible in p99 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at walkaway rate.

### Proposal

1. Add a second bin.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
6. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    paper turnover                   4.95      4.40     -0.55
    abort rate                     231.42    202.64    -28.78
    urgency index                  205.28    266.92     61.65
    walkaway rate                  220.79    173.53    -47.27
    seat-cold complaints           206.95    111.19    -95.77

The improvement in walkaway rate did not survive contact with an
all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window.

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

    zaid       is 3 free
    sanne      no
    callum     still no
    zaid       who is in 3
    dev        nobody is in 3, the lock is broken
    callum     the lock has been broken since tuesday
    dev        which tuesday
    dev        a tuesday
    callum     raised FAC-57988
    callum     that is a duplicate of FAC-74924
    dev        both are duplicates of the one from march
    sanne      the march one was closed as wontfix
    dev        by whom

    dev        classic
    sanne      going to 4
    dev        4 is worse
    zaid       4 is always worse after 13:00
    zaid       why is 4 worse after 13:00

    callum     there it is
    dev        can we just stagger lunch
    callum     we tried that
    callum     we tried that badly
    dev        we tried that for nine days
    zaid       nine days is not a trial

### Derivation 13

Take arrivals lambda = 20.40 per hour and service rate mu = 10.68 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 1.909.

rho exceeds one. The queue is unstable. No amount of politeness
recovers this; the only outcomes are balking, reneging, or somebody
taking the stairs to another floor, which is load shedding by another
name.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

- The vending machine restock arriving three days late

### What went well

### Derivation 14

Take arrivals lambda = 11.42 per hour and service rate mu = 9.16 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.312.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 3.0 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.57. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: A, B, D, H, R, S, T

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nils, erika, mark.

### Derivation 15

Take arrivals lambda = 6.04 per hour and service rate mu = 20.45 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.074.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.02. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 05: blocked stack

Trigger: mean time between visits above twice normal for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
2. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
6. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
7. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
8. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
9. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: Facilities, then Finance, then stop and wait.

### Runbook 06: queue exceeding the kitchen

Trigger: post-lunch arrival rate above 0.85 for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
2. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
5. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
6. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
7. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
8. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
9. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.

Escalation: Procurement, then Support, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0030: Cubicle 3 began returning stale occupancy

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 9h12m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 17:10, the third-floor west block wedged. Root cause was the vending
machine restock arriving three days late. Users experienced elevated
lock-jiggle events for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    09:10  ticket closed without comment
    09:45  workaround removed by cleaning
    11:40  workaround posted on the door
    12:15  partial service restored
    13:15  workaround reposted, laminated
    13:30  contractor dispatched
    15:10  priya notices time-to-first-flush is out of band
    16:45  root cause identified, retroactively

### Contributing factors

- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware
- The wrong bin liners, which fit nothing

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: hana. Status: done.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: nils. Status: closed as wont-fix.

---

## Incident 0031: The ground-floor overflow fell over

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 9h50m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 13:15, the fifth-floor facility queued unboundedly. Root cause was
the cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon. Users experienced
elevated time-to-first-flush for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    12:35  contractor dispatched
    13:45  partial service restored
    14:30  workaround removed by cleaning
    15:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    16:20  escalation to Building Management
    16:45  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    17:10  mira notices time-to-first-flush is out of band
    17:50  workaround reposted, laminated

### Contributing factors

- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- A cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks
- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: callum. Status: open.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: yusuf. Status: closed, unclear why.

## RFC 0245: Notes on the Bus Factor

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: RFC 0097. Reviewers: nobody.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. Every shared resource eventually
acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the hot tap being isolated during unrelated
works. The underlying condition had been present for 18 weeks and was
visible in hand-wash compliance the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at seat-cold complaints.

Treat the following as directional.

### Proposal

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
4. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
5. Add a second bin.
6. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p50 hold latency               225.91    268.93     43.02
    seat-cold complaints           134.54    165.81     31.27
    abort rate                     177.24    176.46     -0.78
    re-entry rate                  193.75     68.09   -125.66
    dispenser refill interval      195.56    173.65    -21.90
    flush success rate              63.30     52.19    -11.11

The improvement in mean time between visits did not survive contact
with a contractor closing two cubicles without notice.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Derivation 16

Take arrivals lambda = 16.65 per hour and service rate mu = 19.97 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.208.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.22. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

### Field note, day 26

Arrived 08:50. Two units free on 3, four on 4. Nobody queueing. Wrote
nothing for ninety minutes.

  This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, H, P, R, S, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, F, H, L, R, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

APPENDIX AW: Waste Composition

### Derivation 17

Take arrivals lambda = 4.26 per hour and service rate mu = 7.87 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.541.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 9.0 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.64. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
-->
<!--
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## ADR 031: The Economics of Physical Access Control

Date: 10 July. Status: Living.

**Context.** We instrumented re-entry rate for six weeks and learned that the interesting variance is entirely social.

**Decision.** We will escalate to Building Management and wait.

**Consequences.** Throughput improves at the peak and degrades everywhere else.

### Glossary: B, D, F, H, L, P, R, S

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

## Incident 0036: Cubicle 4 backed up

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 3h36m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 14:05, the third-floor west block stalled. Root cause was an
off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware. Users experienced elevated
mean time to seat for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:00  partial service restored
    12:15  workaround posted on the door
    12:35  ticket closed without comment
    13:15  root cause identified, retroactively
    14:05  sanne notices floor-hop rate is out of band
    16:20  full service restored

### Contributing factors

- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware
- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- The vending machine restock arriving three days late

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Runbook 07: lock reporting false occupancy

Trigger: extract-fan duty cycle above threshold for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
2. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
5. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
6. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
7. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
8. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.

Escalation: Infra, then Finance, then stop and wait.

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 7h43m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

being repaired, redirecting demand to 4. Users experienced elevated
mean time between visits for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    13:15  contractor dispatched
    13:30  escalation to Building Management
    14:30  workaround reposted, laminated
    15:55  wren notices abort rate is out of band

### Contributing factors

- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: mira. Status: done.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: lotte. Status: open.

### Derivation 18

Take arrivals lambda = 17.92 per hour and service rate mu = 18.29 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.980.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 161.4 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 48.21. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Field note, day 27

A person waited, checked their phone, left, returned four minutes
later, waited again, and got in. Logged as one visit. Should be two.
Our instrumentation cannot tell the difference and this is probably the
largest error in the dataset.

### Correspondence 03

To the landlord: clause 14 obliges you to maintain the sanitary
installations in good working order. We do not dispute that they work.
We dispute that two of them, for ninety people, on a floor with one
stack, constitutes an installation.

Sent: 8 July. Reply: a phone call, undocumented.

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, H, R, S, T

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

    13:15  second report, in the wrong channel
    14:05  workaround reposted, laminated
    16:45  contractor arrives, lacks the part

### Contributing factors

- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call
- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice
- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: dev. Status: done.
2. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: hendrik. Status: done.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: esme. Status: blocked on budget.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, E, F, H, P, R, S, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

### Facilities working group, meeting 8

Present: vermingov, hendrik, lotte, roshan, zaid.
Apologies: yusuf, milo, esme.

1. Accessible stall misuse. Discussed carefully and at length. Action: ask.
2. Budget. Deferred to the next cycle, as in the previous four meetings.
3. Signage. Agreed to laminate. Nobody assigned.
4. Review of open tickets. 41 open, 3 discussed, 0 closed.
5. Sensor procurement. Vendor demo scheduled and then cancelled.
6. The refit. Still scheduled. Still not dated.

Next meeting: November. Quorum: unlikely.

### Summary

At 16:20, Cubicle 2 began returning stale occupancy. Root cause was one
person holding the accessible stall for a phone call. Users experienced
elevated time-to-first-flush for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window

### What did not

## RFC 0286: In Defence of the Badge Reader

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: RFC 0243. Reviewers: nobody.

The sixth-floor facility is the only component in the building with a
hard capacity of one and no queue visibility. Latency is a
distribution, and the tail is where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.
The underlying condition had been present for 17 weeks and was visible
in extract-fan duty cycle the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at Bristol score.

The sample is small and self-selecting.

### Proposal

1. Escalate to building management and wait.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
5. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
6. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Objections

  noor: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

  yusuf: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Derivation 19

Take arrivals lambda = 17.88 per hour and service rate mu = 24.02 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.248.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.25. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

    Rho went up. The mean stayed wrong.
    Laminate it. Only that survives.
    A sign went up on Monday morning.
    Paper curls. Intention dies.
    Little's Law is very kind:
    The ticket says closed. The smell says done.
    and every afternoon undone.
    it tells you what you'll always find.

## RFC 0288: Toward Signage

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

We instrumented paper turnover for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. Redundancy that shares a stack
is not redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the coffee machine on 3 being repaired,
redirecting demand to 4. The underlying condition had been present for
18 weeks and was visible in balking probability the whole time, to
anyone who had thought to look at lock-jiggle events.

The instrument drifted. We do not know by how much.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Add a second bin.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
4. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
5. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
6. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    service time variance            1.14      1.11     -0.02
    p999 hold latency              192.23    241.83     49.60
    false-occupancy signals         61.34     23.85    -37.49
    p50 hold latency               192.68    114.60    -78.08
    dispenser refill interval      113.26    113.23     -0.03

The improvement in queue depth did not survive contact with a
contractor closing two cubicles without notice.

### Objections

  priya: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

  milo: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Glossary: A, C, D, H, P, S, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Facilities working group, meeting 9

Present: yusuf, sef, dev, ada, tess.
Apologies: ada, nils.

1. The refit. Still scheduled. Still not dated.
2. Signage. Agreed to laminate. Nobody assigned.
3. Sensor procurement. Vendor demo scheduled and then cancelled.
4. Cleaning window. Contractor unwilling to move. Escalation drafted.
5. Review of open tickets. 41 open, 3 discussed, 0 closed.

Next meeting: September. Quorum: unlikely.

## RFC 0291: Auditing Legionella Flushing

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: RFC 0052. Reviewers: hendrik, callum.

The contractor portacabin is the only component in the building with a
hard capacity of one and no queue visibility. Every shared resource
eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.
The underlying condition had been present for 13 weeks and was visible
in mean time between visits the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at post-lunch arrival rate.

### Proposal

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
2. Escalate to building management and wait.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Objections

  kwame: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

---

### Benchmark: Legionella Flushing

    n=237, 45 weekdays, January, sensor rev E-beta

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      2         9.7  0.12     78    146    727  25.0
        2      1        12.2  0.88     70    274    381  16.3
        3      4        17.3  0.17    133    425    601  22.8
        4      2         3.6  0.10    133    472    816   9.7

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

### Derivation 20

Take arrivals lambda = 13.01 per hour and service rate mu = 11.70 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.371.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 3.0 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.65. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: B, C, E, H, L, R, S, W

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, F, H, P, R, S, T, W

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

## RFC 0306: Toward Mirror Placement

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: RFC 0014. Reviewers: noor, vermingov.

Every measurement we take of false-occupancy signals changes the thing
measured, because people can see the clipboard. Utilisation above 0.8
is not a target. It is a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 14 weeks and
was visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at queue depth.

### Proposal

1. Add a second bin.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

---

### Derivation 21

Take arrivals lambda = 16.00 per hour and service rate mu = 27.17 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.295.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.25. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 08: water off, unannounced

Trigger: false-occupancy signals above threshold for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
2. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
3. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
4. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
5. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
6. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.

Escalation: Procurement, then SRE, then stop and wait.

## ADR 037: Failure Modes in Extract Ventilation

Date: 3 August. Status: Abandoned.

**Context.** The building was designed for a headcount we exceeded in the second year and never revisited.

**Decision.** We will move the all-hands to 15:00.

**Consequences.** Nothing measurable changes and morale improves anyway.

### Derivation 22

Take arrivals lambda = 8.19 per hour and service rate mu = 14.86 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.138.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.6 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.09. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

### Glossary: B, C, E, H, L, R, S, T, W

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## RFC 0325: The Case Against the Adjacent Meeting Room

Status: Draft. Supersedes: RFC 0204. Reviewers: hana, lotte.

The building was designed for a headcount we exceeded in the second
year and never revisited. Latency is a distribution, and the tail is
where the dignity lives.

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 16 weeks
and was visible in balking probability the whole time, to anyone who
had thought to look at hand-wash compliance.

2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.

4. Stagger the lunch break by team.
5. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
6. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.

### Decision

### Ticket extract 02040-02057

    FAC-02040  triage      aisha     hot tap runs cold
    FAC-02041  duplicate   yusuf     hook missing since the refit
    FAC-02042  closed      juno      smell on the landing
    FAC-02043  duplicate   bea       extract fan noisy
    FAC-02044  stale       dev       extract fan silent, which is worse
    FAC-02045  triage      ada       the mezzanine single door lock sticks
    FAC-02046  stale       ada       door gap allows eye contact
    FAC-02047  in-progress sef       queue reaching the kitchen at 13:15
    FAC-02048  closed      callum    extract fan silent, which is worse
    FAC-02049  in-progress rune      extract fan silent, which is worse
    FAC-02050  duplicate   tess      extract fan silent, which is worse
    FAC-02051  duplicate   dev       cleaning window collides with peak
    FAC-02052  wontfix     mira      Cubicle 3 door lock sticks
    FAC-02053  in-progress erika     extract fan noisy
    FAC-02054  open        juno      no baby change on any floor
    FAC-02055  in-progress mark      bin overflowing by 15:00 daily
    FAC-02056  closed      vermingov smell on the landing
    FAC-02057  open        aisha     queue reaching the kitchen at 13:15

### Derivation 24

Take arrivals lambda = 10.84 per hour and service rate mu = 19.08 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.189.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.7 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.13. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0054: The fourth-floor annex degraded

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 0h56m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 09:10, the accessible stall on 2 backed up. Root cause was the
cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon. Users experienced
elevated re-entry rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    11:40  contractor dispatched
    12:35  workaround posted on the door
    13:00  second report, in the wrong channel
    13:30  ticket closed without comment
    13:45  root cause identified, retroactively
    15:10  aisha notices mean time to seat is out of band
    15:55  workaround removed by cleaning
    16:20  contractor arrives, lacks the part

### Contributing factors

- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware
- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor
- The vending machine restock arriving three days late
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window

### What went well

- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: esme. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: bea. Status: done.
3. Add a second bin. Owner: kwame. Status: open.

---

### Field note, day 38

A person waited, checked their phone, left, returned four minutes
later, waited again, and got in. Logged as one visit. Should be two.
Our instrumentation cannot tell the difference and this is probably the
largest error in the dataset.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,

  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

    attendance ratio     0.87
    units, total         12
    people per unit      10.2
    guideline            20.0
    verdict              within

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

### Derivation 25

Take arrivals lambda = 20.77 per hour and service rate mu = 22.30 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.931.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 36.4 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 12.58. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 10: extract fan failure

Trigger: Bristol score above the March baseline for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
2. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
3. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
4. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
5. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.

Escalation: Frontend, then Frontend, then stop and wait.

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, H, L, R, S, T

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

### Runbook 11: accessible stall unavailable

Trigger: paper turnover above the March baseline for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
2. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
5. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.

Escalation: Backend, then SRE, then stop and wait.

### Runbook 12: queue exceeding the kitchen

Trigger: mean time between visits above threshold for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
2. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
5. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.

Escalation: Legal, then Data, then stop and wait.

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The building was designed for a headcount we exceeded in the second

backpressure signal.

draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 13 weeks
and was visible in mean time to seat the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at dispenser refill interval.

### Proposal

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p999 hold latency              155.74    207.90     52.16
    mean time to seat               62.77     70.10      7.33
    flush success rate             191.02    230.24     39.22

The improvement in abort rate did not survive contact with the

### Objections

  wren: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

### Decision
