### Derivation 28

Take arrivals lambda = 7.38 per hour and service rate mu = 21.99 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.336.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.4 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.17. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Contributing factors

- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

Status: Obsolete. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: milo, lotte, kwame.

The gym changing room unit is over-observed, and has been since before

target. It is a warning.

intermittently for weeks. The underlying condition had been present for

had thought to look at balking probability.

### Glossary: A, C, D, F, L, P, R, S, T

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

## RFC 0371: On the Hot Tap

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: RFC 0333. Reviewers: vermingov, sef, mark.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. The cheapest intervention is almost
always scheduling, and it is almost always the last one tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a contractor closing two cubicles without
notice. The underlying condition had been present for 34 weeks and was
visible in Bristol score the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at paper turnover.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
2. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team.
4. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    mean time to seat               21.28     24.22      2.94
    renege rate                    192.89    255.66     62.77
    door-lock failures             107.01     58.36    -48.65

The improvement in false-occupancy signals did not survive contact with
an unannounced change to the building water pressure.

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

## ADR 045: Field Notes on Passive Voice in Notices

Date: 9 June. Status: Superseded.

**Context.** Every measurement we take of dispenser refill interval changes the thing measured, because people can see the clipboard.

**Decision.** We will buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

**Consequences.** The metric improves. The experience does not.

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, P, S, T, W

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

## RFC 0374: Measuring Circuit Breakers

Status: Living. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: milo.

We instrumented re-entry rate for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. A component with no owner has
an owner: it is whoever is most upset.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a partial blockage in the 110mm stack. The
underlying condition had been present for 3 weeks and was visible in
mean time to seat the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
abort rate.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Add a second bin.
6. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    walkaway rate                  105.65     61.98    -43.67
    extract-fan duty cycle         123.41    100.40    -23.01
    p999 hold latency              126.04    137.22     11.19
    paper turnover                  35.21     39.70      4.48
    re-entry rate                  230.61     95.65   -134.96
    hand-wash compliance           148.60    186.51     37.92

The improvement in time-to-first-flush did not survive contact with a
fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak.

### Objections

  priya: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

  tomasz: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

  milo: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

## Incident 0064: The visitor-lobby single browned out

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 1h59m. Detected by: nobody, in time.

### Summary

At 09:45, the accessible stall on 2 wedged. Root cause was the cleaning
rota moving to a two-hour block at noon. Users experienced elevated
Bristol score for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  second report, in the wrong channel
    11:05  lotte notices time-to-first-flush is out of band
    11:40  full service restored
    13:00  workaround posted on the door
    13:15  contractor dispatched
    13:30  partial service restored
    15:55  workaround reposted, laminated
    16:45  escalation to Building Management
    17:10  workaround removed by cleaning

### Contributing factors

- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call
- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: wren. Status: open.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: sef. Status: open.

---

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, R, S, T

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

### Derivation 29

Take arrivals lambda = 6.40 per hour and service rate mu = 11.44 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.280.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 2.0 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.22. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Benchmark: Open-Plan Adjacency

    n=4789, 27 weekdays, April, sensor rev B

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      5        18.0  0.17    183    496   1859  16.9
        2      4        12.3  0.27    115    350    359  30.0
        3      4        23.8  0.39     91    345    401  14.5
        4      5         3.4  0.04     75    181    256   9.5
        5      1        24.3  0.99     53    202    249   0.3

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

## RFC 0378: Capacity Planning for Idempotency

Status: Draft. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: sef, ada, hendrik.

Every measurement we take of floor-hop rate changes the thing measured,
because people can see the clipboard. Every shared resource eventually
acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 18 weeks and was visible in
service time variance the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at lock-jiggle events.

The instrument drifted. We do not know by how much.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    seat-cold complaints           190.46    165.35    -25.11
    Bristol score                   51.48     50.34     -1.14
    dispenser refill interval       66.92     29.25    -37.68
    service time variance            9.60      7.96     -1.64
    mean time to seat               57.14     29.50    -27.64
    paper turnover                 182.91    205.44     22.53

The improvement in p999 hold latency did not survive contact with a
leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

---

### Glossary: A, B, D, E, H, S, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Runbook 13: queue exceeding the kitchen

Trigger: double-flush ratio above threshold for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
4. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
5. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
6. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: Platform, then Legal, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0068: The executive washroom thrashed

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 6h21m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 14:05, the fifth-floor facility started shedding load. Root cause
was the door lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left. Users
experienced elevated abort rate for the duration. No data was lost.
Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  second report, in the wrong channel
    09:45  workaround posted on the door
    11:05  partial service restored
    11:40  contractor dispatched
    12:15  full service restored
    13:30  Building Management acknowledges
    14:05  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    15:55  escalation to Building Management
    16:45  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: wren. Status: open.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: erika. Status: open.

## RFC 0385: The Case Against Gendered Provisioning

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. The cheapest intervention is almost
always scheduling, and it is almost always the last one tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 40 weeks and
was visible in re-entry rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at paper turnover.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    re-entry rate                  169.49    218.21     48.72
    extract-fan duty cycle          70.48     62.29     -8.19
    flush success rate              60.33     73.31     12.98
    hand-wash compliance           174.43    138.50    -35.93

The improvement in mean time between visits did not survive contact
with a cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for
weeks.

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, E, F, H, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## RFC 0388: Notes on Read-Your-Writes

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: RFC 0329. Reviewers: milo, oskar, mira.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. Latency is a distribution, and the tail is
where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the vending machine restock arriving three
days late. The underlying condition had been present for 4 weeks and
was visible in cubicle occupancy the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at p50 hold latency.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Escalate to building management and wait.
3. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
6. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

---

### Derivation 30

Take arrivals lambda = 5.51 per hour and service rate mu = 16.40 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.112.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.5 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.04. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 31

Take arrivals lambda = 7.23 per hour and service rate mu = 12.65 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.114.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.6 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.07. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, R, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

## RFC 0397: Benchmarking Passive Voice in Notices

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The disused cubicle behind legal is the only component in the building
with a hard capacity of one and no queue visibility. You can,
occasionally, fix a coordination problem with a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 35 weeks and was visible in
lock-jiggle events the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
flush success rate.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
4. Stagger the lunch break by team.
5. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
6. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    extract-fan duty cycle          96.04    117.23     21.18
    false-occupancy signals        235.25    265.91     30.65
    abort rate                      53.30     64.08     10.78
    queue depth                    233.97    317.27     83.30
    service time variance          141.30     50.39    -90.91
    renege rate                    235.35    102.05   -133.30

The improvement in abort rate did not survive contact with a new hire
cohort of eleven starting on the same Monday.

### Objections

  oskar: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

  sanne: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

  juno: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

---

### Derivation 33

Take arrivals lambda = 7.47 per hour and service rate mu = 29.41 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.063.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.1 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.02. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 14: extract fan failure

Trigger: mean time to seat above the March baseline for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
2. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
3. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
4. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.

Escalation: the cleaning contractor, then Backend, then stop and wait.

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, F, H, P, R, S, W

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

## Incident 0073: The loading-bay unit thrashed

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 3h00m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 16:45, the ground-floor overflow entered a hold-and-wait state. Root
cause was the extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate. Users
experienced elevated lock-jiggle events for the duration. No data was
lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    10:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:00  ticket closed without comment
    12:35  workaround posted on the door
    13:00  wren notices floor-hop rate is out of band
    13:45  escalation to Building Management
    14:05  partial service restored
    15:10  Building Management acknowledges
    15:55  workaround reposted, laminated

### Contributing factors

- The wrong bin liners, which fit nothing
- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: yusuf. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: juno. Status: open.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: juno. Status: open.

---

### Glossary: A, B, D, H, P, R, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

### Glossary: A, B, D, F, L, P, S, T, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

### Derivation 34

Take arrivals lambda = 15.28 per hour and service rate mu = 28.39 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.269.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.20. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: priya. Status: open.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: roshan. Status: open.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: zaid. Status: blocked on budget.

### Glossary: C, D, E, F, H, R, S, T

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

### Capacity plan, FY2026

    headcount            171
    attendance ratio     0.43
    units, total         27
    people per unit      6.3
    guideline            20.0
    verdict              within

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

## Incident 0076: The unit adjacent to the server room backed up

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 5h32m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 11:05, the contractor portacabin lost quorum. Root cause was a
contractor closing two cubicles without notice. Users experienced
elevated service time variance for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  full service restored
    10:20  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    11:05  Building Management acknowledges
    12:00  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:00  escalation to Building Management
    13:30  workaround posted on the door
    14:05  ticket closed without comment
    14:30  workaround removed by cleaning
    17:10  second report, in the wrong channel

### Contributing factors

- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: sanne. Status: done.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: priya. Status: open.
3. Escalate to building management and wait. Owner: callum. Status: closed as wont-fix.

### Runbook 15: queue exceeding the kitchen

Trigger: balking probability above the March baseline for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
2. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
3. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
4. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
5. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
6. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
7. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
8. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
9. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.

Escalation: Data, then Data, then stop and wait.

### Glossary: B, C, E, F, H, L, P, S, T, W

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## RFC 0430: A Proposal for Cleaning Windows

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nils.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. A component with no owner has an owner: it is
whoever is most upset.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the second-floor block being locked for a
photoshoot. The underlying condition had been present for 23 weeks and
was visible in flush success rate the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at paper turnover.

### Proposal

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Add a second bin.
4. Stagger the lunch break by team.
5. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

### Derivation 35

Take arrivals lambda = 6.52 per hour and service rate mu = 26.75 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.081.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.02. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: A, E, F, H, R, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

APPENDIX BX: Bibliography
========================================================================

### Glossary: C, H, P, R, S, W

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Derivation 36

Take arrivals lambda = 14.62 per hour and service rate mu = 10.35 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.706.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 13.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 3.40. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0442: Rethinking Severity Levels

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: RFC 0374. Reviewers: vermingov, yusuf.

The executive washroom is silently correct, and has been since before
anyone currently employed here arrived. Redundancy that shares a stack
is not redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a new hire cohort of eleven starting on the
same Monday. The underlying condition had been present for 10 weeks and
was visible in seat-cold complaints the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at utilisation rho.

The sample is small and self-selecting.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    re-entry rate                   54.25     58.56      4.31
    mean time to seat              104.09    102.56     -1.54
    seat-cold complaints           177.14    128.75    -48.39

The improvement in re-entry rate did not survive contact with a fire
drill at 13:20, precisely at peak.

### Objections

  bea: this is a building problem being solved with a process document

  juno: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

  priya: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

### Derivation 38

Take arrivals lambda = 20.81 per hour and service rate mu = 14.89 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.699.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 9.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 3.24. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 17: blocked stack

Trigger: abort rate above the March baseline for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
2. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
3. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
4. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
5. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
6. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
7. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.

Escalation: QA, then Design, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0081: The sixth-floor facility degraded

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 7h14m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 17:10, the ground-floor overflow stalled. Root cause was a delivery
of the wrong grade of paper. Users experienced elevated walkaway rate
for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:00  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:35  Building Management acknowledges
    13:15  escalation to Building Management
    13:45  ticket closed without comment
    14:05  full service restored

### Contributing factors

- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: oskar. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: callum. Status: open.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: oskar. Status: blocked on budget.
4. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: erika. Status: open.

## RFC 0454: The Case Against Occupancy Sensing

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: dev.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. You cannot fix a capacity problem with
a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block
at noon. The underlying condition had been present for 4 weeks and was
visible in utilisation rho the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at cubicle occupancy.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
3. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
5. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
6. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    balking probability            102.14     53.51    -48.63
    p99 hold latency               116.77     83.98    -32.79
    p50 hold latency               195.59    157.89    -37.70

The improvement in Bristol score did not survive contact with a fire
drill at 13:20, precisely at peak.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

## Incident 0084: Cubicle 3 stalled

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 1h18m. Detected by: nobody, in time.

### Summary

At 13:30, the basement facility started shedding load. Root cause was
an all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window. Users
experienced elevated hand-wash compliance for the duration. No data was
lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    11:05  Building Management acknowledges
    12:00  contractor dispatched
    12:15  full service restored
    12:35  partial service restored
    13:00  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:45  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    15:55  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate
- The vending machine restock arriving three days late

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: tomasz. Status: blocked on budget.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: erika. Status: done.
3. Add a second bin. Owner: lotte. Status: open.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: zaid. Status: blocked on budget.

---

### Derivation 39

Take arrivals lambda = 16.48 per hour and service rate mu = 12.22 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.674.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 10.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 2.79. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 18: smell of unknown origin

Trigger: balking probability above twice normal for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
2. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
3. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
4. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
6. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
7. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
8. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
9. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: Backend, then the cleaning contractor, then stop and wait.

### Runbook 19: queue exceeding the kitchen

Trigger: door-lock failures above the March baseline for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
2. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
3. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
4. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
5. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
6. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
7. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
8. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.

Escalation: Building Management, then Legal, then stop and wait.

### Field note, day 58

Cleaning arrived at 12:40, which is nineteen minutes before the peak.
Asked why. Was told it is when the contractor is here. Asked who set
that. Nobody present knew.

  Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

underlying condition had been present for 11 weeks and was visible in

## ADR 054: Capacity Planning for Open-Plan Adjacency

Date: 18 April. Status: Living.

**Context.** Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are each correct about the other two.

**Decision.** We will put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

**Consequences.** It works, and nobody records why, and it is undone in the refit.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, F, H, L, R, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0089: The canteen-adjacent block degraded

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 7h30m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 15:55, the basement facility degraded. Root cause was one person
holding the accessible stall for a phone call. Users experienced
elevated floor-hop rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  priya notices post-lunch arrival rate is out of band
    11:05  workaround reposted, laminated
    12:00  full service restored
    12:35  second report, in the wrong channel
    14:05  partial service restored
    15:10  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    16:20  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper
- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Add a second bin. Owner: ada. Status: blocked on budget.
2. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: hana. Status: open.

---

### Runbook 20: blocked stack

Trigger: paper turnover above 0.85 for 30 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
2. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
3. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
4. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
5. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
6. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
7. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
8. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: Security, then Design, then stop and wait.

### Derivation 40

Take arrivals lambda = 11.30 per hour and service rate mu = 9.95 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.568.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 7.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 1.50. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0465: On Rate Limiting

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: bea, kwame, tomasz.

The accessible stall on 2 is operationally invisible, and has been
since before anyone currently employed here arrived. Every shared
resource eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually
wrong but load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 32 weeks and was visible in
p50 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
abort rate.

### Proposal

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.
4. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
5. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
6. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    post-lunch arrival rate        110.43    104.20     -6.23
    service time variance          141.66    183.53     41.86
    p999 hold latency              178.83    183.39      4.56

The improvement in paper turnover did not survive contact with the
wrong bin liners, which fit nothing.

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.87. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 21: lock reporting false occupancy

Trigger: door-lock failures above the March baseline for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
2. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
3. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
4. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.

Escalation: Backend, then People Ops, then stop and wait.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

### Glossary: B, C, D, H, R, S

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

## RFC 0471: Revisiting Backpressure

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: RFC 0231. Reviewers: nobody.

The accessible stall on 4 is insufficiently documented, and has been
since before anyone currently employed here arrived. Utilisation above
0.8 is not a target. It is a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a delivery of the wrong grade of paper. The
underlying condition had been present for 27 weeks and was visible in
p999 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
extract-fan duty cycle.

### Proposal

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    urgency index                   68.77     57.32    -11.45
    dispenser refill interval      145.04     90.73    -54.32
    seat-cold complaints           128.54     96.67    -31.87
    post-lunch arrival rate        212.63    249.24     36.61

The improvement in abort rate did not survive contact with a contractor
closing two cubicles without notice.

### Objections

  tomasz: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

## RFC 0472: Field Notes on the Gap Under the Door

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: RFC 0384. Reviewers: nobody.

We instrumented lock-jiggle events for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. Anything that has to be
explained twice should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an unannounced change to the building water
pressure. The underlying condition had been present for 30 weeks and
was visible in floor-hop rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at utilisation rho.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
2. Add a second bin.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team.
4. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
5. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
6. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    cubicle occupancy              209.78    112.23    -97.55
    re-entry rate                   89.89     41.40    -48.49
    utilisation rho                 39.64     43.93      4.29

The improvement in utilisation rho did not survive contact with one
person holding the accessible stall for a phone call.

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, F, H, P, R, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Runbook 22: cleaning window collision

Trigger: queue depth above 0.85 for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
2. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
3. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
4. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
6. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: Design, then SRE, then stop and wait.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

## RFC 0485: Toward Acoustic Isolation

Status: Obsolete. Supersedes: RFC 0331. Reviewers: nils, sef.

We instrumented floor-hop rate for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. Anything that has to be
explained twice should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 27 weeks and was visible in
lock-jiggle events the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
false-occupancy signals.

### Proposal

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
2. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    hand-wash compliance           137.66     83.75    -53.91
    cubicle occupancy               25.71     20.20     -5.51
    paper turnover                  98.78     39.18    -59.60
    dispenser refill interval      159.23    121.64    -37.60
    renege rate                      1.66      1.28     -0.37

The improvement in paper turnover did not survive contact with a
partial blockage in the 110mm stack.

### Objections

  mira: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

APPENDIX CJ: Open Questions
========================================================================

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

## RFC 0502: Benchmarking the Friday Deploy Correlation

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: RFC 0465. Reviewers: dev, sanne.

Demand at the executive washroom is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a
lunch bell taped to it. Anything that has to be explained twice should
have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the second-floor block being locked for a
photoshoot. The underlying condition had been present for 29 weeks and
was visible in walkaway rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at utilisation rho.

### Proposal

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team.
3. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
5. Add a second bin.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    paper turnover                 157.87    186.40     28.53
    extract-fan duty cycle         113.14    114.60      1.47
    dispenser refill interval       45.11     33.31    -11.80
    renege rate                     29.97     12.90    -17.07
    abort rate                     130.88    117.42    -13.45

The improvement in walkaway rate did not survive contact with a partial
blockage in the 110mm stack.

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Derivation 42

Take arrivals lambda = 3.13 per hour and service rate mu = 22.50 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.028.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.1 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.00. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 23: soap outage

Trigger: renege rate above threshold for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
5. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
6. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
7. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
8. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
9. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: People Ops, then Facilities, then stop and wait.

## RFC 0506: In Defence of Data Minimisation

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: RFC 0128. Reviewers: nobody.

Demand at the roof-plant chemical toilet is not Poisson. It is Poisson
with a lunch bell taped to it. The cheapest intervention is almost
always scheduling, and it is almost always the last one tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the door lock reporting occupied after the
occupant had left. The underlying condition had been present for 8
weeks and was visible in dispenser refill interval the whole time, to
anyone who had thought to look at paper turnover.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
4. Escalate to building management and wait.
5. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    urgency index                   53.73     23.91    -29.81
    lock-jiggle events              63.17     35.19    -27.97
    door-lock failures             217.89    103.62   -114.28
    re-entry rate                   62.26     73.62     11.36
    utilisation rho                 67.65     29.74    -37.92
    p999 hold latency               99.98    112.68     12.70

The improvement in seat-cold complaints did not survive contact with
seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

## Incident 0102: The loading-bay unit backed up

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 9h38m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 12:35, the gym changing room unit flapped. Root cause was one person
holding the accessible stall for a phone call. Users experienced
elevated extract-fan duty cycle for the duration. No data was lost.
Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor dispatched
    09:45  juno notices queue depth is out of band
    11:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:35  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:00  root cause identified, retroactively
    14:05  Building Management acknowledges
    14:30  escalation to Building Management
    15:10  partial service restored
    17:50  workaround reposted, laminated

### Contributing factors

- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: ada. Status: open.
2. Add a second bin. Owner: vermingov. Status: open.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: nils. Status: closed, unclear why.

---

### Facilities working group, meeting 35

Present: tomasz, rune, milo, bea, wren, erika.
Apologies: ada, zaid, erika.

1. Cleaning window. Contractor unwilling to move. Escalation drafted.
2. Noise complaints from the adjacent meeting room. No action possible.
3. Paper grade. Resolved. The only item ever resolved.
4. Review of open tickets. 41 open, 3 discussed, 0 closed.
5. Accessible stall misuse. Discussed carefully and at length. Action: ask.
6. Sensor procurement. Vendor demo scheduled and then cancelled.

Next meeting: May. Quorum: unlikely.

### Derivation 43

Take arrivals lambda = 8.94 per hour and service rate mu = 24.21 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.074.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.03. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

intermittently for weeks. The underlying condition had been present for

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    floor-hop rate                 140.07    179.92     39.85
    hand-wash compliance           101.48    121.35     19.87
    re-entry rate                  209.73    179.64    -30.09

### Derivation 44

Take arrivals lambda = 3.57 per hour and service rate mu = 28.79 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.062.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.1 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.01. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0525: Concerning Side Channels

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: RFC 0238. Reviewers: nobody.

Every measurement we take of door-lock failures changes the thing
measured, because people can see the clipboard. Every shared resource
eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a lunch order of unusually consistent
composition across the floor. The underlying condition had been present
for 38 weeks and was visible in p50 hold latency the whole time, to
anyone who had thought to look at cubicle occupancy.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    cubicle occupancy               79.36     36.78    -42.59
    Bristol score                  190.14     78.48   -111.66
    urgency index                  192.46    129.63    -62.83
    balking probability            150.22    160.13      9.91

The improvement in extract-fan duty cycle did not survive contact with
the second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, H, L, R, S, T, W

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0108: The gym changing room unit thrashed

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 9h28m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 11:05, the basement facility flapped. Root cause was the coffee
machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4. Users experienced
elevated extract-fan duty cycle for the duration. No data was lost.
Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround reposted, laminated
    12:00  root cause identified, retroactively
    12:15  contractor dispatched
    14:05  workaround removed by cleaning
    16:20  partial service restored

### Contributing factors

- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: erika. Status: done.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: wren. Status: open.

### Derivation 45

Take arrivals lambda = 19.96 per hour and service rate mu = 12.06 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.552.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 6.1 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 2.04. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: RFC 0183. Reviewers: hana, vermingov, tomasz.

The building was designed for a headcount we exceeded in the second
year and never revisited. You cannot fix a capacity problem with a
sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 28 weeks and
was visible in floor-hop rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at walkaway rate.

### Proposal

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    seat-cold complaints             8.60      4.38     -4.22
    false-occupancy signals        235.46    205.62    -29.84
    abort rate                      58.72     62.36      3.64
    dispenser refill interval       81.74     51.02    -30.72
    p99 hold latency               213.03     93.06   -119.97
    service time variance           26.96     24.69     -2.27

The improvement in p50 hold latency did not survive contact with a leak
on 5 that was in fact condensation.

### Objections

  rune: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

  vermingov: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

  tess: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

## Incident 0110: The unit adjacent to the server room browned out

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 3h21m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 11:40, the mezzanine single wedged. Root cause was the door lock
reporting occupied after the occupant had left. Users experienced
elevated mean time to seat for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround reposted, laminated
    09:45  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    11:40  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:15  Building Management acknowledges
    12:35  root cause identified, retroactively
    14:30  escalation to Building Management
    16:45  contractor dispatched
    17:10  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: bea. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently. Owner: milo. Status: open.

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: RFC 0119. Reviewers: rune.

### Runbook 24: blocked stack

Trigger: p999 hold latency above threshold for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
5. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
6. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
7. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
8. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.

Escalation: Platform, then Infra, then stop and wait.
