    15:55  sef notices urgency index is out of band

### Contributing factors

- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: tomasz. Status: open.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: juno. Status: open.

---

### Glossary: B, F, H, L, P, R, S, T

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

## RFC 0552: Concerning Cron Drift

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: RFC 0183. Reviewers: kwame, tomasz, milo.

We instrumented flush success rate for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. The cheapest intervention is
almost always scheduling, and it is almost always the last one tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the vending machine restock arriving three
days late. The underlying condition had been present for 24 weeks and
was visible in queue depth the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at Bristol score.

### Proposal

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
3. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
4. Add a second bin.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    post-lunch arrival rate        196.48    205.03      8.56
    flush success rate             182.65    215.42     32.76
    balking probability            105.67    108.06      2.39
    mean time to seat               96.32     49.94    -46.38
    seat-cold complaints            23.50     23.31     -0.20
    floor-hop rate                 209.27     91.86   -117.42

The improvement in renege rate did not survive contact with the door
lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Derivation 46

Take arrivals lambda = 11.29 per hour and service rate mu = 22.03 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.513.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 2.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.54. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, F, H, R, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

## RFC 0557: In Defence of the Security Guard Route

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: dev, erika.

Demand at the unit adjacent to the server room is not Poisson. It is
Poisson with a lunch bell taped to it. Observability without ownership
produces dashboards and nothing else.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 20 weeks
and was visible in re-entry rate the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at urgency index.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
5. Stagger the lunch break by team.
6. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    lock-jiggle events             109.46     96.21    -13.25
    cubicle occupancy              209.86    280.73     70.87
    paper turnover                 228.01    191.27    -36.74
    hand-wash compliance           145.66     98.20    -47.46
    mean time to seat              151.01    121.62    -29.39
    double-flush ratio              75.45     95.77     20.32

The improvement in utilisation rho did not survive contact with the
vending machine restock arriving three days late.

### Objections

  erika: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

  zaid: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

  rune: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

## Incident 0115: Cubicle 4 wedged

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 1h42m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 13:00, the executive washroom browned out. Root cause was the
extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate. Users experienced
elevated urgency index for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    11:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    11:40  workaround reposted, laminated
    12:15  ada notices hand-wash compliance is out of band
    12:35  workaround posted on the door
    13:00  escalation to Building Management
    13:30  contractor dispatched
    16:20  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    17:10  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    17:50  workaround removed by cleaning

### Contributing factors

- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation
- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: tess. Status: open.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: wren. Status: open.

## RFC 0570: Rethinking the Split Brain

Status: Draft. Supersedes: RFC 0086. Reviewers: mark, nils.

Every measurement we take of Bristol score changes the thing measured,
because people can see the clipboard. Politeness is a rate limiter with
no backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a new hire cohort of eleven starting on the
same Monday. The underlying condition had been present for 26 weeks and
was visible in door-lock failures the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at utilisation rho.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
5. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.

### Objections

  wren: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

---

### Derivation 47

Take arrivals lambda = 19.05 per hour and service rate mu = 29.07 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.218.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.6 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.18. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

**Context.** The loading-bay unit degrades gracefully right up to the point where it does not, and there is no warning band in between.

**Decision.** We will buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

**Consequences.** It works, and nobody records why, and it is undone in the refit.

## RFC 0571: Modelling the Gap Under the Door

Status: Deferred. Supersedes: RFC 0356. Reviewers: milo, tomasz, hana.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. Utilisation above 0.8 is not a target. It is a
warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a lunch order of unusually consistent
composition across the floor. The underlying condition had been present
for 19 weeks and was visible in queue depth the whole time, to anyone
who had thought to look at p99 hold latency.

### Proposal

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Add a second bin.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    Bristol score                  177.74     87.28    -90.46
    queue depth                    146.42    102.32    -44.10
    p99 hold latency               223.54    187.10    -36.44
    hand-wash compliance           179.56    139.85    -39.72
    abort rate                      87.17     68.17    -19.01

The improvement in cubicle occupancy did not survive contact with one
person holding the accessible stall for a phone call.

### Objections

  hana: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

  mira: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

  tess: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

---

## RFC 0572: Capacity Planning for the Laptop Question

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: RFC 0351. Reviewers: nobody.

Every measurement we take of flush success rate changes the thing
measured, because people can see the clipboard. The correct number of
spare cubicles is not zero, and finance has never agreed with this.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.
The underlying condition had been present for 27 weeks and was visible
in p999 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at flush success rate.

### Proposal

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Escalate to building management and wait.
3. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
4. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
5. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
6. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    time-to-first-flush            150.38    197.31     46.93
    paper turnover                   2.53      0.93     -1.60
    queue depth                    121.61    111.68     -9.93

The improvement in double-flush ratio did not survive contact with a
partial blockage in the 110mm stack.

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

## RFC 0573: Toward Acoustic Isolation

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: RFC 0052. Reviewers: nobody.

Demand at the unit adjacent to the server room is not Poisson. It is
Poisson with a lunch bell taped to it. Redundancy that shares a stack
is not redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 17 weeks and was visible in
re-entry rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at p99
hold latency.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
2. Add a second bin.
3. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
4. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
5. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
6. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    service time variance          183.35    249.65     66.30
    cubicle occupancy              194.58    111.26    -83.32
    lock-jiggle events              56.24     36.86    -19.37
    re-entry rate                   66.75     78.88     12.13

The improvement in flush success rate did not survive contact with a
new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same Monday.

### Objections

  mira: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

  milo: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

  priya: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, L, P, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0117: The executive washroom began returning stale occupancy

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 1h45m. Detected by: nobody, in time.

### Summary

At 13:45, the third-floor east block lost quorum. Root cause was the
wrong bin liners, which fit nothing. Users experienced elevated p50
hold latency for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    11:40  aisha notices p50 hold latency is out of band
    12:35  Building Management acknowledges
    15:10  partial service restored
    15:55  full service restored

### Contributing factors

- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation
- The door lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left
- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: lotte. Status: open.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently. Owner: oskar. Status: open.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: erika. Status: done.

---

### Glossary: A, C, D, H, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Field note, day 82

Queue formed at 13:11 and cleared at 13:38. Four walkaways, all toward
the stairs, none toward the lift. People will climb rather than wait in
view of the kitchen.

  This survived review only because review was cancelled.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

## RFC 0577: Concerning Cache Coherence

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. Every shared resource eventually acquires a
folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the wrong bin liners, which fit nothing. The
underlying condition had been present for 27 weeks and was visible in
renege rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at flush
success rate.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Escalate to building management and wait.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
4. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
5. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
6. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

## Incident 0120: The contractor portacabin regressed

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 8h59m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 09:10, the roof-plant chemical toilet thrashed. Root cause was the
cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon. Users experienced
elevated paper turnover for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor dispatched
    12:00  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    12:15  partial service restored
    14:30  workaround posted on the door
    17:10  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: milo. Status: done.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: aisha. Status: open.
3. Add a second bin. Owner: tomasz. Status: closed, unclear why.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: roshan. Status: closed as wont-fix.

---

### Derivation 48

Take arrivals lambda = 18.11 per hour and service rate mu = 24.75 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.183.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.5 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.16. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, H, P, R, S, T

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

### Contributing factors

- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

## Incident 0123: Cubicle 2 queued unboundedly

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 9h20m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 13:15, the canteen-adjacent block backed up. Root cause was the
coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4. Users
experienced elevated mean time between visits for the duration. No data
was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  tomasz notices floor-hop rate is out of band
    11:05  ticket closed without comment
    11:40  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    12:35  second report, in the wrong channel
    17:50  contractor arrives, lacks the part

### Contributing factors

- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware
- A cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks
- The vending machine restock arriving three days late

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: mira. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: mira. Status: blocked on budget.

---

Next meeting: December. Quorum: unlikely.

### Runbook 25: queue exceeding the kitchen

Trigger: time-to-first-flush above threshold for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
2. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
3. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
4. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
5. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.

Escalation: Health and Safety, then Data, then stop and wait.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

## RFC 0618: Toward Leader Election

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. You cannot fix a capacity problem with a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.
The underlying condition had been present for 20 weeks and was visible
in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at p99 hold latency.

### Proposal

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    utilisation rho                102.18     70.09    -32.09
    Bristol score                   72.61     34.46    -38.15
    door-lock failures             146.81     96.47    -50.34
    cubicle occupancy              182.34    218.48     36.15
    floor-hop rate                 150.51    197.83     47.32
    p50 hold latency               143.03    200.10     57.07

The improvement in door-lock failures did not survive contact with one
person holding the accessible stall for a phone call.

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

---

### Derivation 49

Take arrivals lambda = 19.77 per hour and service rate mu = 23.43 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.281.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.0 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.33. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0127: The third-floor west block stalled

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 5h49m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 11:05, the third-floor west block regressed. Root cause was seasonal
demand shift nobody had modelled. Users experienced elevated queue
depth for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    11:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:35  ticket closed without comment
    14:05  partial service restored
    15:10  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    16:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    16:45  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- A cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks
- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: priya. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Escalate to building management and wait. Owner: lotte. Status: closed, unclear why.
3. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: zaid. Status: blocked on budget.

---

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, E, F, H, L, R, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Inventory audit 08

    item                     qty   spec                 last checked
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    seat, standard             20   white, spare 2       Jun 2025
    door closer                12   spare, 1 held        Mar 2020
    bin liner, 40L             13   black, 500           Jun 2022
    grab rail                  28   600mm, spare 0       Mar 2024
    bin liner, 90L             17   clear, 200           Sep 2025
    hook                       29   spare 14, unfitted   Apr 2021

Fourteen hooks have been held in stores since the refit. Nobody has
authority to fit them. The absence of hooks is the second most common
complaint in the corpus.

### Derivation 50

Take arrivals lambda = 13.54 per hour and service rate mu = 24.72 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.110.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.07. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 51

Take arrivals lambda = 20.75 per hour and service rate mu = 29.70 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.349.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.1 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.38. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0128: The basement facility degraded

### Summary

dispenser that dispensed only air. Users experienced elevated
time-to-first-flush for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

    11:05  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:00  contractor dispatched
    13:15  Building Management acknowledges
    14:05  workaround reposted, laminated

    15:55  workaround posted on the door

    17:10  second report, in the wrong channel

### Contributing factors

- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

## RFC 0622: Rethinking Night Cleaning

Status: Draft. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: juno, erika, milo.

Every measurement we take of walkaway rate changes the thing measured,
because people can see the clipboard. Every shared resource eventually
acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the wrong bin liners, which fit nothing. The
underlying condition had been present for 36 weeks and was visible in
utilisation rho the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
urgency index.

### Proposal

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
2. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
3. Add a second bin.
4. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.

### Objections

  priya: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to
  collect

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

## RFC 0623: Against Read-Your-Writes

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: RFC 0469. Reviewers: bea, ada.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. You cannot fix a capacity problem with a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the extract fan being on a timer nobody could
locate. The underlying condition had been present for 31 weeks and was
visible in lock-jiggle events the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at utilisation rho.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Escalate to building management and wait.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
4. Add a second bin.
5. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

Status: Obsolete. Supersedes: RFC 0471. Reviewers: wren, erika, milo.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. Every shared resource eventually
acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

photoshoot. The underlying condition had been present for 37 weeks and
was visible in flush success rate the whole time, to anyone who had

5. Escalate to building management and wait.
6. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

works. The underlying condition had been present for 7 weeks and was
visible in mean time to seat the whole time, to anyone who had thought

## RFC 0626: On the Accessible Stall

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: RFC 0507. Reviewers: mark.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. Politeness is a rate limiter with no
backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a partial blockage in the 110mm stack. The
underlying condition had been present for 10 weeks and was visible in
balking probability the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at p99 hold latency.

The sample is small and self-selecting.

### Proposal

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------

    headcount            110

    people per unit      6.1

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

person cared.

## Incident 0131: Cubicle 2 entered a hold-and-wait state

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 2h33m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 11:40, the third-floor east block wedged. Root cause was the wrong
bin liners, which fit nothing. Users experienced elevated service time
variance for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  tess notices flush success rate is out of band
    10:20  second report, in the wrong channel
    13:00  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:15  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    13:45  escalation to Building Management
    15:10  root cause identified, retroactively
    16:20  workaround posted on the door
    17:50  Building Management acknowledges

### Contributing factors

- A cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate
- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak

### What went well

- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: milo. Status: done.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: ada. Status: done.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: rune. Status: closed as wont-fix.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: dev. Status: open.

## RFC 0632: Benchmarking Soap as a Shared Resource

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: sanne, yusuf.

Every measurement we take of hand-wash compliance changes the thing
measured, because people can see the clipboard. Anything that has to be
explained twice should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the wrong bin liners, which fit nothing. The
underlying condition had been present for 28 weeks and was visible in
seat-cold complaints the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at balking probability.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
3. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p99 hold latency               142.30    158.23     15.94
    floor-hop rate                  76.20     35.30    -40.90
    re-entry rate                  105.77     38.56    -67.20

The improvement in double-flush ratio did not survive contact with the
cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon.

### Objections

  bea: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

---

### Capacity plan, FY2019

    headcount            377
    attendance ratio     0.38
    units, total         11
    people per unit      34.3
    guideline            20.0
    verdict              over by 71%

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

### Benchmark: the Single-Occupancy Unit

    n=3175, 20 weekdays, July, sensor rev B

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      4        12.8  0.13    186    655   2123   3.3
        2      5        23.8  0.17    180    314   1830   2.5
        3      5         6.5  0.10     88    346    424  17.7
        4      4        20.6  0.15    156    429   1466  14.1
        5      5         5.5  0.07     47    182    218  11.6
        6      2        21.8  0.52     66    107    295  13.5
        7      2         9.6  0.29     78    300    282  10.4

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

## RFC 0636: Failure Modes in Open-Plan Adjacency

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: hana, vermingov.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. Latency is a distribution, and the
tail is where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was one person holding the accessible stall for a
phone call. The underlying condition had been present for 12 weeks and
was visible in post-lunch arrival rate the whole time, to anyone who
had thought to look at double-flush ratio.

This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
4. Add a second bin.

### Objections

  yusuf: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

  wren: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

---

### Derivation 52

Take arrivals lambda = 16.79 per hour and service rate mu = 12.61 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.266.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.7 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.48. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

Status: Draft. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: roshan, rune.

each correct about the other two. A component with no owner has an
owner: it is whoever is most upset.

The immediate trigger was the extract fan being on a timer nobody could
locate. The underlying condition had been present for 39 weeks and was
visible in queue depth the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at abort rate.

The sample is small and self-selecting.

### Proposal

1. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
2. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
4. Stagger the lunch break by team.

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------

    dispenser refill interval      182.90    139.78    -43.12
    service time variance          117.31    118.67      1.36
    mean time between visits       186.03     87.84    -98.19

The improvement in utilisation rho did not survive contact with an
off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware.

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

### Runbook 26: smell of unknown origin

Trigger: double-flush ratio above threshold for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
2. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
3. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
4. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
5. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
6. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
7. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.

Escalation: Frontend, then Facilities, then stop and wait.

### Runbook 27: queue exceeding the kitchen

Trigger: queue depth above 0.85 for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
4. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
5. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
6. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
7. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
8. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.

Escalation: the cleaning contractor, then Infra, then stop and wait.

### Glossary: C, D, E, H, S, T, W

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0135: The roof-plant chemical toilet degraded

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 1h29m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 15:55, the loading-bay unit degraded. Root cause was the extract fan
being on a timer nobody could locate. Users experienced elevated
post-lunch arrival rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    10:20  Building Management acknowledges
    11:40  full service restored
    12:00  second report, in the wrong channel
    17:10  root cause identified, retroactively

### Contributing factors

- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack
- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak
- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: oskar. Status: blocked on budget.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: tess. Status: closed as wont-fix.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: hana. Status: open.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently. Owner: dev. Status: closed as wont-fix.

### Derivation 54

Take arrivals lambda = 11.75 per hour and service rate mu = 24.80 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.474.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 2.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.43. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0654: Instrumenting Livelock

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: tess, vermingov, dev.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. Observability without ownership produces
dashboards and nothing else.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the extract fan being on a timer nobody could
locate. The underlying condition had been present for 20 weeks and was
visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at renege rate.

This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Proposal

1. Add a second bin.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
5. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    door-lock failures              19.78      9.29    -10.50
    extract-fan duty cycle         218.89    236.74     17.85
    false-occupancy signals        192.60    150.56    -42.04
    walkaway rate                   20.01      7.62    -12.39
    double-flush ratio              44.99     24.26    -20.73
    cubicle occupancy                3.04      3.65      0.61

The improvement in walkaway rate did not survive contact with an
unannounced change to the building water pressure.

  milo: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

## RFC 0655: Rethinking Threat Modelling

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The disused cubicle behind legal is the only component in the building
with a hard capacity of one and no queue visibility. The correct number
of spare cubicles is not zero, and finance has never agreed with this.

photoshoot. The underlying condition had been present for 29 weeks and
was visible in abort rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at door-lock failures.

Treat the following as directional.

### Proposal

1. Add a second bin.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
5. Escalate to building management and wait.

lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor.

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

## Incident 0137: The basement facility entered a hold-and-wait state

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 5h52m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 15:10, the sixth-floor facility started shedding load. Root cause
was a contractor closing two cubicles without notice. Users experienced
elevated balking probability for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  root cause identified, retroactively
    11:40  workaround reposted, laminated
    13:00  Building Management acknowledges
    14:05  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    16:45  partial service restored

### Contributing factors

- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: kwame. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: noor. Status: blocked on budget.

### Runbook 28: accessible stall unavailable

Trigger: mean time to seat above twice normal for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
2. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
3. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
4. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
5. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
6. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
7. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
8. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
9. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.

Escalation: Facilities, then Legal, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0138: The unit adjacent to the server room flapped

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 4h09m. Detected by: the queue.

### Summary

At 12:15, the contractor portacabin began returning stale occupancy.
Root cause was a contractor closing two cubicles without notice. Users
experienced elevated extract-fan duty cycle for the duration. No data
was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    12:00  partial service restored
    12:15  contractor dispatched
    13:00  Building Management acknowledges
    13:30  ticket closed without comment
    16:45  workaround posted on the door

### Contributing factors

- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: oskar. Status: done.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: esme. Status: open.

---

### Capacity plan, FY2020

    headcount            599
    attendance ratio     0.40
    units, total         26
    people per unit      23.0
    guideline            20.0
    verdict              over by 15%

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

## RFC 0663: Instrumenting Starvation

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: zaid, mira.

The basement facility is the only component in the building with a hard
capacity of one and no queue visibility. Latency is a distribution, and
the tail is where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 21 weeks and was visible in
utilisation rho the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
service time variance.

### Proposal

1. Add a second bin.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.
4. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
5. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
6. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

### Objections

  mark: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

  zaid: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

  lotte: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

---

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

### Facilities working group, meeting 51

Present: priya, tomasz, kwame, rune, esme.
Apologies: rune, noor, sef.

1. Review of open tickets. 41 open, 3 discussed, 0 closed.
2. Noise complaints from the adjacent meeting room. No action possible.
3. Cleaning window. Contractor unwilling to move. Escalation drafted.
4. The refit. Still scheduled. Still not dated.
5. Sensor procurement. Vendor demo scheduled and then cancelled.

Next meeting: September. Quorum: unlikely.

## Incident 0139: The disused cubicle behind legal flapped

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 8h48m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 13:15, the gym changing room unit stalled. Root cause was a leak on
5 that was in fact condensation. Users experienced elevated balking
probability for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  workaround reposted, laminated
    10:20  full service restored
    11:40  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:15  Building Management acknowledges
    14:30  workaround removed by cleaning
    15:55  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    16:20  contractor dispatched
    16:45  rune notices abort rate is out of band
    17:50  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: ada. Status: done.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: aisha. Status: done.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: tomasz. Status: blocked on budget.

## RFC 0665: Revisiting Threat Modelling

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

Demand at the lobby singles is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a lunch
bell taped to it. Every shared resource eventually acquires a folklore,
and the folklore is usually wrong but load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 40 weeks and
was visible in dispenser refill interval the whole time, to anyone who
had thought to look at extract-fan duty cycle.

### Proposal

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
2. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    extract-fan duty cycle         131.77    154.74     22.97
    abort rate                      22.79     30.58      7.78
    queue depth                    110.12     76.54    -33.58
    p99 hold latency                74.72    101.67     26.95
    flush success rate             204.73    269.20     64.47

The improvement in utilisation rho did not survive contact with a
partial blockage in the 110mm stack.

### Objections

  sef: this is a building problem being solved with a process document

  roshan: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

  milo: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

## RFC 0666: Preliminary Findings on Vendor Lock-In

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: RFC 0327. Reviewers: ada, noor, erika.

Every measurement we take of utilisation rho changes the thing
measured, because people can see the clipboard. Utilisation above 0.8
is not a target. It is a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 31 weeks
and was visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at urgency index.

This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Escalate to building management and wait.
3. Add a second bin.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    urgency index                  173.18    215.42     42.24
    seat-cold complaints            14.31     15.22      0.91
    p999 hold latency              114.60    160.42     45.82
    paper turnover                  26.19     31.45      5.26
    p50 hold latency               167.45     66.28   -101.18
    queue depth                    224.78    301.82     77.04

The improvement in urgency index did not survive contact with an
unannounced change to the building water pressure.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

## RFC 0670: Capacity Planning for Remote Work as Load Shedding

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: rune, noor, wren.

We instrumented p999 hold latency for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. You cannot fix a capacity
problem with a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 40 weeks
and was visible in p50 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at flush success rate.

The instrument drifted. We do not know by how much.

### Proposal

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
4. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.

### Objections

  esme: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

## RFC 0671: Measuring Hook Availability

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: kwame, milo.

We instrumented cubicle occupancy for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. Anything that has to be
explained twice should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was one person holding the accessible stall for a
phone call. The underlying condition had been present for 34 weeks and
was visible in p999 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at renege rate.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Add a second bin.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p999 hold latency               64.58     43.90    -20.68
    double-flush ratio             181.82    123.29    -58.54
    time-to-first-flush            176.62     79.01    -97.61

The improvement in false-occupancy signals did not survive contact with
the coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4.

### Objections

  noor: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

  bea: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

  sef: we are solving for the average and the average is not the
  problem

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

## RFC 0672: On Procurement Lead Times

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: RFC 0486. Reviewers: dev, sanne.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. Redundancy that shares a stack is not
redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an unannounced change to the building water
pressure. The underlying condition had been present for 32 weeks and
was visible in mean time between visits the whole time, to anyone who
had thought to look at walkaway rate.

This was measured once, badly, and never repeated.

### Proposal

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

## RFC 0676: Measuring Batch Windows

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: noor.

The mezzanine single is the only component in the building with a hard
capacity of one and no queue visibility. Politeness is a rate limiter
with no backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a cistern refill valve that had been failing
intermittently for weeks. The underlying condition had been present for
23 weeks and was visible in extract-fan duty cycle the whole time, to
anyone who had thought to look at mean time to seat.

This survived review only because review was cancelled.

### Proposal

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
4. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
5. Escalate to building management and wait.
6. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    paper turnover                  52.56     43.15     -9.41
    dispenser refill interval      156.38     91.65    -64.72
    urgency index                  221.46    273.32     51.85
    door-lock failures             207.47    116.36    -91.11
    time-to-first-flush            231.63    212.07    -19.56

The improvement in dispenser refill interval did not survive contact
with the cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon.

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

---

### Derivation 57

Take arrivals lambda = 14.96 per hour and service rate mu = 16.10 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.929.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 48.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 12.19. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0144: The unit adjacent to the server room flapped

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 6h00m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 13:00, the visitor-lobby single began returning stale occupancy.
Root cause was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. Users
experienced elevated hand-wash compliance for the duration. No data was
lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  vermingov notices mean time to seat is out of band
    10:20  workaround posted on the door
    14:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    15:10  workaround removed by cleaning
    16:45  full service restored
    17:10  ticket closed without comment
    17:50  contractor dispatched

### Contributing factors

- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor
- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- The door lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: lotte. Status: open.
2. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: milo. Status: done.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: tess. Status: closed as wont-fix.
4. Add a second bin. Owner: priya. Status: blocked on budget.

---

### Derivation 58

Take arrivals lambda = 12.69 per hour and service rate mu = 20.91 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.152.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.5 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.11. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, H, P, S, T, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0145: The fifth-floor facility began returning stale occupancy

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 3h22m. Detected by: the queue.

### Summary

At 11:40, the sixth-floor facility browned out. Root cause was the
coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4. Users
experienced elevated false-occupancy signals for the duration. No data
was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  full service restored
    12:35  partial service restored
    13:00  workaround removed by cleaning
    13:45  workaround reposted, laminated
    15:10  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    15:55  contractor dispatched
    16:20  sef notices abort rate is out of band
    16:45  workaround posted on the door
    17:10  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday
- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Add a second bin. Owner: nils. Status: open.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: sef. Status: blocked on budget.

### Facilities working group, meeting 56

Present: hana, tess, sanne, zaid.
Apologies: nils, bea, aisha.

1. Noise complaints from the adjacent meeting room. No action possible.
2. Sensor procurement. Vendor demo scheduled and then cancelled.
3. Paper grade. Resolved. The only item ever resolved.
4. Budget. Deferred to the next cycle, as in the previous four meetings.
5. Lunch staggering. Agreed in principle. Opposed in practice.

Next meeting: October. Quorum: unlikely.

### Derivation 59

Take arrivals lambda = 7.73 per hour and service rate mu = 27.92 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.277.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.11. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 5 weeks and was visible in

## Incident 0147: Cubicle 3 lost quorum

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 4h22m. Detected by: nobody, in time.

### Summary

At 12:15, the lobby singles flapped. Root cause was the hot tap being
isolated during unrelated works. Users experienced elevated p99 hold
latency for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  root cause identified, retroactively
    11:05  workaround reposted, laminated
    12:00  hana notices p99 hold latency is out of band
    12:15  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    12:35  second report, in the wrong channel
    13:15  partial service restored
    16:45  workaround removed by cleaning

### Contributing factors

- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.

### Action items

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: ivo. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Add a second bin. Owner: vermingov. Status: closed, unclear why.
3. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: tomasz. Status: blocked on budget.

---

### Derivation 60

Take arrivals lambda = 21.26 per hour and service rate mu = 28.31 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.751.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 6.4 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 2.27. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## ADR 098: Field Notes on Severity Levels

Date: 19 August. Status: Superseded.

**Context.** The sixth-floor facility is thermally unpleasant, and has been since before anyone currently employed here arrived.

    headcount            345

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

Status: Obsolete. Supersedes: RFC 0169. Reviewers: ivo.

the interesting variance is entirely social. Every shared resource

load-bearing.

The immediate trigger was a delivery of the wrong grade of paper. The
underlying condition had been present for 7 weeks and was visible in
double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
time-to-first-flush.

3. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.

### Runbook 29: cleaning window collision

Trigger: double-flush ratio above 0.85 for 30 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
2. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
3. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
4. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
5. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
6. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.

Escalation: Platform, then Frontend, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0150: The basement facility lost quorum

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 1h46m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 16:20, the accessible stall on 2 fell over. Root cause was the
second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot. Users experienced
elevated cubicle occupancy for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    10:20  zaid notices hand-wash compliance is out of band
    11:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:15  escalation to Building Management
    13:00  workaround reposted, laminated
    13:15  Building Management acknowledges
    15:10  full service restored
    16:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    17:50  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- The vending machine restock arriving three days late
- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call

### What went well

- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: vermingov. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: aisha. Status: closed, unclear why.
3. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently. Owner: vermingov. Status: blocked on budget.

    FAC-04236  triage      zaid      bin overflowing by 15:00 daily
    FAC-04237  closed      erika     queue reaching the kitchen at 13:15

### Derivation 61

Take arrivals lambda = 19.41 per hour and service rate mu = 24.93 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.389.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.5 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.50. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.
