## RFC 0919: A Proposal for Vendor Lock-In

Status: Deferred. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: ivo, ada.

Demand at the roof-plant chemical toilet is not Poisson. It is Poisson
with a lunch bell taped to it. Latency is a distribution, and the tail
is where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled.
The underlying condition had been present for 28 weeks and was visible
in p50 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at extract-fan duty cycle.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Escalate to building management and wait.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
4. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
5. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
6. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    floor-hop rate                 113.95     53.25    -60.70
    hand-wash compliance            77.84     51.96    -25.88
    p99 hold latency                70.51     50.97    -19.54
    queue depth                    121.36     67.12    -54.24
    urgency index                    6.92      4.51     -2.41

The improvement in time-to-first-flush did not survive contact with the
hot tap being isolated during unrelated works.

### Objections

  rune: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

    esme       canteen
    mark       there it is
    erika      can we just stagger lunch
    esme       we tried that

### Derivation 83

Take arrivals lambda = 7.10 per hour and service rate mu = 19.70 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.090.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.04. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 84

Take arrivals lambda = 3.20 per hour and service rate mu = 15.14 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.070.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.02. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, H, L, R, S, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

## Incident 0200: The third-floor west block wedged

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 4h47m. Detected by: the queue.

### Summary

At 15:55, Cubicle 4 backed up. Root cause was the second-floor block
being locked for a photoshoot. Users experienced elevated double-flush
ratio for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    13:15  full service restored
    13:30  workaround reposted, laminated
    15:55  root cause identified, retroactively
    16:45  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    17:10  sanne notices renege rate is out of band
    17:50  contractor dispatched

### Contributing factors

- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: yusuf. Status: open.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: vermingov. Status: open.
3. Escalate to building management and wait. Owner: tomasz. Status: open.
4. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: sef. Status: open.

## RFC 0930: Field Notes on Extract Ventilation

Status: Draft. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: mark, milo.

The executive washroom is the only component in the building with a
hard capacity of one and no queue visibility. The cheapest intervention
is almost always scheduling, and it is almost always the last one
tried.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the coffee machine on 3 being repaired,
redirecting demand to 4. The underlying condition had been present for
16 weeks and was visible in door-lock failures the whole time, to
anyone who had thought to look at floor-hop rate.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
4. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    double-flush ratio             103.53    120.48     16.95
    time-to-first-flush             51.23     40.52    -10.71
    lock-jiggle events             237.28    249.45     12.16

The improvement in urgency index did not survive contact with the
coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4.

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

---

### Glossary: B, C, D, H, L, P, R, S, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0201: The basement facility began returning stale occupancy

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 1h10m. Detected by: nobody, in time.

### Summary

At 16:20, the ground-floor overflow thrashed. Root cause was the hot
tap being isolated during unrelated works. Users experienced elevated
walkaway rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  escalation to Building Management
    10:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:00  contractor dispatched
    13:15  Building Management acknowledges
    13:30  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    14:30  workaround reposted, laminated
    16:45  workaround posted on the door
    17:10  root cause identified, retroactively

### Contributing factors

- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor
- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: erika. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Add a second bin. Owner: dev. Status: blocked on budget.

## ADR 145: Formalising the Laptop Question

Date: 21 August. Status: Abandoned.

**Context.** The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the corridor does the work.

**Decision.** We will escalate to Building Management and wait.

**Consequences.** We buy eighteen months. We do not use them.

### Runbook 38: lock reporting false occupancy

Trigger: mean time to seat above twice normal for 30 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
2. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
3. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
4. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
5. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
6. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
7. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.

Escalation: Design, then Design, then stop and wait.

## RFC 0934: Observations on Rate Limiting

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: lotte.

Cubicle 5 degrades gracefully right up to the point where it does not,
and there is no warning band in between. Latency is a distribution, and
the tail is where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was one person holding the accessible stall for a
phone call. The underlying condition had been present for 28 weeks and
was visible in p999 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at renege rate.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Escalate to building management and wait.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
4. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    lock-jiggle events              32.06     42.14     10.08
    time-to-first-flush            101.68    140.35     38.67
    abort rate                      24.55     17.50     -7.05

The improvement in renege rate did not survive contact with the door
lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left.

### Objections

  rune: we are solving for the average and the average is not the
  problem

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

---

### Derivation 87

Take arrivals lambda = 13.23 per hour and service rate mu = 19.55 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.338.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.6 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.35. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

## ADR 146: Failure Modes in Chronic Illness at Work

Date: 5 February. Status: Superseded.

**Context.** Every measurement we take of lock-jiggle events changes the thing measured, because people can see the clipboard.

**Decision.** We will put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

**Consequences.** The metric improves. The experience does not.

### Glossary: B, C, E, F, H, L, T

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

### Glossary: B, D, E, F, H, L, R, S, T, W

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

    10:20  full service restored
    11:05  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:35  ticket closed without comment
    14:05  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    14:30  workaround posted on the door
    16:20  partial service restored

### Contributing factors

- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware
- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: hana. Status: done.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: rune. Status: open.
3. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: milo. Status: blocked on budget.
4. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: wren. Status: done.

## RFC 0943: Measuring Rate Limiting

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

Demand at the sixth-floor facility is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a
lunch bell taped to it. Latency is a distribution, and the tail is
where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the hot tap being isolated during unrelated
works. The underlying condition had been present for 32 weeks and was
visible in p50 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at p999 hold latency.

### Proposal

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
5. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
6. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    floor-hop rate                  80.04     74.59     -5.45
    walkaway rate                  111.09     89.35    -21.74
    extract-fan duty cycle         169.73    176.53      6.80
    flush success rate              58.43     25.39    -33.04

The improvement in lock-jiggle events did not survive contact with a
contractor closing two cubicles without notice.

### Objections

  erika: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: RFC 0726. Reviewers: ivo.

interesting variance is entirely social. The cheapest intervention is

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

### Derivation 89

Take arrivals lambda = 16.51 per hour and service rate mu = 12.62 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 1.308.

rho exceeds one. The queue is unstable. No amount of politeness
recovers this; the only outcomes are balking, reneging, or somebody
taking the stairs to another floor, which is load shedding by another
name.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Benchmark: Water Pressure

    n=1435, 15 weekdays, September, sensor rev E-beta

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      2        10.3  0.13    147    370    822  18.9
        2      4         7.4  0.15     91    150    496  27.6
        3      1         4.5  0.30    110    334   1012   2.8
        4      5        10.1  0.08     90    309    656  20.5

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: RFC 0331. Reviewers: nobody.

Cubicle 3 degrades gracefully right up to the point where it does not,
and there is no warning band in between. A component with no owner has
an owner: it is whoever is most upset.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 12 weeks and was visible in
double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
utilisation rho.

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
4. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
5. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    mean time to seat                0.71      0.49     -0.22
    abort rate                      58.86     60.71      1.86
    walkaway rate                  187.55    249.43     61.87
    p50 hold latency                30.76     34.90      4.14

### Glossary: B, C, D, H, L, S, T, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0205: The gym changing room unit entered a hold-and-wait state

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 7h34m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 13:30, the loading-bay unit regressed. Root cause was a partial
blockage in the 110mm stack. Users experienced elevated queue depth for
the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround removed by cleaning
    11:40  ticket closed without comment
    13:00  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    13:45  escalation to Building Management
    16:45  workaround reposted, laminated
    17:50  contractor arrives, lacks the part

### Contributing factors

- The wrong bin liners, which fit nothing
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: nils. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: nils. Status: open.
3. Add a second bin. Owner: mark. Status: closed as wont-fix.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, F, H, L, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## RFC 0957: Against Backfill Jobs

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: RFC 0490. Reviewers: kwame, aisha, hana.

The fourth-floor annex is the only component in the building with a
hard capacity of one and no queue visibility. Politeness is a rate
limiter with no backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 17 weeks
and was visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at extract-fan duty cycle.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
2. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Derivation 90

Take arrivals lambda = 6.18 per hour and service rate mu = 10.12 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.611.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 9.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.96. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Runbook 39: no paper, all floors

Trigger: abort rate above 0.85 for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
6. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.

Escalation: People Ops, then Facilities, then stop and wait.

## RFC 0971: Instrumenting the Right to Be Forgotten

Status: Living. Supersedes: RFC 0834. Reviewers: nobody.

### Channel excerpt: #facilities

    ivo        is 3 free
    priya      no
    priya      still no
    nils       who is in 3
    priya      nobody is in 3, the lock is broken
    ivo        the lock has been broken since tuesday
    nils       which tuesday
    priya      a tuesday
    priya      raised FAC-82490
    priya      that is a duplicate of FAC-31834
    nils       both are duplicates of the one from march
    nils       the march one was closed as wontfix
    ivo        by whom
    ivo        by someone who left
    priya      classic
    nils       going to 4
    ivo        4 is worse
    nils       4 is always worse after 13:00
    ivo        why is 4 worse after 13:00
    ivo        canteen
    priya      there it is
    priya      can we just stagger lunch
    priya      we tried that
    ivo        we tried that badly

### Derivation 91

Take arrivals lambda = 16.81 per hour and service rate mu = 19.23 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.175.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.7 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.19. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Field note, day 150

Overheard: 'I just go to 5, it's always free.' Went to 5. It was always
free. It is also two flights up and has no hot water. Capacity that
costs enough is not capacity.

### Glossary: A, B, D, F, H, L, R, S, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

## RFC 0979: Notes on Escalation Paths

Status: Deferred. Supersedes: RFC 0501. Reviewers: yusuf, sef.

The canteen-adjacent block is quietly heroic, and has been since before
anyone currently employed here arrived. Politeness is a rate limiter
with no backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a delivery of the wrong grade of paper. The
underlying condition had been present for 39 weeks and was visible in
dispenser refill interval the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at p99 hold latency.

### Proposal

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
3. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
4. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
5. Escalate to building management and wait.
6. Stagger the lunch break by team.

### Objections

  ivo: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

---

### Derivation 92

Take arrivals lambda = 3.77 per hour and service rate mu = 20.81 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.091.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.02. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0984: A Retrospective on Documentation Rot

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: dev, kwame, mira.

Demand at the executive washroom is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a
lunch bell taped to it. Every shared resource eventually acquires a
folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 4 weeks and was visible in
abort rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
floor-hop rate.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
5. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Objections

  nils: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

  callum: we should measure for another quarter before touching
  anything

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

---

### Capacity plan, FY2026

    headcount            236
    attendance ratio     0.88
    units, total         18
    people per unit      13.1
    guideline            20.0
    verdict              within

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

### Derivation 93

Take arrivals lambda = 16.93 per hour and service rate mu = 7.72 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 1.096.

rho exceeds one. The queue is unstable. No amount of politeness
recovers this; the only outcomes are balking, reneging, or somebody
taking the stairs to another floor, which is load shedding by another
name.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0216: Cubicle 3 queued unboundedly

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 9h16m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 13:00, the fourth-floor annex stalled. Root cause was a delivery of
the wrong grade of paper. Users experienced elevated balking
probability for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    11:05  priya notices door-lock failures is out of band
    11:40  partial service restored
    12:35  Building Management acknowledges
    13:45  second report, in the wrong channel
    16:20  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice
- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: mark. Status: done.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: aisha. Status: open.

---

### Runbook 40: water off, unannounced

Trigger: time-to-first-flush above the March baseline for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
4. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
5. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
6. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
7. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
8. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.

Escalation: SRE, then Legal, then stop and wait.

### Glossary: B, D, E, F, H, L, P, S, T, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, H, R, S, T, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Derivation 94

Take arrivals lambda = 9.79 per hour and service rate mu = 14.12 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.693.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 9.6 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 1.56. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 0996: Standardising the Accessible Stall

Status: Obsolete. Supersedes: RFC 0025. Reviewers: callum, dev.

We instrumented double-flush ratio for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. Anything that has to be
explained twice should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 27 weeks
and was visible in mean time between visits the whole time, to anyone
who had thought to look at balking probability.

### Proposal

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
4. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
5. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
6. Move the all-hands to 15:00.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p999 hold latency               65.72     76.04     10.33
    lock-jiggle events             116.32    102.01    -14.30
    service time variance          227.27    303.53     76.26
    re-entry rate                  234.23    305.55     71.32
    dispenser refill interval       81.28     41.05    -40.23
    time-to-first-flush             31.93     32.34      0.40

The improvement in abort rate did not survive contact with a partial
blockage in the 110mm stack.

### Objections

  vermingov: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

  callum: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to
  collect

  hendrik: we are solving for the average and the average is not the
  problem

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

---

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

### Benchmark: the Lunch Peak

    n=4503, 42 weekdays, November, sensor rev C

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      1        21.2  0.99    134    255    891  16.9
        2      5         7.3  0.10     24     74    128  33.9
        3      3        12.6  0.27     66    180    319  20.3
        4      4         5.3  0.11    113    197    500   9.4
        5      4        15.0  0.26    145    427   1227  21.3

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

### Glossary: D, F, H, R, S, W

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

### Field note, day 159

Cleaning arrived at 12:40, which is nineteen minutes before the peak.
Asked why. Was told it is when the contractor is here. Asked who set
that. Nobody present knew.

### Runbook 41: extract fan failure

Trigger: post-lunch arrival rate above 0.85 for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
4. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
5. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
6. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
7. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
8. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.

Escalation: Backend, then Finance, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0226: The contractor portacabin regressed

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 8h34m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 09:10, the ground-floor overflow began returning stale occupancy.
Root cause was a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation. Users
experienced elevated hand-wash compliance for the duration. No data was
lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround removed by cleaning
    11:05  Building Management acknowledges
    12:00  escalation to Building Management
    12:35  partial service restored
    13:15  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:45  contractor dispatched
    14:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    15:10  full service restored
    16:45  rune notices re-entry rate is out of band

### Contributing factors

- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack

### What went well

- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: ada. Status: done.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: hana. Status: closed, unclear why.
3. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: noor. Status: open.
4. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: ivo. Status: open.

### Runbook 42: no paper, all floors

Trigger: queue depth above 0.85 for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
2. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
3. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
4. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.

Escalation: QA, then the plumbing subcontractor, then stop and wait.

## RFC 1022: Failure Modes in Dashboards Nobody Opens

Status: Deferred. Supersedes: RFC 0283. Reviewers: esme, milo.

The accessible stall on 4 is well-intentioned, and has been since
before anyone currently employed here arrived. Every shared resource
eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was one person holding the accessible stall for a
phone call. The underlying condition had been present for 15 weeks and
was visible in hand-wash compliance the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at cubicle occupancy.

### Proposal

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
4. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    re-entry rate                  147.35    187.89     40.54
    mean time between visits        69.46     78.45      8.98

The improvement in Bristol score did not survive contact with a
delivery of the wrong grade of paper.

  wren: this is a building problem being solved with a process document

  priya: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to
  collect

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

## Incident 0227: The basement facility backed up

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 9h30m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 15:10, Cubicle 5 regressed. Root cause was one person holding the
accessible stall for a phone call. Users experienced elevated re-entry
rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  full service restored
    11:40  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:35  workaround posted on the door
    13:15  workaround removed by cleaning
    13:45  Building Management acknowledges
    14:05  contractor dispatched
    14:30  escalation to Building Management
    15:10  root cause identified, retroactively

- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: sanne. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Add a second bin. Owner: priya. Status: open.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: erika. Status: closed, unclear why.

## Incident 0228: The disused cubicle behind legal thrashed

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 8h27m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 16:20, the third-floor east block thrashed. Root cause was a cistern
refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks. Users
experienced elevated p999 hold latency for the duration. No data was
lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    10:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    12:00  contractor dispatched
    13:00  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:30  ticket closed without comment
    15:10  Building Management acknowledges
    16:45  lotte notices mean time between visits is out of band
    17:10  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    17:50  workaround reposted, laminated

### Contributing factors

- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- The vending machine restock arriving three days late
- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: tess. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently. Owner: aisha. Status: open.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: bea. Status: blocked on budget.

---

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 24 weeks and

## RFC 1029: Preliminary Findings on Mirror Placement

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

Demand at the loading-bay unit is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a
lunch bell taped to it. Latency is a distribution, and the tail is
where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a partial blockage in the 110mm stack. The
underlying condition had been present for 31 weeks and was visible in
dispenser refill interval the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at lock-jiggle events.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
2. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    door-lock failures              31.98     15.20    -16.78
    lock-jiggle events              34.09     34.29      0.20
    extract-fan duty cycle         204.06    251.47     47.42
    urgency index                  197.32    179.52    -17.80
    dispenser refill interval      207.73    167.80    -39.93

The improvement in extract-fan duty cycle did not survive contact with
the hot tap being isolated during unrelated works.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

### Runbook 43: cleaning window collision

Trigger: seat-cold complaints above the March baseline for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
4. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
5. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
6. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
7. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
8. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.

Escalation: Infra, then the cleaning contractor, then stop and wait.

### Derivation 96

Take arrivals lambda = 4.74 per hour and service rate mu = 11.31 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.210.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.4 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.11. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0231: The ground-floor overflow lost quorum

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 6h40m. Detected by: the queue.

### Summary

At 12:00, Cubicle 1 regressed. Root cause was a partial blockage in the
110mm stack. Users experienced elevated floor-hop rate for the
duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  full service restored
    11:40  root cause identified, retroactively
    12:35  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:00  workaround removed by cleaning
    14:30  Building Management acknowledges
    15:55  escalation to Building Management
    16:45  second report, in the wrong channel
    17:10  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- A cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call

### What went well

- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: ada. Status: open.
2. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: ivo. Status: open.
3. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: milo. Status: closed, unclear why.

sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled.
The underlying condition had been present for 21 weeks and was visible
in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at extract-fan duty cycle.

The sample is small and self-selecting.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.

    headcount            252

been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

## Incident 0233: The contractor portacabin queued unboundedly

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 0h37m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 12:35, the roof-plant chemical toilet browned out. Root cause was
the second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot. Users experienced
elevated extract-fan duty cycle for the duration. No data was lost.
Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  ivo notices p50 hold latency is out of band
    11:05  full service restored
    11:40  partial service restored
    13:45  workaround removed by cleaning
    14:30  second report, in the wrong channel
    16:45  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Add a second bin. Owner: bea. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: ada. Status: blocked on budget.

---

Present: dev, bea, ivo, mark, priya, aisha.
Apologies: wren.

1. Signage. Agreed to laminate. Nobody assigned.
2. Accessible stall misuse. Discussed carefully and at length. Action: ask.
3. Paper grade. Resolved. The only item ever resolved.
4. Noise complaints from the adjacent meeting room. No action possible.
5. Sensor procurement. Vendor demo scheduled and then cancelled.
6. Budget. Deferred to the next cycle, as in the previous four meetings.

Next meeting: April. Quorum: unlikely.

### Runbook 44: water off, unannounced

Trigger: flush success rate above threshold for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
2. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
3. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
4. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
5. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
6. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
7. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
8. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.

Escalation: QA, then Infra, then stop and wait.

### Facilities working group, meeting 82

Present: tomasz, zaid, ivo, hana, sanne, nils.
Apologies: tess.

1. Budget. Deferred to the next cycle, as in the previous four meetings.
2. Noise complaints from the adjacent meeting room. No action possible.
3. Sensor procurement. Vendor demo scheduled and then cancelled.
4. The refit. Still scheduled. Still not dated.
5. Accessible stall misuse. Discussed carefully and at length. Action: ask.
6. Cleaning window. Contractor unwilling to move. Escalation drafted.
7. Paper grade. Resolved. The only item ever resolved.

Next meeting: October. Quorum: unlikely.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

## Incident 0234: The fourth-floor annex lost quorum

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 9h10m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 09:10, the basement facility browned out. Root cause was the vending
machine restock arriving three days late. Users experienced elevated
flush success rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    11:05  partial service restored
    12:15  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:30  sef notices cubicle occupancy is out of band
    13:45  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    15:10  Building Management acknowledges
    15:55  second report, in the wrong channel
    17:50  workaround reposted, laminated

### Contributing factors

- A partial blockage in the 110mm stack
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday
- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Add a second bin. Owner: ada. Status: open.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: callum. Status: done.
3. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: ada. Status: open.
4. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: oskar. Status: closed, unclear why.

## RFC 1055: Against Sampling

Status: Withdrawn. Supersedes: RFC 0886. Reviewers: zaid, wren, erika.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. Utilisation above 0.8 is not a target. It is a
warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an unannounced change to the building water
pressure. The underlying condition had been present for 18 weeks and
was visible in utilisation rho the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at post-lunch arrival rate.

### Proposal

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
3. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
4. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
5. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
6. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    floor-hop rate                  67.71     74.77      7.06
    balking probability            161.32     67.59    -93.72
    p50 hold latency               141.99    139.18     -2.81
    double-flush ratio             207.28    119.75    -87.53

The improvement in utilisation rho did not survive contact with an
all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window.

### Objections

  mark: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

  kwame: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

### Decision

Accepted. Nobody was assigned. It happened anyway, slowly, because one
person cared.

### Runbook 45: no paper, all floors

Trigger: door-lock failures above twice normal for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
2. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
3. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
4. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
5. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
6. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.

Escalation: Procurement, then People Ops, then stop and wait.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

### Runbook 46: cleaning window collision

Trigger: service time variance above twice normal for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
2. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
3. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
4. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
5. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.

Escalation: Facilities, then Infra, then stop and wait.

### Glossary: A, C, D, E, F, R, S

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

## Incident 0237: Cubicle 1 entered a hold-and-wait state

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 1h32m. Detected by: the queue.

### Summary

At 14:05, the mezzanine single wedged. Root cause was an unannounced
change to the building water pressure. Users experienced elevated
dispenser refill interval for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    12:00  workaround posted on the door
    12:35  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:15  Building Management acknowledges
    14:30  full service restored
    16:20  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- The wrong bin liners, which fit nothing
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot
- The vending machine restock arriving three days late

### What went well

- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Add a second bin. Owner: aisha. Status: closed, unclear why.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: sanne. Status: open.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

### Runbook 47: smell of unknown origin

Trigger: queue depth above 0.85 for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
2. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
3. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
4. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
6. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
7. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.

Escalation: Frontend, then Design, then stop and wait.

## RFC 1081: Field Notes on the Security Guard Route

Status: Deferred. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: ada, rune, noor.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. Redundancy that shares a stack is not
redundancy.

The immediate trigger was the wrong bin liners, which fit nothing. The
underlying condition had been present for 9 weeks and was visible in
service time variance the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at lock-jiggle events.

### Proposal

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
2. Stagger the lunch break by team.
3. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
4. Move the all-hands to 15:00.

### Objections

  yusuf: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to
  collect

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

---

### Derivation 97

Take arrivals lambda = 5.62 per hour and service rate mu = 8.10 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.231.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 2.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.21. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0238: Cubicle 3 started shedding load

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 5h01m. Detected by: nobody, in time.

### Summary

At 14:05, Cubicle 2 thrashed. Root cause was a contractor closing two
cubicles without notice. Users experienced elevated utilisation rho for
the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround posted on the door
    11:05  ticket closed without comment
    11:40  full service restored
    12:35  workaround reposted, laminated
    13:15  workaround removed by cleaning
    14:05  escalation to Building Management
    15:10  partial service restored
    16:45  second report, in the wrong channel

### Contributing factors

- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works
- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: juno. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: roshan. Status: done.

### Runbook 48: extract fan failure

Trigger: queue depth above threshold for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
4. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
5. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
6. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
7. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
8. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
9. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.

Escalation: Legal, then the plumbing subcontractor, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0241: The roof-plant chemical toilet fell over

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 1h30m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 15:55, the third-floor west block began returning stale occupancy.
Root cause was a new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same Monday.
Users experienced elevated mean time between visits for the duration.
No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  workaround removed by cleaning
    11:40  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:30  escalation to Building Management
    13:45  workaround posted on the door
    17:10  partial service restored

### Contributing factors

- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor
- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate

### What went well

- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: esme. Status: open.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: wren. Status: open.

## RFC 1091: On Data Minimisation

Status: Draft. Supersedes: RFC 0123. Reviewers: nobody.

Demand at the mezzanine single is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a
lunch bell taped to it. Redundancy that shares a stack is not
redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 15 weeks and
was visible in double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at mean time between visits.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
2. Escalate to building management and wait.
3. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    paper turnover                  81.74    112.42     30.68
    urgency index                  152.64    197.78     45.13
    false-occupancy signals        179.35    144.82    -34.53
    service time variance          173.41    220.14     46.73
    extract-fan duty cycle          16.88     23.31      6.43

The improvement in time-to-first-flush did not survive contact with the
vending machine restock arriving three days late.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: RFC 0228. Reviewers: erika.

interesting variance is entirely social. Every shared resource
eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the wrong bin liners, which fit nothing. The
underlying condition had been present for 39 weeks and was visible in
queue depth the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
double-flush ratio.

### Proposal

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
5. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    Bristol score                   17.45     10.20     -7.25
    abort rate                     233.96    304.22     70.25
    post-lunch arrival rate         53.22     68.64     15.42

The improvement in re-entry rate did not survive contact with a new
hire cohort of eleven starting on the same Monday.

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

## RFC 1100: Against the Bus Factor

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: sanne, zaid, roshan.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. Utilisation above 0.8 is not a target.
It is a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak. The
underlying condition had been present for 20 weeks and was visible in
time-to-first-flush the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at utilisation rho.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
3. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
4. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
5. Stagger the lunch break by team.
6. Escalate to building management and wait.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    paper turnover                 201.03    133.89    -67.14
    service time variance           82.87     46.81    -36.06
    walkaway rate                   52.30     38.37    -13.93
    lock-jiggle events             190.21    160.64    -29.56
    time-to-first-flush             82.63     54.57    -28.06

The improvement in seat-cold complaints did not survive contact with an
unannounced change to the building water pressure.

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

---

### Derivation 98

Take arrivals lambda = 16.68 per hour and service rate mu = 27.86 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.120.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.08. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0245: Cubicle 1 backed up
