### Derivation 99

Take arrivals lambda = 16.99 per hour and service rate mu = 12.06 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.470.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 4.4 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 1.25. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Benchmark: Depreciation of Fixtures

    n=869, 25 weekdays, May, sensor rev C

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      1         8.1  0.35     48    170    399  21.7
        2      1         6.8  0.31     99    173   1177  18.8
        3      2        21.2  0.86    134    515   1391   1.9
        4      5        18.9  0.12     81    162    676   2.7
        5      2        10.8  0.36    125    438    787   9.9
        6      4        17.3  0.30     56    128    373  27.1

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Why does nothing get fixed?**

  Things get fixed. The median time is nineteen days and nobody closes
  the ticket, so it looks like nothing does.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

## RFC 1114: Field Notes on the Postmortem Template

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: hendrik, priya, roshan.

Demand at the roof-plant chemical toilet is not Poisson. It is Poisson
with a lunch bell taped to it. A component with no owner has an owner:
it is whoever is most upset.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a partial blockage in the 110mm stack. The
underlying condition had been present for 30 weeks and was visible in
double-flush ratio the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
balking probability.

### Proposal

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team.
4. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
5. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
6. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.

### Objections

  sef: nobody asked the people who actually use the accessible stall

### Decision

Withdrawn by the author after the underlying fixture was replaced for
unrelated reasons.

---

### Derivation 100

Take arrivals lambda = 6.95 per hour and service rate mu = 10.61 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.131.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.10. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

Trigger: re-entry rate above 0.85 for 10 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

6. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
7. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.

Escalation: Security, then Finance, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0249: Cubicle 4 lost quorum

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 8h10m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 09:45, Cubicle 1 browned out. Root cause was the vending machine
restock arriving three days late. Users experienced elevated
time-to-first-flush for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    10:20  full service restored
    11:05  second report, in the wrong channel
    13:00  workaround reposted, laminated
    13:15  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:30  Building Management acknowledges
    13:45  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    16:20  partial service restored
    16:45  contractor dispatched

### Contributing factors

- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- An off-by-one in the occupancy sensor firmware

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.

### What did not

- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: rune. Status: open.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: hendrik. Status: open.

### Glossary: B, C, D, E, F, R, S, T

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, P, S, T, W

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cascade.** one floor closing and taking two others with it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Peak.** 13:15, plus or minus eight minutes, all year.

**Shed.** capacity loss disguised as behaviour change.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0250: The gym changing room unit started shedding load

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 0h28m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 12:15, the sixth-floor facility degraded. Root cause was the
second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot. Users experienced
elevated p99 hold latency for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  contractor dispatched
    12:15  workaround reposted, laminated
    12:35  root cause identified, retroactively
    16:45  workaround removed by cleaning
    17:50  contractor arrives, lacks the part

### Contributing factors

- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call
- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.

### Action items

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: zaid. Status: done.
2. Add a second bin. Owner: wren. Status: closed as wont-fix.
3. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: nils. Status: blocked on budget.

## RFC 1126: Capacity Planning for Head-of-Line Blocking

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: wren.

The building was designed for a headcount we exceeded in the second
year and never revisited. Utilisation above 0.8 is not a target. It is
a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the coffee machine on 3 being repaired,
redirecting demand to 4. The underlying condition had been present for
37 weeks and was visible in service time variance the whole time, to
anyone who had thought to look at extract-fan duty cycle.

### Proposal

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    service time variance          173.13    178.49      5.36
    re-entry rate                  114.00     42.07    -71.93
    seat-cold complaints            20.24     27.42      7.18

The improvement in renege rate did not survive contact with a fire
drill at 13:20, precisely at peak.

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

## RFC 1127: Formalising Acoustic Isolation

Status: Deferred. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: mira, sanne, wren.

The executive washroom is unremarkable, and has been since before
anyone currently employed here arrived. Redundancy that shares a stack
is not redundancy.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 3 weeks and was
visible in seat-cold complaints the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at time-to-first-flush.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Escalate to building management and wait.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
5. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
6. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    double-flush ratio              42.73     51.63      8.90
    floor-hop rate                 187.41    173.79    -13.62
    paper turnover                 211.87    178.29    -33.58
    abort rate                     155.32    191.30     35.97
    service time variance          190.47    248.14     57.67
    p99 hold latency               108.01    111.37      3.36

The improvement in p99 hold latency did not survive contact with the
cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon.

### Objections

  milo: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

  vermingov: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

  bea: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

### Runbook 51: water off, unannounced

Trigger: walkaway rate above twice normal for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
2. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
3. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
4. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
5. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
6. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.

Escalation: the cleaning contractor, then Frontend, then stop and wait.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

## Incident 0257: Cubicle 1 stalled

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 7h00m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 11:05, Cubicle 4 regressed. Root cause was a leak on 5 that was in
fact condensation. Users experienced elevated Bristol score for the
duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    09:45  workaround reposted, laminated
    11:05  Building Management acknowledges
    13:00  workaround removed by cleaning
    17:10  root cause identified, retroactively

### Contributing factors

- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- A cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks
- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.

### Action items

1. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: tomasz. Status: open.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: priya. Status: open.

---

### Derivation 101

Take arrivals lambda = 8.72 per hour and service rate mu = 8.39 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.208.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.27. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 102

Take arrivals lambda = 11.60 per hour and service rate mu = 19.43 per

report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Facilities working group, meeting 87

Present: roshan, kwame, dev.
Apologies: vermingov.

1. Cleaning window. Contractor unwilling to move. Escalation drafted.
2. Review of open tickets. 41 open, 3 discussed, 0 closed.
3. Accessible stall misuse. Discussed carefully and at length. Action: ask.
4. Signage. Agreed to laminate. Nobody assigned.
5. Budget. Deferred to the next cycle, as in the previous four meetings.
6. Paper grade. Resolved. The only item ever resolved.

Next meeting: July. Quorum: unlikely.

### Runbook 52: smell of unknown origin

Trigger: queue depth above threshold for 15 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
2. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
3. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
4. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
5. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
6. Confirm with your own eyes. Sensors lie in exactly this scenario.
7. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
8. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
9. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.

Escalation: the plumbing subcontractor, then Procurement, then stop and wait.

### Field note, day 185

Arrived 08:50. Two units free on 3, four on 4. Nobody queueing. Wrote
nothing for ninety minutes.

### Derivation 103

Take arrivals lambda = 21.05 per hour and service rate mu = 7.57 per
hour with c = 1 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 2.782.

rho exceeds one. The queue is unstable. No amount of politeness
recovers this; the only outcomes are balking, reneging, or somebody
taking the stairs to another floor, which is load shedding by another
name.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 104

Take arrivals lambda = 12.79 per hour and service rate mu = 17.08 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.187.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.17. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 1144: On Starvation

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. Anything that has to be explained twice
should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was one person holding the accessible stall for a
phone call. The underlying condition had been present for 15 weeks and
was visible in p999 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at time-to-first-flush.

### Proposal

1. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team.
4. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------

    urgency index                  156.04    143.98    -12.06

    service time variance           68.97     37.48    -31.49

The improvement in service time variance did not survive contact with a
delivery of the wrong grade of paper.

### Objections

  zaid: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

  milo: this is a building problem being solved with a process document

  juno: this optimises a metric we chose because it was easy to collect

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

### Benchmark: Hand Hygiene

    n=2268, 40 weekdays, June, sensor rev E-beta

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      5        12.6  0.06    128    380   1313  29.6
        2      4        14.2  0.29     61    203    189  21.1
        3      5        25.7  0.41    126    459    658  32.2
        4      3        19.3  0.46     83    292    328  33.7
        5      1        18.6  0.99    165    345   1522  27.1
        6      1        21.0  0.89    158    427   1201  22.9

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

### Glossary: B, D, F, H, R, S, W

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Herd.** the simultaneous arrival caused by a shared calendar.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Walkaway.** balk, but with visible annoyance.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

## Incident 0260: The executive washroom flapped

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 4h09m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 11:40, the mezzanine single regressed. Root cause was seasonal
demand shift nobody had modelled. Users experienced elevated abort rate
for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    11:40  Building Management acknowledges
    12:35  workaround removed by cleaning
    13:15  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    15:10  full service restored
    15:55  second report, in the wrong channel
    16:20  workaround reposted, laminated
    17:10  contractor dispatched
    17:50  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: erika. Status: open.
2. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: ada. Status: blocked on budget.
3. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: mark. Status: open.
4. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: roshan. Status: done.

### Runbook 53: soap outage

Trigger: time-to-first-flush above twice normal for 30 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Raise the ticket, then link it in the channel. Both, always.
2. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
3. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
4. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
5. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
6. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
7. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
8. When restored, remove your own sign. Stale signs cost more than none.
9. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.

Escalation: Infra, then Data, then stop and wait.

### Field note, day 193

Overheard: 'I just go to 5, it's always free.' Went to 5. It was always
free. It is also two flights up and has no hot water. Capacity that
costs enough is not capacity.

  We are not confident in this number.

### Derivation 105

Take arrivals lambda = 15.93 per hour and service rate mu = 15.96 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.333.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 1.9 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.50. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: A, C, D, E, F, S

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

    units, total         13
    people per unit      29.2
    guideline            20.0
    verdict              over by 46%

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

## Incident 0266: Cubicle 1 stalled

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 8h41m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 13:00, the accessible stall on 4 queued unboundedly. Root cause was
the second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot. Users experienced
elevated renege rate for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    09:10  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    13:45  priya notices utilisation rho is out of band
    15:10  root cause identified, retroactively
    15:55  ticket closed without comment
    16:20  contractor dispatched

### Contributing factors

- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: bea. Status: closed as wont-fix.
2. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: mira. Status: open.

---

### Derivation 106

Take arrivals lambda = 21.25 per hour and service rate mu = 10.40 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.409.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 4.0 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 1.41. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

    FAC-07051  triage      yusuf     no baby change on any floor
    FAC-07052  stale       hendrik   flush handle requires two hands

    FAC-07054  open        dev       hot tap runs cold
    FAC-07055  closed      roshan    door gap allows eye contact

### Derivation 107

Take arrivals lambda = 20.40 per hour and service rate mu = 16.21 per
hour with c = 2 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.629.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 6.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 2.14. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 108

Take arrivals lambda = 14.66 per hour and service rate mu = 21.50 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.170.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.6 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.14. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Glossary: B, C, D, F, R, S

**Backpressure.** the corridor. There is no other mechanism.

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Drain window.** the ten minutes after a meeting block ends.

**False occupancy.** a lock reporting engaged with nobody behind it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

## Incident 0267: The canteen-adjacent block backed up

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 0h35m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 15:10, the lobby singles began returning stale occupancy. Root cause
was an all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window. Users
experienced elevated walkaway rate for the duration. No data was lost.
Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  partial service restored
    10:20  root cause identified, retroactively
    13:15  second report, in the wrong channel
    13:45  Building Management acknowledges
    15:10  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    15:55  workaround posted on the door

### Contributing factors

- The wrong bin liners, which fit nothing
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: nils. Status: open.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: oskar. Status: open.

## RFC 1196: Instrumenting the Christmas Party

Status: Superseded. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: noor.

The building was designed for a headcount we exceeded in the second
year and never revisited. Utilisation above 0.8 is not a target. It is
a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a contractor closing two cubicles without
notice. The underlying condition had been present for 29 weeks and was
visible in door-lock failures the whole time, to anyone who had thought
to look at false-occupancy signals.

### Proposal

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
4. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    false-occupancy signals        114.28     93.93    -20.35
    renege rate                    177.45    224.26     46.82
    cubicle occupancy               53.41     50.56     -2.86

The improvement in floor-hop rate did not survive contact with seasonal
demand shift nobody had modelled.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Benchmark: Offboarding

    n=750, 48 weekdays, January, sensor rev B

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      1         4.2  0.13     63    180    335  26.7
        2      4        10.6  0.19    183    414    801   7.7
        3      4        25.4  0.55    109    412    963  13.9
        4      1        13.4  0.36    110    228   1086  25.7
        5      5        13.8  0.18    120    375    443  24.5
        6      5         7.4  0.10     98    217    924   9.8

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Why write it here?**

  Because a wiki page would have been deleted in the migration and this
  file has survived four.

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

### Derivation 109

Take arrivals lambda = 5.67 per hour and service rate mu = 18.78 per
hour with c = 4 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.076.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.3 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.02. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

### Derivation 110

Take arrivals lambda = 10.35 per hour and service rate mu = 18.57 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.111.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.4 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.07. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0269: The sixth-floor facility regressed

Severity: SEV-2. Duration: 7h58m. Detected by: a complaint.

### Summary

At 13:00, the gym changing room unit fell over. Root cause was the
extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate. Users experienced
elevated double-flush ratio for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  workaround removed by cleaning
    11:40  ticket closed without comment
    13:00  full service restored
    13:15  contractor dispatched
    15:10  workaround reposted, laminated
    15:55  second report, in the wrong channel
    16:45  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    17:10  escalation to Building Management
    17:50  contractor arrives, lacks the part

### Contributing factors

- A lunch order of unusually consistent composition across the floor
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation
- The door lock reporting occupied after the occupant had left
- A fire drill at 13:20, precisely at peak

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.

### Action items

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: roshan. Status: open.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: aisha. Status: closed, unclear why.
3. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: priya. Status: blocked on budget.
4. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: ivo. Status: open.

## Incident 0270: The contractor portacabin queued unboundedly

bin liners, which fit nothing. Users experienced elevated queue depth
for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Contributing factors

- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Glossary: B, D, E, F, H, R, S, T

**Balking.** declining to join a queue on sight of its length.

**Dwell.** total occupancy time, including the part that is not service.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Floor-hop.** seeking capacity on another storey.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Stack.** the shared 110mm pipe that makes redundancy fictional.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

## RFC 1204: Capacity Planning for Door Locks

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: ivo, mark, kwame.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. Anything that has to be explained
twice should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 28 weeks and was visible in
false-occupancy signals the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at p999 hold latency.

The instrument drifted. We do not know by how much.

### Proposal

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

## Incident 0271: The unit adjacent to the server room entered a hold-and-wait state

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 1h13m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 14:05, Cubicle 4 lost quorum. Root cause was seasonal demand shift
nobody had modelled. Users experienced elevated cubicle occupancy for
the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor dispatched
    12:00  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:15  partial service restored
    13:15  workaround removed by cleaning
    13:45  workaround reposted, laminated
    16:20  escalation to Building Management
    16:45  root cause identified, retroactively
    17:10  callum notices mean time to seat is out of band
    17:50  workaround posted on the door

### Contributing factors

- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The runbook referenced a contractor no longer under contract.

### Action items

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: sef. Status: open.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: priya. Status: closed as wont-fix.
3. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights. Owner: esme. Status: done.
4. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: ada. Status: closed as wont-fix.

## RFC 1207: Deprecating Cache Coherence

Status: Abandoned. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: nobody.

The system has no admission control. It has a corridor, and the
corridor does the work. Every shared resource eventually acquires a
folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the extract fan being on a timer nobody could
locate. The underlying condition had been present for 20 weeks and was
visible in paper turnover the whole time, to anyone who had thought to
look at dispenser refill interval.

Treat the following as directional.

### Proposal

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.
4. Add a second bin.
5. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
6. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    p50 hold latency                53.16     50.59     -2.58
    post-lunch arrival rate        169.93     71.95    -97.98
    service time variance          112.29     98.17    -14.13

The improvement in urgency index did not survive contact with a cistern
refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks.

### Objections

  noor: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

  bea: this is a building problem being solved with a process document

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Runbook 54: soap outage

Trigger: mean time between visits above twice normal for 30 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
2. Close the affected unit physically. A sign is not a closure.
3. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
4. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.
5. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
6. Record the start time. Nobody ever records the start time.
7. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.

Escalation: Design, then Support, then stop and wait.

## ADR 198: Notes on Shelf Space

**Consequences.** Nothing measurable changes and morale improves anyway.

## Incident 0272: The sixth-floor facility browned out

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 2h12m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 10:20, the contractor portacabin fell over. Root cause was a cistern
refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks. Users
experienced elevated re-entry rate for the duration. No data was lost.
Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  contractor dispatched
    11:05  workaround reposted, laminated
    12:00  partial service restored
    13:00  workaround posted on the door
    13:45  full service restored
    14:05  escalation to Building Management

### Contributing factors

- One person holding the accessible stall for a phone call
- The extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The workaround was documented before it was forgotten.

### What did not

- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: ivo. Status: done.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: rune. Status: open.

## Incident 0274: The ground-floor overflow fell over

Severity: SEV-3. Duration: 4h25m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 13:15, the fourth-floor annex queued unboundedly. Root cause was the
second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot. Users experienced
elevated time-to-first-flush for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  workaround posted on the door
    12:15  Building Management acknowledges
    13:15  ticket closed without comment
    13:30  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    14:30  second report, in the wrong channel

### Contributing factors

- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- A contractor closing two cubicles without notice
- The cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Move the all-hands to 15:00. Owner: tess. Status: open.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: noor. Status: open.
3. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked. Owner: ada. Status: open.

## RFC 1212: Failure Modes in Observability

Status: Proposed. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: wren, yusuf, hendrik.

We instrumented walkaway rate for six weeks and learned that the
interesting variance is entirely social. Every shared resource
eventually acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a leak on 5 that was in fact condensation.
The underlying condition had been present for 18 weeks and was visible
in walkaway rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
urgency index.

### Proposal

1. Add a second bin.
2. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
3. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

---

### Derivation 112

Take arrivals lambda = 5.79 per hour and service rate mu = 20.07 per
hour with c = 5 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.058.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.2 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.02. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## RFC 1213: Instrumenting the Five-Year Refit

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: erika, rune.

Nobody owns this. Three teams believe somebody else does, and they are
each correct about the other two. The correct number of spare cubicles
is not zero, and finance has never agreed with this.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 40 weeks and was visible in
Bristol score the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
double-flush ratio.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
3. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Escalate to building management and wait.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    urgency index                   47.28     37.54     -9.75
    mean time between visits       138.38    142.84      4.46
    time-to-first-flush            187.97    170.40    -17.57
    renege rate                    168.07    113.60    -54.47

The improvement in queue depth did not survive contact with the vending
machine restock arriving three days late.

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

## Incident 0275: The sixth-floor facility degraded

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 6h36m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 16:45, the executive washroom wedged. Root cause was a contractor
closing two cubicles without notice. Users experienced elevated
utilisation rho for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    10:20  ada notices mean time to seat is out of band
    11:40  workaround posted on the door
    12:00  second report, in the wrong channel
    12:35  escalation to Building Management
    13:45  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    14:30  ticket closed without comment
    15:10  workaround removed by cleaning
    15:55  contractor dispatched
    17:50  root cause identified, retroactively

### Contributing factors

- A soap dispenser that dispensed only air
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window
- An unannounced change to the building water pressure
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation

### What went well

- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: noor. Status: open.
2. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: lotte. Status: closed, unclear why.
3. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: kwame. Status: open.

## Incident 0276: The executive washroom thrashed

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 6h50m. Detected by: the dashboard, six hours late.

### Summary

At 12:35, the gym changing room unit backed up. Root cause was an
all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window. Users experienced
elevated time-to-first-flush for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    11:05  workaround reposted, laminated
    12:35  workaround removed by cleaning
    13:15  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:30  escalation to Building Management
    15:10  full service restored
    15:55  second report, in the wrong channel

### Contributing factors

- The wrong bin liners, which fit nothing
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.
- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- There was no owner, so there was no pager.

### Action items

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: hendrik. Status: open.
2. Add a second bin. Owner: vermingov. Status: open.
3. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: nils. Status: blocked on budget.

## RFC 1215: Instrumenting Physical Access Control

Status: Obsolete. Supersedes: RFC 0151. Reviewers: tess.

Demand at the fifth-floor facility is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a
lunch bell taped to it. Politeness is a rate limiter with no
backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was one person holding the accessible stall for a
phone call. The underlying condition had been present for 37 weeks and
was visible in dispenser refill interval the whole time, to anyone who
had thought to look at re-entry rate.

This section was written after the decision and should be read
accordingly.

### Proposal

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
2. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
3. Escalate to building management and wait.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
6. Increase paper stock by one case per week.

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

## RFC 1216: Concerning the Single-Occupancy Unit

Status: Accepted, unimplemented. Supersedes: RFC 1049. Reviewers: erika, ada, aisha.

The loading-bay unit is budgetarily orphaned, and has been since before
anyone currently employed here arrived. The correct number of spare
cubicles is not zero, and finance has never agreed with this.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 3 weeks
and was visible in mean time between visits the whole time, to anyone
who had thought to look at abort rate.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    balking probability            105.84    108.20      2.35
    walkaway rate                  149.20    208.27     59.07
    service time variance           16.02     20.03      4.01
    time-to-first-flush             35.75     21.48    -14.26
    hand-wash compliance           184.73    203.74     19.01
    seat-cold complaints           140.88    153.83     12.95

The improvement in hand-wash compliance did not survive contact with a
cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks.

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

## RFC 1217: Against Cache Coherence

Status: Living. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: lotte, bea.

The third-floor east block is budgetarily orphaned, and has been since
before anyone currently employed here arrived. Utilisation above 0.8 is
not a target. It is a warning.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an off-by-one in the occupancy sensor
firmware. The underlying condition had been present for 12 weeks and
was visible in time-to-first-flush the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at balking probability.

Two of the authors disagree with this paragraph and were outvoted.

### Proposal

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Escalate to building management and wait.
3. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
4. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
5. Add a second bin.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    dispenser refill interval       14.84      9.69     -5.15
    cubicle occupancy              231.24    221.89     -9.34
    mean time to seat               91.63     36.87    -54.75

The improvement in p999 hold latency did not survive contact with the
cleaning rota moving to a two-hour block at noon.

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

---

### Benchmark: Head-of-Line Blocking

    n=3023, 49 weekdays, April, sensor rev A

    floor  units  arrivals/h  util   p50s   p95s   p99s  balk%
    -----------------------------------------------------------
        1      1         7.6  0.22    138    383   1226   2.5
        2      3        15.9  0.14    132    383    787  14.6
        3      5        14.0  0.14    181    309   1390  19.8
        4      4         9.2  0.09    123    216    411  31.5
        5      3        24.3  0.20     45    109    232  20.5

Note that rho is computed per floor, not per unit, which flatters every
floor with more than two cubicles and defames the mezzanine.

## RFC 1219: Deprecating the Hot Tap

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: RFC 0982. Reviewers: kwame, esme, erika.

The gym changing room unit degrades gracefully right up to the point
where it does not, and there is no warning band in between. Politeness
is a rate limiter with no backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an unannounced change to the building water
pressure. The underlying condition had been present for 24 weeks and
was visible in post-lunch arrival rate the whole time, to anyone who
had thought to look at cubicle occupancy.

### Proposal

1. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
4. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Decision

Superseded before it was read.

Date: 1 May. Status: Accepted.

**Context.** The canteen-adjacent block is the only component in the building with a hard capacity of one and no queue visibility.

**Decision.** We will publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

**Consequences.** One team absorbs the cost so that four teams do not notice it.

## RFC 1220: Instrumenting Seat Thermal Mass

Status: Obsolete. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: mark, bea.

Demand at the fourth-floor annex is not Poisson. It is Poisson with a
lunch bell taped to it. Latency is a distribution, and the tail is
where the dignity lives.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a partial blockage in the 110mm stack. The
underlying condition had been present for 3 weeks and was visible in
service time variance the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at balking probability.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Escalate to building management and wait.
2. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
3. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
5. Move the all-hands to 15:00.
6. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently.

### Objections

  aisha: this is a building problem being solved with a process
  document

### Decision

Accepted. Implemented in part. The part that was implemented was the
sign.

### Runbook 55: accessible stall unavailable

Trigger: paper turnover above threshold for 5 minutes, or one credible verbal report.

1. Redirect: name the specific alternative floor, not 'another floor'.
2. Check whether the previous fix is still in place. It usually is not.
3. If it is smell, ventilate before you diagnose.
4. Write two sentences in the ticket before closing it.
5. Escalate to Building Management only after the ticket exists.
6. If it is water, isolate before you escalate.
7. Post in the channel with floor, unit, and time. Photo if decent.

Escalation: Finance, then Health and Safety, then stop and wait.

## Incident 0278: The third-floor east block stalled

Severity: SEV-1. Duration: 9h48m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 12:00, the unit adjacent to the server room fell over. Root cause
was an unannounced change to the building water pressure. Users
experienced elevated mean time between visits for the duration. No data
was lost. Some dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  contractor dispatched
    10:20  second report, in the wrong channel
    11:05  partial service restored
    12:00  workaround posted on the door
    12:15  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    15:55  Building Management acknowledges
    16:20  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    16:45  root cause identified, retroactively
    17:10  oskar notices balking probability is out of band

### Contributing factors

- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper
- The second-floor block being locked for a photoshoot
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window

### What went well

- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The escalation path worked, once found.
- Two people independently reached the same diagnosis.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.

### Action items

1. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days. Owner: kwame. Status: open.
2. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: mira. Status: done.
3. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen. Owner: bea. Status: open.
4. Ask people, politely, once, in writing. Owner: roshan. Status: open.

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: aisha, yusuf, roshan.

Demand at the contractor portacabin is not Poisson. It is Poisson with
a lunch bell taped to it. You can, occasionally, fix a coordination
problem with a sign.

### Context

The immediate trigger was the wrong bin liners, which fit nothing. The
underlying condition had been present for 18 weeks and was visible in
flush success rate the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
time-to-first-flush.

We are not confident in this number.

### Proposal

1. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
2. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
3. Buy a second kettle, for unrelated reasons that worked.
4. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
5. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
6. Add a second bin.

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    flush success rate             173.27    188.80     15.54
    mean time between visits       121.75     53.06    -68.69
    urgency index                  142.01     80.33    -61.68

The improvement in door-lock failures did not survive contact with a
cistern refill valve that had been failing intermittently for weeks.

### Decision

Accepted with reservations, all of which turned out to be correct.

## Incident 0279: The roof-plant chemical toilet stalled

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 9h58m. Detected by: a person.

### Summary

At 13:30, the fourth-floor annex started shedding load. Root cause was
the extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate. Users experienced
elevated queue depth for the duration. No data was lost. Some dignity
was.

### Timeline

    12:00  workaround posted on the door
    12:35  contractor dispatched
    13:00  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:15  second report, in the wrong channel
    13:30  full service restored
    16:20  partial service restored
    16:45  workaround removed by cleaning

### Contributing factors

- The coffee machine on 3 being repaired, redirecting demand to 4
- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window
- A new hire cohort of eleven starting on the same monday

### What went well

- The escalation path worked, once found.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.

### What did not

- There was no owner, so there was no pager.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- The same incident occurred in March and was not written up.

### Action items

1. Increase paper stock by one case per week. Owner: kwame. Status: open.
2. Do nothing and let the load shed itself. Owner: ivo. Status: open.

## RFC 1229: Preliminary Findings on Open-Plan Adjacency

Status: Accepted with reservations. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: erika, mark.

Every measurement we take of false-occupancy signals changes the thing
measured, because people can see the clipboard. Anything that has to be
explained twice should have been designed differently once.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 3 weeks and was visible in
urgency index the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look at
utilisation rho.

### Proposal

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal.
4. Stop publishing the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    mean time between visits        27.47     26.70     -0.77
    p99 hold latency                54.97     41.08    -13.89
    hand-wash compliance            34.93     28.93     -6.00
    p50 hold latency               117.56    163.66     46.10
    balking probability            157.14    165.08      7.94
    dispenser refill interval      129.29     80.67    -48.62

The improvement in seat-cold complaints did not survive contact with
the extract fan being on a timer nobody could locate.

### Objections

  roshan: the cost of the change exceeds the cost of the queue

  noor: we are solving for the average and the average is not the
  problem

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

## RFC 1230: Modelling the Split Brain

Status: Accepted. Supersedes: none. Reviewers: lotte.

The failure is never the fixture. The failure is the fourteen days
between noticing and reporting. Every shared resource eventually
acquires a folklore, and the folklore is usually wrong but
load-bearing.

### Context

The immediate trigger was an all-hands scheduled over the natural
draining window. The underlying condition had been present for 13 weeks
and was visible in p50 hold latency the whole time, to anyone who had
thought to look at seat-cold complaints.

Treat the following as directional.

### Proposal

1. Stagger the lunch break by team.
2. Publish the queue depth on a screen in the kitchen.
3. Post a sign, which worked for eleven days.
4. Put the extract fan on a contactor tied to the lights.
5. Increase paper stock by one case per week.
6. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.

### Objections

  kwame: measuring for another quarter is how the last one died

### Decision

Rejected on cost. Revisited eleven months later at higher cost.

    false-occupancy signals        181.26    159.58    -21.68

### Field note, day 210

Queue formed at 13:11 and cleared at 13:38. Four walkaways, all toward
the stairs, none toward the lift. People will climb rather than wait in
view of the kitchen.

### Glossary: A, B, C, D, E, H, L, R, S, T, W

**Abort.** leaving the queue before service. Counted only when observed.

**Bristol.** a seven-point ordinal scale. Ordinal. Not interval. Stop averaging it.

**Cleaning window.** the interval during which capacity is zero and demand is not.

**Cold start.** the first visit of the day, when the seat is at ambient.

**Dignity.** the unmeasured variable that every measured variable is a proxy for.

**Escalation.** telling somebody who can also not fix it.

**Head-of-line.** one slow occupant delaying an entire queue with no overtaking.

**Hold.** voluntary deferral. The dominant failure mode and the least logged.

**Laminate.** the only durable communication medium in the building.

**Renege.** abandoning a queue after joining it.

**Rho.** utilisation. Above 0.8, stop reading the mean.

**Sign.** an intervention with a half-life of eleven days.

**Tail.** where the complaints come from and the averages do not.

**Ticket.** a message in a bottle addressed to a colleague who has left.

**Window.** any interval Facilities considers agreed and nobody else does.

### Capacity plan, FY2024

    headcount            321
    attendance ratio     0.56
    units, total         24
    people per unit      13.4
    guideline            20.0
    verdict              within

The guideline figure is regulatory, not experiential. It assumes
uniform arrival across an eight-hour day. Arrival is not uniform.
Compliance and adequacy are unrelated quantities and the building has
been fully compliant for every year of its occupancy.

### Derivation 113

Take arrivals lambda = 21.06 per hour and service rate mu = 26.22 per
hour with c = 3 servers. Then rho = lambda / (c mu) = 0.268.

Expected waiting time in queue is roughly 0.8 minutes. Little's Law
gives expected queue length L = lambda W = 0.29. The number people
report experiencing is consistently higher, because waiting is measured
in dread, not minutes.

As rho approaches one the waiting term diverges hyperbolically. This is
the single most important fact in the entire document and it is why
adding one cubicle to a saturated floor produces a change people
describe as transformative while the spreadsheet describes it as
marginal.

## Incident 0288: The disused cubicle behind legal began returning stale occupancy

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 7h10m. Detected by: the cleaner.

### Summary

At 16:45, the third-floor east block wedged. Root cause was an
all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window. Users experienced
elevated hand-wash compliance for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:45  contractor dispatched
    10:20  second report, in the wrong channel
    11:05  escalation to Building Management
    11:40  ticket closed without comment
    12:15  partial service restored
    13:00  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    13:45  full service restored
    15:55  workaround reposted, laminated

### Contributing factors

- An all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window
- The hot tap being isolated during unrelated works
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.
- The escalation path worked, once found.

### What did not

- The dashboard showed green throughout.
- Nobody checked whether the previous fix had been applied.

### Action items

1. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: ivo. Status: done.
2. Unlock the mezzanine single permanently. Owner: oskar. Status: closed, unclear why.
3. Stagger the lunch break by team. Owner: nils. Status: open.

### Frequently asked, rarely answered

**Q. Is anyone actually reading this?**

  It is inside an HTML comment. So: statistically, no. Practically,
  you.

**Q. Can we get a live occupancy display?**

  We had one. It made people time their visits to avoid being seen
  timing their visits. Net negative.

**Q. Is this a serious document?**

  The queueing theory is correct. The rest is a place to put it.

**Q. Who do I tell?**

  Facilities, in the channel, with a photo. Not verbally. Verbal
  reports have a documented survival rate of zero.

**Q. Why are there only two on this floor?**

  The building predates the headcount by nine years.

**Q. Why is the peak at 13:15?**

  Because the canteen closes at 14:00 and every calendar in the company
  has a 13:00 boundary.

## RFC 1245: Revisiting Quorum Loss

Status: Rejected. Supersedes: RFC 0280. Reviewers: mark, kwame, esme.

The ground-floor overflow degrades gracefully right up to the point
where it does not, and there is no warning band in between. Politeness
is a rate limiter with no backpressure signal.

### Context

The immediate trigger was a soap dispenser that dispensed only air. The
underlying condition had been present for 25 weeks and was visible in
seat-cold complaints the whole time, to anyone who had thought to look
at extract-fan duty cycle.

The instrument drifted. We do not know by how much.

### Proposal

1. Do nothing and let the load shed itself.
2. Ask people, politely, once, in writing.
3. Add a second bin.
4. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex.
5. Move the all-hands to 15:00.

### Measurements

    metric                        before     after      delta
    ---------------------------------------------------------
    post-lunch arrival rate        180.38    219.89     39.51
    mean time to seat               78.78     51.86    -26.92
    lock-jiggle events             226.83    123.55   -103.28
    hand-wash compliance           126.26    157.16     30.90

The improvement in extract-fan duty cycle did not survive contact with
an all-hands scheduled over the natural draining window.

### Objections

  mira: we should measure for another quarter before touching anything

  sef: the last three interventions all worked for under a month

### Decision

Deferred pending the refit, which has itself been deferred.

---

## Incident 0289: The fifth-floor facility started shedding load

Severity: SEV-4. Duration: 7h08m. Detected by: smell.

### Summary

At 13:00, the loading-bay unit queued unboundedly. Root cause was an
unannounced change to the building water pressure. Users experienced
elevated p50 hold latency for the duration. No data was lost. Some
dignity was.

### Timeline

    09:10  root cause identified, retroactively
    11:40  contractor arrives, lacks the part
    12:35  first report, verbally, to the wrong team
    13:30  esme notices dispenser refill interval is out of band
    14:05  workaround posted on the door
    16:20  ticket closed without comment

### Contributing factors

- A delivery of the wrong grade of paper
- Seasonal demand shift nobody had modelled
- A leak on 5 that was in fact condensation

### What went well

- Somebody put up a sign within twenty minutes.
- The fourth-floor annex absorbed the redirected load without complaint.
- Nobody blamed the cleaner, who had reported it first.

### What did not

- The first report went nowhere for four hours.
- The alert threshold was set from a single week in August.
- The dashboard showed green throughout.

### Action items

1. Redirect traffic to the fourth-floor annex. Owner: mira. Status: open.
2. Reopen the disused cubicle behind legal. Owner: tess. Status: open.
3. Escalate to building management and wait. Owner: sanne. Status: blocked on budget.
4. Replace the flush valve with the older, louder model. Owner: erika. Status: blocked on budget.

---

========================================================================
APPENDIX EZ: THE LEDGER
========================================================================

What follows is the remainder. Volume I closed by counting itself.
Volume II does the same, at scale, because a document that sets itself
a line target and then stops one line short is a document that has
learned nothing from the section on error budgets.

Each line below is a line. That is its whole function. It is the purest
expression of the thesis in either volume: capacity exists to be
filled, and a resource with no admission control will be filled to
exactly the limit it was given and not one unit further.
